bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland State and local correctional officials to ensure that incarcerated individuals have access to their identification documents, including birth certificates, Social Security cards, and photo IDs or driver's licenses, upon their release. It mandates that correctional facilities record and safeguard these documents during the intake process and assist individuals in obtaining or renewing them within specified timeframes before they are released from custody.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and local correctional facility managing officials
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals in Maryland State and local correctional facilities
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, this bill is not anticipated to have a material financial impact on State or local government operations or finances. The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services already maintains interagency agreements and procedures to facilitate the process of obtaining identification for individuals prior to their release.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Commissioner of Correction and state correctional facilities, which are divisions of this department, are the primary implementers of the bill's mandates. They are responsible for intake documentation checks, safekeeping of identification, and the administrative process of obtaining birth certificates and ID cards for incarcerated individuals.

The MVA is directly responsible for issuing the driver's licenses and photo identification cards mentioned in the bill. The legislation requires correctional facilities to coordinate with the MVA for the renewal of these documents and ensures that alternative correctional IDs meet MVA standards.

The bill requires state and local correctional officials to obtain birth certificates for incarcerated individuals. In Maryland, the Division of Vital Records, which manages birth certificates, is located within the Department of Health, and the fiscal note confirms their involvement via existing interagency agreements.
As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT oversees the modal agency responsible for the licensing and identification services central to the bill's implementation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice policy and works to reduce recidivism. The bill's focus on ensuring individuals have proper identification upon release is a key component of reentry strategy and recidivism reduction policy.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Department of Health. They would be responsible for reviewing and drafting the interagency agreements (MOUs) necessary to facilitate the sharing of sensitive records like birth certificates and social security information.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Motor Vehicle Administration from requiring a parent or legal guardian of a minor at least 15 years of age to cosign or be present at the time of submission of the minor's application for an identification card; and requiring the Administration to adopt regulations establishing acceptable forms of documentation  establishing proof of residency that a minor at least 15 years of age may use in an application for an identification card.
Title: Motor Vehicle Administration - Identification Cards - Issuance to Minors
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth
Private Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Motor Vehicle Administration from requiring a parent or legal guardian to be present or cosign for an identification card application for a minor at least 15 years old. It also requires the Administration to adopt regulations specifying acceptable forms of residency documentation for these minors, such as school records or verification from homeless service providers, and allows for the issuance of identification cards that are not compliant with the federal REAL ID Act if necessary.
stakeholders: Minors aged 15 and older, including those who may lack parental support or standard residency documentation such as homeless youth and students.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not materially affect State finances or operations, as the Motor Vehicle Administration can implement the changes with existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Motor Vehicle Administration to change its identification card application requirements for minors aged 15 and older and requires the agency to adopt new regulations regarding acceptable forms of documentation for proof of residency.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Department of Transportation is responsible for overseeing the implementation of this legislation and the resulting regulatory changes.

The bill specifies that records from child welfare agencies and documentation from social services or homeless service providers—entities managed or overseen by the Department of Human Services—are acceptable forms of residency proof for minors.

The bill identifies school enrollment records, report cards, and transcripts issued by schools (overseen by the Department of Education) as valid forms of documentation for a minor's identification card application.
The legislation explicitly includes court documents as an acceptable form of residency proof, which may increase requests for such documentation from the judicial branch.

The bill aims to facilitate the issuance of identification cards to minors, including vulnerable populations like homeless youth and those in foster care, which aligns with this office's mission to support the well-being of Maryland's children.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Motor Vehicle Administration and would likely be involved in the review and drafting of the new regulations required by this bill.
The bill lists health insurance documents as acceptable residency proof; as the department responsible for Medicaid and public health records, this may involve documentation issued by the agency.

The bill's focus on enhancing access to state-issued identification for minors, particularly those in underinvested communities or facing homelessness, aligns with the team's mission to enhance economic mobility.

Synopsis: Authorizing each county board of education to use a chaplain as a volunteer aide in schools to provide support services to students.
Title: County Boards of Education - Volunteer Aides - School Chaplain
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/20 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes local boards of education to use chaplains as volunteer aides in schools to provide support services to students. These volunteers are intended to assist regular school employees rather than replace educational personnel, and they are treated as agents of the county board for purposes of liability insurance and workers' compensation.
responsible_party: Maryland County Boards of Education and County Superintendents
stakeholders: Public school students, volunteer chaplains, and local school systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no impact on State finances. Local school systems are expected to implement the bill's provisions using existing resources. While the bill designates chaplains as agents for insurance purposes, any resulting impact on workers' compensation or liability claims is expected to be minimal. Local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of Maryland's public education system, the Department of Education is the primary body affected by changes to policies regarding school personnel and volunteer aides. This bill directly amends the Education Article concerning how county boards use volunteers in schools.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. This bill, involving the use of religious chaplains in public schools, may require legal review or defense regarding constitutional issues like the Establishment Clause.

The bill explicitly states that volunteer chaplains shall be considered agents of the county board for the purpose of workers' compensation coverage under the Maryland Workers' Compensation Act, which this commission administers and adjudicates.

The Center provides a coordinated approach to school safety and supportive learning environments. The introduction of chaplains as volunteer aides for 'support services' intersects with the agency's mission to foster safe and supportive school climates.

The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws. The use of chaplains in public schools could lead to inquiries or complaints regarding religious discrimination, inclusivity, or public accommodations.

Synopsis: Altering the circumstances under which an equity court is authorized to grant visitation rights to a grandparent of a child to include that the petition for visitation rights was filed after an action for divorce, annulment, custody, or paternity was filed by a parent of the child; and requiring an equity court to grant certain visitation rights if the child resided with the grandparent for at least 12 months, or the child's parent, who is the child of the grandparent, is deceased, and the court finds it in the best interests of the child.
Title: Family Law - Grandparent Visitation
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.

bill_summary: This bill updates the rules for when a court can grant grandparents the right to visit their grandchildren. It allows a court to grant visitation if there is a pending divorce or custody case and it is in the child's best interest. It also requires a court to grant visitation if the child lived with the grandparent for at least a year or if the grandparent's child (the parent) has died, provided it is in the child's best interest and does not interfere with the parent-child relationship.
stakeholders: Grandparents seeking visitation, their grandchildren, and parents involved in legal proceedings regarding divorce, custody, or paternity.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill does not materially impact the operations or finances of the State Judiciary or local circuit courts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the standards and procedures for grandparent visitation petitions in the state's equity courts, for which the Administrative Office of the Courts provides central operational, legal, and technological support.

The Department of Aging is tasked with protecting the rights and improving the quality of life for older adults in Maryland; this legislation directly impacts the legal rights and family involvement of the state's grandparent population.

The Department of Human Services manages child support and paternity services; the bill specifically identifies the filing of a paternity action as a trigger for allowing a grandparent to petition for visitation rights.

This office focuses on the well-being of Maryland's children and families; the bill's provisions regarding child residency with grandparents and family support networks are relevant to the agency's mission of building comprehensive support networks for children.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and the Judiciary and may be involved in advising on or defending the constitutionality of the revised standards for grandparent visitation.

Synopsis: Authorizing a county board of education to adopt an open enrollment policy to authorize certain students to attend, free of charge, a public school in a county other than the county where the student is domiciled with the student's parent or guardian, subject to certain requirements; requiring county boards to include certain students in full-time equivalent enrollment counts; and directing certain funding to the county in which certain students are enrolled in a public school under an open enrollment policy.
Title: Public Schools - Open Enrollment - Policies and Funding
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/25 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Maryland county boards of education to adopt open enrollment policies, allowing students to attend public schools in a county other than the one where they reside. The bill establishes requirements for application processes, reporting school capacity, and a funding mechanism where education dollars follow the student from the sending county to the receiving county, with the State covering any per-pupil funding gaps.
stakeholders: Maryland public school students, parents, and county boards of education.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates an indeterminate fiscal impact on state and local governments. Local funding is shifted from sending counties to receiving counties based on the lesser of their respective per-pupil costs. Additionally, the State is mandated to pay the difference to the receiving county if the sending county's per-pupil spending is lower. Total expenditures depend on the number of participating students and the specific per-pupil funding levels of the involved jurisdictions; specific dollar estimates are currently unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public school system, MSDE is responsible for implementing educational policies, managing student enrollment counts (FTE), and administering the state funding formulas that this bill modifies for open enrollment.

The bill creates a direct fiscal mandate for the State to fund the difference in local current expenses per student between sending and receiving counties, which DBM must account for in the annual state budget and revenue projections.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which will be impacted by the new state funding obligations for inter-county school enrollment.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the General Assembly and MSDE regarding the legality of inter-county funding transfers and compliance with federal and state anti-discrimination laws mentioned in the bill.

The bill's provision for students to attend schools outside their domicile county could shift student populations, affecting school capacity utilization and long-term capital planning for school construction.
As the state's chief financial officer responsible for paying state bills and distributing revenues, the Comptroller would be involved in the transfer of state funds to receiving county boards.

The bill impacts students with disabilities who may seek to use open enrollment, requiring the department to coordinate with school systems to ensure integrated settings and appropriate service delivery across county lines.
The MLDS Center would likely track and analyze the data of students participating in open enrollment to determine the impact of these policies on student performance and workforce outcomes.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Technology Development Corporation to establish a grant and loan program to provide grants and loans for Long COVID innovation; requiring the Corporation to contract with an independent review committee composed of scientific experts in the field of Long COVID; establishing the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund under the administration of the Corporation as a special, nonlapsing fund; and requiring that the interest earnings of the Fund be credited to the Fund.
Title: Maryland Technology Development Corporation - Long COVID Innovation Grant and Loan Program
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/10 at 2:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Medical Conditions -see also- AIDS; COVID-19; rabies
Public Corporations and Instrumentalities -see also- HBE
Technology -see also- AeroT; BioT; EnergyT; InfoT; MedT; etc

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to establish the Long COVID Innovation Grant and Loan Program and the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund. TEDCO must contract with an independent scientific review committee to evaluate research proposals for Long COVID treatment and provide annual progress reports on funded projects.
stakeholders: Public and private entities in Maryland involved in life sciences research and manufacturing, including public four-year institutions of higher education and small biomedical businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, general fund expenditures increase by $10,000,000 annually starting in FY 2027 to capitalize the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund. Special fund revenues and expenditures increase correspondingly as the fund receives appropriations and awards grants and loans. TEDCO will use a portion of these funds for administrative costs, including staffing and peer review committee expenses. Public higher education institutions and small businesses may receive funding through the program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: TEDCO is the primary implementing agency tasked with establishing the Long COVID Innovation Grant and Loan Program, administering the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund, and contracting with scientific review committees.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund separately and invest its money.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the Maryland Long COVID Research Fund.
The bill creates a significant annual general fund expenditure of $10 million, which falls under DBM's responsibility for budget development and supervision of budget execution.
The fiscal note identifies public four-year institutions as potential recipients of the grants and loans for Long COVID research and innovation.
As a public research university, Morgan State University is a likely applicant and recipient for the Long COVID innovation grants and loans established by the bill.
As an independent public honors college, Saint Mary's could receive and spend grants or loans through the program for eligible research projects.
The Governor is responsible for including the fund's appropriation in the annual budget and receives a mandatory annual report on the program's progress.
The bill focuses on Long COVID, a significant public health issue. While TEDCO administers the funds, MDH provides related public health policy and local health department oversight.

The program supports research, product development, and manufacturing in the life sciences sector, which aligns with the Department of Commerce's mission to stimulate Maryland's economy and attract businesses.
The commission coordinates statewide policy for public and private universities, many of which would be the primary entities conducting the research funded by the bill.
The Board oversees significant state expenditures and procurement contracts; the creation of a $10 million grant program and related special fund involves fiscal oversight under their purview.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the creation of an independent scientific peer review committee to review, evaluate, and rank research proposals for the program.
OAG serves as legal counsel to TEDCO and would likely review the regulations, contracts for the review committee, and grant agreements mandated by the bill.
OLA will be responsible for conducting fiscal compliance and performance audits of the new Maryland Long COVID Research Fund and TEDCO's administration of the program.
The program requires reporting on the economic impact of the grants and loans, which may involve student and workforce data sets managed by the MLDSC.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Secretary of Higher Education to allow certain private career schools to advertise certain information and collect contact information from potential new students before receiving a certificate of approval from the Maryland Higher Education Commission to operate a private career school in the State under certain circumstances; requiring an approved private career school to advertise only information relating to the opening of the private career school and include a certain disclosure; etc.
Title: Higher Education - Private Career Schools - Advertising
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Private Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows the Secretary of Higher Education to authorize applicants for private career schools to advertise their upcoming opening and collect contact information from potential students before receiving a final certificate of approval. Such schools must include a disclosure that their certification is pending and are strictly prohibited from collecting any fees or entering into enrollment agreements until they are officially approved.
stakeholders: Private career school applicants and potential students
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Higher Education Commission can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources. There is no direct effect on State revenues or local government finances. The bill may have a meaningful positive fiscal impact on small business private career schools by allowing them to build prospective student lists prior to receiving official approval to operate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note indicates that MHEC requested a full-time staff specialist to manage the workload created by this bill. DBM would be responsible for reviewing such personnel and budget requests in future budget cycles.

As the state's central regulatory body for for-profit career schools, the Commission is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation, including adopting regulations and approving pre-opening advertising requests.

The agency is the primary regulator for private career schools in Maryland. The bill grants the Secretary of Higher Education specific authority to approve advertising and contact collection before a school receives its final certificate of approval.

If an applicant's request to advertise is denied or if a school is cited for violating the advertising restrictions set forth in the bill, OAH would likely adjudicate any resulting administrative disputes.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and commissions. It would be involved in drafting the regulations required by the bill and advising MHEC on legal compliance regarding the pre-approval advertising process.

Synopsis: Authorizing a county board of education to develop and establish income eligibility guidelines and procedures for payment of costs for a post college and career readiness (post-CCR) pathway, except under certain circumstances; extending the time period to 2030 during which the State Board and the Accountability and Implementation Board may limit the number and types of dual enrollment as a post college and career readiness pathway; etc.
Title: Public High Schools - Post College and Career Readiness Pathways - Alterations
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Intergovernmental Cooperation -see also- AdmAgn; Cmts; etc.
Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows local school boards to establish income eligibility guidelines for covering the costs of specific high-level college preparatory programs, such as International Baccalaureate (IB) and Advanced Placement (AP) courses. Students from families with incomes below 400% of the federal poverty level must continue to receive these programs at no cost. Additionally, the bill extends the timeline for limiting dual enrollment types through 2030, restructures the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee, and mandates that state agencies use a unified list of priority occupations for curriculum and credentialing standards.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education, State Board of Education, Accountability and Implementation Board, and County Boards of Education
stakeholders: Public high school students, parents and guardians, local school systems, and the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State revenue or expenditures as it does not alter education aid formulas. At the local level, school system expenditures may decrease, potentially significantly, because districts may choose to stop covering program fees for students whose family incomes exceed the established threshold. However, a specific dollar estimate for this decrease is unavailable as it depends on individual local board decisions and student participation rates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for public education policy, graduation requirements, and College and Career Readiness (CCR) standards. This bill directly alters CCR pathway options, requires the State Board to adopt regulations for these pathways, and includes the State Superintendent on the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee.

The Secretary of Labor is a member of the CTE Committee, and the agency's Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning is responsible for approving the registered and youth apprenticeship programs that serve as primary post-CCR pathways. The agency is also required to use the list of priority occupations and career pathway information developed under the bill for curriculum alignment.

The Secretary of Higher Education is a member of the CTE Committee. The bill impacts dual enrollment policies involving postsecondary institutions and requires the Commission to use the list of priority occupations and career pathway information for its programs.

The CTE Committee is established as a unit within the Governor's Workforce Development Board (GWDB). The GWDB is responsible for collaborating on career pathway information, adopting the final list of priority occupations, and overseeing the committee's performance of duties.

The Secretary of Commerce is a mandatory member of the CTE Committee. The bill's focus on aligning CTE programs and curriculum with 'high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand' occupations directly supports the Department of Commerce's mission to stimulate the economy and support workforce training.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill significantly alters the purpose, composition, and duties of the CTE Committee and repeals the CTE Skills Standards Advisory Committee, both of which fall under this category of executive bodies.

The Governor's Office is responsible for policy coordination and executive branch oversight. The Governor (jointly with the President of the Senate and Speaker of the House) is responsible for appointing seven members and the chair of the CTE Committee.

The bill requires the tracking of progress toward statewide CTE goals, including industry-recognized credentials. The MLDS Center is the state's central repository for the linked student and workforce data necessary to perform this monitoring and assessment.

The bill authorizes the CTE Committee to employ additional staff as provided in the state budget. As the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM oversees the budget execution and personnel policies for the staff and agencies involved.

As the state's public higher education system, USM institutions are key providers of dual enrollment programs. The bill's changes to dual enrollment limits and the integration of CTE with postsecondary programs directly impact USM operations and curriculum alignment.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State is a partner in dual enrollment pathways. The bill's requirements regarding CTE integration and career pathway alignment for postsecondary institutions affect its academic offerings.
As a public college, St. Mary's is impacted by policies regarding dual enrollment and the state's unified system of career progression and CTE integration.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions. It will be responsible for advising the CTE Committee, MSDE, and the GWDB on the legal aspects of restructuring the committees and implementing new regulations for post-CCR pathways.

Synopsis: Altering provisions related to the rates the Department of State Police sets for towing companies involved in police-initiated towing of motor vehicles to include the towing and recovery of light-duty vehicles; defining "light-duty towing" as towing and recovery of a vehicle including trailers or semitrailers with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 pounds or less; and altering the duties of the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Towing and Recovery.
Title: Public Safety - Department of State Police - Police-Initiated Towing - Alterations
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled
bill_summary: The bill expands the scope of police-initiated towing and recovery rates set by the Department of State Police to include light-duty vehicles (10,000 pounds or less). It renames the existing rate-setting committee, expands its responsibilities to include light-duty vehicles and insurance-related reporting, and mandates that light-duty towing rates cannot exceed 80% of the maximum rates for medium-duty towing.
stakeholders: Towing companies, vehicle owners and operators (especially those with light-duty vehicles), the Department of State Police, and insurance companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Department of State Police can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources, and State revenues are not materially affected. Local government finances and operations are also not materially impacted. There is a potential meaningful impact on small business tow companies due to the regulation of light-duty towing rates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of State Police is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It is responsible for establishing and maintaining the tow list, setting approved rates for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty towing, adjudicating complaints against tow companies, and providing staff support to the oversight committee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill renames and significantly alters the statutory duties and scope of the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Towing and Recovery, expanding its advisory role to include light-duty towing and insurance reporting.

The Maryland Insurance Administration is granted a seat on the rate-setting committee, and the bill specifically mandates that the committee examine and report on insurance matters related to out-of-state vehicle registration and the costs associated with cargo and debris cleanup.

The Secretary of Transportation is responsible for appointing a representative from the Maryland Transportation Authority Police to the rate-setting committee, and the bill impacts two of its primary administrations (SHA and MDTA).
The Administrator of the State Highway Administration is responsible for appointing a representative to the rate-setting committee to advise on highway-related towing and recovery matters.

The Maryland Transportation Authority Police is specifically required to have a representative on the rate-setting committee to provide expertise on towing operations involving toll facilities and related law enforcement needs.

Synopsis: Authorizing a police officer who is denied a certain right to apply to the circuit court at any time before a hearing is held by the hearing board for an order that directs the law enforcement agency to show cause why the right should not be granted.
Title: Police Discipline - Order to Show Cause
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Police Conduct -see also- Ethics; Law Enforcement

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a police officer who is denied a right granted under the state's laws relating to police accountability and discipline to apply to a circuit court for an order to show cause. This order directs the law enforcement agency to explain why the denied right should not be granted. The application must be made before a hearing is held by a trial board.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Maryland State and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Police officers and State, county, and local law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to have a material impact on State or local government operations or finances. The Department of Legislative Services notes that applications for show cause hearings in the circuit courts are expected to be few in number.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes police officers to apply to the circuit court for an order to show cause, creating a new legal procedure that the judicial branch must administer.

As the state's primary law enforcement agency, its officers would be directly affected by this change in disciplinary procedure, and the agency would be the respondent in show cause orders filed by its employees.

The OAG serves as the legal representative for state agencies; it would likely be responsible for representing state law enforcement agencies in circuit court when an officer applies for a show cause order.
The MDTA maintains its own nationally accredited police force, which is subject to state police disciplinary and accountability laws.
MDOT oversees several modal administrations with law enforcement components, including the Maryland Transit Administration police and the Maryland Transportation Authority police.
The DNR manages the Natural Resources Police, whose officers are subject to the disciplinary proceedings modified by this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees correctional facilities and probation services, employing personnel who may be classified as police officers under the Public Safety Article for disciplinary purposes.
DGS oversees the Maryland Capitol Police, whose officers would be affected by these changes to disciplinary rights and court procedures.
USM institutions employ campus police officers who are subject to the statewide police accountability and discipline process.
The Comptroller's office employs enforcement and investigative staff with police powers who are subject to these disciplinary regulations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for overseeing and regulating Maryland's statewide emergency medical services (EMS) network and prehospital care, MIEMSS manages the standards and registration for automated external defibrillator (AED) programs across the state.

The Maryland Department of Health sets broad public health policy and oversees safety initiatives; the widespread availability of AEDs in first responder vehicles is a significant component of the state's public health and emergency response strategy.

The department coordinates the state's preparedness and response efforts for emergencies. Ensuring that local law enforcement, as key first responders, carry life-saving medical equipment like AEDs aligns with their mission to ensure state resilience.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation and enforcement of new laws added to the Public Safety Article, such as these equipment requirements for local law enforcement.

Synopsis: Excluding certain charitable contributions from a limitation on the amount of itemized deductions allowed for certain individuals under the Maryland income tax; and applying the Act to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

bill_summary: This bill excludes charitable contribution deductions from a state-mandated 7.5% reduction of itemized deductions that applies to taxpayers with a federal adjusted gross income exceeding $200,000 ($100,000 for married individuals filing separately).
stakeholders: High-income Maryland taxpayers with federal adjusted gross income exceeding the specified thresholds who claim itemized deductions for charitable contributions.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are estimated to decrease by $84,600,000 in FY 2027, with annual revenue losses continuing through FY 2031. Local income tax revenues are projected to decrease by approximately $41,500,000 in FY 2027 and by similar amounts annually thereafter. The Comptroller’s Office is expected to implement the changes using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing changes to the Maryland income tax code. The bill directly modifies how itemized deductions are calculated for high-income taxpayers, which the Comptroller must administer.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The bill is projected to decrease state general fund revenues by $84.6 million in FY 2027 and significant amounts thereafter, directly impacting the state budget and fiscal projections managed by this department.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget. A significant reduction in general fund revenue (over $80 million annually) requires executive-level policy coordination and adjustments to the Governor's proposed budget.

The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals from final decisions of state taxing authorities. Changes to the tax code regarding itemized deductions and charitable contribution limitations may lead to increased administrative litigation or appeals concerning tax assessments.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides legal counsel to state agencies like the Comptroller. It may be required to provide statutory interpretation of the bill's amendments to the Tax - General Article.

bill_summary: Known as 'Mason’s Law,' this bill requires Maryland municipalities to inventory all public and private open drainage inlets and prioritize them based on public safety risks. Municipalities must install safety improvements, such as approved grating systems or fencing, on existing high-risk inlets by April 1, 2031, and incorporate such systems into all new drainage inlet construction. The bill also directs $250,000 annually from the State's comprehensive flood management grant program between fiscal 2029 and 2031 to provide matching funds for these municipal improvements.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment and Maryland Municipalities
stakeholders: Maryland residents, municipal governments, and private property owners with drainage inlets
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a state mandate to use $250,000 annually from the comprehensive flood management grant program for fiscal years 2029 through 2031 to assist municipalities with costs. Local governments are expected to see a significant increase in expenditures to conduct inventories and install improvements, with estimated costs ranging from $1,500 to $2,000 per drainage inlet. While the bill does not directly name state agencies for compliance, there may be operational impacts on the Maryland Department of Transportation for permitting and oversight.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of the Environment is the primary agency responsible for the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program, which is amended by the bill to include specific grants for municipal drainage inlet improvements. The agency is also tasked with adopting regulations for the grant program.

The bill requires the Board of Public Works to approve grants provided through the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program, including the new grants created for municipal drainage inlet improvements.

The Department's State Clearinghouse must review grant applications, and the Department coordinates with MDE to review local flood control operations. Additionally, the Maryland Historical Trust, within this agency, is used to prioritize certain grant awards.

The bill requires the Department of Emergency Management to coordinate with the Department of the Environment on the review and approval of local response plans for automated flood warning projects funded under the same grant program.
DBM is responsible for the state budget and supervising budget execution, including the specific $250,000 annual carve-out from the flood management grant program for fiscal years 2029 through 2031.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller must approve the grants and expenditures authorized under the comprehensive flood management program.
The Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which approves the grants, and manages the state debt proceeds that are often used to fund the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program.
The Governor oversees the executive branch, proposes the state budget (including potential appropriations for this program), and serves as a member of the Board of Public Works.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of the Environment and the Department of Planning regarding the implementation of the bill and the development of new regulations.
According to the fiscal note, MDOT may be required to permit and supervise the construction of improvements if municipal drainage inlets connect to State-owned highways.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Maryland counties and municipalities to regulate the 'tree of heaven' and other invasive trees identified on the Maryland Prohibited Invasive Plant List. Local governments may adopt ordinances to prohibit the sale, planting, or growth of these trees, establish civil fines for violations, and create bounty or native tree replacement programs to incentivize their removal.
responsible_party: The governing body of a county or municipality
stakeholders: Maryland county and municipal governments, property owners, nurseries, plant dealers, plant brokers, and landscaping businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. Local government expenditures may increase if they choose to establish bounty or native tree replacement programs, while revenues may increase from the collection of civil fines for ordinance violations. The fiscal impact is indeterminate as it depends on local adoption. Small businesses such as nurseries may incur compliance costs, while landscaping businesses may benefit from increased demand for tree removal services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines 'listed invasive trees' as any tree on the 'Maryland Prohibited Invasive Plant List' posted by the Maryland Department of Agriculture. The agency is the primary authority responsible for maintaining this list and regulating invasive plant species in the state.

The bill requires that invasive trees be identified and removed according to methodology and species pages published by the University of Maryland Agriculture Extension, which is a key service unit of the University System of Maryland.

As the agency responsible for managing Maryland's forests and natural resources, the Department of Natural Resources is impacted by policy regarding invasive trees like the tree of heaven, which crowd out native plants. The agency is also cited as an information source in the fiscal note.

The fiscal note indicates that the bill may have a meaningful impact on small businesses, specifically affecting nurseries that may be prohibited from selling certain trees and landscaping businesses that may be hired for removal and eradication.

The bill impacts local government regulatory powers and land use, areas where the Department of Planning provides policy guidance and technical assistance to ensure sustainable growth and environmental preservation.

This multi-agency initiative focuses on protecting the Chesapeake Bay and preserving natural resources; the regulation of invasive species and the promotion of native tree replacement programs align with its core mission.

The bill authorizes local governments to establish civil fines for violations of invasive tree ordinances, which may result in increased litigation or appeals handled within the state judicial system.

The OAG may be required to provide legal counsel to the Department of Agriculture regarding the enforcement of the Prohibited Invasive Plant List and the interaction between state law and new local ordinances.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies (MDA, DNR, and MDP) involved in implementing and coordinating the state's response to invasive species and local government regulation.

The Maryland Department of the Environment is responsible for environmental protection; the management of invasive species is relevant to its mission of restoring and protecting the state's land and water quality.

Synopsis: Altering certain terminology throughout the Annotated Code that refers to a clergyman to refer to a member of the clergy and churches to refer to faith institutions and places of worship; and defining "faith institution" as any Christian, Jewish, Islamic, Buddhist, or Hindu congregation, or any other religious society, congregation, or denomination.

bill_summary: This bill updates the Maryland Annotated Code by replacing gendered and religious-specific terminology with neutral language. Specifically, it changes references to 'clergyman' to 'member of the clergy' and replaces 'church' with terms like 'faith institution' or 'place of worship.'
stakeholders: Clergy members, faith institutions, religious organizations, and State agencies that utilize the Maryland Annotated Code.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is technical in nature and has no effect on State or local governmental operations or finances. The Fiscal Note indicates that there are no expenditure or revenue changes associated with this legislation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill updates terminology in the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding the privilege of clergy members not to testify and the Family Law Article regarding the statutory text of marriage licenses issued by the courts.
The bill amends the State Government Article to update the Archives' mandate to collect and preserve records of faith institutions (formerly church records).

The bill amends several sections of the Education Article related to the operation of noncollegiate educational institutions by faith institutions, school facility usage, and student health screening exemptions based on religious tenets.

The bill updates terminology in the Health - General and Health Occupations Articles regarding clergy visits to patients, nursing care provided by religious organizations, and the certification of spiritual healing institutions.

The bill modifies the Labor and Employment Article regarding unemployment insurance coverage for faith institutions and the Business Regulation Article regarding cemetery ownership and trader's licenses.
The bill amends the Transportation Article to update definitions and regulations for buses owned by faith institutions and signage identifying places of worship.
The bill updates regulations in the Transportation Article specifically related to outdoor signs along highways that identify places of worship.
The bill updates terminology in the Transportation Article affecting the classification and regulation of buses owned or operated by faith institutions.

The bill updates terminology in the Tax - General Article related to sales and use tax exemptions for faith institutions and the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article regarding license holder event types.
The bill updates terminology in the Public Safety Article regarding fire safety inspections for places of worship and the Criminal Law Article regarding restricted zones for certain weapons.
The bill amends the Natural Resources Article to update terminology defining 'safety zones' for hunting near places of worship.
The bill updates terminology in the Environment Article regarding public building definitions and physical hazard assessments near places of worship for permit denials.
The bill updates the Family Law Article regarding the terminology for clergy members as mandated reporters in child abuse and neglect cases.

As the state's chief legal officer, the OAG will provide guidance on the implementation of these terminology updates across multiple articles of the Maryland Code, including consumer protection and commercial law.

The agency manages official records and oversees charitable organizations, making the terminology updates for religious entities and faith institutions relevant to its regulatory and record-keeping functions.
The bill amends the Economic Development Article regarding noncollegiate educational institutions operated by faith institutions, which falls under the broader scope of economic and community assets.
The bill modifies the Education Article regarding the enrollment of students in religious educational institutions and the specific terminology for their programs.
The bill updates terminology in the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which is the primary regulatory framework overseen by this administration.
The bill amends the Real Property Article regarding damages for the eminent domain 'taking' of structures such as places of worship, impacting state real estate and facility planning.

The bill updates terminology in the Public Safety Article regarding structure definitions used in emergency management and disaster response contexts.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the enforcement of state laws, making the statewide terminology updates to the Annotated Code relevant to its administrative leadership.
The bill includes a minor update in the Business Regulation Article cemetery exemption list where state veterans' agencies are listed alongside faith institutions.

bill_summary: This bill establishes employment protections for members of the Maryland General Assembly, prohibiting employers from terminating, threatening, or coercing them because of their legislative duties. It restricts employers from forcing these members to use personal leave (annual, sick, or vacation) for legislative responsibilities and prohibits requiring them to work specific night or early-morning shifts if they have performed legislative duties for at least four hours that day. The protections apply year-round but specifically exclude campaigning on behalf of any candidate. Employers who violate these provisions are subject to a fine of up to $1,000.
responsible_party: The Maryland Department of Labor and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Members of the Maryland General Assembly who have outside employment and their public and private sector employers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State and local expenditures are expected to increase minimally and are absorbable within existing resources. State and local revenues may see a minimal increase from fines not exceeding $1,000 per violation for cases heard in District or circuit courts. As of 2026, there are six known State employees who are also members of the General Assembly.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is a primary regulatory body for labor and workplace laws. This bill creates new statutory employment protections and prohibitions against discrimination or discharge for employees serving in the General Assembly, which falls under the agency's broad mission to protect workers and enforce labor laws.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is responsible for managing state employee resources and policies. The bill directly impacts the leave and scheduling rights of state employees who are also members of the General Assembly, and the fiscal note specifically mentions DBM's data regarding these individuals.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and its agencies. It will be responsible for providing legal counsel on the interpretation, implementation, and enforcement of these new employment protections, particularly for state-employed members of the General Assembly.

The judicial branch will be responsible for adjudicating cases where employers violate the bill's provisions. The fiscal note anticipates a minimal increase in court revenues due to the $1,000 fine for violations, which would be processed through the District and Circuit Courts managed by the AOC.

PERB oversees collective bargaining and labor relations for state and public school employees. Since the bill mandates specific leave and scheduling protections for these workers, disputes regarding these rights could fall under the board's jurisdiction as labor-related controversies or unfair labor practices.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates statewide policy initiatives. This bill affects the operations of executive agencies whose employees may also serve in the General Assembly, and the Governor is responsible for enforcing state laws, including those relating to public sector employment.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the use of portable solar electric generating facilities by eligible customer-generators for the purpose of net energy metering. Portable solar is defined as a moveable solar electric photovoltaic facility with a generating capacity of up to 120 kilowatts that is designed to connect via a standard 120-volt outlet to offset the customer's electricity requirements.
stakeholders: Eligible customer-generators (residential and commercial), electric companies, and small solar businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no impact on state finances as the Public Service Commission can absorb implementation costs within existing budgeted resources. Local government operations and finances are not expected to be materially affected. Small solar businesses may see a potential meaningful positive impact due to the expansion of eligible technology for net metering.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulator for public utilities in Maryland. The bill explicitly requires the Commission to mandate that electric utilities develop standard contracts or tariffs for net energy metering for portable solar facilities and to report annually to the General Assembly on the status of the net metering program.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the Public Service Commission. Since this bill involves net metering tariffs and utility rate structures, the OPC would advocate for consumers' interests in how these portable solar systems are integrated into the grid.

The MEA is responsible for maximizing energy efficiency and promoting renewable energy. The bill aligns with its mission to diversify the State's energy resource mix and manage incentives for solar energy, including those funded through the Strategic Energy Investment Fund.

The DNR's Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) is responsible for conducting studies on the Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (RPS) and the overall costs and benefits of energy resources in Maryland, both of which are directly mentioned in the fiscal note as being related to the bill's implementation.

As the state's official green bank, the MCEC advances the adoption of clean energy technologies. They may be involved in providing financing solutions for residential or commercial users to acquire the portable solar facilities authorized by the bill.

The MDE implements environmental laws and climate change initiatives. Expanding net metering for portable solar facilities supports the state's goals for carbon reduction and clean energy adoption, which are central to MDE's environmental protection mission.

DGS manages state-owned facilities and leads sustainability and energy conservation initiatives for the state government. They could potentially utilize portable solar generating facilities to offset electricity consumption at state properties.

DHCD administers energy efficiency programs and community revitalization investments. Portable solar units could be integrated into affordable housing projects or weatherization programs to reduce energy costs for low-to-moderate-income residents.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and the General Assembly. They would likely be involved in reviewing the new regulations and tariffs for legal sufficiency and representing the State in any related legal challenges.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts to reduce the state's carbon footprint and promote sustainable development, goals that are directly supported by expanding access to solar energy through portable generating facilities.

The Department of Commerce promotes economic development and clean energy jobs. Authorizing a new category of solar equipment could stimulate the market for businesses that manufacture or install these portable systems.

bill_summary: This bill requires applicants for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) for overhead transmission lines to include evidence that they considered advanced transmission technologies and alternative planning processes in their internal planning. It also mandates that owners or operators of overhead transmission lines submit reports to the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) every four years, starting in 2026, regarding transmission congestion and the feasibility of using technologies like grid-enhancing hardware, high-performance conductors, or energy storage to address congestion.
stakeholders: Electric companies, owners and operators of overhead transmission lines, utility ratepayers, and local communities near proposed transmission routes.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) special fund expenditures are estimated to increase by approximately $500,000 annually starting in FY 2027 to hire outside consultants and technical experts to analyze congestion reports and CPCN applications. These expenditures are offset by a corresponding increase in special fund revenues through assessments charged to regulated public service companies. Impact on local government finances is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulator and lead implementing agency for this bill. It is responsible for the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) process, reviewing evidence of advanced transmission technologies, and processing the new quadrennial transmission congestion reports.

As the independent agency representing residential utility consumers, OPC is a key stakeholder in CPCN proceedings and will utilize the reports and evidence required by the bill to advocate for ratepayer value and cost efficiency.

DNR plays a critical role in the CPCN review process through its Power Plant Research Program, assessing the environmental impact of proposed transmission lines and providing recommendations that the PSC must consider.

The MEA advises the Governor on energy policy and coordinates energy planning across state agencies. The shift toward advanced transmission technologies and grid efficiency directly aligns with MEA's mission to maximize energy efficiency and renewable energy adoption.

MDE is involved in the CPCN process for utility projects to ensure compliance with state and federal environmental laws regarding land and water quality, which are specific considerations for transmission line routing.

MDP provides technical assistance and data analysis for land use planning during the CPCN process, which is relevant to the bill's requirements for analyzing alternative routes and environmental impacts of transmission lines.
DBM oversees the fiscal and personnel aspects of the bill, including the management of the PSC's special fund assessments which will increase to pay for consultants needed to implement the bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the PSC, DNR, and other state agencies involved in the regulation of utilities and the review of CPCN applications.
The OAH may provide Administrative Law Judges to preside over contested administrative hearings regarding utility licensing and PSC decisions.
The Board may be involved in the acquisition or transfer of State property or rights-of-way required for new overhead transmission line projects authorized under the CPCN process.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development and environmental protection across MDE and MDP, which relates to the bill's focus on mitigating environmental impacts of energy infrastructure.
MCEC's mission to advance clean energy products and technologies relates to the bill's promotion of advanced transmission technologies and energy storage used as transmission.
The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives for the executive branch and coordinates intergovernmental relations regarding utility regulation and the state's energy goals.

stakeholders: Registered voters of Baltimore County, candidates for the Baltimore County Board of Education, and current and future members of the Baltimore County Board of Education
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no direct effect on State finances. Any local fiscal impact for Baltimore County is expected to be minimal, as costs associated with the new redistricting process are assumed to be absorbed within the county's existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and retains the statutory authority to appoint four members to the Baltimore County Board of Education as maintained under the proposed bill.

The Maryland State Department of Education oversees the 24 local school systems; this bill directly alters the governance and election structure of the Baltimore County Board of Education.
The Department of Planning serves as the state's center for census data and provides technical assistance for redistricting and the creation of new geographic boundaries for school board districts.

The State Board of Elections is responsible for administering elections and managing the voter registration system, which must be updated to reflect the seven new school board districts established by the bill.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in the recruitment and vetting process for the four appointed members of the Baltimore County Board of Education.

bill_summary: This bill allows registered massage practitioners to continue practicing beyond October 31, 2026, without being required to convert their registration to a license. It also modifies educational requirements for out-of-state applicants, requiring 750 contact hours while providing options to supplement hours through continuing education or work experience. Additionally, the bill updates license reinstatement and reactivation procedures, requires criminal history checks for practitioners on inactive status, and removes the formal hearing requirement for the Board to impose a $100 penalty for failing to notify it of a name or address change.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners
stakeholders: Licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, out-of-state massage therapy license applicants, and the State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's changes to administrative and licensing procedures do not materially affect State finances and have no impact on local government finances. There is a potential meaningful impact on small businesses, as registered massage practitioners may continue practicing under their current credentials beyond the previous 2026 deadline without needing to meet additional licensure requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly regulates the State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners, which is a unit within the Maryland Department of Health. The department is responsible for the administration of licensure and registration for massage therapy practitioners and implementing the procedural changes described.

The bill specifies that applicants for massage therapy licensure must graduate from institutions approved by the Maryland Higher Education Commission and sets specific contact hour requirements for curricula that must align with commission standards.

As the agency responsible for overseeing postsecondary education and approving institutions in Maryland, it is directly referenced in the bill as the authority for approving massage therapy education programs required for licensure.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners. Changes to administrative penalty procedures, hearing requirements, and regulatory criteria for licensure require legal review and guidance from this office.

The bill repeals the requirement for certain administrative penalties to be subject to formal hearing provisions. This change directly affects the administrative adjudication framework that often involves the Office of Administrative Hearings for contested board decisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires criminal history records checks for the reinstatement and reactivation of massage therapy credentials. These checks are typically processed through the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS) within this department.

The Maryland State Police are involved in the processing of background checks and criminal history information utilized by state licensing boards for verifying the qualifications of applicants and practitioners.

Synopsis: Requiring units of State government to ensure that at least 50% of the unit's total dollar value of procurement contracts for print and digital advertising is being made directly to local news organizations.
Title: Procurement - Advertising - Local News Organizations (Local Newspapers for Maryland Communities Act of 2026)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland State government units to ensure that at least 50% of their total dollar value of procurement contracts for print and digital advertising is awarded directly to local news organizations, with exceptions for out-of-state tourism promotion and employee recruitment.
stakeholders: Local news organizations, State government agencies, and media professionals residing in or near Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill may create operational inefficiencies for State agencies required to verify the eligibility of news organizations. While no direct expenditure is specified, there may be an indeterminate decrease in general fund revenues if shifts in advertising platforms reduce the effectiveness of lottery promotions. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note identifies a specific negative fiscal impact on this agency, noting that shifting advertising funds away from broader platforms could reduce lottery sales and general fund revenues.

As the primary procurement authority for the state, this agency is responsible for overseeing procurement regulations and would likely lead the implementation of the new 50% spending mandate for all units.

This agency conducts significant advertising to attract businesses and promote Maryland's assets; while out-of-state tourism promotion is exempt, its other marketing activities are subject to the bill.
The bill explicitly mentions and exempts out-of-state tourism promotion from the procurement requirements, directly affecting this agency's advertising strategy and spend distribution.
As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM oversees budget execution and procurement policies, ensuring that units comply with state spending goals and fiscal regulations.
The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts and ensures that executive branch spending aligns with state laws, including new procurement mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office monitors socioeconomic procurement programs across the state and may be involved in tracking compliance with the bill's local news organization spending goals.
The Department of Health is a major advertiser for public health campaigns and local health services, making it heavily subject to the operational changes required by the 50% spending mandate.
As a multi-modal agency with extensive public notification and service-related advertising needs, MDOT will face significant operational shifts in its media procurement.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding procurement compliance and the application of the bill's specific criteria for local news organizations.
DoIT may be required to provide technical assistance in verifying audience location data and digital platform metrics as required by the bill's definitions.
The agency conducts significant advertising for workforce programs and recruitment; while out-of-state recruitment is exempt, in-state activities are impacted by the spending mandate.
In addition to serving on the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller manages revenue-related advertising that will be subject to the bill's procurement restrictions.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Treasurer provides oversight for state contracts and manages the funds utilized for these procurement activities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency adjudicates bid protests and contract disputes, which may increase as vendors challenge the application of the bill's new and specific local news organization criteria.

Synopsis: Altering the information that is required to be included on the signature page of a petition seeking to place a question on the ballot and with a question on the ballot; requiring that a certain summary included on the signature page of a petition seeking to place a question on the ballot and a certain statement about a question on the ballot be written in plain language; requiring certain boards of elections to post the text of ballot measures for at least 90 days before the general election; etc.
Title: Election Law - Petitions and Ballot Questions - Contents, Plain Language Requirement, and Procedures
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Senate Rules
