Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse

bill_summary: This bill prohibits Maryland State entities and political subdivisions from assigning a Confederate name to any real property owned by the State or local government, including streets, buildings, parks, and subdivisions. The prohibition is prospective, meaning it only applies to property named after the bill's effective date and does not require the renaming of existing property.
responsible_party: State entities in the executive, legislative, and judicial branches, and political subdivisions including counties, municipalities, school districts, and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission.
stakeholders: State and local government agencies, Maryland residents, and users of public infrastructure such as schools, parks, and roads.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. Because the requirements apply only to the naming of new property or future naming decisions and do not mandate the renaming of existing assets, there is no identified fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of General Services is the primary operational support agency for the state, responsible for the planning, design, and management of state-owned facilities. As the bill prohibits Confederate naming of State-owned buildings, DGS is the primary implementing agency for new facility naming conventions.

The Department of Transportation oversees the state's highways, bridges, and transit systems. Since the bill specifically includes 'streets' and 'buildings' within the definition of real property, MDOT's modal administrations (like SHA and MTA) are directly restricted in how they name new infrastructure.

The Department of Natural Resources manages over 500,000 acres of public lands, including state parks. The bill's definition of real property includes 'parks,' making DNR a primary agency affected by the prohibition when naming new conservation areas or park facilities.

The bill explicitly applies to all units in the Judicial branch. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational support for the Maryland Judicial Branch and would be responsible for ensuring compliance for any new judicial buildings or facilities.

The University System of Maryland manages a vast network of campuses and academic buildings. As a state entity, it must comply with the naming prohibition for all new real property across its 12 institutions.

The State Archives is the central depository for government records and historical research. It is identified as an information source for the bill and would likely be consulted to verify whether a proposed name commemorates a person or entity that served the Confederacy.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures, including the acquisition and naming of major state buildings and capital projects. It would serve as a high-level enforcement body for the bill's provisions during the procurement and project approval process.

The Maryland Stadium Authority plans, finances, and builds sports, entertainment, and educational facilities (including public schools). As a state agency involved in the construction of new real property, it is subject to the naming restrictions.

The MDTA manages toll bridges, tunnels, and roads. As an independent state agency that constructs and operates major transportation infrastructure, it must adhere to the prohibition on Confederate names for new facilities.

The bill's definition of 'political subdivision' includes 'school districts.' While naming is often a local board function, MSDE provides oversight and leadership for the state's public education system and facility construction standards.

The Department of Health manages numerous state-owned facilities, including hospitals and local health department buildings, and would be restricted from using Confederate names for any new real property acquisitions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees state correctional facilities and pretrial detention centers. Any new facilities or buildings within its jurisdiction would be subject to the bill's naming restrictions.

As a state agency and independent university with its own Board of Regents, Morgan State University would be prohibited from assigning Confederate names to any newly constructed or acquired real property on its campus.
As an independent unit of state government, the college is a 'State entity' under the bill and must comply with the naming restrictions for any new campus buildings or real property.

The Adjutant General oversees the Maryland Military Department, which manages armories and other military facilities. The bill's restrictions apply to any new real property assigned by this department.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal interpretations of what constitutes a 'Confederate name' or 'voluntary service' under the bill's definitions.

The Department of Planning oversees the Maryland Historical Trust and provides land use policy guidance. It may play a role in advising agencies and local governments on the historical context of names for new subdivisions or landmarks.
As the head of the Executive Branch, the Governor's Office oversees the agencies implementing this policy and ensures that new state real property is named in accordance with the law.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a county or municipal corporation to grant, by law, a credit against the county or municipal corporation property tax on real property if use of the real property has been converted from a retail service station to other certain uses; prohibiting the application of the credit unless the underground storage tanks located on or formerly located on the real property have been permanently closed; and applying the Act to all taxable years after June 30, 2026.
Title: Property Tax Credit - Retail Service Station Conversions
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Baltimore City, counties, and municipal corporations to grant a property tax credit for real property that has been converted from a retail service station to a residential, retail, or mixed-use property. To qualify for the credit, any underground storage tanks on the property must be permanently closed according to Department of the Environment regulations. The credit is intended to help cover the costs of removing these tanks and remediating associated contamination. Certain types of businesses, such as discount stores, tobacco shops, and liquor stores, are excluded from the retail uses eligible for the credit.
responsible_party: Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City, governing bodies of Maryland counties and municipal corporations, and the Maryland Department of the Environment
stakeholders: Owners of retail service stations, local governments, and small businesses involved in property remediation and redevelopment
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no state fiscal impact because a provision for state reimbursement was removed. Local property tax revenues may decrease starting in fiscal 2027 if local governments choose to grant the credit. The exact financial impact is indeterminate as it depends on local adoption and the number of eligible properties; however, the State Department of Assessments and Taxation identifies approximately 2,300 properties currently classified as retail service stations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly prohibits the property tax credit from being granted unless underground storage tanks on the property have been permanently closed in accordance with the regulations of the Department of the Environment (MDE). MDE's regulatory framework for tank closure and remediation is the primary gatekeeper for credit eligibility.

The Comptroller regulates the motor fuel, alcohol, tobacco, and electronic smoking device industries. The bill specifically defines 'retail use' to exclude several entities regulated by the Comptroller, including licensed retailers of cigarettes, tobacco, electronic smoking devices, and Class A retail alcoholic beverage license holders.

The bill aligns with the department's mission of promoting sustainable growth and community revitalization by providing an incentive to repurpose former service stations—often underutilized or contaminated land—into residential or productive retail sites.

By authorizing a tax credit for the conversion of service stations into residential or mixed retail and residential use, the bill directly supports the department's goals of fostering affordable housing and community redevelopment.

As the state's primary economic development agency, Commerce is impacted by legislation that provides financial incentives for business expansion, job creation, and the conversion of commercial real estate into new retail uses.

This agency provides the second level of administrative review for disputes regarding property tax assessments and credits. If taxpayers are denied the credit authorized by local governments under this bill, they may appeal to this board.

The Maryland Tax Court adjudicates appeals from final decisions of taxing authorities and local boards. It would serve as the final administrative venue for legal disputes concerning the application or valuation of this property tax credit.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Aging to provide resources, training, grants, and other support to the Maryland Access Point network to create dementia-friendly communities through community-based efforts; and requiring the Maryland Access Point network to provide certain public awareness and educational materials to communities regarding community-based ways to support individuals with dementia.
Title: Department of Aging - Maryland Access Point - Dementia-Friendly Communities
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:45 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Aging to provide resources, training, grants, and support to the Maryland Access Point (MAP) network to establish dementia-friendly communities. It also mandates that the MAP network provide public awareness and educational materials to help communities support individuals with dementia, reduce stigma, and create safe, inclusive environments.
stakeholders: Individuals living with dementia, their families and care partners, the Maryland Access Point network, local governments, first responders, local businesses, and community groups.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, state general fund expenditures increase by at least $144,700 in fiscal 2027, covering the cost of a dementia-friendly coordinator and the printing and distribution of educational materials. Costs are projected to increase annually to approximately $177,700 by fiscal 2031. Local governments may see an indeterminate increase in revenues and expenditures if the Maryland Department of Aging provides grant funding to local Maryland Access Point offices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primarily tasks the Department of Aging with providing resources, training, and grants to the Maryland Access Point network to create dementia-friendly communities. The fiscal note indicates the department will require additional staff and funding to fulfill these mandates.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate with the Maryland Department of Health (MDH). Furthermore, MDH is involved in existing dementia public awareness programs and hosts the Virginia I. Jones Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Council mentioned in the fiscal note.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Department of Disabilities. The program serves individuals with disabilities as well as older adults.
The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Department of Human Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.

The fiscal note identifies a significant increase in general fund expenditures ($144,700 in FY 2027 and more in subsequent years) for staff and materials, which falls under DBM's fiscal and personnel management responsibilities.
The bill requires the Maryland Access Point network to facilitate specialized training for first responders, of which the Maryland State Police is a primary state-level entity.

The bill seeks to make physical environments safe, accessible, and easy to navigate through clear signage and infrastructure, which relates to the operational duties of MDOT agencies like the State Highway Administration.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note highlights the role of the Virginia I. Jones Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Council, which is an advisory body tasked with updating the State Plan on Alzheimer’s Disease and related issues.

Synopsis: Requiring a county board of education to develop and adopt a policy on the use of personal electronic devices during school hours; requiring the policy to restrict or limit the use of personal electronic devices by students during school hours, except for any purpose documented in the student's education program or Section 504 plan, to monitor or address a student's health issue, or for certain educational purposes; and requiring the policy to be published on the county board's website and in student handbooks.

bill_summary: This bill requires each Maryland county board of education to develop and adopt a policy regarding student use of personal electronic devices during school hours. The policy must prohibit device use for elementary and middle school students and limit device use for high school students, though exceptions are allowed for documented health issues, special education needs (IEP or 504 plans), or specific educational purposes directed by staff.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and county boards of education
stakeholders: Public school students, teachers, school administrators, and local county boards of education
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education and local boards of education can implement the policy development, adoption, and review requirements using existing resources. The bill is not expected to affect state or local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Maryland State Department of Education (the 'Department') to review student technology use policies for elementary and middle school students every two years. MSDE is also the primary oversight body for the local boards of education that must develop and adopt these policies.

As an independent unit within the Department of Education, the Center provides a coordinated approach to school safety. Technology use, specifically personal electronic devices like smartphones, is a significant factor in school safety and environment, and the agency is listed as a primary information source in the bill's fiscal note.

The bill includes specific exemptions for students using personal electronic devices as part of an Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Section 504 plan. The Department of Disabilities is the principal agency for coordinating services and inclusive policies for residents with disabilities, including students.

The bill allows an exception for students to use personal electronic devices to monitor or address documented health issues. The Department of Health oversees public health policies and coordinates with local health departments that often support school health services and requirements.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the Department of Education and state agencies. They would be responsible for providing legal counsel regarding the implementation and enforcement of technology use policies and related disciplinary measures like in-school suspensions.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from disposing of yard waste collected on the grounds of a State building or State highway in single-use plastic container; requiring a person to collect yard waste on the grounds of a State building or State highway in a container that will not be discarded with the yard waste or in a compostable paper bag; and requiring all yard waste collected on the grounds of a State building or State highway to be disposed of in a certain manner under certain circumstances.
Title: State Buildings and State Highways - Collection and Disposal of Yard Waste
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Plants -see also- Invasive Species; Trees; Weeds
Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse

bill_summary: This bill prohibits State employees and contractors from using single-use plastic containers to collect or dispose of yard waste from State buildings and highways. It requires the use of reusable containers or compostable paper bags and mandates disposal at organics or natural wood waste recycling facilities if such a facility is within a 30-mile radius and has capacity. The bill excludes noxious weeds and invasive species.
responsible_party: State agencies managing State buildings and highways, including the Department of General Services, Maryland Department of Transportation, and Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: State employees and private contractors involved in landscaping and yard waste collection on State property
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures may increase slightly due to the higher cost of compostable paper bags compared to plastic ones and potential transport or disposal fees. However, the fiscal impact is not expected to be significant. No impact on State revenues or local government finances is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill applies to yard waste collected on the grounds of State buildings and facilities, including the training sites and readiness centers managed by the Maryland Military Department.

The bill applies to 'State buildings,' which include facilities used by the Judicial Branch. The AOC provides operational and financial support to the state's courts and would be responsible for compliance with yard waste disposal rules at court facilities.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurement contracts, including those for landscaping and waste management services that will be affected by the bill's container and disposal requirements.
The authority manages state-owned properties within the Canal Place Heritage Area, which are subject to the bill's requirements for yard waste collection and disposal.
The bill specifically excludes 'noxious weeds' as designated by the Department of Agriculture from its requirements, making the agency responsible for defining the scope of this exemption.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the budget and personnel impacts across multiple fund types resulting from potential increases in costs for compostable bags and disposal fees.

The bill defines 'State building' to include educational facilities owned or operated by the State, which may include specific facilities under the oversight or management of the Department of Education.

DGS is the primary operational support agency for the construction and maintenance of state-owned facilities. It will be a lead agency in implementing the yard waste collection and disposal standards across its managed portfolio.
The Maryland Department of Health operates various institutional facilities and hospitals with significant grounds that generate yard waste subject to the bill's requirements.
DHS operates local department offices and facilities whose groundskeeping activities must comply with the new disposal and collection standards.
DJS operates secure residential facilities for youth; these grounds are considered State buildings/improved areas subject to the bill's requirements.

The bill specifically includes State parks and recreation centers in the definition of 'State building.' DNR is a primary land manager for the state and will be significantly impacted by the change in yard waste disposal practices.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages extensive correctional facility grounds throughout the state, which generate substantial yard waste that must now be diverted to specific recycling facilities.
The bill's title and definitions explicitly include 'State highways' and 'public mass transportation accommodations' such as terminals or stations, making MDOT a primary implementing agency.
The department manages state veteran cemeteries and the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home, which are State-owned improved areas that generate yard waste.

The bill relies on definitions of 'organics recycling facility' and 'natural wood waste recycling facility' from the Environment Article, and MDE regulates the facilities where yard waste must be diverted.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch operations and policy implementation related to the management of state facilities and environmental initiatives.
As an independent agency managing an outdoor history museum and archaeological park on state-owned land, it must comply with the bill's yard waste disposal rules.
The corporation manages the Reginald F. Lewis Museum, which is a state-owned structure subject to the bill's yard waste collection requirements.

MES provides technical and operational environmental services to state agencies, including waste management and recycling. It may be called upon to help agencies comply with the bill's disposal requirements.
As a state agency with two campuses, MSD is responsible for managing its grounds in accordance with the bill's yard waste collection and disposal mandates.
The MSA plans and manages major sports and entertainment facilities and state-owned properties, which are subject to the bill's yard waste requirements.
MSP manages barracks and other state-owned buildings across Maryland that are subject to the new yard waste collection standards.
MTA is specifically referenced through the inclusion of public mass transportation accommodations in the definition of a 'State building.'
MDTA manages toll facilities and adjacent lands that fall under the bill's definition of 'State highway,' requiring compliance for its landscaping activities.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the bill's definition of 'State building,' making Morgan State University directly responsible for compliance.
MVA operates various branch offices and facilities across the state that are considered State buildings subject to the bill.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to state agencies regarding the modification of landscaping and waste disposal contracts to ensure compliance with the bill.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the bill's definition of 'State building,' making the college directly responsible for compliance.
As the agency responsible for the majority of non-toll State highways, SHA is a primary entity impacted by the bill's highway yard waste collection and disposal rules.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the definition of 'State building.' USM campuses manage significant grounds and were specifically mentioned in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Requiring that the salary of certain Sheriffs to be equal to the salary of certain State's Attorneys.
Title: Courts - Sheriffs' Salaries - Alterations
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill mandates that the annual salaries of Sheriffs in 16 Maryland counties (Allegany, Calvert, Caroline, Carroll, Cecil, Dorchester, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Kent, St. Mary’s, Somerset, Talbot, Washington, Wicomico, and Worcester) be set equal to the annual salary of the State’s Attorney for the same county.
responsible_party: County governments (County Commissioners and County Councils) of the 16 affected counties
stakeholders: County Sheriffs in Allegany, Calvert, Caroline, Carroll, Cecil, Dorchester, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Kent, St. Mary’s, Somerset, Talbot, Washington, Wicomico, and Worcester counties.

The bill alters the salaries of Sheriffs, who are constitutional officers and law enforcement officials often participating in the State Retirement and Pension System. Changes in pensionable salary affect the agency's administration of contributions and future benefit liabilities.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. The bill involves constitutional considerations regarding the timing of salary adjustments for public officials, an area where the OAG (via the Counsel to the General Assembly) frequently provides guidance.

The State Superintendent of Education is a statutory member of the commission. Additionally, the department is one of the agencies required to jointly provide staff for the commission's operations.

The Maryland State Archives is explicitly required to have a representative on the commission and is one of the agencies responsible for providing joint staff support.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the State of Maryland from purchasing gasoline-powered leaf blowers beginning July 1, 2026. Starting January 1, 2031, the State and any contractors or subcontractors working on State-owned land are prohibited from using gasoline-powered leaf blowers. The bill exempts emergency response, firefighting, and wildland fire suppression activities and requires the State to comply with local government standards that are more stringent than the State's requirements.
responsible_party: Each agency in the Executive Branch of State government
stakeholders: Maryland State agencies, state contractors and subcontractors, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. However, the bill creates a mandate for State agencies to transition to alternative equipment, likely resulting in increased expenditures for new purchases and potential increases in contract costs for landscaping services on State property.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary operational support and procurement agency, DGS is directly impacted by the prohibition on purchasing gasoline-powered leaf blowers and the requirement to ensure contractors and subcontractors comply with use restrictions on state-owned land.

MDOT manages extensive state-owned grounds including highway roadsides, transit stations, and airports. The bill specifically mentions MDOT facilities regarding emergency response exemptions and imposes a significant operational shift for its maintenance crews and contractors.

DNR manages over 500,000 acres of public land, including state parks and forests. The bill directly affects its grounds maintenance operations and includes specific exemptions for wildland fire suppression and prescribed burns, which are DNR responsibilities.

The bill codifies these new regulations within the Environment Article of the Maryland Code. As the primary agency for environmental protection, MDE is responsible for the policy area the bill addresses.

USM governs 12 institutions with significant campus acreage. The prohibition on the purchase and use of gasoline-powered leaf blowers will require a large-scale transition to electric equipment for campus facilities management.

DBM oversees state budget execution and procurement policies. The transition from gasoline to electric equipment will have fiscal impacts across multiple agencies that DBM must manage and account for in state budget planning.

MES provides operational environmental services to state and local governments. In its role as a service provider or contractor on state lands, it must comply with the bill's use prohibitions.
The Maryland Military Department manages armories and military facilities with grounds that require maintenance, necessitating compliance with the bill's restrictions.
As an independent state agency with a large urban campus, MSU must monitor and enforce its own compliance with the purchase and use bans for its grounds maintenance.
As an independent state agency with a residential campus, the college will need to transition its landscaping equipment to comply with the bill.
The Commission manages an outdoor living history museum and archaeological park with significant grounds, making the equipment restrictions relevant to its operations.
MSP maintains numerous barracks and facilities across the state which require groundskeeping, impacting their facility management and equipment purchasing.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal advice to various state agencies regarding the interpretation and enforcement of the new requirements and the interaction with local government standards.

It expands eligibility for the Housing Innovation Fund, the Housing Innovation Pilot Program, and the Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program to include local school boards and municipal corporations. stakeholders: Teachers and employees of local school systems, county boards of education, municipal corporations, and nonprofit organizations

Local school boards and municipal corporations gain eligibility for state financial assistance through the Housing Innovation Fund and related programs. The Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program tax credit cap remains at $3,500,000 annually, and the bill does not create new spending mandates or revenue changes.

DHCD is the primary agency responsible for administering the Housing Innovation Fund, the Housing Innovation Pilot Program, and the Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program, all of which are expanded by this bill to include educator workforce housing.

bill_summary: This bill allows individuals to petition for the expungement of any misdemeanor or felony conviction after a specified waiting period following the completion of their sentence, parole, probation, and mandatory treatment. Misdemeanors require a 5-year waiting period, while felonies require a 7-year waiting period. A court may grant the expungement based on a finding of 'good cause,' taking into account the nature of the crime, the person's character, public safety risk, rehabilitation success, and the impact of the conviction on the person's ability to secure housing, employment, and education. If a petition is denied, the decision cannot be appealed, and the petitioner must wait at least three years before filing again for the same conviction.
stakeholders: Individuals with criminal records (misdemeanors and felonies), the Maryland court system, and state and local law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill will likely increase administrative and judicial expenditures due to the creation of a new petition process, required court hearings for each petition, and the resulting processing of expungement orders by the Judiciary and law enforcement agencies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new cause of action for expungement petitions and requires the judicial branch to conduct hearings and make specific factual findings for any misdemeanor or felony conviction.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency maintains the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS) and supervises individuals on parole or probation; it is responsible for verifying sentence completion and executing the expungement of records.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender will be the primary agency representing indigent individuals who seek to petition for expungement under the expanded criteria, leading to a significant increase in caseload.
As the primary repository for state criminal records, the Maryland State Police must process court-ordered expungements and ensure police records are properly removed or shielded.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategy and coordinates policy regarding recidivism and public safety, which are directly impacted by broader expungement eligibility.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding implementation and represents the state in the judicial proceedings where expungement is sought.
DBM is responsible for managing the fiscal impact and personnel needs across state agencies resulting from the significantly increased administrative workload created by the bill.
The MVA maintains records for vehicle-related misdemeanors and felonies that may become eligible for expungement under this bill.
The bill requires petitioners to complete mandatory treatment before filing; MDH oversees behavioral health and may be involved in certifying or managing records of such treatment.
The court must consider the impact of a conviction on a person's ability to secure housing, which aligns with the department's mission to ensure residents have access to secure housing.
The court is required to consider the impact of a conviction on a person's ability to secure public assistance, a program area managed by DHS.
DoIT may be required to provide technical support and infrastructure updates to ensure that expungement orders are correctly reflected across interconnected state databases.
The bill explicitly requires the court to consider the impact of a conviction on a person's ability to obtain professional licensing, which is regulated by this department.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and the annual state budget, both of which are affected by the significant expansion of expungement eligibility and the associated fiscal costs.
This office focuses on reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility, goals that are supported by removing criminal record barriers to parental employment.
As the central depository for permanent state and judicial records, the Archives must comply with expungement orders for any qualifying historical or permanent records in its possession.
The expungement of felony convictions can impact the accuracy of the statewide voter registration system and records regarding voter eligibility.
This team identifies and pilots novel initiatives to enhance economic mobility and reduce poverty, which are key factors the court must consider in granting an expungement under this bill.
The court must consider the impact of a conviction on a person's ability to secure education, which relates to the department's leadership over educational access.

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of a 'drug trafficking crime' to include the misdemeanors of possessing cannabis with intent to distribute and the cultivation or manufacture of cannabis. This change means that individuals who possess, use, or carry a firearm in relation to these cannabis-related misdemeanors can be charged with a felony carrying a mandatory minimum prison sentence of five to ten years.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals charged with cannabis-related distribution or cultivation offenses, law enforcement agencies, and State and local correctional systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are expected to increase minimally for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services due to the application of mandatory minimum incarceration penalties. Local expenditures may decrease minimally as some individuals who would have served time in local jails are instead committed to State correctional facilities. While the average cost per incarcerated individual is estimated at $5,838 per month, total aggregate fiscal impact estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly impacts this department by expanding the definition of drug trafficking crimes to include certain misdemeanors, which will result in longer incarceration periods and increased general fund expenditures for state correctional facilities as noted in the fiscal note.
The judicial branch is responsible for the adjudication of these new felony charges and the application of mandatory minimum sentences, directly affecting court operations and caseload management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency will face an increased workload as their attorneys will be required to defend indigent clients against new felony enhancements and significant mandatory minimum sentences in cases that were previously classified as misdemeanors.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing criminal laws and will be tasked with investigating and charging individuals under this expanded definition of drug trafficking crimes involving firearms.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for managing the state's general fund, which will see a minimal increase in expenditures due to the expanded application of incarceration penalties for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.

The bill's focus on cannabis-related misdemeanors (possession with intent to distribute and unauthorized cultivation) intersects with the MCA's role in overseeing the state's cannabis regulatory framework and public health outcomes.

bill_summary: This bill permits Maryland municipalities to authorize their code enforcement, parking enforcement, and traffic enforcement officers to use body-worn cameras while performing their duties. It includes these municipal officers in the definition of law enforcement officer for legal exceptions to wiretapping and electronic surveillance prohibitions, allowing them to record audio in the course of duty provided the municipality adopts a formal ordinance and publishes a usage policy consistent with Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission standards.
stakeholders: Municipal code, parking, and traffic enforcement officers, municipal governments, and the general public who interact with these officers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to have a material fiscal impact on State government. Locally, the fiscal impact is indeterminate and contingent on whether a municipality chooses to adopt an ordinance or resolution to authorize body-worn cameras. If a municipality implements the program, expenditures would increase to develop policies and to obtain and maintain camera equipment and recorded data. No specific dollar estimates are provided in the Fiscal Note.

bill_summary: This bill allows sole owners and certain co-owners (joint tenants or tenants by the entirety) of marine vessels and motor vehicles to designate a beneficiary on the vehicle or vessel title to whom ownership will transfer upon the death of the last surviving owner. These transfers occur outside of the formal estate administration process, allowing for more streamlined asset transfer upon death.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Department of Transportation's Motor Vehicle Administration
stakeholders: Sole and co-owners of motor vehicles and marine vessels in Maryland, designated beneficiaries, creditors, the Department of Natural Resources, and the Motor Vehicle Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) and the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) are expected to increase as owners pay fees (typically $20 to $40) to update certificates of title with beneficiary designations. The Fiscal Note estimates potential increases of $269,540 for DNR and $1,000,000 for TTF in fiscal 2027 based on specific adoption scenarios. General fund revenues may decrease minimally due to reduced probate fees and inheritance taxes, as vehicles and vessels would pass outside of probate estates. There is no local fiscal impact.

The bill explicitly tasks the Motor Vehicle Administration (referred to as the Administration in the Transportation Article) with expanding its current transfer-on-death registration process to include co-owned motor vehicles.

The bill allows vessels and motor vehicles to pass to beneficiaries outside of estate administration, which directly affects the Registers of Wills by potentially reducing the volume of probate estates and the collection of associated probate fees and inheritance taxes.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT will see fiscal impacts to the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) from title fees, and the bill affects MDOT's modal administration duties.

The AOC supports the judicial branch, including the Orphans' Courts; since the bill allows specific assets to bypass probate, it affects the workload and nature of estate-related proceedings overseen by the judiciary.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies like the DNR and MVA, and will likely assist in developing the necessary regulations and forms to implement the bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy; the Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law once it is passed.

bill_summary: This bill expands the legal protections for certain spousal trusts, specifically Spousal Lifetime Access Trusts (SLATs). It provides that an individual who creates an irrevocable trust for their spouse is not considered the settlor of that trust for creditor purposes if they later become a beneficiary through a power of appointment. This designation protects the trust's assets and income from being seized or attached by the original creator's creditors.
stakeholders: Trust settlors, spouses of settlors, beneficiaries of irrevocable trusts, and legal creditors.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. The bill clarifies estate and trust law regarding creditor access to trust assets, which primarily affects private legal interests. There are no explicitly stated financial mandates or revenue changes for state or local governments, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the support agency for the Maryland Judicial Branch, the AOC is relevant because the bill modifies the Estates and Trusts Article, which governs the legal interpretation of trusts and creditor rights—matters frequently adjudicated in the state's courts.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector. Since the bill concerns the legal status of trust settlors and mentions the reimbursement of taxes on trust income or principal, it may have implications for the administration and collection of state income or inheritance taxes.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides counsel on the interpretation of state laws. This bill makes substantive changes to the Estates and Trusts Article regarding the definition of a trust settlor and creditor protection, requiring legal oversight.

The Register of Wills is the primary state agency responsible for the administrative probate of estates and the collection of inheritance taxes. Changes to the classification of trust settlors and spousal trusts directly impact estate administration and tax liability assessments under their jurisdiction.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Department of Natural Resources to allow bow hunting for deer and turkey on Sundays throughout their respective hunting seasons statewide in Maryland.
stakeholders: Bow hunters, small businesses (including outfitters and equipment retailers), farmers, and residents in areas with significant deer or turkey populations.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government finances. However, it may have a meaningful economic impact on small businesses due to increased hunter expenditures and potential reductions in agricultural crop damage and deer-vehicle collisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Department of Natural Resources is authorized by this bill to establish Sunday hunting for deer and turkey using a bow and arrow. The agency manages hunting seasons, enforces conservation laws through its Natural Resources Police, and oversees the regulations amended by this legislation.

The expansion of hunting opportunities is intended, in part, to manage deer populations which cause significant crop damage. The Department of Agriculture represents the interests of the farming community that would benefit from reduced agricultural losses.

The fiscal note indicates that a reduction in the deer population may lead to a decrease in deer-vehicle collisions. MDOT, specifically through the State Highway Administration, is responsible for highway safety and infrastructure maintenance affected by such incidents.

The fiscal note highlights a potential meaningful economic impact on small businesses related to hunting, such as lodging, food, and equipment providers. The Department of Commerce is responsible for supporting economic growth and the state's competitive position in these sectors.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and would be responsible for ensuring the new regulations comply with existing state and federal law, as well as defending the agency in any related litigation.
The Council addresses challenges in Maryland's 18 rural counties, where hunting is a significant cultural and economic activity and where agricultural damage from deer populations is most prevalent.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Department of Natural Resources. The Governor is responsible for policy initiatives regarding environmental conservation and rural affairs mentioned in the bill's scope.

Synopsis: Authorizing a person to file a petition for expungement of a disposition under a certain provision of law if the disposition was included in a case that was disposed of by the court with a no finding designation or designated by the court as having been terminated without finding.

bill_summary: The bill expands eligibility for criminal record expungement under Section 10-110 of the Criminal Procedure Article. It allows individuals to file a petition for expungement if a charge for an eligible offense was disposed of by a court with a 'no finding' designation or was part of a case designated as having been 'terminated without finding.'
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals with criminal charges resulting in 'no finding' or 'terminated without finding' dispositions for eligible offenses, the Maryland Judiciary, and State's Attorneys.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $11,740 in fiscal 2027 only for the Judiciary to update expungement-related forms, brochures, and instructional materials. While the total number of eligible cases is unknown due to current case management terminology, the Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services may experience an operational impact from processing additional petitions. Local government finances and operations are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Judiciary is the primary agency responsible for processing expungement petitions and issuing court orders; the fiscal note explicitly details their costs for updating forms and brochures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency manages the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS), which serves as the central repository for Maryland criminal records and is responsible for processing all expungement orders.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent clients and frequently assists them in filing petitions for expungement to clear their records.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, it maintains police records that are subject to expungement under the bill's provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice policy and coordinates state strategies regarding public safety and record management.
The Archives is the central depository for permanent government records and must ensure that expunged records in its possession are removed from public inspection.
The MVA maintains records that may be impacted by expungement orders, particularly those related to offenses under the Transportation Article mentioned in the bill.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the management and security of transportation-related records subject to the bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation of expungement laws and represents the state in related legal proceedings.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the bill and coordinates relevant policy initiatives.

Synopsis: Repealing and establishing the methodology used to calculate the weekly benefit amount; altering the taxable wage base used to determine employer contributions to the Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund and the amount of earned wages subtracted from a weekly benefit amount; requiring the Maryland Department of Labor to determine and make available online the State annual average wage applicable to the rate of contribution; requiring, beginning in 2027, the maximum weekly benefit to be 40% of the state average weekly wage; etc.
Title: Unemployment Insurance Modernization Act of 2026
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/11 at 2:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Insurance -see also- Health Ins; MAIF; Motor Vehicle Ins

bill_summary: The Unemployment Insurance Modernization Act of 2026 updates the Maryland unemployment insurance system by replacing fixed dollar amounts for benefits and employer contributions with formulas tied to the State's average wages. It establishes a new methodology for calculating weekly benefit amounts, phases in a maximum weekly benefit of 40% of the State average weekly wage by 2027, and increases the employer taxable wage base to 16% of the State average annual wage by 2029. Additionally, it modifies the treatment of earned wages and dependent allowances for claimants.
stakeholders: Unemployed individuals in Maryland, Maryland employers, and the Maryland Department of Labor.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a significant increase in both revenues to the Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund (via an increased taxable wage base) and expenditures from the Fund (via increased weekly benefit amounts). The taxable wage base is shifted from a fixed $8,500 to 16% of the State average annual wage by 2029, and the maximum weekly benefit is phased into 40% of the State average weekly wage by 2027. Because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the source text, specific total dollar estimates for these revenue and expenditure changes are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for administering the Unemployment Insurance program. The bill requires the Department and the Secretary of Labor to establish new methodologies for benefit amounts, taxable wage bases, and state average wage calculations.

The bill explicitly states that compensation for serving as an election judge for a local board of elections may not be included when computing wages subtracted from unemployment benefits. The State Board of Elections oversees these local boards.

The bill alters the taxable wage base used to determine employer contributions to the Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund, which significantly impacts the cost of doing business and the economic climate in Maryland.

As the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for monitoring the fiscal impact on the state budget, including the state's own costs as an employer contributing to the Unemployment Insurance system.
The OAH adjudicates contested cases involving the Department of Labor, including unemployment insurance benefit disputes which may arise from the new methodologies established by this bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and would be involved in the drafting and legal review of regulations required by the bill to carry out the modernization of unemployment insurance.

The Treasurer's Office manages and protects state funds. While the Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund is separate, the Treasurer's role in state financial management and banking relates to the handling of large-scale state revenues and distributions.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives like unemployment insurance modernization, and the Governor proposes the annual state budget which is affected by these fiscal changes.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is concerned with the collection of state revenues and the overall fiscal health of Maryland funds, including those impacted by changes in employer contribution rates.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that beginning in the 2028-2029 school year, Maryland public middle schools must start instruction no earlier than 8:00 a.m. and public high schools no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The State Board of Education may grant waivers for compelling reasons, though a lack of funding is explicitly excluded as a valid reason. Additionally, local school boards and charter schools must conduct a public information campaign during the 2027-2028 school year to educate the community on the health and academic impacts of sleep deprivation and the benefits of later start times.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Education and local county boards of education
stakeholders: Middle and high school students, parents, teachers, school administrators, and local boards of education
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. At the local level, fiscal impacts vary significantly by jurisdiction; while some counties like Anne Arundel already comply and expect no impact, others face substantial costs primarily due to increased transportation needs. For example, Frederick County Public Schools estimates first-year costs exceeding $11,000,000 with annual recurring costs of $6,000,000 for additional buses, drivers, and maintenance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary state agency overseeing public and charter schools, MSDE and the State Board of Education are responsible for granting waivers for school start times and assisting local boards with required public information campaigns regarding sleep deprivation.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Board of Education and MSDE, particularly concerning the statutory requirements for school hours and the legal framework for granting or denying start-time waivers.
The shifting of instruction start times for middle and high schools impacts the deployment and coordination of school safety personnel and protocols, which are overseen by this agency.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; this bill involves a significant change in statewide education policy and student health initiatives.

bill_summary: This constitutional amendment requires all Maryland counties to transition to a charter home rule form of government by December 31, 2032. It mandates that each county charter provide for a county executive and a county council with members elected from councilmanic districts. The bill establishes a specific procedure for adoption, requiring boards of county commissioners to appoint charter boards by 2029 and vote on the resulting charters by 2032, while phasing out code home rule provisions once charters are adopted.
responsible_party: Maryland County Boards of Commissioners, Charter Boards, and the State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Residents and local government officials in Maryland counties currently operating under commission or code home rule systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text. Financial implications include costs to counties for appointing charter boards, administrative support for drafting charters, and mandatory newspaper publications. Additionally, the State Board of Elections will incur costs to include the amendment on the 2026 general election ballot, and affected counties will incur expenses to restructure their local governments into executive and council-based branches.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor has a constitutional role in receiving election returns for constitutional amendments, as specified in the bill, and the office manages intergovernmental relations with county executives and local entities.
As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG provides critical legal counsel on the constitutional amendment process and the legal framework for county home rule and legislative authority.

The agency provides technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments regarding administrative structures and land use planning, both of which are significantly affected by a transition to charter home rule.

The agency maintains the Maryland Manual On-Line, which is the official record of state and local government structures, and would be responsible for documenting these constitutional and structural changes.
The agency is responsible for supervising the statewide referendum for this constitutional amendment and overseeing the transition to councilmanic district-based voting required by the bill.
As the principal custodian of the state's official records, the Secretary of State manages the filing and certification of laws and constitutional amendments.

Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

bill_summary: This bill prohibits merchants from refusing cash payments or charging higher prices for cash transactions for 'essential consumer goods' (such as food, water, hygiene products, health products, and fuel) for in-person transactions totaling less than $300 between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. It establishes exceptions for transactions involving denominations over $20 or for merchants that provide free on-site cash-to-prepaid card conversion devices. Violations are designated as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices subject to specific civil penalties enforced after two opportunities for compliance.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
stakeholders: Retail merchants, small businesses, and Maryland consumers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's penalty provisions are not expected to have a material impact on State or local finances. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division can handle the bill's enforcement and administrative requirements with existing resources. Small businesses may experience a meaningful operational impact if they are currently cashless and must adapt to accept cash for essential goods. Civil penalties of up to $500 for initial noncompliance and $1,000 for subsequent violations are established, though no specific revenue estimate is provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Division of Consumer Protection within the Office of the Attorney General with enforcing the new regulations, providing merchants with opportunities to comply, and recovering civil penalties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note indicates that the bill will have a meaningful impact on small businesses, as those that currently operate on a cashless basis will be required to change their operational policies to accept cash for essential goods.

The Comptroller regulates the motor fuel industry. Since 'fuel' is specifically listed as an essential consumer good under the bill, the agency's regulated entities will be directly impacted by the cash acceptance mandate.

The bill defines 'food' (including human and animal food) as an essential consumer good. The Department of Agriculture provides leadership for the agricultural community and oversees food quality assurance and marketing.
As the state's primary economic development agency, Commerce is relevant due to the bill's impact on retail establishments and the broader business environment in Maryland.
The bill includes medicine and health products as essential consumer goods. The Department of Health regulates health care professionals and facilities, including those that may retail these items.
The Department of Labor is responsible for protecting consumers and regulating various industries and businesses in the state, which are the primary entities impacted by this retail mandate.

The team is tasked with addressing economic mobility and reducing child poverty. Ensuring that low-income or unbanked residents can purchase essential goods using cash is directly aligned with their mission of enhancing economic mobility.

Older adults are a demographic that may disproportionately rely on cash transactions. The department's mission to protect the rights and quality of life for seniors makes this consumer protection bill relevant to their advocacy work.
Residents with disabilities may face barriers to electronic banking or digital payments. This bill ensures they maintain access to essential goods through cash payments.
The department serves residents in economic need, who are more likely to be unbanked or underbanked and dependent on cash for essential purchases like food and hygiene products.

bill_summary: This bill exempts certain accredited religious educational institutions from the requirement to obtain a certificate of approval from the Maryland Higher Education Commission, provided they have been in continuous operation in Maryland since before January 1, 2013.
stakeholders: Accredited religious educational institutions and students pursuing religious vocations or purposes.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Higher Education Commission estimates that the bill will have no significant impact on its administrative operations, special fund revenues, or expenditures. Local governments are not affected, and there is no impact on small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency mentioned in the bill, MHEC is responsible for issuing Certificates of Approval (COA) and regulating postsecondary institutions. The bill directly alters MHEC's regulatory requirements by exempting certain accredited religious institutions from the COA process.

This agency is the central regulatory and coordinating board for all postsecondary education in Maryland. It is directly responsible for implementing and overseeing the changes to the Certificate of Approval process for religious educational institutions as mandated by the bill.

The OAG serves as the chief legal counsel for MHEC. They would be responsible for providing legal guidance on the implementation of the bill's exemptions and ensuring that the new regulations comply with state and federal law, including First Amendment considerations.

The MLDS Center links student data from partner agencies, including MHEC. Changes in which institutions are required to obtain approval or register with MHEC could affect the scope and consistency of student data collected and analyzed for state-wide reporting.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state and oversees MHEC's budget. While the fiscal note indicates a minimal impact, DBM is responsible for monitoring changes in the special fund revenues and expenditures related to institutional application and renewal fees.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. Since the bill modifies the regulatory authority of an executive commission (MHEC) and relates to educational policy, it falls under the administrative oversight of the Governor.

Synopsis: Requiring a unit of State government to provide a certain debriefing of a contract award to certain persons on request; adding an exemption to the prohibition on an individual who assists in the drafting of specifications, an invitation for bids, or a request for proposals from submitting a bid or proposal or assisting in the submission of a bid or proposal; requiring a procurement contract to include a certain clause pertaining to certain contract modifications related to changes in State law; etc.

Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill updates Maryland's State procurement laws to improve transparency and streamline procedures. Key changes include requiring debriefings for unsuccessful offerors upon request, establishing a conflict-of-interest exception for providing information that does not create an unfair competitive advantage, and requiring contract clauses that allow for equitable adjustments when performance costs rise due to changes in State law. It also synchronizes and clarifies the timelines and processes for bid protests and contract claims across construction and non-construction contracts.
responsible_party: Office of State Procurement (within the Department of General Services) and State procurement units.
stakeholders: State agencies, prime contractors, subcontractors, and unsuccessful bidders or offerors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's implementation is expected to be handled with existing State resources, and no direct impact on revenues is anticipated. However, the Fiscal Note suggests that changes to procurement ethics could lead to an increase in bid protests, which may cause project delays and indeterminate cost overruns. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Office of State Procurement, which is housed within the Department of General Services, with establishing guidelines and procedures for contract debriefings. As the central procurement authority, DGS is the primary agency responsible for implementing these procedural changes.

The bill requires that contract debriefings occur before recommended awards are presented to the Board for approval. The Board also oversees the fiscal integrity of procurement contracts and modifications affected by the bill's provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly alters the timelines, procedures, and final actions related to bid protests and contract claims, which are the primary matters adjudicated by this board. Changes to appeal rights directly impact the board's caseload and operations.

The bill mandates that procurement officers seek legal advice from the Office of the Attorney General on all legal issues raised in protests and contract claims, increasing the agency's mandatory consultative workload.

As a major multi-modal procurement unit responsible for massive infrastructure and service contracts, MDOT is heavily impacted by changes to construction claim procedures being extended to all contracts and new debriefing requirements.

The Department of Health conducts significant procurement for services and facilities and is specifically identified as an impacted agency in the fiscal analysis regarding changes to protest and claim procedures.
The bill includes specific provisions related to nonvisual access clauses for information technology and impacts DoIT's role in coordinating statewide IT procurement strategy and contracts.
As a major public entity with significant procurement activity, USM is subject to the changes in state procurement law and is specifically noted as an impacted agency in the fiscal note.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM oversees budget execution and state agency efficiency, which are impacted by changes in procurement timelines and the potential for cost overruns from contract delays.
The Comptroller serves on the Board of Public Works, which must approve the contracts and modifications subject to the bill's new transparency and procedural rules.
The State Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works and oversees state funds used in the procurement contracts affected by these procedural changes.

OLA is responsible for auditing state agency compliance with laws; it will be tasked with ensuring agencies adhere to the new transparency, debriefing, and certification requirements in the procurement process.

The Governor oversees the executive branch units implementing these changes and is the final approval authority for the bill; the Office of State Procurement is within the Executive Department's administrative scope.

In consultation with the Maryland Department of Labor, the program provides incarcerated individuals at the Baltimore City Correctional Center with the opportunity to serve as paid apprentices in state or local government agencies or with private entities. The program focuses on skilled trades to help participants develop marketable job skills and earn money prior to their release. The pilot program is established as a three-year initiative.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to conduct studies on the use of emerging technologies—such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and biometrics—to improve the safety and transparency of Maryland's gambling environment. bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of 'baby food' to include infant cereal, making it subject to existing toxic element testing and labeling requirements. Manufacturers must test representative samples of their products monthly for toxic elements—specifically arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury—and make the results publicly available on their websites without requiring purchase verification. The bill also mandates that baby food labels include QR codes for accessing test results, requires specific disclosures for online sales, and requires manufacturers to retain certificates of analysis for at least five years.
stakeholders: Manufacturers of baby food and infant cereal, the Maryland Department of Health, and consumers with children under the age of two.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. The bill is not expected to affect state revenues or have a material impact on local government finances. The financial impact on small businesses is anticipated to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Health - General article and tasks the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) with receiving baby food test results and managing consumer reports of non-compliance. MDH's Center for Food Processing is the primary entity responsible for licensing and inspecting food facilities to ensure compliance with these new testing and labeling requirements.

OLA conducts fiscal and compliance audits of executive branch agencies. They would be responsible for auditing the Department of Health to ensure the agency is properly executing and enforcing the baby food safety and labeling mandates established by this bill.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state. While the fiscal note suggests the impact can be handled with existing resources, DBM oversees the allocation of these resources and the long-term fiscal planning for the Department of Health as it takes on additional oversight duties.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the enforcement of state laws. This bill expands the regulatory authority of the Department of Health, an executive agency, regarding public health and food safety standards.

The bill imposes new testing and labeling costs and administrative burdens on baby food manufacturers and processors operating within the state, which is a matter of interest to the Department of Commerce as the state's economic development and business advocacy agency.

bill_summary: The Comprehensive Community Safety Funding Act establishes an 11% excise tax on the gross receipts of federally licensed firearms dealers derived from the retail sale of firearms, firearm accessories, and ammunition. The tax applies to sales made in Maryland and to sales made to Maryland residents by out-of-state dealers who meet certain revenue or transaction thresholds. Collected revenues are designated for distribution to several state funds focused on violence prevention, trauma services, and victim support.
stakeholders: Federally licensed firearms dealers, Maryland residents purchasing firearms or ammunition, victims of homicide and their survivors, and public health and safety organizations focused on trauma and violence prevention.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a new state revenue source via an 11% excise tax on the gross receipts from sales of firearms and ammunition. Revenue is distributed as follows: 26% to the Maryland Violence Intervention and Prevention Program Fund, 26% to the Center for Firearm Violence Prevention and Intervention, 20% to the Coordinated Community Supports Partnership Fund, 20% to the Survivors of Homicide Victims Grant Program, 4% to the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, and 4% to the R Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center. Implementation is phased, beginning with large retailers on July 1, 2027, and extending to all other dealers on July 1, 2028. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for administering, collecting, and distributing the new firearm, firearm accessory, and ammunition excise tax. This includes managing tax returns, performing audits, and overseeing the administrative cost account for the tax.

The bill distributes 26% of the new tax revenue to the Center for Firearm Violence Prevention and Intervention within the Department of Health and 4% to the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, which the Department oversees.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is a major beneficiary of the tax revenue, receiving 26% for the Maryland Violence Intervention and Prevention Program Fund and 20% for the Survivors of Homicide Victims Grant Program.

The bill distributes 20% of the net excise tax revenue to the Coordinated Community Supports Partnership Fund, which is managed under the Education Article and overseen by the Department of Education.
The Tax Court will have jurisdiction over appeals related to the final determinations made by the Comptroller regarding assessments, revisions, or refunds of the new firearm excise tax.
As the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office is responsible for the custody, investment, and management of the various state funds receiving distributions from the new excise tax.

DBM is responsible for estimating revenues and overseeing the execution of the state budget; the creation of a new excise tax and multiple dedicated funds has significant fiscal planning and personnel implications for the state.
MHCC is the regulatory body within the Department of Health that administers the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, which receives a 4% distribution of the excise tax revenue under this bill.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Comptroller regarding the implementation and enforcement of the new tax and represent the state in any litigation or appeals resulting from tax assessments.

The bill defines firearms and dealers by reference to the Public Safety Article, which MSP regulates. Additionally, sales to law enforcement agencies and officers are specifically exempted from the excise tax.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties (misdemeanors and perjury) for willful failure to file returns or filing false returns, which will be adjudicated within the state's court system.
OLA will be responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of the Comptroller’s administration and the various funds receiving the new tax revenue.

As the executive authority overseeing GOCPP and the state budget, the Governor's Office is responsible for the high-level policy coordination and the proposed annual budget impacted by these new revenue streams.
DoIT may be required to support the Comptroller's office in upgrading or creating IT infrastructure and secure data systems to handle the registration and processing of the new excise tax returns.
The Maryland National Guard is explicitly listed as an entity exempt from the 11% excise tax on the purchase of firearms, accessories, and ammunition.
