bill_summary: This bill establishes the Purple Star Colleges Program to recognize institutions of higher education and private career schools that provide support and services for military-connected students. It also modifies the definition of 'military-connected student' for the existing Purple Star Schools Program to align with state law, specifically including dependents of service members killed in the line of duty.
stakeholders: Military-connected students (service members, veterans, spouses, and dependents), public and private institutions of higher education, and private career schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Maryland Higher Education Commission increase by $43,800 in FY 2027 and $46,400 in FY 2028 to hire a contractual half-time program manager to establish program criteria and regulations. Participation by public four-year institutions, community colleges, and private career schools is voluntary; while seeking the designation may increase their operational expenditures, these costs are expected to be absorbable. The Maryland State Department of Education can update regulations for the existing Purple Star Schools Program using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Higher Education Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering the new Purple Star Colleges Program, including establishing criteria for designation, reviewing applications, and adopting regulations.
The bill amends the definition of 'military-connected student' for the existing Purple Star Schools Program, which is overseen and managed by the Maryland State Department of Education.

The program directly serves and recognizes institutions that support veterans, service members, and their dependents, which aligns with this agency's mission to assist Maryland's military-connected families in securing services.
As the state's primary public higher education system, its constituent institutions are eligible to apply for and benefit from the Purple Star College designation established by this bill.
As an independent public university, Morgan State University is eligible to seek designation under the Purple Star Colleges Program to support its military-connected students.
As Maryland's public honors college, it is eligible to participate in the program and seek recognition for its services to military-connected students.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Maryland Higher Education Commission to consult with the Maryland College Collaboration for Student Veterans Commission—a body that falls under this category—to develop program criteria and regulations.

The fiscal note indicates a need for general fund expenditures to hire contractual personnel at the Maryland Higher Education Commission to manage the new program, which requires DBM's fiscal oversight.

The Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives and oversees the executive branch; this bill creates a new executive program and requires regulatory adoption that aligns with state policy priorities regarding veterans.

Synopsis: Requiring certain hospitals licensed in the State to comply with certain staffing standards to establish and maintain a clinical staffing committee and to implement a clinical staffing plan; requiring each staffing committee to develop a staffing plan; requiring the chief nursing executive of each hospital to produce a draft clinical staffing plan and submit it to the clinical staffing committee of the hospital; requiring, beginning in 2028, by July 1 each year, each hospital to implement a clinical staffing plan; etc.
Title: Hospitals - Clinical Staffing Committees and Plans - Establishment (Safe Staffing Act of 2026)
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

bill_summary: The Safe Staffing Act of 2026 requires licensed hospitals in Maryland (excluding state-run facilities) to establish clinical staffing committees and implement annual clinical staffing plans. These plans must be developed by the hospital's chief nurse executive and finalized by a committee consisting of both managers and employees, taking into account patient acuity, staff skill mix, and federal staffing standards.
responsible_party: Licensed hospitals and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Hospital clinical staff (including nurses, certified nursing assistants, and technicians), hospital administrators, and hospital patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates that the bill does not directly affect state or local governmental operations or finances. While the bill requires hospitals to establish committees and implement staffing plans, it is expected to have no direct state expenditure or revenue impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new part to the Health - General Article, which falls under the regulatory purview of the Maryland Department of Health. As the agency responsible for licensing hospitals and health care facilities in the State, MDH (specifically the Office of Health Care Quality) oversees compliance with health care standards and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation referenced in the bill.

The HSCRC is an independent agency within MDH that regulates hospital rates and revenues. Mandatory clinical staffing plans and committees will directly impact hospital labor costs and operational expenses, which are critical factors in the Commission's 'all-payer' rate-setting system and cost-containment efforts.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving the quality of care. Staffing levels are a key metric in assessing hospital performance and quality, making this legislation relevant to their mission of increasing accountability and informing public health policy.

The bill focuses on workforce management within hospitals, including the creation of committees comprised of employees (nurses, aides, technicians). This intersects with the Department of Labor's role in protecting workers and overseeing workplace safety and labor-related standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees the state's emergency medical services and trauma systems. Clinical staffing levels in hospitals significantly impact hospital capacity and the ability to accept emergency patients, which directly affects ambulance 'wall time' and overall EMS system efficiency.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and other executive agencies. They would be responsible for advising on the implementation of these new statutory requirements and representing the State in any enforcement actions or legal challenges related to the new staffing regulations.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates health policy initiatives. The bill requires the Governor's final approval and aligns with broad executive branch goals regarding public health safety and healthcare workforce standards.

Synopsis: Requiring research facilities that are located in the State and required to submit an Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service Form 7023 to pay contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund to the Department of Agriculture, rather than the Maryland Department of Health; and establishing that a research facility that fails to pay the contribution required by the Act may be subject to a civil penalty of not more than $1,000 per day.
Title: Human-Relevant Research Fund - Collection of Contributions - Responsible Entity
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Agriculture -see also- Agritourism; Cannabis Prd; Farm; etc.

Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

Scientific Research -see also- ChemTst; MedRsrch; Studies

bill_summary: This bill transfers the responsibility for collecting annual contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund from the Maryland Department of Health to the Maryland Department of Agriculture. Research facilities in the state that are required to submit a federal Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Form 7023 must pay these contributions based on the number of animals used in research. The collected funds are distributed to the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to provide grants and loans for research into human-relevant alternatives to animal testing.
stakeholders: Research facilities using animals for testing in Maryland, including public and private higher education institutions, the Maryland Department of Agriculture, and the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO).
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures for the Maryland Department of Agriculture increase by $42,900 in FY 2027 (growing to $54,200 by FY 2031) to hire a half-time administrative officer for collection and compliance tracking. Special fund revenues for the Human-Relevant Research Fund (HRRF) administered by TEDCO will continue and may increase if collection efforts under the Department of Agriculture are more successful than previous efforts. While total potential annual revenue was previously estimated at $915,000, only $185,000 has been collected to date.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transfers the responsibility for collecting annual contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund from the Department of Health to the Department of Agriculture. The agency will require additional staff to manage collection and tracking compliance.

TEDCO administers the Human-Relevant Research Fund (HRRF). The bill changes the entity that collects and distributes the funds into the HRRF, which may impact the efficiency and volume of revenue received for the fund's grants and loans.
The bill repeals the Department of Health's authority and responsibility to collect contributions from research facilities for the Human-Relevant Research Fund.

Several public senior institutions of higher education within the University System of Maryland are research facilities subject to the animal research contribution requirements and may also be eligible for grants from the HRRF.
As a public research university, Morgan State may be among the institutions required to pay the research facility contribution or may apply for research funding through the HRRF.
The fiscal note indicates a need for a new half-time position at the Department of Agriculture to implement the bill, which falls under DBM's oversight of personnel and state expenditures.
The bill maintains civil penalties for research facilities that fail to pay the required contribution, which may result in litigation or administrative actions within the judicial system.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the agencies involved (MDA, MDH, and TEDCO) regarding the transfer of statutory duties and the enforcement of civil penalties.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is involved in the oversight of state revenue collection and the distribution of funds into special accounts like the HRRF.
The Treasurer's Office manages state funds and special fund accounts. The HRRF is a special, nonlapsing fund that receives the contributions collected under this bill.
As an independent public honors college, it may be subject to the contribution requirements if it operates a research facility submitting APHIS Form 7023, or it may apply for HRRF grants.

Synopsis: Establishing a certain rebuttable presumption that a statement made by a minor during a custodial interrogation is involuntary and is inadmissible in a juvenile or criminal proceeding against the minor if the law enforcement officer intentionally used information known by the officer to be false in order to elicit the statement.
Title: Custodial Interrogation of Minors - Admissibility of Statements (Exonerated 5 Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth

bill_summary: This bill, known as the Exonerated 5 Act, establishes a rebuttable presumption that a statement made by a minor during a custodial interrogation is involuntary and inadmissible in juvenile or criminal proceedings if a law enforcement officer intentionally used information known to be false to elicit the statement. This presumption may only be overcome by clear and convincing evidence that the statement was voluntary and not made in response to the false information.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and State and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Minors, law enforcement officers, State's Attorneys, defense attorneys, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the bill text. No specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are identified; however, the bill may result in an increase in the number of suppression hearings and associated legal costs for the State and local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary law enforcement agency for the state, the Maryland State Police are directly impacted by this bill, which changes the rules for conducting custodial interrogations of minors and the admissibility of resulting statements in court.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Office of the Public Defender represents indigent minors in juvenile and criminal proceedings. This bill establishes a new rebuttable presumption that benefits their clients and provides a significant legal tool for defense in custodial interrogation cases.

The Administrative Office of the Courts must ensure that the Maryland Judicial Branch is prepared to apply this new evidentiary standard in juvenile and criminal proceedings, potentially impacting court procedures and hearing lengths regarding the admissibility of statements.

The Department of Juvenile Services is responsible for youth in the juvenile justice system. The bill's changes to the admissibility of statements in juvenile proceedings directly affect the legal outcomes and rehabilitative pathways for the youth under their supervision.

The Office of the Attorney General represents the state in criminal appeals. This bill creates a new legal standard for the admissibility of statements that will likely be the subject of future litigation and appeals that the OAG must handle.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and manages public safety funds. This legislation, known as the Exonerated 5 Act, represents a significant shift in public safety policy regarding the treatment of minors in the justice system.

MCSS oversees school safety personnel and certification. To the extent that school resource officers or other law enforcement personnel under their purview conduct custodial interrogations of minors on school grounds, this law would apply to their conduct.

MDOT oversees the Maryland Transportation Authority Police and the Maryland Transit Administration Police. These law enforcement officers must comply with the bill's requirements during custodial interrogations of minors.

The Department of Natural Resources includes the Natural Resources Police, who are state law enforcement officers capable of conducting custodial interrogations that would be subject to the bill's provisions.
DGS manages the Maryland Capitol Police. These officers must adhere to the bill's standards regarding the use of false information during the interrogation of minors.

The University System of Maryland institutions maintain campus police forces. Officers in these departments would be subject to the new standards when interrogating minors involved in incidents on campus property.
As a state agency with its own police force, Morgan State University's law enforcement officers are impacted by the changes to interrogation protocols and evidence admissibility for minors.
St. Mary's College of Maryland maintains a campus security and/or law enforcement presence that must comply with the bill's regulations concerning custodial interrogations of minors.

Synopsis: Establishing the Commission on Historic, Cultural, and Civic Contributions in Education to study and make recommendations to the State Board of Education and the Maryland Higher Education Commission about certain lessons currently taught in public schools; requiring the Commission to study school calendars and make recommendations to the State Board and the General Assembly; and requiring the State Board to identify existing courses and materials to be updated into professional development courses under certain circumstances.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on Historic, Cultural, and Civic Contributions in Education to evaluate and improve the inclusion of diverse histories and cultures in Maryland's K-12 education system. The commission is responsible for studying current curriculum standards, instructional materials, and school calendars to ensure they accurately reflect the contributions and experiences of diverse groups, including Indigenous, African American, LGBTQ+, and disabled communities. It requires recommendations to be made to the State Board of Education for curriculum updates and to the Maryland Higher Education Commission for teacher training improvements.
stakeholders: Maryland public school students, K-12 educators, institutions of higher education, and members of diverse racial, ethnic, cultural, and social communities.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures will increase by $56,400 in fiscal year 2027 to cover the costs of a half-time education program specialist at the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to staff the commission. Projected costs increase annually, reaching $73,300 by fiscal year 2031. Local school systems may incur indeterminate costs related to future curriculum updates or professional development based on the commission's recommendations, although these are expected to align with existing curriculum review cycles.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It is required to provide staffing for the new Commission, and the State Board of Education (within MSDE) must review the Commission's recommendations and update Pre-K through Grade 12 educational standards accordingly.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's primary purpose is to establish the Commission on Historic, Cultural, and Civic Contributions in Education, which fits the definition of an executive commission created to address specific government policy issues.

The Commission is mandated to make recommendations to the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) regarding updates to teacher preparation programs to include instruction on the history of diverse people.
The Secretary of Disabilities is responsible for recommending a member to represent the state's disabled community on the Commission.
The Chancellor of the University System of Maryland is required to nominate/select a representative from a USM institution to serve on the Commission.

The bill requires a representative on the Commission from a Historically Black College or University (HBCU) that is a separate entity from the University System of Maryland; Morgan State University is the state's independent public HBCU.
The fiscal note indicates a general fund expenditure increase of $56,400 in FY 2027 to cover staffing and operational costs for the Commission, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget.

The Commission is required to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor annually, and the Governor may still have appointment roles or administrative oversight over the reporting process.
The bill (in its original form and through the involvement of the Commission on Indian Affairs) references cultural and ethnic commissions managed under GOCI for nominating members to the Commission.

As the legal representative for all state agencies, the OAG may be required to provide counsel to MSDE and the State Board regarding the implementation of new educational standards and the Commission's regulatory compliance.

Synopsis: Establishing the Foster Care Transition Grant Program in the Department of Human Services to provide for the economic security of individuals aging out of the out-of-home placement program; providing that, beginning in fiscal year 2028, an individual can become eligible for a foster care transition grant of $1,000 for 1 year under certain circumstances; providing that payments made under the Program may not be considered income or resources for purposes of determining eligibility for certain benefits; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Foster Care Transition Grant Program within the Maryland Department of Human Services to provide economic security for individuals aging out of foster care. Beginning in fiscal year 2028, the program provides eligible individuals with a $1,000 monthly grant for one year. To qualify, an individual must have been in an out-of-home placement on their 18th birthday and have turned 18 on or after October 1, 2026. The bill also mandates annual reporting on recipient demographics and outcomes.
stakeholders: Individuals aging out of the Maryland foster care system (out-of-home placement) who reach age 18 on or after October 1, 2026.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures increase by $479,500 in FY 2027 for contractual staff and one-time information technology costs. Expenditures peak at $4,077,900 in FY 2028 as grant payments begin and are estimated at approximately $3,170,000 annually for FY 2029 through FY 2031. The program and its associated costs terminate on September 30, 2031. There is no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Foster Care Transition Grant Program within this department. DHS is responsible for implementing the program, determining eligibility, issuing the $1,000 monthly grants, and submitting annual outcome reports to the General Assembly.

The fiscal note explicitly states that DoIT will incur $378,000 in one-time programming costs in FY 2027 to update and maintain the Enrollment and Eligibility System (E&E) for managing the distribution of funds, plus annual maintenance costs thereafter.

The bill specifies that grants issued under the program may not be considered income for determining eligibility for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is administered by the Department of Health.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM will oversee the significant general fund expenditure increases (estimated at over $3 million annually) required for the grants and contractual staff, and manage the associated budget execution.
The bill mandates that program grants are not considered income for State and federal financial aid and college support programs, which MHEC administers and coordinates.
The bill provides that the grants may not be considered income for purposes of the Maryland Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), which the Comptroller's office manages and administers.

MHBE is responsible for determining eligibility for Medicaid and financial assistance; the bill's requirement to exclude the grant from income calculations directly impacts their eligibility determination processes.

The program directly aligns with GOC's mission to reduce child poverty and improve access to economic opportunities for vulnerable youth, specifically those transitioning out of the foster care system.

The team is specifically charged with identifying and piloting initiatives to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility; this grant program serves as a direct policy tool for these objectives.

The bill requires annual reporting on outcome measures such as employment and housing status; GOPI utilizes such data-driven metrics to oversee the implementation of the Governor's priorities and ensure government responsiveness.

OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like DHS and MDH. They may be required to review the bill's income exclusion provisions against federal law, a potential conflict noted in the fiscal note.
OLA will likely conduct fiscal compliance audits of the new program within DHS to ensure the appropriate distribution of millions in state general funds.
The center links student and workforce data; they may assist in analyzing the long-term effectiveness of the grant program on the employment and educational outcomes of foster care transition youth.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and DHS. The Governor is responsible for proposing the budget that will fund this multi-million dollar program.
As the provider of higher education for many transition-age youth, the system is impacted by how these grants are treated in financial aid calculations for its students.
MSU, as a public university, will be affected by changes in how state financial aid and college support programs are calculated for students receiving these transition grants.
As a public honors college, it is impacted by the bill's provisions regarding the exclusion of transition grants from financial aid eligibility assessments for its students.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Energy Administration to conduct a study on the potential for land-based wind energy generation in the State and the siting of land-based wind energy generating systems in the State; authorizing the Administration to use available funds in the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund to conduct the study; and requiring by December 1, 2026, the Administration to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor and certain committees of the General Assembly.
Title: Maryland Energy Administration - Study on Land-Based Wind Energy
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Energy Administration to conduct a study on land-based wind energy generation in Maryland. The study must evaluate the total potential for land-based wind energy, identify potential locations, and investigate mitigation strategies that allow wind energy systems to operate alongside military radar technologies. The Administration is authorized to use the Strategic Energy Investment Fund for this study and must report its findings to the Governor and General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Maryland Energy Administration, land-based wind energy developers, military installations using radar technology, and Maryland state legislators
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill authorizes the Maryland Energy Administration to use existing money within the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to cover the costs of the study.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MEA is the primary agency responsible for conducting the study on land-based wind energy, assessing potential siting, and reporting findings to the Governor and General Assembly.

The bill specifically requires the study to investigate mitigation efforts for military radar technologies, such as ADAMS, which directly involves the military readiness and operations overseen by the Adjutant General.
The PSC is the regulatory body for utility-scale energy generation and siting in Maryland; the results of this study will directly impact the planning and regulation of future wind energy projects.
Land-based wind siting significantly impacts natural resources, wildlife habitats, and state-owned lands, which are managed and protected by DNR.
MDP is responsible for land use planning and providing technical assistance for infrastructure development, making them a key stakeholder in the siting and potential assessment of wind energy.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including MEA, and is the recipient of the mandated report and recommendations.
The bill authorizes the use of funds from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) to conduct the study, requiring fiscal oversight by DBM regarding budget execution and personnel.
The assessment of wind energy potential has significant implications for economic development, job creation, and attracting green industry businesses to Maryland.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MEA and would likely assist in interpreting the statutory requirements for the study and any regulatory implications.
MDE is the lead agency for renewable energy goals and environmental protection, making the study's findings on sustainable energy generation highly relevant to their mission.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from operating an immigration detention facility at a building, structure, or facility that was not originally designed and constructed for the purpose of housing or detaining individuals.

bill_summary: This emergency bill prohibits any person from operating an immigration detention facility in a building, structure, or facility that was not originally designed and constructed specifically for the purpose of housing or detaining individuals.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals detained for federal civil immigration violations, private entities or persons operating detention facilities, and State and local government units.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing the state's correctional facilities and being governed by the Correctional Services Article, which this bill amends, DPSCS is directly impacted by changes to laws regulating detention facilities.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies on the interpretation and enforcement of this new prohibition on immigration detention facility operations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, directly advising the Governor on policies related to detention and law enforcement standards.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for enforcing state laws. This bill impacts executive policy regarding intergovernmental agreements and the use of facilities for detention.

DGS manages state-owned facilities, real estate leasing, and construction. They are relevant because the bill establishes specific requirements for the 'original design and construction' of buildings used for detention.

The Board approves significant state expenditures, including the acquisition, lease, and transfer of state property, which would be subject to the restrictions on facility use for immigration detention.

DJS operates secure residential and detention facilities. While focused on youth, shifts in the legal standards for detention facilities within the Correctional Services Article are relevant to their operational oversight.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP may be involved in the enforcement of state laws or coordination with local agencies regarding the legal operation of detention facilities.

MCCR enforces anti-discrimination laws and monitors state contracts. Immigration detention facilities often involve civil rights considerations that fall under their monitoring and educational mandate.

bill_summary: This bill reclassifies the crime of knowingly making a threat against a State official, local official, State's Attorney, or Public Defender from a misdemeanor to a felony. It also increases the maximum penalties for this offense from three years imprisonment and a $2,500 fine to 10 years imprisonment and a $5,000 fine.

stakeholders: State and local officials (including the Governor, General Assembly members, and judges), State's Attorneys, Public Defenders, and individuals charged with making threats against these officials.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances. Reclassifying the offense from a misdemeanor to a felony will likely shift cases from the District Court to the circuit courts and may lead to longer sentences for some offenders. The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services reported minimal activity for this specific offense in fiscal 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor and Governor-elect are explicitly listed in the bill as State officials protected by increased criminal penalties for threats.
The Lieutenant Governor and Lieutenant Governor-elect are explicitly listed in the bill as State officials protected by increased criminal penalties for threats.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly includes assistant Public Defenders as protected parties under the reclassified felony prohibition against threats.

bill_summary: This bill exempts psychiatric health care facilities and psychiatric or mental health services from the requirement to obtain a Certificate of Need (CON) before being established, operated, or expanded. fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text; therefore, specific dollar estimates are unavailable. However, the bill eliminates the Certificate of Need requirement for psychiatric services, which typically involves administrative review and application fees, potentially reducing fee revenue for the state and decreasing administrative expenditures for the Maryland Health Care Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Health Care Commission is the primary agency responsible for planning for the state's health system needs and administering the Certificate of Need (CON) process. This bill directly removes psychiatric facilities and mental health services from their regulatory oversight via the CON process.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) oversees behavioral health services and the state's Medicaid program. Altering the requirements for establishing psychiatric facilities impacts MDH's health policy, equitable access to care, and the regulatory environment for health care professionals and facilities.

As the independent agency regulating hospital rates and revenues, the HSCRC is impacted because any increase in psychiatric bed capacity or the establishment of new psychiatric health care facilities affects hospital cost growth and the state's 'all-payer' hospital financing system.

The Governor's Office oversees health policy initiatives and coordinates the executive branch. This bill represents a significant shift in health care regulation and the state's approach to mental health infrastructure, which are key policy priorities.

DBM is responsible for fiscal planning and estimating revenues. Deregulating psychiatric facility establishment could lead to increased facility capacity, potentially impacting state expenditures for Medicaid and other behavioral health funding streams.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Department of Health and its commissions. They would be responsible for advising on the legal implementation of this exemption and representing the state in any related litigation regarding the certificate of need process.

The Lieutenant Governor chairs advisory councils related to mental health and coordinates specific policy initiatives delegated by the Governor, making changes to psychiatric facility regulation relevant to their portfolio.

As the agency responsible for attracting new businesses and stimulating the economy, removing regulatory barriers (CON) for psychiatric facilities may incentivize private healthcare investment and facility expansion in Maryland.

DHS assists vulnerable populations, including those in foster care or requiring protection from neglect, who frequently require access to the psychiatric and mental health services affected by this bill.

DJS is responsible for treating youth in the juvenile justice system. The availability of psychiatric health care facilities is critical for the rehabilitation and placement of youth requiring mental health treatment.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees the rehabilitation and health of justice-involved individuals. The expansion of psychiatric services and facilities impacts the landscape of treatment options for individuals in or transitioning from state correctional facilities.

The department advocates for veterans' benefits, including health care. Changes that increase the supply of psychiatric facilities directly impact the resources available to veterans and their families in Maryland.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS coordinates the statewide emergency medical services network. The establishment of new psychiatric facilities would impact EMS routing, prehospital care coordination, and the designation of specialty referral centers for psychiatric crises.

The department works to improve service delivery for residents with disabilities, including those with psychiatric disabilities. The bill's impact on facility availability is highly relevant to their mission of community living and integrated services.

OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including appeals of Certificate of Need decisions. Removing the CON requirement for psychiatric facilities would reduce the future volume of such administrative disputes handled by the agency.

The Maryland Department of Health oversees public health policy and the Medicaid program. While the mandate primarily affects private insurance, the department maintains a significant interest in cancer prevention strategies and health equity.

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to increase the mandatory retirement age for Maryland judges from 70 to 73. The bill includes transition provisions whereby judges currently in office as of November 3, 2026, generally remain subject to the age 70 retirement limit, while the new age 73 limit applies to those appointed or elected thereafter.
responsible_party: Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts) and State Retirement Agency
stakeholders: Maryland State judges, Maryland voters, and the State Retirement and Pension System
fiscal_impact_summary: If approved by voters, the amendment is projected to reduce State pension liabilities by $21,700,000 and reduce normal costs by $1,500,000. There is no estimated impact on local finances or small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The AOC provides operational, legal, and financial support to the Maryland Judicial Branch. The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting candidates for judicial vacancies. Altering the mandatory retirement age changes the frequency and timing of these vacancies.

The Treasurer oversees state funds and pension investments, and holds a key position on the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System, which includes the Judges' Retirement System affected by this bill.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the state and its agencies, including the Judiciary and the Governor. They would provide legal counsel regarding the implementation and interpretation of this constitutional change.

The Department's representation on the Oversight Committee on Quality of Care in Nursing Homes and the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee is affected by the bill's membership revisions.

The bill significantly alters reporting requirements for specialized intervention services, shifting focus to grade 3 literacy proficiency, and removes MSDE representation from the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee.
The Department chairs the Maryland Green Purchasing Committee, which sees membership changes under the bill, and remains a member of the Customer Council.

The bill repeals several of the Department's reporting mandates (e.g., Hepatitis B and C, cancer registry) and alters its representation on various boards, such as the Oversight Committee on Quality of Care in Nursing Homes and the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board.
The bill modifies the Interagency Council on Homelessness, making the Secretary the permanent chair and authorizing compensation for members with lived experience of homelessness.
The bill repeals the Two-Generation Family Economic Security Commission and the Commission on Trauma-Informed Care, both of which were units within the Department.
The Department's Secretary is a member of the Maryland Green Purchasing Committee, which undergoes composition changes.

The bill repeals a reporting requirement for the Department regarding voter registration efforts at one-stop career centers and maintains its representation on the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board.
The bill repeals the Department's requirement to report on nutria eradication and modifies its reporting on State park maintenance projects.
The Department's representation on the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee is updated by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the Criminal Justice Information Advisory Board, which provides advice to the Secretary, and modifies the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board membership.
The bill modifies the membership of the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee, which provides guidance to MDOT and other agencies.
The bill repeals several working groups within the Environment Article and alters the membership of the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly repeals or modifies the membership, reporting, and operational mandates of numerous executive-branch commissions and task forces.
The bill is a departmental initiative to streamline executive branch efficiency and affects various boards and commissions appointed by the Governor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency houses the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board, which is modified by the bill, and its Executive Director serves on the Cannabis Public Health Advisory Council.
The bill is linked to the Government Modernization Initiative, which is coordinated by GOPI to enhance government efficiency.
The Board is consulted by the Maryland Department of Health to identify health care workforce shortage areas for preceptor tax credit eligibility.
The Commission is represented on the Customer Council, which undergoes membership changes under the bill.
The Administration's Director is a member of the Cannabis Public Health Advisory Council, which is modified by the bill.
The Director was a member of the now-repealed Renewable Fuels Incentive Board, with duties transferred to the Department of Agriculture.
The bill requires the Commission to collaborate with the Office of Minority Health and Health Disparities on the 'Health Care Disparities Policy Report Card'.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Defender is a member of the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board and was a member of the now-repealed Alternative Response Advisory Council.
The agency is impacted by the repeal of the Criminal Justice Information Advisory Board and changes to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Maryland Green Purchasing Committee, which is modified by the bill.
The MVA Administrator is a member of the Cannabis Public Health Advisory Council, which has its membership composition revised.
The Attorney General is a member of the Justice Reinvestment Oversight Board, which undergoes membership changes.
The Chancellor of the USM is a member of the Maryland Green Purchasing Committee, which undergoes membership revisions.

Synopsis: Establishing the Curbside Voting Pilot Program to test the viability of curbside voting in the State; establishing requirements governing curbside voting; and requiring the State Board to report to the General Assembly on the implementation of the Pilot Program by September 1, 2031.
Title: Election Law - Curbside Voting - Pilot Program
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/18 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: House Bill 641 establishes the Curbside Voting Pilot Program to test the viability of curbside voting in Maryland. The State Board of Elections is required to select three counties (representing small, medium, and large voter populations) to implement the program, allowing registered voters to cast paper ballots or use ballot marking devices outside designated early voting and election day polling locations. The State Board must adopt regulations for the program and submit a report on its implementation to the General Assembly by September 2031.
responsible_party: The Maryland State Board of Elections and local boards of elections in designated pilot counties
stakeholders: Registered voters in the three selected pilot counties, the Maryland State Board of Elections, and local election boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a state and local mandate to implement and administer a curbside voting pilot program in three counties. Expenditures will increase for the State Board of Elections and the affected local boards to cover the costs of ballot marking devices, signage, training for election judges, and the preparation of a formal implementation report. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for implementing, administering, and regulating the Curbside Voting Pilot Program, including designating participating counties, certifying voting systems, and reporting findings to the General Assembly.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal counsel for the State Board of Elections and will be responsible for advising on the implementation of the pilot program and the drafting of new election regulations.

As the agency responsible for coordinating services for individuals with disabilities, it is relevant to the bill's focus on ballot accessibility, voter assistance, and the preservation of secrecy for voters with mobility issues.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for managing the budget execution and personnel requirements associated with the fiscal impact of implementing a new pilot program across three counties.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the State Board of Elections, coordinates policy initiatives, and is responsible for proposing the budget funding required for the pilot program.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advocates for equal access to public resources for deaf and hard of hearing residents, which is relevant to ensuring that the curbside voting process and communication with election judges are inclusive.
The bill requires local boards to consider accessibility by public transportation and proximity to dense concentrations of voters when designating curbside voting locations.

Synopsis: Requiring each electric company to report to the Public Service Commission, on or before April 1 each year, geographic and demographic data on all customers impacted by certain service outages and rate increases within the immediately preceding year.
Title: Electric Companies - Service Outages and Rate Increases - Report on Customer Impact
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill requires each electric company in Maryland to report geographic and demographic data annually to the Public Service Commission (PSC) regarding customers impacted by service outages and rate increases. The reports must cover outages lasting two hours or longer, scheduled maintenance outages, and any outages occurring during inclement weather, including service restoration times.
stakeholders: Maryland electric companies, municipal electric utilities (in Berlin, Easton, Hagerstown, Thurmont, and Williamsport), and electric service customers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect State or local government finances or operations. It is assumed that both the Public Service Commission and the affected municipal electric utilities can manage the new reporting requirements using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires electric companies to report geographic and demographic data regarding service outages and rate increases to the Public Service Commission (PSC) each year. This information is directly related to the PSC's primary responsibility of regulating public utilities to ensure safe, reliable, and economical services.

The Office of the People's Counsel (OPC) is the primary advocate for Maryland's residential utility consumers. The geographic and demographic data required by this bill regarding rate increases and service outages is essential for the OPC's mission to represent consumer interests in proceedings before the Public Service Commission.

The Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) advises the Governor and General Assembly on state energy policy. Data on service reliability and the impact of rate increases on different demographics and regions is highly relevant to the MEA's role in coordinating state-level energy planning and resource management.

The Department of Human Services (DHS) provides energy assistance to residents in economic need. Information on rate increases and service reliability, specifically when linked to demographic data, is relevant to DHS for identifying and assisting vulnerable populations who may be disproportionately affected by utility costs.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and the General Assembly. The OAG may be involved in the interpretation and enforcement of the new reporting requirements for electric companies.

The Maryland Department of Aging (MDoA) advocates for the quality of life for older adults. Geographic and demographic data on utility outages and rate increases is relevant to the department, as seniors are often more physically vulnerable during outages and financially impacted by rising utility costs.

The Maryland Department of Disabilities coordinates services for residents with disabilities. Data regarding service outages is critical as many individuals with disabilities rely on electricity for life-sustaining medical equipment and assistive technology.

The Governor's Office oversees executive agencies like the PSC and MEA and coordinates state policy. Data on utility reliability and affordability across Maryland informs the Governor's policy initiatives regarding infrastructure and economic equity.

Synopsis: Altering certain educational and experiential qualifications for a license to practice certified public accountancy.
Title: Certified Public Accountants - Licensure - Qualifications
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: This bill modifies the requirements for becoming a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) in Maryland by providing alternative combinations of education and work experience. It allows applicants with a bachelor's degree and a concentration in accounting to qualify for licensure by completing 4,000 hours of practical work experience over at least two years, serving as an alternative to the requirement of 150 semester hours of college credit. Additionally, it extends the maximum period to complete the required work experience from three to six years.
stakeholders: Prospective certified public accountants, accounting firms, and the State Board of Public Accountancy.
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Board of Public Accountancy can implement the bill's changes using existing resources. State special fund revenues may increase minimally if the alternative pathways lead to more individuals seeking licensure. There is no impact on local government finances. Small business accounting firms may experience a meaningful positive impact by having a larger pool of qualified applicants for licensure.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor houses the State Board of Public Accountancy, which is the primary entity responsible for licensing CPAs. The bill directly alters the educational and experiential qualifications that the Board must regulate and enforce.

As the state's regulatory and coordinating board for postsecondary education, this commission oversees the academic standards and degree programs that applicants must complete to meet the new CPA licensure pathways.

Many institutions within the University System of Maryland offer the accounting degrees and credit hours required for CPA licensure; changes to these pathways directly affect their student enrollment and curriculum planning.
Morgan State University offers baccalaureate and master's programs in accounting; the bill's changes to licensure pathways directly impact their students' degree requirements and career preparation.
As a public institution of higher education, the college provides academic programs that may serve as a foundation for CPA licensure under the bill's altered degree and experience requirements.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Board of Public Accountancy and will be responsible for advising the board on the implementation and legal interpretation of the new licensure regulations.

As the state's chief financial officer and auditor, the Comptroller's Office employs many CPAs and is impacted by changes to the professional standards and the recruitment pipeline for accountants in Maryland.

As the central personnel agency, DBM may need to adjust state job classifications or recruitment policies for accounting positions if the requirements for obtaining a CPA license are significantly altered.

Synopsis: Altering the application requirements for a certain property tax exemption for a dwelling house owned by the surviving spouse of a disabled veteran.
Title: Property Tax - Exemption for Dwellings of Surviving Spouses of Disabled Veterans - Application
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill allows the surviving spouse of a disabled veteran to use Dependency and Indemnity Compensation documentation from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs as proof of a veteran's disability when applying for a property tax exemption on their home, serving as an alternative to a formal certification or disability rating decision.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Surviving spouses of disabled veterans, local governments, and the Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues (Annuity Bond Fund) are estimated to decrease by approximately $1,700,000 annually starting in FY 2027. Local property tax revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $20,000,000 annually starting in FY 2027. The state revenue decrease may require an increase in the State property tax rate or a general fund appropriation to cover debt service on general obligation bonds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly affects the application process and eligibility requirements for property tax exemptions for the surviving spouses of disabled veterans, a key constituent group that the department is tasked with supporting and advocating for regarding state benefits.

The fiscal note indicates that the bill will significantly decrease revenue to the Annuity Bond Fund, which is managed by the Treasurer's Office to pay debt service on the state's general obligation bonds.

As the agency responsible for state revenue estimation and fiscal planning, DBM is impacted by the projected decrease in state property tax revenues and the potential need for general fund appropriations to cover debt service shortfalls.

This board is the primary administrative body responsible for hearing appeals regarding property tax exemptions and credits. It would adjudicate disputes arising from the implementation of the bill's new documentation requirements.

The Maryland Tax Court serves as the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, including real property tax assessments and exemptions, making it a critical entity for appeals related to this legislation.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees the collection of state revenues, including the state property taxes that will be reduced by this expansion of exemptions.

The Board of Public Works oversees state fiscal integrity and general obligation bond issuances; the bill's impact on the Annuity Bond Fund, which services these bonds, falls under their broader fiscal oversight.

The OAG would provide legal guidance to state agencies on the interpretation and implementation of the revised application requirements and the use of federal Dependency and Indemnity Compensation documentation.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies implementing this law and is responsible for the state budget, which may require adjustments due to the bill's fiscal impact on the Annuity Bond Fund.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from intentionally or knowingly providing certain assisted reproductive treatment to another using the person's sperm or ovum without the other's written consent to assisted reproductive treatment using the person's sperm or ovum; and establishing a civil cause of action for a violation of the Act.

Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/31 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records
Reproductive Matters -see also- Abortion; BrthCntr; Preg

bill_summary: This bill prohibits a person from using their own sperm or ovum during assisted reproductive treatment without the recipient's written consent. Violators face felony charges, including up to 10 years in prison and a $5,000 fine, and are liable for civil damages to the recipient, their partner, or the resulting child.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Patients receiving assisted reproductive treatment, their spouses or domestic partners, children born from such treatments, and healthcare providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures increase by $8,400 in FY 2027 only for one-time programming costs for the Judiciary. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government finances or small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill has a direct fiscal impact on the Judiciary, including $8,400 for one-time programming costs. Additionally, the Administrative Office of the Courts must manage the new civil cause of action and the felony cases established by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison. DPSCS would be responsible for the incarceration and subsequent parole or probation supervision of individuals convicted under this statute.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for providing legal counsel to indigent defendants, the OPD will experience a potential increase in caseload to defend individuals charged with the new felony created by the bill.

As the chief legal officer of the state, the OAG provides counsel on the enforcement of new criminal laws and would represent the state in any appeals resulting from convictions under this new felony.
The bill regulates assisted reproductive treatments, which are healthcare services. MDH oversees the regulation of health care professionals and facilities that provide such treatments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategy, this office is relevant to the development and implementation of new felony statutes and sentencing policies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office was identified as a source of information for the fiscal note and manages medical-related dispute resolutions, which may overlap with the civil causes of action involving medical providers.
As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police may be responsible for investigating criminal allegations of fraud related to assisted reproductive treatment.

Synopsis: Requiring that a medical provider report or physician referral be the primary factor in the Motor Vehicle Administration's decision on whether to issue, refuse, or suspend a driver's license for driver's license holders or applicants who self-report a diagnosis of certain medical conditions; authorizing the Administration in its discretion to require additional documentation, written statements, or other materials and testing related to a diagnosis disclosed by a licensee or an applicant; etc.
Title: Driver Licensing – Self–Reporting of Medical Conditions
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/01 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Medical Conditions -see also- AIDS; COVID-19; rabies

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) to primarily rely on medical provider reports or physician referrals when deciding whether to issue, refuse, or suspend driver's licenses for individuals who self-report certain medical conditions. The MVA is authorized to require additional documentation or testing at its discretion. The bill also mandates the creation of an expedited process for issuing learner's instructional permits to individuals whose medical conditions have improved but who must complete driver education or examinations to regain their license. Finally, the MVA must conduct a review of its medical case review practices and report findings to the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Drivers and license applicants with self-reported medical conditions, medical providers, law enforcement, and the Motor Vehicle Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates that the bill's requirements can be handled using the Motor Vehicle Administration's existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not expected to be materially affected, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), which is a modal administration of MDOT, is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill. The bill regulates MVA licensing decisions, requires the MVA to establish expedited permit processes, and mandates that the MVA conduct a study and report on its medical case review practices.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases involving motor vehicle license suspensions and refusals. This bill changes the statutory criteria and primary factors (medical provider reports) that must be used in making those licensing decisions, directly affecting the standards applied during administrative hearings.

The bill explicitly mentions that law enforcement requests for reexamination serve as a primary exception to the rule that medical reports must be the primary factor in licensing decisions. As the primary state agency enforcing motor vehicle laws, MSP's referrals are a critical component of this process.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the MVA and coordinates policy initiatives. The bill also requires a formal report on medical case review practices to be submitted to the General Assembly from within the executive branch.

The bill centers on medical provider reports and physician referrals for licensing. MDH regulates health care professionals and may be involved in the development of the regulations and standards for the medical documentation required by the MVA.

The bill affects the licensing process for individuals with medical conditions, which often involves Marylanders with disabilities. The department is tasked with advancing accessible transportation and ensuring that state policies are inclusive, making the MVA's medical review standards relevant to their mission.

Synopsis: Requiring the Power Plant Research Program to study and make recommendations on nuclear energy and its role as a renewable energy resource that can effectively combat climate change in the State; and requiring, by September 30, 2027, the Program to report its official findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly.
Title: Power Plant Research Program - Study on Nuclear Energy
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Environment and Transportation; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.
Renewable Energy Sources -see also- Geotherm; Solar; etc.
Scientific Research -see also- ChemTst; MedRsrch; Studies

bill_summary: This bill requires the Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) to study the role of nuclear energy as a renewable energy resource to combat climate change in Maryland. The study includes evaluating the current state of nuclear energy, identifying benefits and potential for new initiatives, and locating sites for new generating stations. PPRP must report its findings and recommendations by September 30, 2027.
responsible_party: Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) within the Department of Natural Resources (DNR)
stakeholders: The Governor, the General Assembly, the Department of Natural Resources, the nuclear energy industry, and Maryland residents.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general or special fund expenditures increase by $218,800 in FY 2027 and $11,600 in FY 2028 to complete the required study and report, specifically for hiring an independent consultant and a part-time contractual site assessor. There is no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill and fiscal note explicitly task the Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), which is an office within the Department of Natural Resources, with conducting the nuclear energy study and reporting the findings.

The study's focus on nuclear energy's role as a renewable resource and its potential in the state's energy portfolio directly aligns with MEA's mission to promote renewable energy and advise the Governor on energy policy.

The bill requires an assessment of adding nuclear energy to the state's Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (RPS) and identifying sites for power plants, both of which are core regulatory responsibilities of the PSC.

The study aims to evaluate nuclear energy's role in combatting climate change and its environmental benefits, which falls under MDE's mandate to implement state laws regarding air quality and environmental restoration.
The report and recommendations must be submitted directly to the Governor, who oversees the state's energy policy and coordinates the initiatives proposed by the study.

The fiscal note identifies a need for additional general or special funds and contractual personnel for the Department of Natural Resources to complete the study, which impacts DBM's personnel and fiscal management duties.
The study is required to include recommendations for growing the nuclear energy industry in Maryland, which aligns with Commerce's mission to stimulate the economy and attract new businesses.
The mandate to identify potential locations for nuclear generating stations involves land use planning and infrastructure development, which are primary functions of the Department of Planning.
The bill explores the potential for State-owned and operated nuclear energy generating stations, which would involve DGS's responsibilities for state real estate management and facility planning.
The OAG would provide necessary legal counsel regarding proposed changes to state energy laws, the Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard, and the legal aspects of power plant siting.
As the state's green bank, the MCEC is relevant to any study seeking to advance the adoption of clean energy technologies and grow the clean energy industry in Maryland.

bill_summary: This bill reduces the minimum age from 65 to 60 for eligible energy customers to qualify for a uniform redetermination process when enrolling in energy assistance programs, such as the Electric Universal Service Program and the Maryland Energy Assistance Program.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services (Office of Home Energy Programs)
stakeholders: Eligible energy customers between the ages of 60 and 64 and Local Administering Agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill primarily alters the purposes for which existing funds may be used. The Department of Human Services and local administering agencies can handle the bill's requirements with existing budgeted resources. While the bill expands the redetermination process to an estimated 1,760 additional households, the Office of Home Energy Programs may adjust benefit levels to stay within available funding, which for fiscal 2027 includes $47,700,000 for the Electric Universal Service Program and $94,700,000 for the Maryland Energy Assistance Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Human Services is the primary implementing agency for the bill, as it houses the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP), which is directly responsible for the redetermination process and the administration of the energy assistance programs mentioned.

The bill specifically reduces the age for special energy assistance redetermination from 65 to 60, aligning with federal definitions of 'older adults' and impacting the demographic served by this department.

The Maryland Energy Administration manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which provides significant funding for the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) affected by the bill's eligibility changes.

The Public Service Commission regulates the utilities that collect ratepayer surcharges used to fund energy assistance programs and oversees programs like the Utility Service Protection Program mentioned in the fiscal note.
The Department of Budget and Management oversees the fiscal planning and execution of the state and federal funds (EUSP and MEAP) that support these energy assistance programs.
This is a departmental bill introduced at the request of the Department of Human Services, part of the Governor's executive branch oversight.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Human Services regarding the implementation of state and federal energy assistance regulations.
Energy assistance programs like MEAP include referrals to weatherization services, which are often administered or supported by the Department of Housing and Community Development.

The fiscal note highlights that households with individuals receiving means-tested Veterans Affairs benefits are categorically eligible for the energy assistance programs affected by the redetermination process changes.

bill_summary: The bill authorizes the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR) to enforce prohibitions against discrimination in educational institutions, spanning from prekindergarten through higher education. It establishes concurrent jurisdiction between the MCCR and the State Superintendent of Schools for investigating and mediating complaints, allows for private civil actions in cases of educational discrimination, and requires higher education bodies to refer discrimination complaints to the MCCR.
stakeholders: Students in prekindergarten through postsecondary education, parents and guardians, public and nonpublic educational institutions, the Maryland State Department of Education, and the Maryland Higher Education Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights expects to implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. There is a potential for significant expenditure increases for higher education institutions and local school systems due to more robust enforcement and increased litigation risks. For illustrative purposes, Prince George's County estimates that adding one attorney to handle increased complaint volumes would cost approximately 250,000 annually.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR) is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It is authorized to enforce prohibitions against discrimination in educational institutions, conduct investigations, mediate complaints, adopt implementing regulations, and initiate civil actions.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), through the State Superintendent, shares concurrent jurisdiction with MCCR for enforcing anti-discrimination laws in schools. The bill alters the Superintendent's enforcement duties and requires joint coordination with MCCR on mediation guidelines.

The Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) is required by the bill to refer any complaints regarding educational discrimination in postsecondary institutions to MCCR for investigation and must oversee compliance within its regulated sector.

The Board of Regents of the University System of Maryland (USM) is mandated to refer discrimination complaints to MCCR. As the governing body for Maryland's public universities, USM and its constituent institutions are subject to the bill's mandates and face significant fiscal impact from potential litigation and enforcement.

The Comptroller is tasked with withholding state funding from schools or programs that fail to remedy or eliminate discriminatory practices upon order from the State Superintendent or notification from MCCR.
The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) is designated as the appellate body to hear cases if a complainant or respondent appeals a decision issued by the State Superintendent or MCCR.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to the implementing agencies (MCCR, MSDE, MHEC) and would represent state educational institutions in the civil actions and appeals authorized by the bill.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State is directly subject to the bill's non-discrimination mandates and enforcement oversight, and the fiscal note indicates a potential increase in legal expenditures.
As a state-operated college, it is subject to the bill's requirements regarding educational discrimination and faces potential litigation and settlement costs as noted in the fiscal analysis.
The bill establishes a private right of action for individuals to bring civil suits in Circuit Court, impacting the judicial branch's caseload and operations.

The Treasurer's Office manages state insurance and liability through the State Insurance Trust Fund; it would be responsible for handling claims and settlements resulting from compensatory or punitive damage awards against state educational entities.

The bill explicitly defines disability and addresses discrimination against students with disabilities, overlapping with the department's mission to ensure inclusive and integrated services across all state programs, including education.

DBM oversees fiscal planning and personnel for state agencies. The bill has potential fiscal impacts on agency staffing for MCCR and MSDE, as well as implications for the withholding of state funding for non-compliant schools.

As a state-operated educational institution, the Maryland School for the Deaf is directly subject to the anti-discrimination prohibitions and enforcement authority granted to MCCR and MSDE under this bill.

DJS operates educational programs within its residential facilities that lead to diplomas or certificates; these programs fall under the bill's definition of educational institutions subject to civil rights oversight.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy. This bill represents a significant shift in executive branch enforcement of civil rights in educational institutions.

This office oversees various ethnic, cultural, and faith-based commissions and is responsible for community engagement, making it the primary entity to coordinate or support the heritage celebrations mentioned in the bill.
The Secretary of State is the custodian of the state's official records, including the executive orders and proclamations issued by the Governor.

The bill requires proclamations to urge educational organizations to observe these months with appropriate programs; as the oversight body for public schools, MSDE is a key stakeholder in implementing these educational activities.

The bill urges cultural organizations to observe these heritage months. The Department of Commerce oversees the state's tourism, film, and arts programs, which are central to Maryland's cultural landscape.
The bill urges educational organizations to observe the commemorative months; the Commission oversees postsecondary institutions that would be encouraged to participate in these programs.
