bill_summary: The Safe Kids Act prohibits online platforms from knowingly creating or distributing unlawful child exploitation material, including content generated by artificial intelligence. The bill establishes a civil cause of action for parents and guardians of affected minors to sue for damages, authorizes enforcement by the Attorney General, and expands criminal statutes to include AI-generated material and protect all minors by increasing the age threshold for victims from 16 to 18.
responsible_party: The Office of the Attorney General and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Minors, parents, legal guardians, and online platforms such as social networks and advertising networks
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The bill establishes criminal penalties including fines of up to $2,500 for first-time misdemeanors and $10,000 for subsequent felony convictions. Additionally, the creation of a new civil cause of action and the expansion of the Attorney General's enforcement authority may increase expenditures for the Maryland Judiciary and the Office of the Attorney General due to an increased caseload.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to seek injunctive or other equitable relief to enforce provisions related to the dissemination and creation of unlawful child exploitation material.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating crimes related to child pornography, which the bill expands to include AI-generated images and victims up to age 18.
The bill creates a new civil cause of action and modifies criminal law, which will directly impact court operations, caseloads, and the judicial process supported by the AOC.

The agency is dedicated to the well-being of Maryland's children; the protection of minors from digital exploitation and AI-generated pornographic material aligns with its core mission.

The center is responsible for comprehensive school safety; the creation and dissemination of exploitation material involving minors is a significant safety threat that impacts the school-age population.

The MSDE oversees the well-being of the state's student population; child exploitation material is a major concern for the safety and development of minors under their jurisdiction.

bill_summary: This bill regulates the land application of sewage sludge containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), specifically PFOA and PFOS. Starting October 1, 2028, it prohibits applying sewage sludge to agricultural or marginal land if PFAS concentrations are 50 parts per billion (ppb) or higher. Sludge with concentrations between 25 and 50 ppb is subject to strict management measures, source tracking studies, and mitigation plans. The bill also authorizes the Maryland Department of the Environment and local authorities to establish pretreatment standards and fees for industrial users that discharge PFAS into wastewater systems.
stakeholders: Sewage sludge generators (wastewater treatment plants), industrial users discharging to wastewater systems, agricultural and marginal landowners, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $248,100 in FY 2027 for the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) to implement and oversee the program, with costs rising to $331,800 by FY 2031. Local government expenditures may increase significantly for jurisdictions whose wastewater treatment plants produce sludge exceeding PFAS thresholds; for example, the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission estimates annual management cost increases between $4,100,000 and $8,200,000. Local revenues may increase through the collection of new rates and fees from industrial users.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill. It is tasked with adopting regulations, establishing monitoring protocols for PFAS, reviewing and approving source tracking studies and mitigation plans from sewage sludge generators, and establishing pretreatment standards for industrial users.

The bill explicitly includes the Maryland Environmental Service (MES) in the definition of a 'sewage sludge generator.' MES operates approximately 90 wastewater treatment plants and will be directly impacted by the new testing, monitoring, and reporting requirements, as well as potential mitigation costs.

The bill mandates that MDE cannot adopt regulations regarding the land application of sewage sludge without the approval of the Department of Agriculture. Additionally, MDA provides recommendations for nutrient requirements on agricultural land where sludge is applied.

The fiscal note indicates that MDE will require three additional positions (one regulatory engineer and two natural resource planners) to implement the bill. DBM is responsible for managing state personnel resources and budget execution for these additions.

The bill may have a meaningful impact on small businesses and industrial users who discharge into wastewater systems, as they may face new pretreatment standards, mitigation costs, and increased rates or fees. The Department of Commerce is the primary agency for business retention and economic development.

The OAH provides an impartial hearing process for contested cases. If MDE determines a sewage sludge generator is out of compliance with an approved mitigation plan and prohibits land application, the generator may appeal the decision through OAH.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MDE and MDA during the regulatory process and represents the state in civil or criminal enforcement actions related to violations of the new sewage sludge and PFAS standards.

The BPW oversees significant state expenditures and procurement contracts. Any major infrastructure projects or large-scale consulting contracts initiated by MDE or MES to address PFAS mitigation may require BPW approval.
The Comptroller manages the collection of state revenues, including the annual generator fees paid by sewage sludge generators into the Maryland Clean Water Fund.

The bill was assigned to the Health Committee in the House. MDH regulates health care facilities and professionals and has a vested interest in public health outcomes related to PFAS contamination in the environment.
The bill requires MDE to consider the nearness of land application sites to sensitive areas such as wetlands and flood plains, which are under the conservation and management purview of DNR.

The bill requires MDE to consider the character of nearby planned land uses and transport routes when adopting regulations for land application, which falls under MDP's land use planning responsibilities.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the primary implementing agencies (MDE and MDA), and the Governor must sign the bill into law and propose the budget for its implementation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO provides financial services to agricultural and seafood industries. Farmers impacted by restrictions on sewage sludge application or those needing to implement new soil management practices may seek assistance through MARBIDCO's programs.
The Treasurer acts as the custodian of state funds and manages the investment of revenues collected in state funds, including those used for environmental programs.
As an urban research institution, MSU may be an industrial user of a wastewater system or participate in research related to the environmental and public health impacts of PFAS.

OLA is responsible for fiscal compliance and performance audits of executive branch agencies; it will likely review MDE's management and enforcement of the new PFAS regulatory framework in future audit cycles.

The RMC advocates for the interests of rural counties. Since the land application of sewage sludge occurs primarily on agricultural and marginal lands in rural areas, the council has a stake in the bill's implementation.
As a state agency and educational institution, the college may be classified as an industrial user discharging into a public wastewater system subject to new pretreatment standards or fees.

This multi-agency initiative promotes sustainable development and environmental protection. The regulation of PFAS in biosolids aligns with the initiative's goals of protecting the Chesapeake Bay and preserving agricultural resources.
USM institutions may be impacted as industrial users of wastewater systems or as research partners providing data on PFAS mitigation and environmental impacts.

bill_summary: This bill expands the requirement for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) to include all transmission lines designed to carry more than 69,000 volts, effectively removing the previous limitation that only applied to overhead lines. It replaces a mandatory CPCN waiver for construction on existing lines with a discretionary waiver based on 'good cause,' requiring the Public Service Commission to consider environmental impacts and costs to ratepayers. Additionally, the Commission must adopt regulations by July 1, 2027, to establish specific criteria for these waivers.
stakeholders: Electric utility companies, Maryland electricity ratepayers, environmental advocacy groups, the Maryland Aviation Administration, and local municipal and county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill creates new administrative requirements for the Public Service Commission, including the development of new regulations and the review of a potentially higher volume of CPCN applications and waiver requests. Ratepayers may be financially impacted as the Commission is now required to consider the cost of construction during the waiver evaluation process.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary regulatory body responsible for issuing Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) for transmission lines. This bill directly modifies the PSC's regulatory authority by expanding the CPCN requirement to all transmission lines (not just overhead), establishing new criteria for waivers, and requiring the PSC to adopt new regulations.

The bill explicitly requires the PSC to consider aviation safety as determined by the Maryland Aviation Administration (MAA) and requires MAA's concurrence with Federal Aviation Administration determinations regarding transmission lines located near public airport runways.

The Department of Planning is specifically named as an entity that must receive immediate notice of any CPCN application and is responsible for evaluating the proposal's significance to State and local plans.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers. The bill adds 'the cost of the construction on ratepayers' as a mandatory consideration for the PSC when determining whether to waive CPCN requirements, which is a core advocacy area for this agency.

The bill requires the PSC to consider environmental impacts, air and water quality, and climate change commitments (specifically citing the Environment Article) when reviewing CPCN applications. MDE is the primary agency for enforcing these standards.

The bill impacts the Maryland Aviation Administration, a modal unit of MDOT, regarding airport safety. It also affects the construction of utility infrastructure that often intersects with state-owned transportation rights-of-way.

DNR typically serves as a 'State unit' in the CPCN review process, evaluating the impact of energy infrastructure on natural resources, fisheries, and wildlife, all of which are considerations under the bill's expanded criteria.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the PSC and other state agencies involved in the CPCN process and would be involved in the drafting of new regulations and any legal challenges related to eminent domain or regulatory changes.

The Department of Agriculture is concerned with the impact of large-scale infrastructure projects on agricultural land and soil conservation, which are components of the environmental and site-use evaluations required by the bill.

Transmission lines frequently traverse rural counties. The Council advocates for rural interests regarding infrastructure development, economic impact, and land preservation, all of which are impacted by changes to CPCN requirements.

The bill references the right of condemnation in accordance with Title 12 of the Real Property Article. Changes to CPCN applicability directly affect the frequency and legal basis for eminent domain cases heard in the state court system.

The bill requires the PSC to consider the effect of transmission lines on 'historic sites.' The Archives and its Commission on Artistic Property are involved in identifying and preserving Maryland's historical record and assets.

The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies (PSC, Planning, MDE, MDOT) involved in the implementation of the bill and is responsible for the overall policy direction regarding state energy infrastructure and climate goals.

The construction of transmission lines and the resulting cost to ratepayers can impact Maryland's economic competitiveness and business environment, which are key concerns for the Department of Commerce.
The bill maintains provisions for emergency repairs to avoid imminent safety hazards or reliability risks, which relates to the department's role in statewide disaster and emergency preparedness.

bill_summary: This bill decouples the Maryland income tax from federal provisions that allow 529 education savings plans to be used for elementary and secondary education expenses. It also prohibits the Governor from participating in a federal tax credit program for K-12 scholarships and requires that employer contributions to certain educational accounts and 529 distributions used for K-12 expenses be added back to Maryland adjusted gross income.
responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland and the Governor
stakeholders: Maryland taxpayers with 529 education savings plans, employers providing educational assistance, and elementary and secondary school students.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an indeterminate increase in State and local income tax revenue by eliminating certain subtractions and exclusions for K-12 education expenses and employer-paid educational contributions. Specific dollar estimates were not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly prohibits the Governor from electing to participate in a specific federal tax credit program for elementary and secondary education scholarships established under the Internal Revenue Code.

As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for implementing and enforcing the new income tax addition and subtraction modifications related to education expenses and employer contributions specified in the bill.

The bill directly impacts the tax treatment of contributions and distributions for the 529 plans managed by this agency, specifically restricting tax benefits when funds are used for elementary and secondary education expenses.

The Treasurer's Office oversees Maryland 529 and its associated investment plans. Changes to the tax status and 'qualified higher education expense' definitions for these accounts directly impact the agency's management of these state funds.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and fiscal planning; changes to tax modifications and decoupling from federal tax changes will result in a notable fiscal impact on the state's general fund.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Governor regarding the limits on executive authority imposed by the bill and advise the Comptroller and Treasurer on the legal implementation of decoupling from federal tax law.
The bill concerns the funding of elementary and secondary education through tax-advantaged accounts and scholarship programs, which falls under the broader policy domain of MSDE.

fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's requirements, including adopting regulations and granting certification extensions, using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary implementing agency responsible for adopting regulations, establishing certification requirements for medical directors, approving equivalent credentials, and granting extensions for good cause.

The OAH may adjudicate contested cases related to the certification status or extension requests of medical directors should disputes arise regarding compliance with the new regulations.

DBM oversees the state's budget and personnel; while the bill is expected to be implemented with existing resources, the agency monitors the administrative impact and regulatory workload on executive departments.
The Department of Disabilities has a relevant interest in nursing home clinical standards, as these facilities provide long-term care for individuals with chronic illnesses and disabilities.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for the bill's implementation and the Governor must sign the legislation into law.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the process for issuing and using Sales and Use Tax Multiple Points of Use (MPU) certificates for digital codes, products, and services. It requires buyers to register with and obtain authorization from the Comptroller to issue these certificates, sets a minimum two-year validity period for authorizations, and establishes procedures for the renewal, denial, and revocation of that authority. Authorized buyers using MPU certificates are responsible for remitting the applicable tax, and the Comptroller must notify vendors if a buyer's authorization has been revoked.

These expenditures are projected to rise to $207,000 by FY 2031. General fund revenues may experience an indeterminate decrease due to potential risks in tax compliance verification and fraudulent certificate use. There is no impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. It is tasked with authorizing buyers to issue multiple points of use (MPU) certificates, managing the registration and renewal process, and revoking authorizations when necessary. The fiscal note indicates a direct impact on the Comptroller's operations, requiring additional personnel and computer programming updates.

As the independent administrative agency that hears appeals from the final decisions of the Comptroller, the Maryland Tax Court is relevant because it would adjudicate any disputes arising from the denial or revocation of MPU certificate authorizations as provided for in the bill.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency for the state. This bill has a notable fiscal impact requiring the hiring of two additional financial compliance auditors and funding for computer system modifications, which falls under DBM's responsibility for budget supervision and personnel management.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Comptroller. It would be responsible for providing legal advice on the implementation of these new tax regulations and representing the Comptroller's office in any litigation or appeals resulting from the enforcement of MPU certificate provisions.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for proposing the annual state budget. The fiscal note indicates a decrease in general fund revenues and an increase in expenditures, which the Governor must account for in the state's fiscal planning.

bill_summary: This emergency bill alters the requirements for a comprehensive rehabilitative prerelease facility for female incarcerated individuals, mandating that it be located in Baltimore City on a site of at least three acres and at least one mile from other correctional facilities. It requires the Department of General Services (DGS) to manage an expedited procurement and construction process and directs the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (DPSCS) to provide gender-responsive and evidence-based rehabilitative services to eligible individuals even before the new facility is completed. The bill also establishes specific amenities for the facility, reporting requirements for the agencies, and oversight by the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and Maryland Department of General Services
stakeholders: Female incarcerated individuals eligible for prerelease status and the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. However, the bill mandates the acquisition of land and the construction of a new prerelease facility in Baltimore City, which will require significant State capital expenditures. Additionally, the requirement to provide comprehensive rehabilitative and gender-responsive services will lead to increased ongoing operational expenditures for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments, including DPSCS and DGS, that are mandated to implement this major correctional policy and facility construction project.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is responsible for approving the significant state contracts and property acquisitions required for the new prerelease facility.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Treasurer oversees the issuance of State bonds and approves the significant expenditures related to the construction of the new facility.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the implementing agencies regarding the expedited procurement process, site acquisition, and contract awarding mandated by the bill.
DBM is responsible for the fiscal planning, budget development, and allocation of funds necessary for the construction and ongoing operation of the new prerelease unit.
DGS is explicitly directed by the bill to lead the procurement process, review proposals, and award contracts for the planning, design, and construction of the new facility.
The bill mandates that the facility include a medical suite and provide substance use and mental health treatment services, which aligns with the department's public health oversight.
The bill requires the facility to provide vocational skills training, industry certification, and job placement services, which are core functions of the Department of Labor.
The bill sets specific land area and location requirements in Baltimore City, involving land use considerations that may fall under the department's planning and policy guidance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is the primary implementing agency responsible for operating the prerelease unit, implementing rehabilitative services, and reporting on the project's progress.
The new facility is required to have access to public transportation, which requires coordination with MDOT's transit systems and infrastructure.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises on criminal justice strategies and manages funds for public safety, directly relating to the bill's goal of reducing recidivism through rehabilitative services.
The Board of Public Works must approve the acquisition of land and the major procurement contracts for the design and construction of the state-owned facility.

The Maryland Food Center Authority manages wholesale produce and seafood markets that serve as critical infrastructure in the food supply chain for the local farms and invasive species providers identified in the bill.

The Rural Maryland Council advocates for the interests of the agricultural and natural resource sectors in rural counties, many of which provide the 'certified local farm' products targeted by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the use of automated crosswalk monitoring systems in Anne Arundel, Montgomery, and Prince George’s counties and their municipalities to cite drivers who fail to stop for pedestrians in crosswalks. It establishes a civil penalty of up to $65 for violations, outlines the process for issuing and contesting citations, and requires that net fine revenue be used for implementation costs and crosswalk safety infrastructure such as beacons and raised crosswalks.
responsible_party: Law enforcement agencies in Anne Arundel, Montgomery, and Prince George's counties and associated municipalities, and the District Court of Maryland.
stakeholders: Motorists and pedestrians in Anne Arundel, Montgomery, and Prince George’s counties.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues from contested cases in the District Court may increase beginning in FY 2027. Local expenditures and revenues will increase for participating jurisdictions to implement systems, though total annual revenue for a jurisdiction is restricted; balances exceeding 10% of a local government's total revenue must be remitted to the State. The District Court estimates a broader automated enforcement system upgrade may cost approximately $1,400,000, though this is not exclusively tied to this bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants exclusive original civil jurisdiction to the District Court for crosswalk monitoring system infractions. It requires the Chief Judge of the District Court to prescribe uniform citation forms, schedule trials, and adopt procedures for collecting civil penalties.

The bill requires authorization from the State Highway Administration (SHA) to use crosswalk monitoring systems on State highways. It also requires local jurisdictions to obtain SHA approval before placing signs on State highways regarding the monitoring systems.

The Motor Vehicle Administration is authorized to refuse, suspend, or deny the registration or reregistration of a motor vehicle if a civil penalty from a crosswalk monitoring system is not paid and the violation is not contested.

As the parent agency for the State Highway Administration and the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the modal administrations responsible for highway safety, signage approval, and vehicle registration sanctions related to the new monitoring systems.

The bill mandates that for any fiscal year where the balance of fines exceeds 10% of a local jurisdiction's total revenue, the excess must be remitted to the Comptroller. The Comptroller also distributes fines from other speed monitoring systems referenced in the bill's amendments.

The bill requires Anne Arundel, Montgomery, and Prince George's counties to submit a detailed report to the Governor by December 1, 2027, regarding the performance, reliability, and effectiveness of the crosswalk monitoring systems.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a regulatory framework for 'large load customers' (commercial or industrial entities with at least 25 MW demand and an 80% load factor). It requires the Public Service Commission to develop specialized interconnection processes and a Demand Response Program for these customers, exempts specific projects from the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity requirement, and mandates a load study fee of at least $1,000 per megawatt to fund low-income energy assistance programs. The Maryland Energy Administration is also required to study surplus interconnection potential across the state.
stakeholders: Large load commercial and industrial electricity customers, data center developers, electric utility companies, and low-income residents who benefit from state energy assistance programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a revenue stream via a mandatory fee of at least $1,000 per megawatt of load for large load customers, with proceeds split between the Electric Universal Service Program and the Department of Housing and Community Development’s EmPOWER Maryland Limited Income Energy Efficiency Program. Specific aggregate dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are unavailable as they depend on the number and size of future large load customer applications. The Public Service Commission and Maryland Energy Administration will also incur administrative costs to implement the new processes and conduct the required study.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Public Service Commission to establish a new interconnection process for large load customers, regulate a new Demand Response Program, set load study fees, and manage the prioritization of interconnection and permitting for specific customers.

The bill requires the Maryland Energy Administration to conduct a comprehensive study of surplus interconnection potential at generating facilities across the State and report its findings to the General Assembly.

The bill provides a direct fiscal impact by allocating 50% of the fees collected from large load customer load studies (not less than $1,000 per megawatt) to the EmPOWER Maryland Limited Income Energy Efficiency Program administered by DHCD.

The bill allocates 50% of the fees collected from large load customer load studies to the Electric Universal Service Program, which is a major energy assistance program managed by the Department of Human Services.

The bill specifies that large load customers must pay the prevailing wage rate to receive prioritization for load studies and interconnection, which falls under the regulatory and enforcement domain of the Department of Labor.

As the representative for residential utility consumers, the Office of the People's Counsel would be concerned with the grid impacts, ratepayer implications, and demand response incentives associated with high-demand 'large load' industrial and commercial users.

The bill impacts 'large load customers,' which are primarily industrial or commercial entities like data centers, and the facilitation of their interconnection is a significant factor in Maryland's economic development and business attraction strategies.

The bill addresses significant state energy policy, grid management, and economic development priorities, requiring coordination across the executive branch and alignment with the Governor's climate and economic goals.

The bill exempts certain projects from the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) process and emphasizes carbon-free assets and behind-the-meter storage, which intersect with MDE's environmental regulation and climate goals.

DNR typically participates in the CPCN process through the Power Plant Research Program; exemptions from CPCN requirements for large load customers and storage facilities would impact their regulatory review workload.

Large load customers with high load factors are often data centers or major IT infrastructure hubs; the bill's provisions on interconnection directly impact the deployment of this critical digital infrastructure in Maryland.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the PSC and MEA regarding the new regulations, study mandates, and the dispute resolution process established for the Demand Response Program.

The development of large-scale industrial loads and their interconnection points has significant land use and sustainable growth implications, which the Department of Planning monitors through its various initiatives.
The bill's focus on energy storage, carbon-free assets, and grid-enhancing technologies aligns with the Center's mission to advance clean energy adoption and innovative energy financing.

bill_summary: This bill requires health care entities—including hospitals, ambulatory surgical facilities, and provider organizations—with at least $10,000,000 in assets or annual revenue to provide 90 days' notice to the Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) and the public before completing a material change transaction such as a merger, acquisition, or affiliation. It repeals certain Certificate of Need (CON) exemptions for mergers and establishes a public interest review process. Under this process, the MHCC Executive Director evaluates transactions for their impact on market competition, costs, quality, equity, and access to care, and has the authority to approve, deny, or impose conditions on the transactions.
stakeholders: Health care entities (hospitals, ambulatory surgical facilities, and provider organizations), medical group practices, health care practitioners, and Maryland health care consumers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill allows the Maryland Health Care Commission to adopt regulations establishing fees for parties involved in material change transactions to reimburse the administrative costs of the review process. Additionally, the Commission may contract with independent experts or consultants to conduct public interest reviews, the costs of which must be paid by the parties to the transaction. The Commission is also authorized to impose civil penalties for violations, not exceeding 1% of the transaction's value. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the bill text, so specific state revenue and expenditure figures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues. Since hospital mergers and consolidations (classified as material change transactions in this bill) directly impact hospital costs and the 'all-payer' system, this bill's oversight of such transactions is highly relevant to their mission.

The bill explicitly preserves the Attorney General's authority to protect the health care market. Additionally, the OAG would represent the Commission in the judicial review processes and enforcement actions established by this legislation.

The bill regulates transactions involving organizations that administer contracts with health insurance carriers. These consolidations in the health provider market can influence insurance rates and market stability, which are overseen by the MIA.

Material change transactions and market consolidations among health care entities can impact the affordability and accessibility of health plans offered on the state exchange, which the MHBE administers.

The bill explicitly references and provides specific exceptions for health care facilities owned and operated by the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families in the context of certificate of need requirements.

This bill will likely have a fiscal impact requiring new personnel or resources for the Maryland Health Care Commission to conduct technical public interest reviews, monitor compliance, and manage the new regulatory workload.
The bill establishes a formal judicial review process in the Circuit Courts for parties aggrieved by the Commission's decisions regarding material change transactions, impacting court operations.

The bill authorizes the Commission to impose civil penalties of up to 1% of the value of a material change transaction, which represents a potential source of state revenue that the Comptroller's office manages.

bill_summary: The County and Municipal Street Lighting Investment Act authorizes Maryland counties and municipalities to acquire street lighting equipment from electric companies via purchase or condemnation. The bill requires local governments to pay the net book value of the equipment and the costs of any necessary preparation work (make-ready work). It mandates that electric companies establish a specific tariff for customer-owned street lighting that excludes certain maintenance fees, allowing local jurisdictions to manage their own lighting infrastructure and potentially implement energy-efficient upgrades like LED technology.
stakeholders: Maryland counties and municipalities, electric companies, and residential and commercial electricity customers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. These jurisdictions may see long-term savings through reduced maintenance and electricity charges under the new customer-owned lighting tariffs. The Public Service Commission will incur administrative costs to review new tariffs and resolve acquisition disputes.

The PSC is responsible for receiving notices of street lighting acquisition, resolving disputes regarding the net book value of equipment or other acquisition terms through its complaint procedures, and issuing final determinations on the adoption of the mandatory customer-owned street lighting tariffs filed by electric companies.

The bill's findings explicitly state that street lighting upgrades provide opportunities to reduce carbon footprints and address climate change through energy-efficient technologies like LED lamps. As the agency dedicated to maximizing energy efficiency and advising the state on energy policy, the MEA is directly relevant to the implementation and policy goals of transitioning to more efficient, customer-owned lighting systems.

The Maryland Department of Transportation, specifically through the State Highway Administration (SHA), manages thousands of miles of roadways. While the bill empowers counties and municipalities to acquire utility-owned streetlights, these local jurisdictions often coordinate infrastructure and safety resources with MDOT SHA along state-numbered highways that run through their boundaries.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and other state agencies. The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial branch where these condemnation cases and jury trials for determining property value would be conducted.

bill_summary: This bill regulates 'companion chatbots' by requiring operators to establish protocols to prevent the production of content related to self-harm, suicide, and sexually explicit conduct, particularly for minor users. It mandates clear warnings that chatbots are not human, limits the collection and use of personal data, and requires operators to establish a complaint system. Additionally, the bill classifies chatbots as products for liability purposes, requires annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention, and makes violations subject to the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health (Office of Suicide Prevention) and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Users of companion chatbots (especially minors), chatbot operators and developers, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase beginning in FY 2027. The Office of the Attorney General anticipates an annual cost of $326,000 for personnel to handle enforcement, although the Department of Legislative Services (DLS) notes the actual fiscal impact will depend on the volume of consumer complaints. While the Maryland Department of Health estimated a need for $382,700 annually, DLS suggests those duties can be managed with existing resources. There is no expected material impact on local government finances or state revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes that companion chatbots are considered products for the purposes of product liability actions, creating new legal pathways for design, manufacturing, and marketing defect lawsuits that will be adjudicated within the state court system.

According to the fiscal note, the bill is expected to increase general fund expenditures for the Office of the Attorney General to support new personnel required for enforcement; DBM is responsible for managing these budgetary adjustments and personnel allocations.

As the state's primary economic development and business advocacy agency, the Department of Commerce is relevant due to the bill's new regulatory requirements and protocols imposed on technology companies operating as companion chatbot developers and operators in Maryland.

The bill includes significant protections for minor users, including content restrictions and mandatory usage warnings, which intersects with the department's mission to ensure the safety and well-being of students in digital environments.

The bill explicitly tasks the Office of Suicide Prevention within the Maryland Department of Health with receiving annual reports from chatbot operators, compiling data on crisis service referrals, and publishing results on its website.

DoIT is the state's lead agency for information technology strategy and data governance. The bill's requirements for AI disclosure and personal data collection limits align with DoIT's oversight of the state's broader AI policy framework and its role on the Governor's AI Subcabinet.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's subject matter directly relates to the ongoing work of the Governor’s AI Subcabinet and the Workgroup on AI Implementation, both of which are mentioned in the fiscal note as bodies coordinating Maryland's response to artificial intelligence.

The bill addresses key executive priorities including child welfare and the ethical regulation of artificial intelligence; the Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementation and the AI Subcabinet mentioned in the analysis.

The bill classifies violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which is enforced by the OAG. The fiscal note indicates that the OAG will require additional staffing and resources to perform the specialized enforcement required by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Governor, with the approval of the Board of Public Works, to transfer funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account (Rainy Day Fund) to the State Disaster Recovery Fund (SDRF). Such transfers are permitted as long as the Rainy Day Fund balance remains at or above 5% of the estimated General Fund revenues for the fiscal year in which the transfer is made.
responsible_party: The Governor, the Board of Public Works, and the Maryland Department of Emergency Management
stakeholders: State and local government agencies and Maryland residents requiring disaster recovery assistance in scenarios where federal disaster declarations are not issued.
fiscal_impact_summary: Because the bill is authorizing in nature, it does not directly affect State finances. Should a fund transfer occur, special fund revenues for the State Disaster Recovery Fund would increase. If a transfer causes the Rainy Day Fund balance to fall below 7.5% of projected general fund revenue, general fund expenditures may increase by at least $50,000,000 in the following year to meet statutory replenishment requirements. Local governments may benefit from receiving additional aid from the State Disaster Recovery Fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Governor to initiate the transfer of funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account to the State Disaster Recovery Fund.
MDEM administers the State Disaster Recovery Fund, which is the direct recipient of the funds transferred under this bill, and may require additional staff to manage a significant influx of funding.
The bill requires the formal approval of the Board of Public Works for any transfer of funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account to the State Disaster Recovery Fund.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM manages the state's budget execution and the State Reserve Fund, which includes the Revenue Stabilization Account.

The Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works and acts as the custodian of state funds, including the Revenue Stabilization Account affected by the bill.
OLA is responsible for fiscal compliance audits of state agencies and funds, and would oversee the legal compliance of these new authorized fund transfers.

The Maryland Transportation Authority is explicitly named throughout the bill text as a unit that withholds retainage and must comply with the new 90-day payment deadline following substantial completion.

USM has independent procurement authority and manages significant construction projects. It was cited in the fiscal note as an affected entity that would need to adjust its contract payment practices.

The IAC oversees the planning and funding of public school construction projects. This bill impacts the timing of payments to contractors for projects managed under their capital improvement programs.

MSA is a major state agency involved in the design and construction of sports facilities and public schools. The shift in retainage payment schedules affects their contract management and project closeout procedures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is responsible for processing state payments and overseeing the fiscal integrity of state contracts affected by this legislation.
The Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works and manages state funds. The agency is involved in the approval of the procurement contracts that will be subject to the new retainage timelines.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency and is responsible for budget execution and long-term fiscal planning. The bill's potential for increased expenditures due to double payments on unfinished work falls under DBM's oversight.

As an independent public urban research university with its own board, Morgan State manages its own construction projects and must comply with state procurement laws regarding contractor payments and retainage.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and reviews procurement contracts. They would be responsible for advising units on the definition of 'substantial completion' and ensuring contract templates comply with the new law.

bill_summary: The Secure the Vote Act of 2026 repeals the use of ballot drop boxes and permanent absentee ballot lists in Maryland. It establishes new requirements for voter registration, including mandatory proof of citizenship, and requires voters to present valid photo identification or specific alternative documentation to vote in person. The bill also restricts absentee voting to individuals facing specific circumstances such as illness or absence from the state, mandates signature verification for all absentee ballots, requires regular comprehensive audits of the voter registration list, and prohibits non-citizens from registering or voting in municipal elections.
stakeholders: Maryland voters, non-citizen residents, state and local election officials, and county public library systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates several new administrative mandates for the State Board of Elections and local boards, including the establishment of a photo identification program at public libraries, the conduct of pre-election voter registration audits, and the implementation of signature verification procedures. While the repeal of ballot drop boxes and special mail-in elections may reduce certain operational costs, the new requirements are expected to result in an overall increase in State and local expenditures. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note with figures was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation, including establishing the voter photo ID program, adopting regulations for proof of citizenship, conducting registration audits, and overseeing municipal election standards.

The bill explicitly requires the State Board and each county public library system to collaborate to operate a program allowing individuals to obtain photo identification for voting purposes at any public library in the State.

The bill requires the State Board to conduct voter registration audits using data from jury commissioners (who fall under the Judiciary/Courts) regarding individuals who report they are not citizens of the United States.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the requirement for ballot drop boxes at the Baltimore City centralized booking facility and modifies absentee voting provisions specifically mentioning incarceration as a valid circumstance for absentee voting.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and land use planning; the bill establishes uniform standards for the conduct of municipal elections, which often intersects with the department's role in local government coordination.
The bill repeals the requirement that student voting plans include ballot drop box siting, which directly affects the Commission's oversight of public and private college policies.

As a state-governed institution, Morgan State University is affected by the repeal of requirements regarding student voting plans, specifically the removal of ballot drop box siting requirements on campuses.

The Office of Legislative Audits is responsible for fiscal and performance audits of state agencies; this bill introduces significant new administrative processes (ID issuance, registration audits) that would be subject to future OLA review.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the State Board of Elections regarding the implementation and defense of these new statutory requirements.
As an independent unit of state government, the college's student voting plans would be impacted by the repeal of the requirement to include ballot drop box siting.
The bill's repeal of ballot drop box siting requirements in student voting plans affects the 12 institutions within the University System of Maryland.

The Adjutant General oversees the state's military forces; the bill identifies 'service in the uniformed services' as a qualifying circumstance for absentee voting, which is relevant to personnel management within the Military Department.
Members of the Maryland National Guard are impacted by changes to absentee voting eligibility, specifically the provision allowing absentee voting for those in uniformed services.

The Secretary of State manages the 'Safe at Home' address confidentiality program; the bill mentions specific verification procedures for voters whose personal information has been deemed confidential.

bill_summary: This bill renames the 'Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard' to the 'Clean Energy Portfolio Standard' and updates associated terminology, such as changing 'Renewable Energy Credits' to 'Clean Energy Credits.' Crucially, it expands the definition of 'Tier 2 renewable sources' to include electricity generated by nuclear power plants and small modular reactors, making them eligible for inclusion in the state's clean energy compliance requirements.

The bill may also impact retail electricity rates for consumers based on changes to utility compliance costs.

bill_summary: The Freedom From Monopolies Act repeals various regulations and licensing requirements for retail electricity and gas suppliers, salespersons, and vendors. The bill eliminates price caps and contract duration limits for residential energy suppliers, reduces the maximum assessment the Public Service Commission (PSC) can levy against utilities for its operating costs, and abolishes a specific division within the PSC. It also renames and modifies the purpose of the Education and Protection Fund to focus specifically on retail choice education.
stakeholders: Retail electricity and gas suppliers, public service companies (utilities), residential and small commercial energy consumers, and the Maryland Public Service Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a significant but indeterminate decrease in state revenue due to halving the maximum assessment rate (from 0.50% to 0.25% of gross operating revenues) that the Public Service Commission may charge public service companies to fund its operations. Additionally, potential revenue from civil penalties will decrease as the maximum fine for violations is lowered from $25,000 to $10,000. Administrative expenditures will be impacted by the abolition of a specific PSC division and the subsequent reassignment of staff, though the bill mandates no diminution in pay or benefits for those employees. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary agency affected by this bill. It oversees the licensing of electricity and gas suppliers, manages the newly named Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund, and is responsible for standard offer service transitions. The bill also reduces the PSC's assessment cap and abolishes a specific division within the Commission.

The bill directly impacts the funding of the Office of the People's Counsel (OPC) via the modified public service company assessment. Additionally, OPC is explicitly named as a party involved in customer complaints, licensing investigations, and market status reporting.

The bill affects the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) through its Strategic Energy Planning Office, which is funded by the assessments modified in the bill. The bill also repeals several provisions related to green energy and renewable energy credits which align with MEA's energy policy role.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to consult with the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General before issuing consumer protection regulations. The OAG also maintains enforcement authority over consumer protection violations related to energy suppliers.

The bill repeals specific provisions that allowed the Department of General Services (DGS) to sell energy under certain conditions and removes them from the definition of energy salespersons/vendors under specific sections.
The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for holding the Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund and managing its investments as specified in the bill.

The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the newly named Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund and has a general interest in the fiscal assessments on public service companies.

The bill involves the transfer and reassignment of state employees within the Public Service Commission and modifies state fund structures, which falls under DBM's personnel and fiscal management oversight.

The bill repeals specific requirements for the Education and Protection Fund to address the State's climate commitments under the Environment Article and modifies reporting requirements for renewable energy credits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires electricity suppliers to document the participation levels of minority business enterprises in activities supporting the creation of renewable energy credits, a reporting requirement relevant to this office's mission.

Synopsis: Prohibiting licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, and third parties directed by licensed massage therapists or registered massage practitioners from placing, publishing, or distributing certain advertisements; and requiring that if an advertisement for massage therapy services lists the name of a licensed massage therapist or registered massage practitioner, the name displayed on the advertisement must be consistent with the name of the individual on the Board issued license or registration.
Title: Health Occupations - Massage Therapy - Advertising
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 23

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: This bill prohibits licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, and third parties from advertising massage therapy services that include prostitution, escort services, or sexual services. It bans advertising on websites known for such services and prohibits language implying sexual activity. Advertisements must include the practitioner's full name and license or registration number. The State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners is required to adopt regulations defining prohibited content and establishing procedures for reporting violations.
responsible_party: State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners
stakeholders: Licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, massage therapy businesses, and the general public
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners can adopt the required regulations using existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not affected, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Health Occupations Article concerning massage therapy. The Maryland Department of Health is responsible for regulating health care professionals and providing oversight for the health-related boards and commissions that implement these standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners, which falls under this category of executive bodies, is the primary entity responsible for adopting the required regulations, defining prohibited advertising content, and establishing reporting procedures for violations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions. It would be responsible for advising the Board of Massage Therapy Examiners on the development of regulations and the legal enforcement of advertising prohibitions.

The bill subjects licensees and registrants to disciplinary hearings under the Health Occupations Article for violations. The OAH conducts these impartial hearings for contested cases involving regulatory enforcement by state health boards.

The bill explicitly prohibits advertising for prostitution, escort, and sexual services. As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police may be involved in investigating criminal activities identified through the reporting of these prohibited advertisements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety and criminal justice strategies for the Governor. The bill's focus on eliminating advertisements for illicit services such as prostitution aligns with broader public safety policies and efforts to combat human trafficking.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the department and boards implementing the bill and coordinates the underlying policy initiatives regarding professional standards and public safety.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "full-time equivalent enrollment" in the calculation for State education aid to include the average number of students enrolled in kindergarten through grade 12 on September 30 and May 31 of the prior school year; requiring the State Department of Education to publish online and submit a certain report to certain standing committees of the General Assembly; and applying the Act to the calculation of education funding for fiscal years beginning after June 30, 2027.
Title: Primary and Secondary Education - Funding Accuracy and Full-Time Equivalent Enrollment Count - Alterations and Report (Education Funding Accuracy Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:35 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Primary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Schools
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: This bill alters the definition of 'full-time equivalent enrollment' used to calculate State education aid and local government funding requirements. Instead of using the student enrollment count from September 30 of the prior school year, the calculation will now use the average of student counts from September 30 and May 31 of the prior school year. The bill also requires the Maryland State Department of Education to publish an annual report on its website starting in 2026 detailing county-level enrollment counts, student categories, and per-pupil funding allocations.
stakeholders: K-12 public school students, local school systems, and county governments in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal impact on the State and local governments is indeterminate beginning in fiscal 2028. State expenditures for education aid will fluctuate based on the new enrollment averaging method, which may result in higher or lower funding compared to current law depending on student mobility throughout the school year. Local school systems will see corresponding changes in State revenue, and county governments will face modified minimum maintenance of effort and local share requirements. While an MSDE analysis of historical data suggested a potential 0.1% decrease in statewide enrollment, actual dollar estimates are unavailable because the impact will vary annually and by jurisdiction.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public education system, MSDE is responsible for calculating Full-Time Equivalent (FTE) enrollment and administering State education aid. The bill directly mandates MSDE to change its counting methodology and requires the agency to produce and publish a detailed annual report on enrollment and funding allocations.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal agency and is responsible for developing the annual state budget. The fiscal note indicates that MSDE provides enrollment data to DBM to calculate the funding formulas for the budget, and the bill's change to the counting timeline may impact DBM's statutory deadlines for budget preparation.

The Governor's Office proposes the annual state budget and coordinates policy initiatives. Since education aid is a major component of state expenditures, changes to the foundation formula and enrollment counting directly affect the Governor's fiscal planning and legislative priorities.

The MLDS Center links student and workforce data from partner agencies like MSDE. Altering the definition of FTE enrollment and requiring new student categories (such as 'whereabouts unknown') impacts the data set maintained and analyzed by the Center.

GOPI utilizes performance metrics to ensure state resources are managed effectively. Because education funding is a significant state investment, changes in how its accuracy is measured and reported fall under GOPI's mandate for improving government accountability and service delivery.

OLA is responsible for fiscal and performance audits of state agencies and local school systems. Changes to the funding formulas and the creation of new reporting requirements for education aid would be subject to OLA's auditing and accountability oversight.

Synopsis: Requiring a person that is not V.A. accredited that is seeking compensation for certain services related to veterans benefits matters to enter into a certain written fee agreement with the recipient of the services that complies with certain laws; requiring the fee agreement to contain a certain notice; requiring a certain notice to be given orally and acknowledged in writing; prohibiting the imposition or collection of a certain fee under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Veterans Benefits Matters - Claim Servicers - Requirements
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill regulates individuals or businesses not accredited by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs that charge for assistance with veterans' benefits claims. It requires these entities to use written fee agreements that include specific disclosures regarding the availability of free services, mandates that these disclosures be provided orally, and prohibits charging fees if the claimant dies before the claim is processed. Violations are categorized as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices, subject to civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and a potential one-year ban on providing such services.
responsible_party: Maryland Attorney General and the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families
stakeholders: Veterans, their dependents and survivors, and non-V.A. accredited individuals or businesses providing veterans' benefits services for compensation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a potential revenue increase for the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund through civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation. It also grants the Attorney General enforcement authority under the Consumer Protection Act. Specific total fiscal estimates are not provided as a formal Fiscal Note was not included with the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families (DVMF) as it regulates services related to veterans benefits matters, defines such matters in the context of the department's administration, and mandates that civil penalties be deposited into the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, which the department manages.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) is tasked with enforcing the provisions of the bill, particularly regarding consumer protection and bringing civil actions in District Court for violations related to unaccredited claim servicers.

The bill grants jurisdiction to the District Court to order civil penalties for violations, which involves the judicial branch's operations and workload overseen by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for the oversight of state revenues, including the collection and accounting of civil penalties directed to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund.

The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for the management and protection of state funds, including the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, which will receive revenues from civil penalties established by this bill.

The Department of Budget and Management is relevant due to its role in supervising budget execution and fiscal planning related to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund and the resources required for enforcement by the Attorney General.

Synopsis: Authorizing a campaign finance entity of a member of the General Assembly, under certain circumstances, to make a disbursement from a campaign account to reimburse the member for certain expenses related to a home security system used at the member's primary place of residence; and authorizing a member of the General Assembly who expends personal funds on certain expenses related to a home security system used at the member's primary place of residence to be reimbursed by the General Assembly.
Title: General Assembly - Home Security System Expenses - Campaign Funds and Reimbursement
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/25 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte

bill_summary: This bill allows members of the Maryland General Assembly to be reimbursed for up to $1,000 per term for expenses related to the acquisition, installation, maintenance, or upgrade of a home security system at their primary residence. Members may seek reimbursement either from their campaign finance entity or from the General Assembly using state funds.
responsible_party: Maryland General Assembly and the State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Members of the Maryland General Assembly
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a potential state expenditure of up to $188,000 per four-year term (based on a $1,000 cap for each of the 188 members). It also allows campaign finance entities to disburse up to $1,000 per term for these expenses, which does not impact state funds. Because the formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, specific total state and local expenditure estimates and administrative costs for auditing are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Election Law Article to regulate campaign finance disbursements for home security systems. It requires campaign finance entities of General Assembly members to submit proof of these disbursements to the State Board and specifically authorizes the State Board to audit these transactions.

As the state's chief financial officer responsible for paying state bills, the Comptroller's office would be involved in processing the state-funded reimbursements for General Assembly members authorized under the newly added Section 2-1805 of the State Government Article.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for budget development and supervision. The bill's authorization of new state-funded reimbursements for General Assembly members creates a recurring fiscal impact that must be managed within the state's budget.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the State and provides counsel to the General Assembly and the State Board of Elections. They would be responsible for providing legal guidance on the implementation and enforcement of these new reimbursement and campaign finance laws.

Synopsis: Requiring the General Assembly to organize and hold a Convention to amend the State Constitution if a majority of the votes cast on the question of calling for a Convention, rather than a majority of voters voting at the election, are for the holding of a Convention; and prohibiting any changes or amendments to the State Constitution adopted by the Convention and submitted to the voters of the State from becoming effective unless the majority of votes cast on the question are in favor of the adoption.
Title: State Constitutional Convention - Question on Ballot - Passage by Majority of Votes Cast
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/09 at 2:30 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill proposes an amendment to the Maryland Constitution to change the voting threshold required to call a State Constitutional Convention and to approve changes recommended by such a convention. Currently, these measures require approval from a majority of all voters participating in the general election; this amendment would require only a majority of the votes cast specifically on that ballot question.
responsible_party: Maryland General Assembly and the Governor
stakeholders: Maryland voters and the Maryland General Assembly
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided. The bill mandates that the constitutional amendment be submitted to voters at the November 2026 general election, which will result in administrative costs for ballot preparation and election processing.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering state elections. This bill requires the board to place a constitutional amendment question on the 2026 ballot and would change the threshold they use to certify the results of future constitutional convention votes.

The Governor's Office is responsible for receiving the election returns for the proposed constitutional amendment and, per Article XIV of the State Constitution, the Governor must issue the official proclamation declaring the adoption of the amendment if it passes.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and the General Assembly regarding the legal sufficiency and interpretation of constitutional amendments and the procedures for state conventions.

The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records, including the laws passed by the General Assembly and the executive proclamations regarding constitutional amendments.

Synopsis: Requiring the Secretary of Human Services to establish and maintain a Guardianship Assistance Program to promote the placement and maintenance of children in permanent guardianship homes by providing guardianship assistance to guardians of minor children; establishing the State Foster Youth Ombudsman in the Department of Human Services; requiring the Ombudsman to provide legal expertise in child welfare, custody and guardianship matters, and appeal and due process; etc.
Title: Family Law and Human Services - Guardianship Assistance Program and State Foster Youth Ombudsman - Establishment (Kanaiyah's Law)
Status: In the House - Returned Passed
