bill_summary: Known as Kanaiyah’s Law, this bill requires the Maryland Department of Human Services to establish and maintain a Guardianship Assistance Program (GAP) to provide monetary and medical aid to guardians of minor children, facilitating permanent placements. It also establishes the State Foster Youth Ombudsman within the Department of Human Services to advocate for children in out-of-home care, investigate their complaints, and provide legal expertise in child welfare, custody, and guardianship matters. Furthermore, the bill prohibits placing children in unlicensed settings and mandates criminal history records checks for adults residing in a guardian's home.
stakeholders: Children in the foster care and child welfare system, legal guardians of minor children, youth in out-of-home care, and local departments of social services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $37,500 in fiscal year 2028 and $50,000 annually thereafter to fund the salary and associated costs for the State Foster Youth Ombudsman position, assuming the Department of Human Services repurposes an existing vacant position. If a new position is created instead, annual costs would be at least $154,000. The Guardianship Assistance Program is expected to have no material fiscal impact as it primarily codifies existing departmental regulations. Local government operations and finances are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for child welfare and social services, DHS is mandated by the bill to establish and maintain the Guardianship Assistance Program and host the newly created State Foster Youth Ombudsman within its department. DHS will manage the eligibility, annual reviews, and administration of monetary and medical assistance for guardians.

DBM is the state's central personnel and budget agency. The fiscal note indicates that DHS will need to work with DBM to repurpose a vacant position (PIN) for the Ombudsman and adjust salary levels. Additionally, DBM will be involved in the long-term fiscal planning and budget execution for the new program's general fund expenditures.

The bill impacts juvenile court proceedings by requiring specific directives in orders granting guardianship and setting procedures for guardianship reviews and the reopening of Child in Need of Assistance (CINA) cases based on new criminal history information.

The OAG serves as legal counsel to state agencies like DHS. The bill requires the State Foster Youth Ombudsman to be an attorney admitted to practice in Maryland. The OAG will likely provide legal guidance on the implementation of the new ombudsman's duties, investigative powers, and regulatory frameworks.

The bill involves expanded requirements and checks related to criminal history records for adults living in the homes of guardians. The Maryland State Police is the primary agency for processing and maintaining records for the State of Maryland.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHS is authorized to terminate guardianship assistance if an adult in the household is under criminal court supervision or required to register with a supervising authority. DPSCS manages the Division of Parole and Probation and the registry mentioned in the bill, providing the necessary data for DHS compliance reviews.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD represents indigent children and parents in juvenile court and CINA proceedings. The creation of a State Foster Youth Ombudsman to investigate complaints and advocate for youth in out-of-home care directly overlaps with the legal interests and protections the OPD seeks for its clients.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including DHS. The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law and proposing the state budget that includes the necessary general fund appropriations for the Ombudsman's salary and program costs.

Synopsis: Requiring the Public Service Commission, in a base rate proceeding, to determine a certain equity market return for certain public service companies; and authorizing the Commission to adjust certain rates based on the equity market return.
Title: Investor-Owned Public Service Companies - Base Rate Proceeding - Equity Market Return
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Environment and Transportation; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill requires the Public Service Commission (PSC), during base rate proceedings for investor-owned gas and electric companies, to determine the current average expected 10-year United States equity market return using multiple objective sources. The PSC is authorized to adjust a company's utility rates based on the risks to the company as compared to this determined equity market return.
stakeholders: Investor-owned gas and electric companies and their customers, including the State, local governments, and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Public Service Commission can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on State or local revenues. While the bill may result in changes to gas and electric utility rates for consumers (including the State and local governments), the specific fiscal impact on rates cannot be reliably estimated at this time.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill, as it must determine the equity market return and may adjust utility rates during base rate proceedings for investor-owned gas and electric companies.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in the very base rate proceedings at the Public Service Commission that this bill seeks to modify, directly impacting their advocacy and evidentiary presentations.

As the agency responsible for the operation and maintenance of state-owned facilities and the central procurement of services, the Department of General Services will be directly impacted by any changes in gas and electric utility rates resulting from the bill's implementation.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees the state's budget execution; any significant changes in utility rates resulting from the bill will affect the operational budget requirements for all state agencies.

The Maryland Energy Administration advises the Governor on energy policy and coordinates planning across state agencies; changes to the regulatory framework for utility rate-setting are relevant to their advisory role.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of a "foster care recipient" to mean an individual who resided in an out-of-home placement on or after the individual's 8th birthday rather than 13th birthday for purposes of determining eligibility for a certain tuition exemption.
Title: Higher Education - Tuition Exemption for Foster Care Recipients - Eligibility
Status: In the Senate - Rereferred to Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.

bill_summary: This bill expands the eligibility for tuition and fee exemptions at Maryland public institutions of higher education for foster care recipients. Specifically, it lowers the age from 13 to 8 at which an individual must have resided in an out-of-home placement (for at least one year and subsequently placed into guardianship, adopted, or reunited with a parent) to qualify for the tuition waiver.
responsible_party: Maryland public institutions of higher education, Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC), and the Maryland Department of Human Services (DHS)
stakeholders: Foster care recipients who were in out-of-home placement on or after their 8th birthday, Maryland public four-year universities, and Maryland community colleges.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to decrease state and local higher education tuition revenues, potentially significantly, starting in FY 2027 as more students become eligible for waivers. The exact impact is indeterminate as it depends on enrollment numbers. However, for context, the average annual tuition and fees for full-time resident undergraduates at public four-year institutions is projected at $11,192 for FY 2027. In FY 2024, community college tuition waivers for foster care recipients totaled approximately $529,870 across 222 recipients.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Human Services is the primary agency responsible for out-of-home placements. The bill directly modifies the definition of a 'foster care recipient' based on placement history managed by this department.

As the state's central regulatory board for postsecondary education, this commission oversees tuition waiver programs and receives annual reports from institutions regarding the number of recipients and the financial impact.
The University System of Maryland oversees 12 public institutions that are required to implement these tuition exemptions, and the bill will lead to a direct reduction in their tuition revenue.

As a public university and state agency, Morgan State University is mandated to provide these tuition exemptions to eligible foster care recipients, resulting in decreased tuition revenues and potential increases in enrollment expenditures.
As a public honors college and independent state agency, the college is required to implement the expanded tuition waiver for foster care recipients defined in this bill.

The Maryland Longitudinal Data System links and analyzes data between MSDE and higher education institutions, specifically tracking outcomes for foster youth which informs the state's fiscal and policy analysis of this program.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors the fiscal impact on the state budget, including the significant tuition revenue decreases and increased enrollment costs for state-operated higher education institutions.

The Maryland State Department of Education provides data on foster care graduation rates and GED completions, which are key components of the eligibility criteria for the tuition exemptions modified by this bill.

Synopsis: Altering the Enterprise Zone Program; altering and repealing certain credits, exemptions, and deductions to the State income, motor fuel, sales and use, tobacco, and property taxes; providing an addition modification under the Maryland income tax for the entire amount of certain deductions under the Internal Revenue Code for dividends paid for real estate investment trusts; requiring the Department of Commerce to evaluate the film production activity tax credit and submit a certain report on or before December 1, 2026; etc.
Title: State Tax Credits, Modifications, and Exemptions - Alterations and Repeal

bill_summary: This bill alters, sunsets, or repeals various Maryland tax programs and credits to change state fiscal policy. It terminates the Enterprise Zone Program in 2031 and the One Maryland Economic Development Tax Credit in 2027, while advancing the termination of the biotechnology investment incentive tax credit to 2026. The bill also modifies income tax rules for Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) by disallowing certain dividend deductions, caps property and income tax credits, repeals sales and use tax exemptions for specific industrial machinery and materials, and reduces a tobacco tax exemption for cigarettes brought from out-of-state.
stakeholders: Maryland business entities (specifically those in biotechnology, film production, and cybersecurity), real estate investment trusts (REITs), local governments, motor fuel dealers, and tobacco consumers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill results in a net State fiscal impact of $13,600,000 in FY 2027. This includes approximately $2,000,000 in revenue increases and $11,700,000 in expenditure decreases (primarily through the elimination of funding for the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Tax Credit). Local highway user revenues are expected to increase by at least $300,000 annually. Future years will see varying revenue increases as specific tax credits sunset and carryforward periods expire.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is directly responsible for administering the income, sales and use, motor fuel, and tobacco taxes, all of which undergo significant alterations, credit sunsets, or exemption repeals under this bill.

Commerce is the primary agency responsible for the state's economic development programs, including the Enterprise Zone, One Maryland, BIITC, Film Production, Cybersecurity, and Security Clearance tax credits, all of which are sunset or significantly modified by the bill.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning; this bill has significant quantified impacts on General Fund and Special Fund revenues and expenditures.

MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF), which is impacted by the repeal of motor fuel tax collection discounts and changes to corporate income tax distributions.
The MVA is specifically responsible for the administration and certification of the Class F vehicle registration tax credit, which the bill alters and limits to Maryland-headquartered entities.
The bill impacts tax credits that can be claimed against the insurance premiums tax, requiring coordination with the Insurance Commissioner for certification of eligible credit amounts.

As a modal administration of MDOT, SHA is funded by the TTF and is affected by changes in motor fuel tax revenue and the repeal of sales tax exemptions for road-building materials like bituminous concrete.
The Department of Labor's workforce development missions are linked to economic development programs like One Maryland and Enterprise Zones, which are designed to incentivize job creation.
MDP oversees the designation of Priority Funding Areas (PFAs), which are a prerequisite for Enterprise Zone designations, a program the bill significantly restricts and sunsets.
As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, the Tax Court will likely adjudicate appeals resulting from the sunset of major tax credits and the repeal of longstanding exemptions.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the Comptroller and Commerce and will be involved in interpreting and defending the bill's extensive changes to the tax code.
The Treasurer manages state funds and sits on the Board of Public Works; the bill's impact on state revenues and the management of special funds falls within the agency's financial oversight duties.
The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and the executive branch; this bill represents a major shift in the state's economic development and fiscal policy priorities.
The bill explicitly adds 'boosting tourism' as a statutory purpose of the Film Production Activity tax credit and requires an evaluation of the credit's effectiveness in achieving this goal.
PTAAB hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and exemptions; the bill's limitations and sunsets of Enterprise Zone property tax credits may result in increased appeals.
The bill repeals tax exemptions for construction in 'target redevelopment areas,' which are defined by their participation in MDE's Voluntary Cleanup Program.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office has a vested interest in the state's socioeconomic programs; several of the sunsetting credits target small and minority-owned businesses in the technology and security sectors.
DHCD utilizes Enterprise Zones and economic development incentives as tools for community revitalization and infrastructure projects, which will be affected by the bill's sunset provisions.

MEDCO supports the state's economy through real estate and financing; the repeal of major tax credits like One Maryland and Enterprise Zones alters the financial tools available for large-scale economic projects.

Synopsis: Prohibiting, on and after January 1, 2035, a person from disposing of a mattress in a landfill, subject to certain exceptions; prohibiting, on and after January 1, 2035, a person from disposing of a mattress in an incinerator, subject to a certain exception; requiring certain producers of mattresses sold at retail in the State or a certain representative organization to submit a plan for the establishment of a Mattress Stewardship Program in the Department of the Environment for approval on or before July 1, 2031; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Mattress Stewardship Program in Maryland, requiring mattress producers to develop and fund a statewide system for the collection, transport, and recycling of discarded mattresses. The program is funded by a stewardship assessment fee added to the purchase price of new mattresses, and the bill prohibits the disposal of mattresses in landfills or incinerators beginning in 2035.
stakeholders: Mattress producers, retailers, consumers, local governments, and waste management entities
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $54,800 in FY 2030 and $60,200 in FY 2031 for initial implementation. Starting in FY 2032, the program's oversight costs are intended to be fully offset by special fund revenues from producer plan and report review fees, projected to reach $72,400 by FY 2034. Local governments may experience a decrease in waste management costs due to the diversion of mattresses from landfills and may receive reimbursements for existing recycling efforts, although they will be subject to the stewardship assessment when purchasing new mattresses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, MDE's Office of Recycling is responsible for reviewing and approving mattress stewardship plans, managing annual reports, adopting regulations, and overseeing program compliance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Maryland Correctional Enterprises (MCE), a unit of DPSCS, is a producer of mattresses and will be subject to the bill's assessment, reporting, and stewardship requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board to oversee program implementation and provide recommendations to the Department of the Environment.
The Comptroller or their designee is a member of the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, and the agency is responsible for accounting for the State Recycling Trust Fund.

The Secretary of Health or their designee serves on the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, and the department has a role in determining disposal protocols for mattresses contaminated by biological fluids or toxins.
The Secretary of Commerce or their designee serves on the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, advising on the program's impact on mattress producers and retailers.
The bill mandates that MDE's Office of Recycling coordinate with MES to study and report on the state's progress in diverting mattresses from landfills and incinerators.
The Governor is responsible for appointing several members to the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, including representatives from industry, environmental groups, and the public.
The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for holding and investing the money in the State Recycling Trust Fund, which will receive fees and penalties from the program.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to MDE for the development of regulations and enforcement of the new stewardship and disposal requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The stewardship plan must describe how minority, women, and veteran-owned businesses will be solicited and supported by the Mattress Stewardship Program.

The bill requires the program to provide examples of recycling programs that create jobs for individuals with disabilities and ensures that collection infrastructure is accessible to disabled residents.
As a consumer of mattresses for judicial facilities, the AOC will be subject to the mattress stewardship assessment and is listed as an information source in the fiscal note.
As a state institution with residential facilities, the university will be impacted by the stewardship assessment on mattress purchases.
USM institutions with student housing will incur additional costs due to the mattress stewardship assessment.
DHCD is identified as a stakeholder in the fiscal note regarding the impact on community waste management and residential sectors.
DJS will be impacted as a consumer of mattresses for its residential youth facilities.
DGS manages state-owned facilities and procurement; it will likely oversee mattress purchases affected by the new stewardship assessment.
The bill contains provisions requiring stewardship organization contracts to guarantee livable wages and benefits for workers, which aligns with the department's labor law enforcement role.

stakeholders: Local governments, nonprofit organizations, and residents of Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards

The bill specifies that the Fund consists of investment earnings, and the Treasurer's Office is responsible for managing and investing state funds. The significant increase in the fund's mandated size impacts the Treasurer's custodial and investment management duties for these specific assets.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the building energy performance standards (BEPS) and related regulations originally established under the Climate Solutions Now Act. It eliminates requirements for the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) to develop and enforce standards for covered buildings (commercial, multifamily residential, or State-owned buildings with a gross floor area of 35,000 square feet or more) to achieve specific greenhouse gas emission reductions by 2030 and 2040.
stakeholders: Owners of commercial and multifamily residential buildings with 35,000 square feet or more, State agencies, local governments, and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State special fund revenues for the Maryland Clean Air Fund will decrease by $900,000 annually beginning in FY 2027 due to the repeal of annual reporting fees. Significant additional revenue losses from foregone alternative compliance pathway fees are expected starting in FY 2031. State and local expenditures are expected to decrease, potentially significantly, as agencies and local jurisdictions will no longer be required to fund or perform building retrofits to meet the repealed energy standards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the department's statutory mandate to develop and implement building energy performance standards and eliminates the annual reporting fees and alternative compliance pathway fees that support its operations.

The bill explicitly amends Section 4-211 of the Housing and Community Development Article, modifying the department's program for providing grants and loans for energy conservation projects in multifamily buildings.

The MEA manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which the fiscal note indicates will likely be required to backfill funding for Department of the Environment staff following the loss of building energy reporting fees.

As the agency responsible for managing and maintaining state-owned facilities, DGS is directly impacted by the repeal of energy performance standards for State-owned buildings exceeding 35,000 square feet.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency; the bill impacts state revenues through foregone fees and affects budget execution and the allocation of state personnel assigned to the repealed program.

The bill repeals the requirement for electric and gas companies to provide building-level energy data to owners for benchmarking purposes, removing a regulatory provision previously overseen within the commission's utility oversight.
MDOT operates numerous large-scale facilities, including airport and port terminals and administrative buildings, that qualify as covered state-owned buildings under the standards being repealed.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the executive branch agencies (MDE and DHCD) responsible for implementing or repealing the regulations and standards addressed in this bill.

The USM governs public universities with a large inventory of buildings that meet the 'covered building' criteria; the repeal eliminates significant compliance costs and future retrofitting requirements for these facilities.

As an independent public urban research university and state agency, Morgan State's campus includes several facilities that would have been required to meet the energy performance standards and associated reporting fees.
The college operates as an independent state agency with facilities that were subject to the building energy performance standards and annual reporting requirements being repealed.

As the state's green bank, the center's mission includes financing energy efficiency projects; the repeal of mandatory building performance standards for the commercial and multifamily sectors is likely to reduce demand for its financial products.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget; the bill repeals a major environmental policy previously established under the Climate Solutions Now Act.
The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and serves on the Board of Public Works, which oversees state expenditures and properties affected by the repeal of building standards.
The Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works and manages state funds and property insurance; the repeal affects the management and required upgrades for state-owned assets.

The board oversees significant state expenditures and the management of state property; the bill changes the fiscal and regulatory requirements for state-owned building improvements and capital projects.

Building energy performance standards impact the state's overall energy demand; the OPC's role in representing utility consumers relates to how these changes affect long-term energy costs and utility planning.
The repeal reduces compliance and operational costs for owners of large commercial buildings, which impacts the economic climate and business retention efforts led by the department.
The department regulates health care facilities like assisted living and nursing homes, which were subject to the performance standards and reporting requirements being repealed.
The AOC provides facility support for the Judicial Branch; court-related facilities are often state-owned buildings that were subject to the energy performance and benchmarking requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note identifies a 'meaningful' small business effect; this office is responsible for monitoring socioeconomic procurement and supporting small business interests affected by state regulations.

The Department of Housing and Community Development is a mandated consultant for the study and manages the housing assistance programs whose eligibility criteria are being evaluated.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Electronic Device Producer Responsibility Program, requiring manufacturers of various electronic devices (such as computers, televisions, and cameras) to participate in and fund a statewide system for the collection, recycling, and reuse of their products. Manufacturers must register with the Maryland Department of the Environment, pay registration and review fees, and form producer responsibility organizations to implement plans that provide free collection and recycling services to households, small businesses, and public agencies.
stakeholders: Electronic device manufacturers, electronic device retailers, Maryland households, small businesses (10 or fewer employees), public sector agencies, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by at least $67,800 in FY 2027 for MDE to hire staff for oversight and enforcement, while special fund revenues increase by at least $146,000 through manufacturer registration fees. Future fee revenue is expected to be adjusted by MDE to cover administrative costs. Local governments are expected to benefit from the bill through financial compensation for collection efforts and free electronics recycling for local agencies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary implementing and regulatory agency for the Electronic Device Producer Responsibility Program. It is responsible for reviewing plans, managing registrations and fees, staffing the Advisory Council, and enforcing compliance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Electronic Device Producer Responsibility Advisory Council, a new body within the executive branch tasked with advising the Department of the Environment on the program's implementation and administration.

The Maryland Environmental Service is explicitly designated for a seat on the new Advisory Council and currently manages electronic waste collection sites on behalf of several counties, meaning its operations may be indirectly impacted by the new producer responsibility system.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for the personnel and budget oversight regarding the new natural resources planner and environmental compliance specialist positions identified in the fiscal note as necessary for the program.

The Department of General Services manages state-owned facilities and handles the procurement and disposal of state property, including electronic devices, making it a relevant 'covered entity' and an information source for the fiscal note.

As the state's lead IT agency, DoIT is impacted by the management of electronic waste and is considered a 'covered entity' under the bill, which entitles it to free electronic device recycling services.
The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for holding, investing, and distributing the funds within the State Recycling Trust Fund, which will receive the manufacturer registration and review fees.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to MDE, oversees enforcement actions, and handles legal matters related to the bill's provisions on state antitrust law exemptions and trade secret protections.
The Comptroller's Office is responsible for accounting for the revenues and expenditures of the State Recycling Trust Fund, which receives fees and penalties under this program.

As a large state educational entity and 'covered entity' under the bill, the University System of Maryland is impacted by changes to electronic device disposal and was a primary information source for the fiscal note.
Morgan State University is a 'covered entity' that will be able to utilize the new recycling program free of charge and was consulted as an information source for the bill's fiscal analysis.

The bill references composting standards established by the Secretary of Agriculture and excludes agricultural equipment from the definition of covered electronic devices; the agency also houses the Rural Maryland Council.
The Maryland Department of Health is a 'covered entity' that generates electronic waste and was an information source for the fiscal impact analysis.

The Department of Transportation is a 'covered entity' under the bill; additionally, the bill's definitions exclude electronic components used in motor vehicles, which is relevant to MDOT's oversight.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Secretary of the Environment, who is responsible for the program's administration and the appointment of many Advisory Council members.

The Rural Maryland Council is relevant due to the bill's specific requirements for rural county representation on the Advisory Council and the mandate to ensure collection site convenience for rural residents.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Labor to pay all collected fees to the Comptroller, who is then responsible for distributing those funds into the newly established Sellers of Travel Services Registration Fund.

DBM is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution. The fiscal note indicates a need for a new Executive Director position and a small general fund appropriation in the first year to cover a projected revenue shortfall.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding the drafting of regulations and the enforcement of the new financial security and registration requirements.
The bill and fiscal note specifically state that the new Sellers of Travel Services Registration Fund may be subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in the bill's implementation and must sign the legislation into law. The fund is established within a cabinet-level department.

As the manager of state funds, the Treasurer's Office would be responsible for any investment activities of the new special fund, particularly since the bill mandates that investment earnings be credited to the General Fund.
The fiscal note identifies $25,000 in one-time information technology start-up costs for the Department of Labor to manage the new registration system, which may require coordination with DoIT.
If the Department of Labor takes enforcement actions or denies registrations, contested cases would likely be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges at the OAH.

Synopsis: Prohibiting behavioral health care providers from using artificial intelligence to provide behavioral health care to a patient; authorizing a behavioral health care provider to use a system that employs artificial intelligence in performing administrative support tasks under certain circumstances; and requiring a behavioral health care provider to obtain certain informed consent from patients if the provider uses a certain system that employs artificial intelligence under certain circumstances.
Title: Health Occupations - Behavioral Health Care Providers - Use of Artificial Intelligence
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Health; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Debt Collection -see also- Attachments and Garnishments
Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: House Bill 995 prohibits behavioral health care providers from using artificial intelligence (AI) to perform clinical functions such as assessment, diagnosis, treatment, or therapeutic communication. Providers are permitted to use AI for administrative support tasks, such as scheduling and billing, provided they ensure data security, enter into confidentiality agreements with AI vendors, provide notice to patients, and independently verify AI-generated output. Additionally, providers must obtain informed consent if an AI system could materially affect clinical decision-making or patient-facing services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and health occupation boards
stakeholders: Licensed behavioral health care providers, patients receiving behavioral health services, and health occupation licensing boards
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health can monitor compliance with the bill using existing budgeted resources. While violations are subject to disciplinary action, including potential civil penalties, such revenues are not expected to materially affect State special funds. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for the health occupation boards that license and certify behavioral health care providers. MDH will be responsible for monitoring compliance and the respective boards will handle disciplinary actions for violations of the AI restrictions.

The Department of Information Technology (DoIT) is the principal agency for the state's AI strategy and cybersecurity. The bill references definitions of AI used in procurement and the fiscal note highlights DoIT's role in governing AI policy and assessing high-risk AI systems.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) provides an impartial hearing process for contested cases involving state agencies. It would be responsible for adjudicating appeals from health occupation boards regarding disciplinary actions taken against providers for violating the bill's AI provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office administers mandatory arbitration for medical malpractice claims. If the use of AI by a behavioral health care provider leads to professional negligence or damages, the claim would likely pass through this agency.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to the health occupation boards and the Department of Health. It also oversees consumer protection, which may be relevant given the bill's informed consent and patient notification requirements.

As a regulatory agency within MDH focused on health system planning, informed decision-making, and accountability, this commission is relevant to the integration of new technologies like AI into the healthcare landscape.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy initiatives. The fiscal note highlights the Governor's role in establishing the AI Subcabinet and overall AI governance strategy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This category includes the Governor's AI Subcabinet, which is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as being responsible for adopting policies regarding high-risk AI and overseeing state AI strategies.

The fiscal note appendix mentions the establishment of an AI Evidence Clinic Pilot Program within the AOC to provide expertise on electronic evidence that may have been altered by AI, which could include behavioral health records.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees correctional facilities where behavioral health care is provided to incarcerated individuals. Staff or contracted providers at these facilities must comply with the bill's AI restrictions.
The department provides behavioral health care to youth within the juvenile justice system. Providers operating under DJS authority would be subject to the bill's limitations on AI use.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) oversees public school systems where behavioral health services are provided. The fiscal note also mentions MSDE's own internal initiatives regarding AI use in schools.

The bill's provisions regarding administrative support tasks include billing insurers. The MIA regulates the insurance market and would be interested in how AI restrictions and informed consent impact healthcare liability and claims processing.

This team tests and pilots novel initiatives for the Governor's priorities. Since the bill regulates a frontier technology in the critical area of health services, the team may be involved in analyzing the impact on service delivery.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Department of Assessments and Taxation to notify a person who files a charter document if the Department does not accept the document; requiring the Department to accept a corrected charter document under a certain circumstance; authorizing certain governing bodies of certain corporations to take certain actions without a meeting of the governing body subject to certain conditions;  repealing the authority of certain persons to maintain a suit in a State court; etc.
Title: Corporations and Associations - Revisions
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Corporations -see also- Municipal Corps; Public Corps & Inst
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill updates Maryland's laws for corporations and partnerships. It requires the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) to notify filers of rejected documents and allows a 30-day window for corrections to retain the original filing date. It permits open-end investment companies to take board actions with majority written consent rather than unanimous consent. The bill also simplifies corporate actions taken under federal bankruptcy orders by removing stockholder approval requirements, repeals criminal penalties for officers of unregistered foreign corporations, and establishes default rules for the adoption and amendment of partnership agreements.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland corporations, open-end investment companies, foreign corporations, partnerships, and limited partnerships
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Department of Assessments and Taxation can implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. There is no anticipated material effect on state revenues and no impact on local government finances. The bill repeals a criminal misdemeanor fine of up to $1,000 for officers of unregistered foreign corporations while maintaining a $200 corporate penalty.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT), which is the primary agency tasked with implementing the document notification and rejection protocols established by the bill.
As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller relies on accurate corporate and partnership registration data from SDAT to enforce tax laws and manage revenue collection.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including SDAT, and would be responsible for interpreting the new statutory requirements regarding charter documents and corporate governance changes.
DBM oversees the budget and personnel of SDAT; while the fiscal note suggests SDAT can implement the bill with existing resources, DBM monitors the execution of these administrative changes.

As the state's economic development agency, Commerce is impacted by changes to corporate law that affect the business climate, specifically governance revisions for investment companies and the ease of business formation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note specifically identifies a potential meaningful impact on small businesses, as the bill provides greater certainty in the formation and resubmission of business entity charter documents.

The bill impacts the judicial branch by altering the standing of foreign corporations to maintain suits in state courts and by providing procedures for state entities to carry out federal bankruptcy court orders.
The MIA regulates insurance companies, many of which are organized as corporations or investment-related entities that may be affected by the revised governance and filing provisions.

The Archives is the central depository for permanent government records, including corporate charter documents filed with the state; changes to filing and acceptance dates affect these historical records.

The Tax Court hears appeals from final decisions of SDAT; while often related to assessments, changes to the legal status and registration requirements of business entities provide critical context for their review.

OLA is responsible for auditing SDAT's fiscal and compliance operations, including ensuring the agency follows the new statutory mandates for notifying filers of rejections and correctly backdating resubmitted documents.

The Secretary of State serves as a custodian of state records and manages various business-related registrations; revisions to the treatment of foreign corporations and partnership agreements overlap with their administrative functions.

Synopsis: Modifying the method by which the Commissioner of Labor and Industry determines a prevailing wage rate; and requiring the Commissioner to vacate a certain prevailing wage rate under certain circumstances.
Title: State Finance and Procurement - Prevailing Wage Rate - Calculation
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Government, Labor, and Elections; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Commissioner of Labor and Industry from surveying or using wage data of employees directly employed by investor-owned gas, electric, or combined utility companies when determining prevailing wage rates. Additionally, it requires the Commissioner to vacate and recalculate a prevailing wage rate if a petition for review shows that prohibited wage data was used in the calculation.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry (Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Construction workers, investor-owned utility companies, contractors, subcontractors, and state and local government agencies managing public works projects.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates that the bill has no state or local fiscal impact. Any potential adjustments to prevailing wage rates are expected to be negligible and will not significantly affect the costs of public works projects. The Maryland Department of Labor is expected to implement the bill using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Commissioner of Labor and Industry, who is part of the Department of Labor, with modifying the method for calculating prevailing wage rates and handling petitions to vacate and recalculate those rates.
As the state's primary agency for construction and procurement, DGS manages public works projects that are subject to the prevailing wage laws affected by this bill.
MDOT oversees extensive highway and transit construction projects (through SHA and MTA) that are major users of prevailing wage classifications affected by this legislation.
The IAC oversees public school construction projects, which represent a significant portion of the projects subject to the state's prevailing wage requirements.

The bill relies on definitions for investor-owned gas and electric companies from the Public Utilities Article, which the PSC administers, and the bill affects how wages for projects involving utility infrastructure are determined.
The Maryland Stadium Authority manages its own prevailing wage program for sports and school construction projects, often using wage rates determined by the Commissioner of Labor and Industry.

Although technically exempt from state prevailing wage law, USM often voluntarily complies with prevailing wage requirements for large construction contracts, making the calculation changes relevant to their project costs.
Similar to USM, Morgan State University is exempt but typically follows prevailing wage requirements for its capital construction projects.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Commissioner of Labor and Industry and would be involved in defending or interpreting the new wage calculation methodology and the petition review process.
The Board of Public Works approves the significant state procurement and construction contracts that are subject to the prevailing wage rates modified by this bill.
As a public honors college with independent status, it is mentioned in the fiscal note as an entity associated with prevailing wage law compliance for its construction projects.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to issue a Class 7 micro-brewery license to the holder of a Class B-D-7 license in the 46th alcoholic beverages district, subject to a certain limitation; requiring the Board to establish a standard template for certain memoranda of understanding by January 1, 2027; authorizing certain holders of certain Class D licenses in the 46th alcoholic beverages district to apply for a 7-day sales privilege under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Baltimore City – Alcoholic Beverages – 46th Alcoholic Beverages District
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill makes several modifications to alcoholic beverages laws in Baltimore City, primarily within the 46th alcoholic beverages district. Key provisions include authorizing the Board of License Commissioners to issue Class 7 micro-brewery licenses to certain Class B-D-7 license holders, establishing a standard template for memoranda of understanding (MOU) between license applicants and neighborhood associations, and allowing the transfer of specific licenses between districts. It also creates a 7-day sales privilege for certain Class D licenses subject to a $15,000 fee and food sales requirements, allows for alcohol donations for nonprofit events at a specific location, and extends the expiration dates for several specific licenses to facilitate transfers or renewals.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage license holders in Baltimore City (specifically the 46th and 40th districts), local neighborhood associations, nonprofit organizations, and alcohol manufacturers and wholesalers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or Baltimore City finances or operations according to the fiscal note. However, it establishes a one-time $15,000 fee for Class D license holders in the 46th district who apply for a 7-day sales privilege; these funds are earmarked for the enforcement of required memoranda of understanding. The bill also extends the expiration of specific licenses for renewal or transfer purposes through 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and serving as the state's principal tax collector. This bill modifies alcoholic beverage license categories, fees, and includes requirements regarding the remission of taxes on donated alcoholic beverages.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City is the primary body tasked with implementing the bill's requirements, including issuing Class 7 micro-brewery licenses, establishing a standard template for memoranda of understanding, and adopting tiered penalty regulations. As a permanent regulatory body established by the General Assembly, it falls under this classification.
The Governor's Office is responsible for the final approval and signing of the bill into law, and the bill is formally presented to this office after being passed.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state boards and agencies. It may be required to provide legal guidance to the Board of License Commissioners regarding the new tiered penalty regulations and standard MOU templates mandated by the bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the holder of a Class 9 limited distillery license to manufacture, rectify, or bottle more than one brand of alcoholic beverage; and authorizing the holder to manufacture or rectify up to 31,000 gallons of product of an entity other than the holder.
Title: Alcoholic Beverages - Class 9 Limited Distillery License - Alteration
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Alcoholic Beverages Manufacturing -see also- Breweries; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows the holder of a Class 9 limited distillery license to manufacture, rectify, or bottle more than one brand of alcoholic beverage and authorizes the holder to produce up to 31,000 gallons of product per year for another brand or entity.
stakeholders: Class 9 limited distillery license holders and small distillery businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local operations or finances. Small businesses holding Class 9 limited distillery licenses may see a meaningful increase in revenue from contract distilling and the ability to maintain multiple brands.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller's summary explicitly states that the agency is responsible for regulating the alcohol, tobacco, and motor fuel industries and collecting state revenues. This bill directly alters the Class 9 limited distillery license, which falls under the agency's primary regulatory and revenue oversight duties as described in the summary.

The bill is identified as having a meaningful impact on small business distilleries by expanding their capacity to manufacture multiple brands and providing opportunities for contract distilling. This aligns with the Department of Commerce's mission to stimulate economic growth, attract and expand businesses, and support Maryland's competitive economic position.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and boards. The agency would be responsible for advising the regulatory bodies on the implementation of these statutory changes to the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article and ensuring the new production and branding limits are legally sound.

Synopsis: Requiring, beginning July 1, 2026, the school mapping data produced with funding from the School Mapping Data Program to contain site- specific labeling for bodies of water in the 1-mile radius surrounding the school grounds.
Title: Public Schools - School Mapping Data - Radius of School Grounds
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/07 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Water -see also- Coastal Bays; Riv,Str,Lks; Wastewater; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires that all school mapping data produced with funding from the School Mapping Data Program include site-specific labeling for bodies of water located within a one-mile radius of the school grounds.
responsible_party: Maryland Center for School Safety (MCSS) and the Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC)
stakeholders: Local school systems, public school students and staff, and local, State, and federal public safety agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact is indeterminate. While the labeling requirement can likely be incorporated into future school maps using existing resources from the School Mapping Data Program (which received a $3,000,000 appropriation in the fiscal 2026 budget), state general fund expenditures and local school system expenditures could increase significantly if the bill is interpreted to require the updating of existing school maps.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Center for School Safety (MCSS) administers the School Mapping Data Program, which is directly modified by this bill to include specific labeling requirements for bodies of water.

The IAC is responsible for developing the mapping standards that schools must follow to comply with the School Mapping Data Program and will need to update these standards to reflect the new requirements.

The Maryland Center for School Safety is an independent unit within the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), which oversees the state's public education system and the schools impacted by these mapping requirements.
The fiscal note indicates that the Department of Information Technology works with the IAC to make data available for the creation of these school maps.
The bill has a potential fiscal impact on state general fund expenditures if additional grant funding is required to update existing maps, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies implementing the program and is responsible for the final approval of the legislation and related budget appropriations.

Synopsis: Requiring a police officer who is on duty at a polling place to obey the authority of the State Administrator, the Deputy State Administrator, or a local election director; providing that, in a polling place, certain individuals have the authority to keep the peace and order the arrest of certain persons; requiring a local election director, while serving in a polling place, to protect certain rights of challengers and watchers; etc.
Title: Election Law - Authority at Polling Places, Early Voting Centers, and Counting Centers - Revisions
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: The bill authorizes the State Administrator, the Deputy State Administrator, and local election directors to maintain order, keep the peace, and order arrests at polling places, independent of election judges. It also updates regulations for accredited challengers and watchers, extending their presence to early voting centers, prohibiting them from handling voting equipment, and requiring that their certificates be submitted to local boards before entry. Additionally, the bill modifies who may designate these individuals, replacing groups of voters with political committees and including persons required to file independent expenditure reports.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections and local election directors
stakeholders: Registered voters, political candidates, political parties, political committees, police officers, and election officials
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no effect on State finances and is not expected to directly affect local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for supervising and administering elections in Maryland, the State Board of Elections is directly impacted by the bill, which grants expanded authority to its State Administrator and Deputy State Administrator to keep the peace and order arrests at polling places and counting centers.

The Office of the State Prosecutor investigates and prosecutes criminal offenses related to the electoral process and election laws. The bill specifies the authority to order arrests for breaches of the Election Law Article, which directly relates to the OSP's prosecutorial mandate.

The bill explicitly requires police officers on duty at polling places to obey the orders of the State Administrator, Deputy State Administrator, and local election directors regarding keeping the peace and making arrests, which affects the conduct and command structure of State Police officers assigned to election security.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as legal counsel to the State Board of Elections. It would be responsible for providing guidance on the implementation of these expanded administrative authorities and the legal protections afforded to police officers acting under the orders of election officials.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. This bill involves the administrative authority of the State Administrator and the interaction between executive branch officials and law enforcement during the election process.

Synopsis: Prohibiting certain facilities from involuntarily transferring or discharging a resident to certain housing or before receiving certain confirmations; altering the information required to be included in a certain notice or new notice; requiring that a certain notice or new notice be provided to certain residents at least a certain period of time before an involuntary discharge or transfer; establishing time requirements that apply to the discharge or transfer of a resident if a new notice of involuntary discharge or transfer is provided; etc.
Title: Nursing Facilities - Involuntary Discharge or Transfer
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 24

NarrowSubjects.Name: Long-Term Care -see also- Continuing Care; Nursing Homes
Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

Vulnerable Adults -see also- DevDisab; EldPers; PhysDisab

bill_summary: This bill prohibits nursing facilities from involuntarily transferring or discharging residents to temporary housing such as hotels or shelters and requires that the receiving facility confirms acceptance before a move occurs. It also updates the requirements for involuntary discharge notices to include specific contact information for advocacy organizations and establishes clear timelines for providing new notices and developing post-discharge care plans.
stakeholders: Nursing facility residents, their families and representatives, nursing facility operators, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, Maryland Legal Aid, and Disability Rights Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's requirements can be handled with the Maryland Department of Health's existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on state revenues or local government finances. The financial impact on small business nursing facilities is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary regulatory agency for nursing facilities. The bill requires the Department to prepare and provide standardized notice forms, receive copies of involuntary discharge notices, and adopt regulations to implement the safe, secure, and sustainable environment standards for post-discharge plans.

The Maryland Department of Aging oversees the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program. The bill requires that this program be included in the standardized notice provided to residents and that the Ombudsman receive a copy of every written notice of involuntary transfer or discharge.

The bill details the hearing process for residents appealing an involuntary discharge or transfer, which is conducted by Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) within the Office of Administrative Hearings. The bill specifically establishes notice requirements and timelines that are triggered by ALJ orders.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Department of Aging. They would likely be involved in drafting the required regulations and representing the agencies in matters related to the enforcement of nursing facility discharge standards.

The bill requires discharge notices to include contact information for Disability Rights Maryland for residents with intellectual or developmental disabilities or mental disorders. As the principal agency coordinating services for this population, the department is relevant to the policy goals of ensuring safe transitions for disabled residents.

Synopsis: Requiring the Anne Arundel County Board of Education and the State Board of Elections, in consultation with the State Department of Education, to establish a pilot program in the county schools to prepare students for a career as an election official.
Title: Anne Arundel County Public Schools - Election Official Career and Technical Education Pilot Program

bill_summary: This bill requires the Anne Arundel County Board of Education and the State Board of Elections, in consultation with the Maryland State Department of Education, to establish a career and technical education pilot program in Anne Arundel County Public Schools designed to prepare students for careers as election officials.
responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of Education and the State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Students in Anne Arundel County Public Schools and election administration agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text. However, the bill mandates the creation and implementation of a new pilot program, which will result in administrative and operational costs for the Anne Arundel County Board of Education and the State Board of Elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the State Board of Elections to establish and develop the career pilot program in partnership with the local school board to prepare students for careers as election officials.

The bill mandates that the pilot program be developed in consultation with the Department of Education, which oversees state educational standards, policies, and Career and Technical Education (CTE) programs.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal agency; it would be responsible for overseeing the budget execution and any potential resource allocations required by the State Board of Elections or MSDE for this pilot.
As the body responsible for Maryland's workforce system strategy, this career-focused pilot program aligns with the board's mission to develop innovative workforce solutions and talent pipelines.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments tasked with the pilot and is responsible for proposing the state budget that would provide the necessary funding.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the State Board of Elections and the Department of Education, and would likely review the program for legal sufficiency.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from manufacturing, selling, delivering, holding, or offering for sale in the State food that contains any ingredient or additive that is prohibited for use in food under regulations adopted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or any other federal law or regulation.
Title: Public Health - Prohibited Ingredients in Food
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/25 at 1:00 p.m.

Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the manufacture, sale, or distribution of food containing certain additives, specifically brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben, and Red 3, along with any other substances prohibited by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or federal law. It establishes criminal and civil penalties for violations.
stakeholders: Food manufacturers, distributors, retailers, consumers, and local health departments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health can likely handle enforcement with existing resources. Penalty revenue is not expected to be material. Local government expenditures may increase starting in fiscal 2028 if local health departments require additional staff to inspect food products in licensed food establishments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency responsible for food safety, licensing food processing plants, and enforcing the Maryland Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which this bill directly amends. Its Center for Food Processing handles the relevant inspections and regulatory oversight.

OAG serves as the legal representative for MDH and the state, providing counsel on the implementation of these regulations and representing the state in civil and criminal enforcement actions or appeals related to violations.
The bill establishes criminal and civil penalties for violations, which will be adjudicated within the Maryland court system managed by the AOC.

MDA oversees food quality assurance and regulatory activities for the state's agricultural and seafood industries; the broad definition of food in the bill may impact products under their general oversight.

MFCA manages regional food distribution and wholesale facilities; since the bill prohibits 'holding' or 'delivering' food with specified ingredients, the businesses operating within MFCA facilities must ensure compliance.
MSDE manages school nutrition and food programs for the public education system, which must comply with state laws regarding food ingredients and safety standards.

As the agency responsible for supporting and attracting businesses, the Department of Commerce is relevant due to the impact of the ingredient prohibition on Maryland's food manufacturing and processing sector.

DBM is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution; they would oversee any fiscal impacts or staffing changes required for MDH or local health departments to enforce the new food standards.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementation and coordinates the broader policy initiatives related to public health and consumer safety addressed by the bill.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Human Services, by May 1, 2028, to develop a certain form for the submission of a written report concerning suspected child abuse or neglect for cases in which the victim is currently at least 18 years old; requiring the Department to consult with certain individuals, entities, and the State's Attorney in the process of developing the form; requiring the form to include certain information including, if known, information on whether the accused individual currently has access to children; etc.
Title: Child Abuse and Neglect - Reporting (Survivor Reporting Reform Act)
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/02 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: This bill requires the Department of Human Services (DHS) to develop a standardized form for mandatory reporters to use when reporting suspected child abuse or neglect in cases where the victim is now an adult. The form, which must be developed by May 1, 2028, must include information such as whether the survivor wants an investigation and if the alleged abuser currently has access to children, and it must be accompanied by a document explaining how the reported information will be used.
stakeholders: Adult survivors of child abuse and neglect, mandatory reporters (including health practitioners, police officers, educators, and human service workers), local departments of social services, law enforcement agencies, and State's Attorneys.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Human Services can implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for child welfare and social services, the Department of Human Services is explicitly mandated by the bill to develop the new survivor reporting form, consult with stakeholders, and make the form available to mandatory reporters.

The bill affects educators and schools, who are designated as mandatory reporters under the Family Law Article and will be required to utilize the newly developed form when reporting suspected abuse or neglect involving adult survivors.

Health practitioners and public health agencies are mandatory reporters under the bill; the Department of Health regulates these professionals and will be involved in ensuring they have access to and utilize the new reporting form.

Police officers are mandatory reporters under the statute, and the bill specifically requires the Department of Human Services to consult with law enforcement agencies during the development of the new reporting form.
The bill specifically mentions juvenile detention centers as institutions whose staff members are mandatory reporters required to follow the new reporting protocols for adult survivors.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note clarifies that human service workers, who are mandatory reporters, include parole and probation officers managed by this department.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the Department of Human Services regarding the form's development and its compliance with the Family Law Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety and victim services policy; the bill's focus on survivor reporting reform aligns with its mission to support victim services and develop criminal justice strategies.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Talbot County Board of Education to operate all the schools within the county using a scheduling model that eliminates early dismissal days to allow for less than 180 school days if the minimal hours of attendance are met; and requiring a school operating under a certain scheduling model to provide certain employees an opportunity to make up lost wages.
Title: Talbot County - Public Schools - School Schedule Options
