bill_summary: The Sacred Places Safety Act prohibits the commission of a crime of violence in medical facilities or places of worship. Violators are guilty of a felony and subject to up to 10 years in prison in addition to any penalty for the underlying crime.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Healthcare facility staff and patients, religious congregations, law enforcement, and the Maryland judicial system.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the text. The creation of a new felony penalty of up to 10 years is expected to increase state expenditures for incarceration and judicial proceedings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The judicial branch, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, is responsible for adjudicating the new felony charges created by this bill and overseeing the sentencing phase for violations occurring in medical facilities or places of worship.

The bill defines 'medical facility' using the regulatory and oversight scope of the Maryland Department of Health, including facilities defined in the Health - General Article and those under the authority of local health officers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new felony offense with a potential 10-year prison sentence that may be served consecutively, directly impacting the correctional population and facility management overseen by this department.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the coordination of public safety policy and the state agencies responsible for enforcing the provisions of the Sacred Places Safety Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office is the state's primary coordinating body for criminal justice strategies and public safety policy, making it a key stakeholder in the implementation of new penalties for crimes of violence in sensitive locations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender will be responsible for providing legal counsel to indigent defendants charged with the new felony created by this bill, which significantly increases the potential period of incarceration for their clients.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating crimes of violence and enforcing criminal statutes across the state, including those occurring in medical or religious facilities.

The OAG provides legal guidance to the state on criminal law and represents the state in criminal appeals, making the establishment of a new statutory felony and sentencing enhancement relevant to their prosecutorial and advisory roles.

Synopsis: Establishing that the exercise by the Public Service Commission of its authority is an essential government function; altering the duties of the Commission and the Executive Secretary of the Commission; providing for the designation of a certain employee as Deputy Executive Secretary of the Commission; requiring the Commission to submit certain information to the Department of Budget and Management each year, keep certain records, and submit to certain audits; etc.
Title: Public Service Commission – Administrative Operations and Personnel Matters (Public Service Commission Flexibility Act)
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Environment and Transportation; Withdrawn

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

NarrowSubjects.Name: Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill grants the Public Service Commission (PSC) greater administrative autonomy by establishing it as an essential government function and requiring it to create an independent personnel management system separate from the State Personnel Management System. It exempts the PSC from most State procurement laws and all State and local taxation, expands the duties of the Executive Secretary, and requires annual independent audits of the commission's financial accounts.
stakeholders: Employees of the Public Service Commission, regulated public utility companies, and the Maryland Department of Budget and Management.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State special fund expenditures increase by a net of $100,600 in FY 2027. This figure accounts for the addition of three human resources positions at the PSC ($325,892 as introduced in the FY 2027 budget) to manage the new independent personnel system, offset by $192,810 in savings from the commission no longer utilizing the Department of Budget and Management's (DBM) shared services. Consequently, DBM reimbursable revenues and expenditures decrease by $192,810 annually starting in FY 2027. The bill also exempts the PSC from State and local taxation and provides procurement flexibility, which may impact operational efficiency.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary subject of the bill, the Commission is granted significant administrative flexibility, including the establishment of an independent personnel management system and exemption from most state procurement laws.

The bill removes Commission employees from the State Personnel Management System (SPMS) overseen by DBM and transitions the Commission's budget process to informational status only, resulting in a loss of reimbursable revenue and oversight.

The bill exempts the Commission from most state procurement laws; however, exempt agencies typically must still have their procurement policies and procedures approved by the BPW to ensure fiscal integrity.
The bill removes DGS oversight of the Commission's procurements, which currently applies once certain thresholds are met, and exempts the Commission from central procurement authority.
The bill explicitly states that the Commission is subject to audit and examination of its accounts and transactions by the OLA at any time.

The bill mandates that the Commission collaborate with the Office of Security Management and submit cybersecurity reports to the State Chief Information Security Officer, both of which are within DoIT.

The bill exempts the Commission from state and local taxation, which falls under the Comptroller's jurisdiction as the state's principal tax collector, and the Comptroller also serves on the Board of Public Works.

The Commission is required to establish its own personnel management system, which may affect collective bargaining and grievance procedures for its employees, who remain under PERB's general jurisdiction for state workers.
The bill defines the Commission's authority as an essential government function and clarifies its status as an independent unit within the Executive Department.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: While the bill exempts the Commission from general procurement law, it explicitly maintains the Commission's obligation to follow Title 14, Subtitle 3 regarding the Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) Program, which GOSBA monitors.
The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and would likely advise the Commission and DBM on the legal transition to an independent personnel and procurement system.

The bill references statutory requirements for record destruction and the role of the Executive Secretary in keeping Commission records, which falls under the Archives' oversight of government records of permanent value.

Synopsis: Altering eligibility for certain services and programs offered by the State Tax Sale Ombudsman to include certain persons acting on behalf of a deceased homeowner or an heir or a legatee of a deceased homeowner; establishing a Legacy Protection Program administered by the Ombudsman to allow heirs who inherit a dwelling to become the record title holder of the dwelling, prevent tax sales of dwellings inherited by heirs, and allow heirs to remain in their homes; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Legacy Protection Program to assist heirs who inherit a home in becoming the record title holder, thereby preventing tax sales and helping them stay in their homes. It expands the authority of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman to assist estates and heirs, creates a Legacy Protection Fund to provide legal assistance and probate grants, and allows certain heirs to claim homeowners' and homestead property tax credits for up to three years even if they are not yet listed as the record title holder.
responsible_party: State Tax Sale Ombudsman within the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
stakeholders: Heirs and legatees of deceased homeowners residing in inherited dwellings, legal services organizations, and county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by 250,000 dollars annually and special fund revenues and expenditures increase by 750,000 dollars annually starting in fiscal year 2028 for the Legacy Protection Program. County governments must collectively pay 500,000 dollars annually to the fund. State and local property tax revenues may decrease starting in fiscal year 2027 due to expanded eligibility for property tax credits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the State Tax Sale Ombudsman to collaborate with the Registers of Wills to develop probate guides. Furthermore, the program provides grants for probate fees and inheritance taxes, which are administered or collected by the Registers of Wills.

DBM is responsible for the state budget process, including the $250,000 mandated appropriation for the Legacy Protection Fund. Additionally, the State Tax Sale Ombudsman is a member of the management service of the State Personnel Management System, which DBM oversees.

The Governor is required by the bill to include a mandated appropriation of $250,000 in the annual budget for the Legacy Protection Fund. The Governor also oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the program.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the newly established Legacy Protection Fund and managing the accrual of interest earnings related to state funds as specified in the bill.

The State Treasurer is responsible for holding, investing, and distributing the money within the Legacy Protection Fund, and coordinates the allocation of interest on state money as affected by this legislation.
The bill's focus on the probate process for heirs to become record title holders involves the judicial system, specifically the Orphans' Courts for which the AOC provides central support.

The bill modifies eligibility and application procedures for the Homeowners' and Homestead property tax credits; the PTAAB is the agency responsible for hearing appeals regarding disputes over these specific tax credits.

The bill's primary goal is to prevent tax sales and allow residents to remain in their homes, which aligns with the mission of the Department of Housing and Community Development to ensure access to safe, secure housing and community revitalization.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the implementing departments regarding the establishment of the Legacy Protection Program, the grant awarding process, and the management of the new special fund.
The Ombudsman is authorized to establish grant eligibility criteria that prioritize elderly heirs, a population directly served and protected by the Department of Aging.

The bill allows the Ombudsman to prioritize low-income and disabled heirs for grants, making the bill relevant to the Department of Disabilities' mission to improve services for residents with disabilities.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Comptroller to settle a claim of the State that is in arrears, regardless of how long the claim has been in arrears, under certain circumstances.

Status: In the House - Returned Passed

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Comptroller of Maryland to settle a State claim against a business entity that has permanently ceased operations regardless of how long the claim has been in arrears, effectively removing the two-year waiting period required for other types of settlements.
stakeholders: Business entities that have permanently ceased operations with outstanding State debt, the Comptroller's Office, and local jurisdictions receiving shared tax revenues.
fiscal_impact_summary: State tax revenues (general and special funds) are projected to increase by approximately $250,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. General fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office will increase by $74,100 in fiscal 2027 for staff to process additional settlements, rising to $98,500 by fiscal 2031. Local income tax and highway user revenues may also see an indeterminate increase.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Comptroller direct authority to settle state claims in arrears for businesses that have permanently ceased operations. The fiscal note explicitly identifies a fiscal impact on the Comptroller's Office, including a potential increase in revenue and the need for a new revenue administrator position to handle the increased volume of settlement claims.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is affected by the bill's impact on state general fund revenues and the budgetary requirement for an additional personnel position within the executive branch to implement the bill's provisions.

The fiscal note indicates that settlements of corporate income tax claims will affect the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) and expenditures for local highway user revenue grants, which are managed under the multi-modal transportation network overseen by MDOT.

The bill requires settlement sums to be paid into the State Treasury. As the chief financial agency responsible for receiving and depositing state funds, the Treasurer's Office is directly involved in the fiscal workflow established by this legislation.

The bill stipulates that the Comptroller must be satisfied that a claim cannot be collected through 'legal process' before settling. The OAG, as the chief legal officer, provides counsel to state agencies regarding the feasibility of legal collection and represents the state in related matters.

The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies authorized to settle these claims and is responsible for the overall fiscal planning and executive branch operations impacted by the bill's revenue and expenditure changes.

Synopsis: Authorizing pharmacists, under certain circumstances, to prescribe, administer, and dispense certain drugs or devices and perform and interpret certain laboratory tests; repealing provisions establishing and governing the Nonoccupational Postexposure Prophylaxis (nPEP) Standing Order Program; and authorizing the Maryland Department of Health to establish certain statewide written protocols relating to the treatment of minor conditions and the prevention and treatment of human immunodeficiency virus.
Title: Health Occupations - Pharmacists - Minor Conditions and HIV Prevention and Treatment (Rapid Testing and Preventive Care Act)
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Finance

NarrowSubjects.Name: Medical Conditions -see also- AIDS; COVID-19; rabies

bill_summary: This bill authorizes pharmacists to order tests for and treat certain minor medical conditions, including influenza, strep throat, and COVID-19, under protocols established by the Maryland Board of Pharmacy. It also repeals the Nonoccupational Postexposure Prophylaxis (nPEP) Standing Order Program, instead authorizing the Maryland Department of Health to create statewide protocols for HIV prevention and treatment medications.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, pharmacy students, and patients seeking treatment for minor conditions or HIV prevention services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by $155,000 in FY 2027, comprising $42,100 in general funds for protocol development and $112,800 in special funds for Board of Pharmacy oversight and staffing. Special fund expenditures continue annually, reaching $146,700 by FY 2031, which may be offset by increased licensing fees. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary implementing agency. The bill authorizes the Department to establish statewide protocols for HIV prevention and treatment, and the State Board of Pharmacy (an agency within MDH) to establish protocols for minor conditions. The fiscal note also identifies a direct increase in MDH expenditures for personnel to implement these protocols.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Board of Pharmacy. It will be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new statewide protocols and assisting in the drafting of regulations required by the bill.

The bill impacts health insurance coverage for drugs and services provided by pharmacists. The MIA regulates the insurance market and must ensure that carriers comply with state laws regarding coverage and the prohibition of prior authorization for certain treatments like HIV postexposure prophylaxis.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency. The bill has a notable fiscal impact requiring the addition of both general fund and special fund positions (contractual and part-time staff) at MDH and the Board of Pharmacy.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access to care. This legislation directly impacts healthcare access by significantly expanding the clinical scope of practice for pharmacists across the state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives. This bill represents a significant shift in public health policy and requires the Governor to propose the associated funding increases in the state budget.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Health Care Commission and the Maryland Medical Assistance Program jointly to study the impact of requiring the Maryland Medical Assistance Program to provide reimbursement for room and board services provided by a hospice house; and requiring the Maryland Department of Health to report its findings to the Senate Finance Committee and the House Health Committee by December 1, 2026.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Health Care Commission and the Maryland Medical Assistance Program to jointly study the impact of providing Medicaid reimbursement for room and board services at hospice houses. The study must analyze potential cost savings associated with hospice care, projected fiscal impacts, and clinical outcomes such as hospital readmission rates and emergency department utilization, with a final report due by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Maryland Medical Assistance Program enrollees, hospice house providers, and the Maryland Department of Health
fiscal_impact_summary: State Medicaid expenditures increase by up to $52,000 in FY 2027 only for contractual services required to complete the study. These costs are expected to be split equally between state general funds ($26,000) and federal funds ($26,000), with federal fund revenues increasing accordingly. bill_summary: House Bill 1153 prohibits health insurance carriers and managed care organizations from downcoding medical claims—unilaterally changing service codes to lower-paying ones—without a clinical documentation review. The bill requires carriers to provide written notice and justification to health care providers before downcoding, allows providers to appeal these decisions, and mandates that final downcoding determinations be made by board-certified or eligible physicians. Additionally, it establishes a fine of up to $10,000 per violation and requires carriers to report downcoding data to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Commissioner and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Health care providers (including physicians, hospitals, and freestanding medical facilities), health insurance carriers, nonprofit health service plans, health maintenance organizations (HMOs), managed care organizations (MCOs), and participants in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill establishes a fine of up to $10,000 for each violation. Financial implications likely include increased administrative costs for the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Department of Health, as well as potential increases in reimbursement expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and state-regulated health plans due to restricted downcoding practices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of health insurance in Maryland, the Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the new prohibitions on downcoding, collecting quarterly reports from carriers on downcoding activities, and administering the fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

The bill explicitly amends the Health - General Article to apply the new downcoding protections to Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) within the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), making the department responsible for oversight of these standards within the state's Medicaid system.

The bill classifies final decisions to downcode a claim leading to nonpayment as 'coverage decisions' under Title 15, Subtitle 10D of the Insurance Article, which are subject to the administrative appeal process often adjudicated by this office.

The commission's role in improving access to health care and increasing accountability in the health system is relevant to regulations that impact provider reimbursement and the financial viability of health services.

bill_summary: This bill limits the use of restrictive housing (solitary confinement) in Maryland correctional facilities by redefining it as confinement for 20 or more hours a day. It restricts placement to a maximum of 15 consecutive days and 20 total days within a 60-day period, while requiring at least 4 hours of out-of-cell time daily. Crucially, the bill prohibits placing members of 'vulnerable populations'—including youth under 22, seniors over 55, pregnant individuals, and those with mental or physical disabilities—in restrictive housing for any duration. The Correctional Ombudsman is tasked with monitoring implementation and reporting results in 2028 and 2030.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals (particularly youth, seniors, and those with disabilities), correctional facility staff, and the Correctional Ombudsman.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Financial implications include potential increases in state and local expenditures for staffing to facilitate the mandated 4 hours of daily out-of-cell time, facility modifications to provide less restrictive environments, and administrative costs for the Correctional Ombudsman to conduct reviews and surveys.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary department responsible for managing state correctional facilities and pretrial detention centers, this bill directly impacts their core operations, housing protocols, and staffing requirements regarding restrictive housing.

The bill regulates the use of restrictive housing for minors and individuals under the age of 22, directly impacting the department's management and rehabilitation of youth within the juvenile justice system.

The bill establishes vulnerable population categories based on mental illness, developmental disabilities, and serious medical conditions, requiring health assessments and clinical treatment plans that involve coordination with health officials.

The mandate to provide at least 4 hours of out-of-cell time and the prohibition of restrictive housing for various populations will likely require significant changes in staffing levels and operational budgets.

The bill specifically designates individuals with various types of disabilities (mental, developmental, physical, and sensory) as vulnerable populations, aligning with the department's mission to ensure inclusive and integrated services.

Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:35 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to authorize the General Assembly to lower the voting age to 16 for Howard County Board of Education elections. If approved by voters in the 2026 general election, the bill would allow individuals at least 16 years old to vote specifically for members of the Howard County Board of Education.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections and Howard County Board of Elections
stakeholders: 16 and 17-year-old residents of Howard County, the Howard County Board of Education, and Howard County voters
fiscal_impact_summary: If the constitutional amendment is approved, State general fund expenditures and Howard County expenditures are each estimated to increase by $149,000 in FY 2027 for one-time programming and pollbook software modifications. In subsequent years, costs for additional ballots are expected to increase by less than $3,000 per election for both the State and Howard County, with the county also facing unquantified costs for personnel and equipment testing.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for supervising and administering elections, the State Board of Elections is the primary entity affected by the bill. The fiscal note indicates the agency will incur significant costs for programming changes to the Agency Election Management System, the voter registration system, and pollbook software to accommodate voters under age 18 in Howard County Board of Education elections.

The bill proposes a constitutional amendment. Under the Maryland Constitution and Section 4 and 6 of the act, the Governor is responsible for receiving the election returns and issuing a proclamation declaring the amendment adopted if ratified by the voters.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact on the state's general fund, requiring an estimated $149,000 in FY 2027 for IT and software modifications. DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and fiscal planning for the state.

The bill requires modifications to the Agency Election Management System (AEMS) and other statewide voter registration databases. DoIT oversees the state's information technology strategy and infrastructure, which includes these centralized systems.

The bill concerns the election of members to the Howard County Board of Education. MSDE oversees local school systems and maintains a general interest in the governance and selection of local boards of education.

The Secretary of State is the custodian of official records, including laws and executive orders. The agency is involved in the processing and recording of constitutional amendments and election certifications.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor, the General Assembly, and state agencies like the Board of Elections. It would likely review the legality of the constitutional amendment and the implementation of the new voting eligibility rules.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Public Service Commission to require a water company, sewage disposal company, or water and sewage disposal company to adopt a certain limited-income mechanism subject to the approval of the Commission; and requiring the Commission to study the feasibility of requiring certain companies to adopt a limited-income mechanism to benefit limited-income customers and to report its findings to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
Title: Water Companies, Sewage Disposal Companies, and Water and Sewage Disposal Companies - Limited-Income Mechanisms
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water
Water -see also- Coastal Bays; Riv,Str,Lks; Wastewater; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to study the feasibility of requiring water and sewage disposal companies to implement limited-income mechanisms to assist low-income customers. Effective July 1, 2027, the PSC is authorized to require these companies to adopt such mechanisms—including programs, credits, or special rates—to benefit customers with incomes at or below 175% of the federal poverty level, or 200% for customers aged 67 and older.
stakeholders: Privately owned water and sewage disposal companies, eligible limited-income residential customers, and other utility ratepayers including local governments and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill can be implemented using the Public Service Commission's existing budgeted resources. There is no material effect on State expenditures or revenues. However, utility rates for non-limited-income customers (including residential, local government, and small business users) may increase as early as fiscal 2028 to fund the mechanisms if they are adopted by the companies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Public Service Commission (PSC) to study the feasibility of limited-income mechanisms for water and sewage companies, authorizes them to require these mechanisms, and expands their evaluation criteria for utility rates.

The Office of the People's Counsel is the statutory advocate for residential utility consumers, including those of private water and sewage services. This bill directly impacts utility rate structures and assistance mechanisms for the consumers they represent.

The bill explicitly requires the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP), which is administered by the Department of Human Services, to certify eligible limited-income customers for participation in these utility mechanisms if required.
The bill specifies that eligible customers may also participate in assistance programs offered by the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) and requires coordination of benefits.
The Public Service Commission is required to report its study findings on the feasibility of these limited-income mechanisms to the Governor by December 1, 2026.

Synopsis: Requiring certain apprenticeship programs utilized in certain State procurements to have at least a 25% completion rate, as determined by the Maryland Department of Labor.
Title: State Procurement - Apprenticeship Program Accountability and Completion
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires apprenticeship programs used for State procurement contracts to maintain a completion rate of at least 25% once they have graduated at least one cohort. The requirement applies to 'covered procurements' valued at $1,000,000 or more, prevailing wage public works worth $250,000 or more, and other public works valued at $500,000 or more. The Maryland Department of Labor is responsible for verifying these completion rates, and contractors who do not utilize a qualifying program must pay into the State Apprenticeship Training Fund.
stakeholders: Contractors and subcontractors on State and local public work projects, registered apprenticeship program sponsors, and State procurement units.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State special fund revenues will increase beginning in FY 2027 as more contractors may pay into the State Apprenticeship Training Fund (SATF) as an alternative to using an apprenticeship program that meets the new criteria; however, a specific estimate is not feasible. Additionally, project costs for State and local governments may increase if the bill reduces the number of eligible bidders or offerors for specified contracts. The Maryland Department of Labor and other State agencies can implement the bill with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for calculating and verifying the 25% completion rate for apprenticeship programs, managing the State Apprenticeship Training Fund, and enforcing the bill's requirements.
DGS houses the Chief Procurement Officer, who is tasked with adopting regulations for 'covered procurements' and managing state construction projects impacted by these apprenticeship standards.
The Secretary of Information Technology must be consulted by the Chief Procurement Officer regarding 'covered procurements' related to IT contracts under Title 3.5.
MDOT oversees massive public works and infrastructure projects (highways, transit, etc.) that utilize state funds and are subject to the bill's apprenticeship completion requirements.
The Board approves significant state procurements and contracts, which will now be subject to these new accountability and completion standards for apprenticeship programs.
The Comptroller is explicitly tasked with accounting for the State Apprenticeship Training Fund and serves on the Board of Public Works which oversees affected contracts.
The State Treasurer is explicitly tasked with holding the State Apprenticeship Training Fund and serves on the Board of Public Works.
The Authority plans and manages large-scale construction projects using state capital funds, making their contracts subject to the new apprenticeship completion rate mandates.
The System and its member institutions frequently manage capital construction projects funded by the state budget that are subject to these apprenticeship standards.
The IAC oversees public school construction projects that use state funds and typically involve the use of apprentices in the building trades.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency overseeing state budget execution and procurement policies, which are altered by these apprenticeship requirements.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies on procurement law and would be responsible for representing the state in enforcement or compliance litigation.
The bill's definition of 'public work' specifically includes infrastructure like waterworks and sewage disposal plants, which are regulated or overseen by MDE.
As a state agency with its own board, Morgan State manages capital projects subject to the bill's procurement and apprenticeship requirements.
As a public honors college, St. Mary's manages construction and procurement activities that are subject to these apprenticeship completion standards.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and procurement policy, and the Governor serves on the Board of Public Works which approves affected contracts.
The Commission is mentioned in the definition of 'public work' regarding structure or work performed by public service companies under their order.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a motor vehicle dealer from delivering a motor vehicle for which two registration plates are required to a buyer or lessee unless the motor vehicle has a certain front registration plate display mechanism or the buyer or lessee signs a written statement acknowledging declined installation of the display mechanism; requiring a motor vehicle dealer to submit certain information on declined installation of a certain front registration plate display mechanism to the Motor Vehicle Administration; etc.
Title: Motor Vehicles - Dealers - Front Registration Plate Display
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/01 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
License Plates -see also- Motor Vehicle Registration
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill prohibits motor vehicle dealers from delivering new vehicles that require two registration plates unless the vehicle is equipped with a front registration plate mounting hardware or display mechanism. Alternatively, a buyer or lessee may sign a written disclosure statement acknowledging they declined the installation, understand that Maryland law requires a front plate, and are aware that failure to display the plate is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500. Dealers must submit these signed statements to the Motor Vehicle Administration on a monthly basis.
stakeholders: Motor vehicle dealers, buyers and lessees of new motor vehicles, and the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration
fiscal_impact_summary: The Motor Vehicle Administration can implement the bill's requirements with existing budgeted resources. While specific dollar estimates are unavailable, the bill may result in an indeterminate decrease in traffic fine revenue due to improved compliance and a potential increase in toll collection revenue by improving the Maryland Transportation Authority's ability to identify vehicles via camera. Failure to display a front plate remains a misdemeanor subject to a fine of up to $500.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) with developing the required disclosure statement for dealers, receiving monthly reports or submissions from dealers regarding buyers who decline front plate hardware, and adopting regulations to implement the new statutory requirements.

As the parent department for the MVA, MDOT is responsible for the overall implementation of transportation laws. Additionally, the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA), a unit within MDOT, is noted in the fiscal note as having a potential impact on toll collection revenues if the bill leads to increased compliance with front plate requirements.

The MDTA relies on front registration plates for toll enforcement via camera systems. The bill's success in increasing the number of vehicles with front plates could improve toll collection accuracy and revenue.

The bill requires the MVA to adopt regulations regarding the use and disclosure of the signed statements to law enforcement for the enforcement of registration plate display laws. The State Police are the primary agency enforcing these traffic laws.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the MVA in developing the new regulations and ensuring the disclosure statements meet constitutional and statutory requirements, especially regarding the use of collected data for law enforcement.
The MVA may require support from DoIT to manage the monthly digital or manual submission of written statements from dealers and the subsequent storage and disclosure of that data to law enforcement.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for various state agencies, including the MVA. If the MVA pursues regulatory enforcement actions against dealers for failing to comply with these reporting requirements, the OAH would likely handle the appeals.

The bill text specifically mentions the Department of Human Services as an entity that is excluded from the definition of a 'dealer' when transferring vehicles under certain programs, clarifying their regulatory standing under the amended law.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing this bill and is responsible for signing the legislation into law.
DBM monitors the fiscal impact of legislation and the execution of the state budget, including potential changes to traffic fine revenues mentioned in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Department of Health to replace the State Medicaid Management Information System mainframe with a modular system.
Title: Department of Information Technology - Workgroup on the Medicaid Management Information System Mainframe System Replacement
Status: In the Senate - Rereferred to Education, Energy, and the Environment and Finance

NarrowSubjects.Name: General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte
Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill requires the Department of Information Technology to convene a workgroup to oversee and assist the Maryland Department of Health in replacing the outdated Medicaid Management Information System (MMIS) mainframe system. The replacement system must be implemented by July 1, 2029, and must improve payment accuracy, security, and performance. The workgroup is required to submit quarterly progress reports and annual activity reports to several legislative committees until the transition is complete.
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, Department of Information Technology, Department of Human Services, Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, Office of the Comptroller, and health insurance policy experts.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Information Technology and other participating state agencies can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. While the bill facilitates the procurement and transition to a new Medicaid Management Information System, it does not directly allocate specific funds for the system itself; however, decisions made by the workgroup may influence future system costs. A 2008 estimate for the system replacement was approximately $111,000,000, but no current funding for the replacement has been requested beyond project planning funds approved for fiscal year 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of Information Technology to convene and lead the workgroup responsible for overseeing the Medicaid Management Information System (MMIS) mainframe replacement.
The MMIS is the primary system for Maryland's Medicaid program, which is managed by MDH. The department is a mandated member of the workgroup and the primary entity responsible for the transition.
The Department of Human Services is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.
The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.
The Comptroller of Maryland is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new workgroup composed of state officials and experts to coordinate interagency work on a specific technological modernization project.

As the state's central procurement authority, DGS is identified as an information source for the fiscal note and will be involved in the competitive bidding and acquisition process for the replacement system.
The Board of Public Works will likely be required to approve the final, high-value procurement contract for the replacement of the state's MMIS mainframe.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the funding and execution of major state IT capital projects such as the MMIS modernization.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Department of Education to develop a model sexual abuse and sexual misconduct response policy that includes, at minimum, certain components; requiring each local school system to adopt a  response policy based on the model policy developed by the Department on or before September 1, 2027, and to post in a conspicuous place on its website a link to a certain centralized statewide resource platform; etc.
Title: State Department of Education - Sexual Abuse and Sexual Misconduct Model Response Policy - Requirements
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Senate Rules

Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop a model sexual abuse and misconduct response policy for local school systems. Each local school system must adopt its own response policy based on this model by September 1, 2027. These policies must include communication plans, electronic record retention for at least one year, and a structured after-action review process for serious incidents. Additionally, school systems must notify parents of credible allegations of misconduct and maintain a centralized resource platform link on their websites.
stakeholders: Public school students, parents and guardians, local school system employees, contractors, volunteers, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education can develop the model policy and resource platform using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State revenues. Local school systems will face increased legal and programmatic expenditures starting in fiscal 2027 to implement the required policies and conduct reviews. Specific expenditure estimates provided in the fiscal note include approximately $265,000 annually for Prince George’s County Public Schools and $160,000 annually for St. Mary’s Public Schools for additional staffing and legal risk management, while other sampled counties expect to absorb costs within existing budgets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. It is tasked with developing the model sexual abuse and misconduct response policy and the centralized statewide resource platform.

As an independent unit within MSDE focused on school safety, the Center is directly involved in developing and delivering the resources, training, and technical assistance necessary to implement safety-related policies in schools.
The bill explicitly requires the record retention requirements and guidelines within the model policy to be developed in collaboration with the State Archives.
The bill requires coordination with child protective services units, which are administered by DHS, and addresses the reporting and investigation of child abuse involving school employees.
The bill's model policy must address coordination with law enforcement agencies regarding investigations and allow for law enforcement to request delays in public communication for serious incidents.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MSDE and will likely be involved in reviewing the model policy for compliance with state law and constitutional protections.

The bill directly aligns with the office's mission to promote the well-being and safety of Maryland's children by establishing standardized protocols for responding to sexual abuse in educational environments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety, GOCPP may be involved in the interagency collaboration required to develop the model response policy, particularly regarding criminal justice implications.

Synopsis: Authorizing Howard County to decrease the maximum speed limit to not less than 15 miles per hour on highways after performing an engineering and traffic investigation; and prohibiting Howard County from implementing a new speed monitoring system to enforce speed limits on highways on which the speed limit has been reduced under the Act.
Title: Howard County - Highways - Speed Limits Ho. Co. 8-26
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/25 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Howard County to lower speed limits on its highways to a minimum of 15 miles per hour, provided an engineering and traffic investigation is conducted first. It also prohibits the county from installing new speed monitoring systems (speed cameras) on any section of a highway where the speed limit has been reduced under this specific authority.
stakeholders: Howard County residents and motorists
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may increase minimally from speeding citations. Howard County expenditures will increase to the extent that engineering and traffic investigations are performed. Local revenues may increase if speed limits are reduced on highways where speed cameras are already in operation; however, the bill prohibits the installation of new speed monitoring systems on these road segments. Specific dollar estimates for these impacts are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency for the State Highway Administration (SHA), MDOT oversees the state's multimodal transportation network. The bill directly impacts highway speed limit regulations which fall under MDOT's broad policy and operational scope.

SHA is the primary agency responsible for approving speed limit alterations made by local authorities on State highways. The fiscal note explicitly mentions that any alteration of a maximum speed limit by Howard County on a part of a State highway is not effective until approved by SHA.
The bill may lead to an increase in speeding citations if speed limits are lowered. These citations are adjudicated in the District Court, which is managed by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle laws and traffic safety on state highways. Lowering speed limits in Howard County would affect their enforcement operations and potentially increase the volume of manual citations issued.

The Comptroller is responsible for receiving excess revenues from local speed monitoring systems if the balance exceeds 10% of a county's total annual revenue. While the bill prohibits new systems, it allows existing ones to continue, which could impact revenue flows handled by the Comptroller.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Department of Transportation and the State Highway Administration, and would be responsible for advising on the implementation and legal compliance of speed limit changes and enforcement prohibitions.

Synopsis: Expanding the authorization to place and use speed monitoring systems on highways in Howard County to include U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard).
Title: Howard County - Speed Monitoring Systems - Expansion of Authorization Ho. Co. 9-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/26 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

bill_summary: This bill expands the authorization for Howard County to place and use speed monitoring systems (speed cameras) on U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard).
stakeholders: Motorists traveling on U.S. Route 1 in Howard County and the Howard County local government.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided with the bill text. The expansion of speed monitoring systems to U.S. Route 1 is expected to generate indeterminate local revenue from civil penalties for speeding violations and involve indeterminate expenditures for the installation and administration of the systems; however, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency for the State Highway Administration (SHA) and the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the enforcement mechanisms for highway safety, including speed monitoring systems on state routes like U.S. Route 1.

SHA is responsible for the maintenance and engineering of state-numbered highways, including U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard). They must review and approve the placement and engineering specifications of speed monitoring systems on state highways.
The MVA is responsible for administrative actions related to speed camera violations, such as placing flags on vehicle registrations for unpaid citations and maintaining driving records.

The Maryland Judicial Branch, through the District Court, adjudicates contested speed monitoring system citations. An expansion of these systems in Howard County may increase the volume of cases processed by the courts.

The Maryland State Police is the primary law enforcement agency responsible for traffic safety on state highways like U.S. Route 1 and often coordinates with local jurisdictions on automated enforcement initiatives.

The Maryland Transportation Authority is explicitly mentioned in the section of the Transportation Article being amended (§ 21–809) regarding its own authority to use speed monitoring systems elsewhere, making the agency relevant to the statutory framework being modified.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MDOT, the State Highway Administration, and the Maryland State Police regarding the implementation and legality of automated enforcement systems on state property.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the state's coordinating body for public safety and advises the Governor on criminal justice and traffic safety strategies, including the use of technology to reduce speeding and crashes.

DBM is responsible for fiscal planning and reviewing the fiscal impact of legislation. This bill may result in increased fine revenue or operational costs for state agencies involved in enforcement and adjudication.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing this law (MDOT, MSP) and must ultimately sign the bill into law.

Synopsis: Altering the matters on which the student member of the Howard County Board of Education may vote.
Title: Howard County Board of Education - Student Member - Voting Ho. Co. 7-26
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill expands the voting rights of the student member of the Howard County Board of Education to include matters such as geographical attendance areas, school construction, property acquisition, donations, school consolidation, student transportation, budgetary matters, and student suspension and expulsion. The student member remains prohibited from voting on certain personnel matters, including the appointment of the superintendent and collective bargaining.
stakeholders: Student member of the Howard County Board of Education and the Howard County Public School System community.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill has no state or local fiscal impact. The changes are procedural and do not directly affect Howard County school finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of Maryland's 24 local school systems, the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is directly interested in statutory changes to the governance and voting procedures of local boards of education.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies regarding the interpretation of the Education Article and would be responsible for reviewing the legality of altering the voting powers of a public board member.

The bill explicitly grants the student member voting rights on matters relating to school construction. The IAC is the independent state unit that oversees the planning and funding of these local capital projects.
The Governor's Office is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the executive department's broader education policy initiatives.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement that a certain individual designate a certain representative as an ex officio member of the Board of Directors of the Howard County Economic Development Authority; altering the frequency of certain Board meetings from at least once each month to at least once every other month; and amending the title of certain staff for the Authority.
Title: Howard County - Economic Development Authority - Alterations Ho. Co. 14-26
Status: In the House - Returned Passed
bill_summary: This bill makes administrative alterations to the Howard County Economic Development Authority. It removes the requirement for a representative from the Mid-Maryland Private Industry Council to serve as an ex officio member of the board, reduces the required frequency of board meetings from once a month to once every other month, and updates the title of the Executive Director to Chief Executive Officer.
stakeholders: Board of Directors of the Howard County Economic Development Authority, Howard County government, and the Mid-Maryland Private Industry Council.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no State fiscal impact and does not materially affect Howard County operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing local legislation passed by the General Assembly into law.
As the primary state agency for economic development, the Department of Commerce maintains collaborative relationships with local entities like the Howard County Economic Development Authority.

The bill removes a representative of the Mid-Maryland Private Industry Council from the Authority's board; the Department of Labor oversees workforce development programs and policies related to such councils.

The board coordinates statewide workforce solutions and partnerships; changes to the representation of workforce-related council members on local economic development boards are relevant to their coordination mission.

Synopsis: Prohibiting certain contractors and vendors from knowingly using public funds to influence the decisions of certain employees to support or oppose a certain employee organization or become a member of an employee organization; and prohibiting certain contractors and vendors from knowingly using public funds or resources to contract with or provide assistance to a person for the purpose of carrying out a certain campaign or engaging in anti-union activities.
Title: State Procurement - Contractors and Vendors - Restrictions on Use of State Funds and Resources
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/06 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits state contractors and vendors from using public funds to influence their employees' decisions to support or join a labor union. It also forbids these entities from using public funds or resources to conduct anti-union campaigns or engage in anti-union activities.
responsible_party: Maryland state agencies and units of government
stakeholders: State contractors, vendors, subcontractors, their employees, and labor organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill limits how contractors use state funds, potentially requiring monitoring by state agencies, but does not specify direct revenue or expenditure changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central procurement authority, DGS is responsible for the oversight of state-owned facilities and the purchase of goods and services. This bill directly regulates the conduct of state contractors and vendors regarding the use of public funds for labor-related activities, requiring DGS to update and enforce procurement standards.

DBM is a principal personnel and fiscal agency that also handles central procurement for various services. It is responsible for supervising budget execution and ensuring that state funds are used efficiently and in compliance with state law, including the new restrictions on contractors and vendors.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves major state expenditures and procurement contracts. This bill creates new statutory requirements for state contracts that the Board must monitor and enforce during the approval process for vendors and contractors.

MDOT is a major modal agency with significant independent procurement authority. It manages a vast network of contractors and vendors who would be subject to these new restrictions regarding the use of public funds for influencing union-related decisions.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and boards. It would be tasked with interpreting the bill's provisions, helping to draft compliant contract language for agencies, and defending the state in potential litigation regarding these procurement restrictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The MSBCA adjudicates bid protests and contract disputes. If a vendor is disqualified for violating these fund-use restrictions or a contract is terminated, the MSBCA would be the body responsible for resolving the resulting legal and factual disagreements.

USM operates with a high degree of procurement autonomy. Its various institutions enter into numerous contracts with vendors and would be responsible for ensuring those contracts comply with the new labor-related funding restrictions.

As a state agency with independent procurement authority, Morgan State University must ensure that its contractors and vendors do not use state-provided funds for the prohibited anti-union activities outlined in the bill.
The college acts as an independent unit of state government and would be responsible for implementing these procurement restrictions within its own contracting and vendor relations.

As a member of the Board of Public Works and the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees significant state expenditures and contract approvals, ensuring they meet the legal requirements established by this bill.

The Treasurer manages state funds and serves on the Board of Public Works, participating in the approval of the contracts that will be governed by these new restrictions on the use of public resources.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and procurement strategy. This bill aligns with the Governor's role in enforcing state laws and proposing the budget, as it impacts the use of public funds across all executive units.

Synopsis: Requiring the Howard County Board of Education to close public schools in the county to students beginning in the 2027-2028 school year in observance of Yom Kippur and Juneteenth and to observe the first day of Diwali, Eid al-Adha, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year, and Rosh Hashanah.
Title: Howard County - Board of Education - Mandatory School Holidays Ho. Co. 11-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch

bill_summary: This bill requires the Howard County Board of Education to close public schools to students for several specific holidays starting in the 2027-2028 school year. The mandated holidays include Yom Kippur, Juneteenth, and the first day of Diwali, Eid Al-Adha, Eid Al-Fitr, Lunar New Year, and Rosh Hashanah.
stakeholders: Students, families, and staff of the Howard County Public School System
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Locally, it is not expected to materially affect Howard County school finances because many of the specified holidays are already observed as noninstructional or professional development days. However, costs may increase if additional instructional days must be added to the calendar to meet state requirements, potentially requiring payments to contractual staff. Specific dollar estimates for these potential costs are not provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees state policy initiatives and coordinates between state agencies and local entities. This bill involves a legislative mandate on a local board of education that requires executive branch oversight through the Maryland State Department of Education.

The bill amends the Education Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland, which is the primary statutory framework overseen by the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE). MSDE is responsible for ensuring that all county boards of education comply with state laws regarding instructional hours and mandatory school days.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. This bill's requirement for public school closures on specific religious and cultural holidays involves potential constitutional and legal review regarding the Establishment Clause and state educational law.

bill_summary: This bill establishes several measures to promote residential housing development and affordability in Maryland. It requires the Governor to set housing production targets for the state and local jurisdictions, mandates that entities owning residential property disclose contact information to the Department of Housing and Community Development, and authorizes local governments to create administrative review processes for housing projects. The bill also provides local jurisdictions with the authority to adjust taxes and fees to incentivize affordable housing construction and discourage speculative landholding, while requiring various state agencies to review and streamline their internal permitting and approval processes.

stakeholders: Residential housing developers, local government authorities, business entities owning residential real estate, community development organizations, and Maryland residents seeking affordable housing.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, state general fund expenditures are expected to increase by $536,900 in FY 2027 and $521,900 in FY 2028 to cover administrative costs for the Department of Planning and the Comptroller's Office to conduct studies, reports, and oversight. Local government revenues and expenditures will be impacted based on discretionary decisions to implement new tax subclasses, transfer taxes, or fee exemptions for affordable housing projects, as well as the administrative costs of establishing new review and preapproval processes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is the primary implementing authority for Section 12-201, which requires the Governor or a designee to establish housing production targets for the State and local jurisdictions and publish annual progress reports.

The Department of Planning is tasked with leading a comprehensive study and report on housing infrastructure (water, sewer, schools, and transportation) and compiling final internal review reports from other state agencies.

The department is responsible for maintaining a registry of entity contact information, conducting a comprehensive internal review of its housing-related processes, and is likely the Governor's designee for establishing housing production targets.
Section 3 requires the Comptroller to evaluate and report on State-level tax policies (such as capital gains) to reduce disincentives for homeowners to downsize or transition to smaller homes.

The department is tasked with a comprehensive internal review, specifically including an evaluation of building code, energy efficiency, and fire safety requirements that impact housing development.
The department is specifically named as one of the agencies required to conduct a comprehensive internal review of processes, procedures, and regulations that impact housing development.
The department is tasked with conducting a comprehensive internal review and coordinating with other departments regarding permits for wetlands and forest conservation as they relate to housing.
The department must be consulted by the Department of Planning for the school facility capacity portion of the comprehensive housing infrastructure report.
The Commission is a required consultee for the school facility capacity assessment within the housing infrastructure study conducted by the Department of Planning.

The bill requires the establishment of metrics to measure progress toward housing production targets, which aligns with GOPI's mission of using data-driven strategies and performance metrics to oversee state priorities.
The department is a relevant consultee for the Comptroller's study on downsizing disincentives, as the bill specifically identifies older adults as a demographic affected by these tax policies.

bill_summary: The Application Store Accountability Act requires application store providers and developers to implement age verification for users and obtain verifiable parental consent before minors (individuals under 18) download or purchase applications or make in-application purchases. It mandates that application stores share age category data with developers, requires notification for significant updates to an application's terms or content, and prohibits the enforcement of contracts against minors without proper parental consent. Violations of the Act are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Application store providers, mobile application developers, parents and legal guardians, and minors residing in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation and allows for the recovery of actual or punitive damages for harmed minors, which may result in an increase in state revenue. The Office of the Attorney General will incur indeterminate costs to adopt regulations and enforce the new subtitle. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, specific total dollar estimates for state expenditures and revenues are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically mandates the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General to adopt regulations for age verification processes and grants it authority to enforce the Application Store Accountability Act as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice.

As the central panel for contested cases, the Office of Administrative Hearings would adjudicate administrative enforcement actions brought by the Division of Consumer Protection against application store providers or developers.
The bill creates a private right of action for harmed minors and allows for civil penalties to be recovered in court, which impacts the Judiciary's caseload and administrative operations.
The implementation of a new regulatory and enforcement framework by the Office of the Attorney General will require fiscal oversight, personnel management, and budget adjustments handled by DBM.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the regulations for placing children with developmental disabilities or mental illnesses in out-of-home care through voluntary placement agreements (VPAs). It prevents local departments of social services from requiring parents to give up legal custody to access treatment, establishes a 5-business-day deadline for assessment meetings and eligibility determinations, and requires trauma-informed training for state staff. Additionally, it makes any child support owed to the State under these agreements prior to the bill's effective date uncollectible and mandates annual data reporting on placement outcomes and hospital stay durations.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services and Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Children with developmental disabilities or mental illnesses, their parents or legal guardians, and local departments of social services.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures increase by $94,700 in FY 2027 for the Department of Human Services to hire a program manager, with annual costs reaching $127,700 by FY 2031. Montgomery County anticipates a local expenditure increase of approximately $162,000 annually for additional social workers and technology upgrades. State revenue from Child Support Foster Care Offsets will decrease due to the elimination of prior debts and new restrictions on seeking child support orders that might impede family reunification.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires juvenile courts to make specific findings regarding the best interests of a child for placements exceeding 180 days and involves court proceedings for the modification of existing child support obligations.

The bill specifically addresses the placement and treatment of children with developmental and mental disabilities, aligning with the department's mandate to coordinate and improve services for residents with disabilities.

MDH is a primary partner in the bill's implementation, required to consult on annual training for local staff, receive referrals for Medicaid-eligible children via local behavioral health authorities, and co-author a joint report on VPA outcomes.

The Governor's Office receives the required joint report from DHS and MDH concerning children in out-of-home placement and the status of voluntary placement agreement reforms.

bill_summary: This bill requires public and nonpublic schools to establish policies and procedures for handling student wandering and elopement. bill_summary: This bill updates the insurance and liability framework for peer-to-peer car sharing programs in Maryland. bill_summary: This bill expands the Maryland Whistleblower Reward Program for tax enforcement. It authorizes the Attorney General and other State agencies to bring tax enforcement actions based on information provided by whistleblowers and extends the program's scope to include taxes imposed under any Maryland law, provided they are collected by or paid to the State. The program targets individual taxpayers with federal adjusted gross income of at least $250,000 and businesses with annual gross receipts or sales of at least $2,000,000, where the tax in dispute exceeds $250,000.
stakeholders: Whistleblowers, high-income individual taxpayers, businesses with high annual gross receipts, the Maryland Comptroller, the Maryland Attorney General, and State agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase State revenue through the collection of unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest from enforcement actions where at least $250,000 is in dispute. These revenues will be partially offset by mandatory award payments to whistleblowers, ranging from 15% to 30% of the total funds collected. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with this text, specific aggregate dollar estimates for revenue and expenditure increases are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for administering the Whistleblower Reward Program, receiving original information, determining award eligibility and amounts, and coordinating with the Attorney General and other State agencies for enforcement.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to bring tax enforcement actions under the Whistleblower Reward Program and requires the office to coordinate with and report assessment information back to the Comptroller.

The bill specifies that determinations made by the Comptroller regarding whistleblower awards may be challenged in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act, which is adjudicated by the Office of Administrative Hearings.

The Department of Labor collects unemployment insurance taxes under the Labor and Employment Article. The bill expands the program to include taxes imposed under 'any other article' and allows State agencies to bring covered enforcement actions.

The Maryland Insurance Administration collects insurance premium taxes. The bill's expansion to include taxes under any article and actions by any State agency makes this administration a potential enforcement partner in the whistleblower program.

The Motor Vehicle Administration, within MDOT, collects vehicle excise taxes. The bill's expansion allows for whistleblower information to be shared with State agencies authorized to enforce such taxes.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court is likely to adjudicate the underlying high-value tax assessments and enforcement actions that trigger whistleblower claims under this program.

The Maryland Cannabis Administration oversees the cannabis industry and related tax compliance. The bill's expansion to include taxes across different articles and involving various State agencies encompasses its regulatory and enforcement scope.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates and ensures compliance for gaming taxes. Under the bill, the agency could potentially be involved in covered enforcement actions resulting from whistleblower information.

The Department of Natural Resources collects vessel excise taxes. The bill expands the whistleblower program to include any tax collected by or paid to the State, potentially involving DNR in enforcement actions.

The bill defines whistleblowers to include individuals who provide information to a law enforcement agency before providing it to the Comptroller, potentially involving the Maryland State Police in initial intake.

The bill defines 'covered enforcement action' to include judicial actions. The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial branch where these tax enforcement cases would be filed and heard.

As the central personnel agency, DBM is relevant due to the bill's provisions protecting state employees from retaliation for participating in the whistleblower program, as well as its role in supervising budget execution and revenue estimation.

bill_summary: This bill establishes legal protections for debtors who have incurred 'coerced debt' as a result of fraud, duress, or abuse within contexts such as domestic violence or human trafficking. It allows debtors to notify creditors to cease collection activities and provides a judicial process for debtors to obtain relief, including declaratory judgments that a debt is coerced and injunctions against further collection efforts. The bill also enables victims to seek damages from the individuals responsible for the coercion and establishes coerced debt as an affirmative defense in collection actions.
stakeholders: Debtors who are victims of coercion or exploitation, creditors, and debt collection agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note states that the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances or operations. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

The bill's triggers for 'coerced debt' include abuse and exploitation of children, which falls under the social services and protection remit of the Department of Human Services.
Law enforcement officers are listed as qualified third parties and police reports are cited as adequate documentation for proving a debt was coerced under the provisions of the bill.

The Secretary of Natural Resources administers the State Lakes Protection and Restoration Fund, which is expanded by the bill to include state-managed lakes.
