bill_summary: This bill transfers the administration of the Electric Universal Service Program from the Public Service Commission to the Office of Home Energy Programs within the Department of Human Services. It also expands the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to include fuel assistance programs in addition to electric assistance for low-income households.
responsible_party: The Office of Home Energy Programs within the Maryland Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Low-income electric customers (at or below 200% of the federal poverty level), electric utility companies, and residential, commercial, and industrial ratepayers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual collection of 37,000,000 dollars from electric customers to fund the Electric Universal Service Program, with 27,400,000 dollars collected from industrial and commercial classes and 9,600,000 dollars from the residential class. It transfers administrative responsibility and personnel from the Public Service Commission to the Department of Human Services. The bill also expands the allowable use of proceeds in the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to include fuel assistance programs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transfers the implementation and administration of the electric universal service program (EUSP), including bill assistance and arrearage retirement, to the Office of Home Energy Programs within this department.

The bill transfers the primary administration of the EUSP away from the Commission to the Department of Human Services, though the Commission maintains oversight and annual reporting responsibilities.
The bill explicitly confirms that this department remains responsible for administering the low-income residential weatherization component of the electric universal service program.

The bill alters the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which the MEA manages, to include providing supplemental funds for fuel assistance programs administered by the Department of Human Services.

The bill directs the Comptroller to collect revenue from electric companies and place it into the electric universal service program fund, and to disburse weatherization funds to the Department of Housing and Community Development.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM will oversee the transfer of employees from the Public Service Commission to the Department of Human Services and manage associated fiscal and budgetary adjustments.
The bill explicitly mandates that the electric universal service program remains subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.
The People's Counsel advocates for residential utility consumers, the primary beneficiaries of the assistance programs being reorganized and funded under this bill.
The reorganization of low-income energy assistance programs aligns with this office's mission to reduce child poverty and support underinvested communities.
This team's mission to enhance economic mobility and reduce child poverty is directly related to the state's strategies for providing energy assistance to low-income residents.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary agencies (DHS, PSC, MEA) involved in the administrative transfer and the implementation of the bill's requirements.
The Governor oversees the executive departments involved in this reorganization and is responsible for the state budget that must reflect the transfer of program funding and personnel.

Synopsis: Establishing that a "qualified project" is a certain residential project that has been subject to retaliatory downzoning; requiring a local jurisdiction to allow the density of a certain qualified project to exceed the density otherwise authorized; and permitting a certain qualified project to consist of certain types of developments with certain density limits under certain circumstances.
Title: Land Use - Qualified Project - Retaliatory Downzoning
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill defines 'qualified projects' as residential developments targeted by 'retaliatory downzoning'—a situation where local officials publicly oppose a project and subsequently reduce its permitted density in a manner inconsistent with professional recommendations. Local jurisdictions are required to allow these projects to exceed standard density limits, permitting middle housing in single-family zones and significantly increased density in multifamily, mixed-use, and nonresidential zones, provided that 15% to 20% of the units are deed-restricted as affordable for at least 40 years.
responsible_party: Local jurisdictions (Maryland counties and municipal corporations)
stakeholders: Residential developers, local government officials, local planning and transportation departments, and residents in need of affordable housing.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. Potential financial impacts include increased local administrative costs for processing development applications and changes to local property tax revenue resulting from increased density and mandatory affordable housing requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article, which the Department of Planning oversees. The agency is responsible for promoting sustainable growth through comprehensive land use planning and providing technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments, all of which are impacted by new mandates on density and retaliatory downzoning.

The bill mandates density bonuses for residential projects and includes specific requirements for affordable housing units and deed restrictions, directly aligning with this agency's mission to ensure access to safe and affordable housing.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG would be involved in providing legal counsel on the interpretation of 'retaliatory downzoning' and defending the state's authority to override local zoning ordinances in these specific cases.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts across Planning and the Environment to manage land use and sustainable development. The bill's density mandates for 'qualified projects' directly interact with the initiative's goals regarding land use and community revitalization.

The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and intergovernmental relations. This bill represents a significant state-level policy intervention into local government zoning authority, a matter of executive branch policy coordination.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning and would need to evaluate any fiscal note or resource requirements for state agencies tasked with monitoring compliance with these new land use provisions.

The creation of a legal definition for 'retaliatory downzoning' and new density rights is likely to lead to increased litigation between developers and local jurisdictions, impacting the workload of the state's judicial branch.

Synopsis: Altering the triennial assessment cycle for real property for property tax purposes to a 5-year cycle.
Title: Property Tax Assessments - 5-Year Assessment Cycle
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill alters the assessment cycle for real property in Maryland from a three-year (triennial) cycle to a five-year (quinquennial) cycle. It adjusts the phase-in of property value increases to occur in one-fifth increments over five years, rather than the current one-third increments over three years, and updates related administrative procedures for revaluations and appeals.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
stakeholders: Real property owners in Maryland, local governments including Baltimore City and Maryland's 23 counties, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the real property assessment and phase-in cycle from three to five years. This change will likely result in a delay of property tax revenue growth for both the State and local governments, as value increases will be spread over a longer duration (five years instead of three). Specific dollar estimates for expenditures or revenue changes were not provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the source material.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is directly responsible for hearing appeals regarding real property valuations. Changing the assessment cycle from 3 to 5 years fundamentally alters their adjudication process, workload timing, and the statutory standards for the cases they review.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, the Tax Court will be responsible for interpreting and applying the new 5-year assessment cycle rules, phased-in value calculations, and appeal rights established by this bill.

The bill specifically amends Section 8-209 regarding farm and agricultural use land, changing the income averaging period used to determine tax classification from a 3-year to a 5-year period. This directly impacts the department's mission to support the economic viability of farming.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. Moving from a 3-year to a 5-year assessment cycle will significantly change the timing and volume of property tax revenue projections, which are critical for state budget development.

The Treasurer manages state funds and oversees the issuance of State bonds. State property tax revenues are typically used to pay debt service on General Obligation bonds; changing the assessment cycle affects the predictability and timing of these funds.

The Board oversees significant state expenditures and bond issuances. Changes to the property tax assessment cycle affect the fiscal projections and revenue streams that support the state's capital projects and fiscal integrity, which the Board monitors.

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller oversees state revenues and fiscal policy, both of which are impacted by changes to property tax assessment cycles and phase-in schedules.

The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch agencies (like SDAT) that implement property tax laws. Changes to the assessment cycle impact the fiscal resources available for executive priorities.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies involved in tax administration and represents the state in civil appeals. This bill introduces new statutory requirements for assessments and appeals that may require legal interpretation or defense.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits and performance evaluations of state agencies. They would be responsible for auditing the transition and adherence to the new 5-year assessment cycle by the relevant tax agencies.

Changes to property tax assessment cycles affect the cost of homeownership and the administration of property tax credits, which are relevant to the department's mission of ensuring access to affordable housing.
While most tax disputes are handled administratively, changes to property tax law can result in litigation that eventually reaches the state's court system, requiring judicial branch support.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "control" of a cannabis business and excluding from the definition certain management services agreements, franchise relationships, and options to purchase; prohibiting the Maryland Cannabis Administration from limiting the acquisition of a certain ownership interest in cannabis businesses; reducing the number of years that a cannabis licensee is prohibited from transferring ownership or control of the license; repealing certain criteria for a certain prohibition on cannabis advertising that targets minors; etc.

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's cannabis laws by altering the definition of business 'control', reducing the mandatory holding period for license transfers from five years to three years, and establishing a process for the Maryland Cannabis Administration (MCA) to approve management services agreements. It also relaxes advertising restrictions to allow outdoor signage and billboards, provided they are at least 500 feet from schools and other specified locations, and increases the maximum criminal fine for unlicensed cannabis sales to $10,000.
stakeholders: Cannabis licensees, management service providers, business investors, and the Maryland public, particularly minors regarding adjusted advertising protections.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Maryland Cannabis Administration increase by $322,213 in FY 2027 for four new administrative positions to oversee management agreements and advertising reviews. Since administrative costs are paid from adult-use cannabis tax revenue, this expenditure results in a $161,107 reduction in General Fund revenues and a $16,111 reduction in county revenues for FY 2027. The bill also increases the maximum fine for the unlicensed sale of cannabis to $10,000 per violation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for the cannabis industry, MCA is responsible for implementing the bill's major provisions, including reviewing management services agreements, providing advertising advisory opinions, and updating data publishing schedules.

The Comptroller distributes cannabis tax revenues. The bill increases MCA's administrative costs, which are deducted from tax collections before the Comptroller distributes remaining funds to the General Fund and other accounts.
Commerce administers the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund, which will see a decrease in revenue as a direct result of the bill's impact on the distribution formula for cannabis sales and use tax.

MDH administers the Cannabis Public Health Fund, which will receive reduced revenue under the bill. Additionally, its Office of Controlled Substances Administration regulates the state's controlled dangerous substance list relevant to THC products.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MCA and will be involved in the development and review of the new regulations and advisory opinion procedures required by the bill.
DBM is responsible for the personnel actions associated with the 4 new staff positions required by MCA to implement the bill, as well as overseeing the resulting shifts in state fund allocations.
OAH would likely adjudicate administrative appeals if MCA denies or conditionally approves management services agreements or takes enforcement action against advertising violations.
MSP is responsible for enforcing criminal laws, including the unlicensed sale or distribution of THC products, which the bill addresses by increasing misdemeanor fines.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This includes the Advisory Board on Medical and Adult-Use Cannabis, which is tasked with studying and making recommendations on the industry regulations being altered by this legislation.
The judicial branch will process and adjudicate the misdemeanor citations and increased fines for the unlicensed sale of cannabis products established by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill increases the value of personal property that is exempt from execution on a judgment, such as household furnishings and appliances, and establishes new exemptions for firearms and motor vehicles used for work or education. It provides significantly higher exemption limits for debtors who are elderly (at least 60 years old) or who have a disability. Additionally, it exempts federal child tax credit and earned income tax credit payments from being seized to satisfy a judgment.
responsible_party: The Maryland Judiciary and local Sheriffs
stakeholders: Judgment debtors, judgment creditors, small businesses, elderly individuals, and individuals with disabilities
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances. There is a potential meaningful negative impact on small businesses that provide goods and services on credit, as higher exemption values and additional exempt categories may reduce their ability to collect on money judgments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding exemptions from execution on a judgment, which is centrally managed and implemented by the judicial branch and its administrative support systems.

As the state's chief tax collector and financial officer, the Comptroller's debt collection and revenue recovery efforts are impacted by changes to property and cash exemptions, particularly the new protections for the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit.

The OAG represents the state and its agencies in civil litigation and debt collection. Changes to statutory exemptions affect the legal strategies and capabilities for recovering funds owed to the state.
The bill creates specific value-based exemptions for motor vehicles necessary for work or education, which relates to the vehicle records and titling managed by the MVA.
The bill establishes specific, higher exemption thresholds (up to $10,000 for household goods and $25,000 for a vehicle) for individuals who are 'elderly' (60 years or older).
The bill establishes specific, higher exemption thresholds for individuals with a disability, as defined in the bill, to protect their essential assets from judgment.
The bill addresses the exemption status of child support payments and the ability to execute judgments against personal injury or workers' compensation recoveries for child support arrearages.
The bill references subrogation rights of the Maryland Department of Health and specifically excludes MDH claims from certain retirement asset protections.
The bill specifies how judgments for child support arrearages may be executed against workers' compensation indemnity benefits.
As the administrator for state employee workers' compensation claims, this agency is impacted by the rules governing the execution on indemnity benefits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender

As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT is relevant to the administration of new policies concerning motor vehicle exemptions.

The bill creates motor vehicle exemptions specifically for students enrolled in institutions of higher education.

bill_summary: House Bill 1521 establishes a State income tax credit to incentivize financial contributions, volunteerism, and the employment of at-risk youth (ages 12 to 25) in designated high-crime or high-poverty zip codes, including all of Baltimore City and Baltimore County. The bill allows for a 50% credit for donations to certified organizations, a $25 daily credit for professional volunteering in schools, and a $1,000 credit per at-risk youth employed for a minimum duration.
stakeholders: At-risk youth, nonprofit organizations, local education agencies, business entities, and individual taxpayers in high-crime or high-poverty areas.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues will decrease by an estimated maximum of $10,000,000 annually between fiscal years 2027 and 2033, as the bill caps the total amount of certified tax credits at this amount per taxable year. Although a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, the bill explicitly limits the Department of Commerce to certifying no more than $10,000,000 in credits each year.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the primary agency responsible for certifying eligible organizations, establishing the tax credit application process, certifying the credit amounts for taxpayers, and reporting annually to the General Assembly on the program's impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is explicitly required to consult with the Department of Commerce to certify eligible organizations and adopt regulations, and it serves as the lead agency for the public safety and juvenile crime prevention aspects of the bill.
As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller's office is responsible for administering the new income tax credits, processing claims, and managing the fiscal impact on state revenue.

The bill designates local education agencies and public schools as eligible organizations for contributions and volunteerism; it also targets youth who are chronically absent or have dropped out of school, which are metrics tracked by MSDE.

The bill's definition of at-risk youth includes individuals involved in prevention or diversion programs under the Human Services Article, as well as those aging out of foster care or experiencing homelessness, both of which fall under DHS jurisdiction.
The bill specifically targets youth involved in the juvenile justice system for support services, development programs, and employment initiatives to reduce juvenile crime.
The bill provides a tax credit for employers who hire at-risk youth, which directly relates to the Department of Labor's mission of supervising workforce development and enforcing labor laws.
The bill's focus on reducing child poverty, youth homelessness, and improving outcomes for underinvested communities aligns directly with the central mission and the ENOUGH Initiative of this office.
DBM oversees the state's revenue estimations and fiscal planning, which will be impacted by the $10 million annual cap on the tax credits established by this bill.

The bill requires that individuals claiming the volunteer credit must be accompanied by school safety personnel while on school grounds, which falls under the safety standards and personnel oversight of this agency.

The bill targets at-risk youth experiencing homelessness and promotes community revitalization in high-poverty ZIP codes, areas managed through DHCD's community investment and homeless solution programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency promotes service and volunteerism to create workforce pathways, aligning with the bill's provisions for professional volunteerism and youth employment credits.

The bill's primary objectives of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility for at-risk youth are the core priorities this team was established to address through novel policy initiatives.
The bill includes faith-based organizations as eligible recipients for supporting at-risk youth, a sector primarily engaged by GOCI through its community and faith-based commissions.

As the administrative support for the Governor, this office oversees the executive branch agencies (Commerce and GOCPP) tasked with implementing the bill and coordinates the broader policy initiative.

Synopsis: Repealing the exemptions for a motor vehicle that is owned by a motor vehicle rental or leasing company or that displays certain registration plates from liability for citations produced as a result of images recorded by a traffic control signal monitoring system or a speed monitoring system.
Title: Traffic Control Signal Monitoring and Speed Monitoring Systems - Exemptions From Liability - Vehicle Rental Companies
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: License Plates -see also- Motor Vehicle Registration

bill_summary: This bill repeals the liability exemptions for motor vehicle rental or leasing companies and holders of certain special registration plates regarding citations produced by traffic control signal monitoring systems (red light cameras) and speed monitoring systems. It expands the definition of 'owner' to include all registered owners and lessees, regardless of the lease duration, thereby making these entities or their drivers subject to civil penalties for violations recorded by automated enforcement systems.
responsible_party: Maryland State Highway Administration, Maryland Transportation Authority, and local jurisdictions or police departments operating automated traffic monitoring systems.
stakeholders: Motor vehicle rental and leasing companies, lessees of rental vehicles, holders of special registration plates, and state and local government agencies that manage traffic monitoring programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an increase in state and local revenue through the collection of civil penalties from previously exempt rental and leased vehicles and special registration plate holders. Specific dollar estimates for the fiscal impact are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note with numerical data was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency for the SHA, MVA, and MDTA, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the multi-modal administrations responsible for implementing and maintaining automated enforcement systems and vehicle registration records.

The SHA is specifically authorized in the bill to operate speed monitoring systems on Interstate 83 and Interstate 695. The repeal of liability exemptions for rental companies and special plate holders directly impacts their citation issuance and revenue collection processes.

The MDTA is explicitly mentioned as the operator of speed monitoring systems on the Intercounty Connector (MD Route 200). Changing the definition of 'owner' to include rental companies directly affects their enforcement operations and revenue stream.

The MVA manages the vehicle registration and titling database used to identify 'owners' for automated citations. They also oversee the special registration plates (manufacturers, dealers, etc.) for which the bill repeals liability exemptions.

Citations from automated monitoring systems are civil penalties that are often contested in the District Court system. Expanding the pool of liable parties (by removing exemptions) may lead to an increase in the volume of cases adjudicated by the Judiciary.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MDOT, SHA, and MDTA. They would be responsible for defending the state's enforcement procedures or handling potential litigation resulting from the removal of exemptions for rental and leasing companies.

DBM oversees state revenue and fiscal planning. This bill will likely have a fiscal impact by increasing citation revenue into state and local funds (like the Strategic Energy Investment Fund or General Fund) that were previously lost to exemptions.

The Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing traffic laws and work in conjunction with automated systems to ensure public safety. Changes to liability definitions impact the overall traffic safety enforcement landscape in the state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDOT, MSP) implementing these programs and is responsible for the overall policy direction regarding traffic safety and state revenue from civil penalties.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits retailers from distributing, selling, or advertising 'unauthorized consumable products,' which include certain tianeptine, kratom, and phenibut products, as well as other substances designated as poisonous or deleterious by the Maryland Department of Health. It authorizes the Field Enforcement Division of the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission to issue citations for violations and allows the Executive Director of the Commission to seize and destroy unauthorized products. The bill also establishes criminal and civil penalties for noncompliance and expands restrictions on advertising these products to minors.
stakeholders: Retailers (including convenience stores, gas stations, and pharmacies), manufacturers, wholesalers, the Maryland Department of Health, and consumers of tianeptine, kratom, and phenibut products.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission and the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes criminal fines of up to $5,000 and various civil penalties, these provisions are not expected to have a material impact on State or local finances or operations. Specific dollar estimates for revenue from fines were not provided as they are not anticipated to be significant.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Health as it modifies the Health – General Article regarding the regulation of kratom, tianeptine, and phenibut products. The Department is required to notify the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission of regulatory changes and the Secretary of Health is responsible for designating deleterious consumable products for enforcement.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primarily concerns the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC), which is an independent executive body. The bill expands the citation powers of the ATCC's Field Enforcement Division and authorizes its Executive Director to seize, confiscate, and destroy unauthorized consumable products.

The bill explicitly authorizes the District Court to order the Comptroller to suspend or revoke tobacco-related licenses (issued under Title 16 of the Business Regulation Article) for violations involving unauthorized consumable products.

The bill empowers the District Court to adjudicate violations, impose fines of up to $5,000, and issue orders for the suspension of business licenses and the forfeiture or destruction of seized contraband products.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission regarding the enforcement of these new regulations and the legal processes for product seizure and forfeiture.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and independent commissions like the ATCC. The office coordinates policy initiatives related to public health and the enforcement of laws prohibiting the sale of dangerous substances.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill introduces new criminal misdemeanor offenses and expands the enforcement capabilities of a public safety division (the FED), which aligns with GOCPP's mission to coordinate statewide criminal justice strategies and public safety policy.

The Field Enforcement Division officers who implement the bill's citation and seizure provisions are required to be sworn police officers and frequently coordinate with other state and local law enforcement agencies on enforcement problems.

DBM is responsible for the personnel and budget oversight of the Commission's Field Enforcement Division, ensuring that officers and employees are provided for in the State budget to carry out these expanded duties.

bill_summary: This bill requires employers with 15 or more employees and all governmental units to provide employees who are parents with at least 20 hours of paid leave per year to attend school functions at their child's elementary or secondary school. Employees may use no more than 2 hours of this leave per month and must provide proof of the school function within 48 hours of the event.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry (Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Maryland employers with 15 or more employees, state and local government agencies, and employees who are parents, stepparents, or legal guardians of children in elementary or secondary schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures may increase starting in fiscal year 2027 due to overtime costs for coverage of employees using the leave, particularly in 24/7 facilities such as prisons and hospitals. While specific dollar estimates are unavailable, the impact is described as potentially significant for some agencies. Small businesses with at least 15 employees may also experience operational disruptions and increased costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Commissioner (of Labor and Industry, within this department) as the enforcement authority responsible for investigating violations and issuing compliance orders. The department must also provide public guidance on the program.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is responsible for implementing the new leave category within the State Personnel Management System, training HR staff, and managing fiscal impacts on state agencies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As an agency with 24/7 facilities (prisons), DPSCS is specifically noted in the fiscal note as potentially incurring significant overtime costs to provide coverage for employees using this paid leave.
MDH operates 24/7 facilities (hospitals) and, according to the fiscal note, may face significant overtime costs to maintain coverage when employees utilize the new paid school function leave.

The leave is specifically for attending functions at elementary and secondary schools overseen by MSDE. Schools will likely be responsible for providing the 'proof of school function' required by the bill for employees to qualify for the leave.
USM is a major state employer with an independent personnel system; the fiscal note identifies it as an agency that will be impacted by the leave requirements and related administrative burdens.
MDOT is a large state employer with varied operational shifts; it was consulted for the fiscal note regarding the impact on state personnel expenditures and operational coverage.
The AOC manages the personnel system for the Judicial Branch and was identified in the fiscal note as an entity impacted by the new leave requirements for its employees.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding the enforcement of the new labor law and to DBM regarding its implementation for state employees.
The bill explicitly states that the leave use must comply with collective bargaining agreements; PERB oversees these agreements and labor disputes for the public sector.
As an independent state agency and large employer, Morgan State University will be required to provide this paid leave to its eligible employees and manage the fiscal and administrative impacts.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Governor to withdraw Maryland from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by January 1, 2027, and establishes specific conditions under which the State may rejoin. It eliminates the utility surcharge for EmPOWER energy efficiency programs and limits the rate for community solar energy bill credits to the electric company's standard offer service generation cost.
responsible_party: Governor of Maryland and the Maryland Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Maryland electric and gas utility customers, utility companies, community solar subscriber organizations, and state agencies receiving Strategic Energy Investment Fund proceeds.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will cause a significant loss of State special fund revenue due to the cessation of carbon allowance sales under RGGI. It also eliminates the EmPOWER surcharge on utility bills, which will reduce costs for ratepayers but remove the cost-recovery mechanism for energy efficiency programs. Specific financial estimates are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note was included in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Governor to withdraw the State from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by a specific date and provides criteria under which the Governor may rejoin. It also mandates specific notifications from the Governor to the Department of Legislative Services.

The bill amends the Environment Article regarding carbon dioxide emissions and the State's participation in RGGI, which is the primary regulatory framework managed by MDE for greenhouse gas reductions from power plants.

MEA manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which receives all proceeds from RGGI auctions. The bill's withdrawal from RGGI would cease these revenue streams, and rejoining would redirect them back to the SEIF.
The bill mandates the PSC to eliminate utility surcharges for the EmPOWER program and restricts the PSC's ability to set community solar tariffs above standard offer service rates.
The bill impacts utility rates for residential consumers by eliminating surcharges and changing community solar bill credits, areas where the OPC is the primary advocate for consumers.

The withdrawal from RGGI and elimination of EmPOWER surcharges have significant fiscal and personnel implications for state programs funded by these mechanisms, requiring DBM's oversight of the state's budget and fiscal planning.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the PSC and MDE regarding the implementation of statutory changes to the Public Utilities and Environment Articles and would handle legal aspects of withdrawing from the RGGI interstate memorandum.
The Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative is an interstate compact/agreement. Maryland's withdrawal directly affects its status and cooperation within this interstate body.
The bill's focus on eliminating energy efficiency surcharges and withdrawing from greenhouse gas initiatives directly impacts the MCEC mission to advance clean energy and energy efficiency products.
Changes to utility surcharges and energy policy affect the cost of doing business in Maryland, which falls under Commerce's role in economic development and business retention.
DHS manages energy assistance programs (like SNAP and OHEP) that are sometimes supported by funds derived from energy initiatives and RGGI proceeds.
DHCD administers energy efficiency and weatherization programs that are frequently funded through EmPOWER and RGGI proceeds.
This multi-agency initiative is focused on reducing the state's carbon footprint, a goal directly impacted by withdrawing from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative.

It also allows distillery premises to be used for events, subject to approval from the Carroll County Health Department for food and beverage service.
responsible_party: Carroll County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Class 1 distillery license holders in Carroll County, the Carroll County Health Department, and the Carroll County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Carroll County revenues may increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027, depending on the permit fees established by the Board of License Commissioners. The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state official responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and issuing manufacturer's licenses. This bill directly references the Class 1 distillery license and its issuance by the Comptroller, and establishes a specific on-premises consumption permit for Carroll County relating to those licenses.

The bill explicitly requires that the authorization to sell, prepare, and serve food and non-alcoholic beverages at these distilleries be approved by the Carroll County Health Department, which operates under the oversight and policy guidance of the Maryland Department of Health.

The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the executive branch departments, such as the Comptroller and the Department of Health, that are involved in alcohol and food safety regulation.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the state and its agencies, including providing counsel on the implementation of new licensing and permitting laws within the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

Synopsis: Authorizing an individual to practice complementary or alternative health care in the State without obtaining a license, certification, or authorization issued under certain provisions of law; establishing certain requirements and limitations regarding the practice of complementary or alternative health care; and providing that certain provisions of this Act do not waive certain claims for relief.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Complementary and Alternative Health Care Practice Act, which authorizes individuals to provide various alternative health services—such as acupressure, aromatherapy, and herbology—without obtaining a license or certification from a state health occupations board. Practitioners are required to provide clients with written disclosures regarding their credentials and services and are strictly prohibited from performing specific medical procedures, including surgery, prescribing controlled substances, and manipulating joints.
stakeholders: Complementary and alternative health care practitioners, health care consumers, and Maryland state health occupation boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health special fund expenditures increase by at least $244,300 in FY 2027 to hire investigative and legal staff for the Board of Physicians and the Board of Pharmacy to handle complaints. These expenditures are projected to grow annually to approximately $319,800 by FY 2031. The bill has no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for the oversight of health care professionals. The bill directly impacts the regulatory framework managed by MDH by allowing individuals to practice various forms of health care without standard licensure. The fiscal note identifies significant special fund expenditure increases for MDH to manage investigative staff for boards such as the Board of Physicians and the Board of Pharmacy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the specific statutory authority of 19 different health occupation boards, including the State Board of Physicians, State Board of Nursing, and State Board of Pharmacy. These boards, which function as permanent regulatory bodies within the executive branch, will have their licensing jurisdiction bypassed for practitioners of complementary and alternative health care.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to all state agencies and boards. The fiscal note specifically anticipates the need for additional part-time legal counsel to support the Boards of Physicians and Pharmacy in handling complaints and legal issues arising from the authorization of unlicensed practitioners.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including MDH and its various health occupation boards. If the boards take enforcement action against alternative practitioners for exceeding the scope of the bill (e.g., performing surgery or prescribing drugs), the OAH would likely handle the appeals.

As a division of MDH that enforces the state's Controlled Dangerous Substance Act, this office is relevant because the bill explicitly prohibits unlicensed alternative health care practitioners from prescribing or dispensing controlled substances. Enforcement of this provision would fall under this agency's purview.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is involved in the creation and management of the new investigator and legal counsel positions identified in the fiscal note as necessary to implement the bill's oversight requirements.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access and accountability. The authorization of a new class of health care providers and the modification of licensing standards are relevant to the commission's broad mandate for health policy planning.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office administers the mandatory arbitration system for medical malpractice claims. Because the bill authorizes practitioners to provide various health services, disputes regarding liability and damages for these services may fall under this office's jurisdiction.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Maryland public schools to allow students in home instruction programs to participate in school-sponsored extracurricular activities, including athletics and interscholastic sports, provided the local school system approves. It requires schools to prioritize students enrolled at the school over non-enrolled students if space in an activity is limited.
responsible_party: Maryland local school systems and individual public schools
stakeholders: Homeschool students, public school students, and local school administrators
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific estimates is not included in the provided text. Potential financial implications involve minor administrative costs for local school systems to coordinate and oversee the participation of homeschool students in school-sponsored activities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for overseeing Maryland's public education system and setting statewide educational policies and standards, MSDE is highly relevant. This bill directly concerns the eligibility of students in home instruction programs to participate in public school extracurricular activities and references COMAR guidelines, which fall under MSDE's regulatory authority.

The OAG serves as the legal representative for the Maryland State Department of Education and all state agencies. They would likely be required to provide legal guidance and interpretation regarding the implementation of this new statutory section, particularly concerning liability, equal access, and the rights of non-enrolled students.

It requires residential condominiums, cooperatives, and homeowners associations to register annually and authorizes the commission to provide training, technical assistance, and a dispute resolution process for community members and governing bodies.
stakeholders: Owners and governing bodies of common ownership communities (condominiums, cooperatives, and homeowners associations), developers, and professional community managers in Baltimore County.
fiscal_impact_summary: State operations and finances are not materially affected. Baltimore County expenditures will increase to the extent that the county establishes the commission or modifies existing operations to comply with the bill's requirements. While the bill authorizes the collection of reasonable fees for registration and dispute resolution services to offset costs, the formal Fiscal Note does not provide specific dollar estimates for revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a local commission on common ownership communities in Baltimore County with the authority to resolve disputes. It specifically outlines procedures for appealing commission decisions to the court system and allows courts to stay civil actions related to these communities if a dispute has been filed with the local commission. The Administrative Office of the Courts is also identified as an information source in the bill's fiscal note.

The bill adds a new Title 11C to the Maryland Real Property Article. The Office of the Attorney General is the primary legal representative for the state and provides counsel on the interpretation and enforcement of state laws, including real property and consumer protection matters which often overlap with the governance of common ownership communities like HOAs and condominiums.

bill_summary: This bill reduces the number of years (from three to two) that an individual or their parent or guardian must have filed Maryland income tax returns to qualify for an out-of-state tuition exemption at public institutions of higher education under the Maryland Dream Act. It also updates residency verification requirements for students to maintain their tuition status until they are awarded a degree.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission and the governing boards of public institutions of higher education
stakeholders: Undocumented students, their parents or legal guardians, Maryland public four-year universities, and Maryland community colleges
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2029 to accommodate additional full-time equivalent students in community college funding formulas, with estimated increases of $5,400 to $13,600 per student. The Maryland Higher Education Commission estimates an initial $20,000 increase in scholarship awards for the first cohort of newly eligible students, potentially rising to $80,000 after four years. Tuition revenues at public institutions may decrease minimally; for context, four-year institutions and community colleges reported revenue losses of $6,600,000 and $2,400,000 respectively in fiscal 2025 due to existing Dream Act exemptions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is the primary regulatory and coordinating board for higher education in Maryland. It is responsible for overseeing the out-of-state tuition exemption policies, collecting annual reports from institutions regarding qualifying students, and administering state-funded scholarship programs (like the EEA and Promise scholarships) whose eligibility is directly impacted by changes in tuition status.

USM oversees 12 public institutions that must implement the revised eligibility criteria for tuition exemptions. These institutions will experience direct fiscal impacts through potential shifts in tuition revenue and adjustments to enrollment classifications.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State is directly responsible for applying the new tax-filing requirement to determine student eligibility for in-state tuition rates and may see associated impacts on tuition revenue.

As Maryland's public honors college, St. Mary's is directly affected by the change in tuition exemption criteria for undocumented students and the resulting impact on tuition revenue and student eligibility reporting.

The bill's eligibility criteria are based on Maryland income tax returns. The Comptroller's Office is the custodian of these records and plays a role in the verification process for students or parents/guardians seeking the tuition exemption.

DBM oversees the state budget and the funding formulas for higher education institutions (including the Cade and BCCC formulas). Changes in resident student enrollment counts resulting from this bill can affect state general fund expenditure requirements.

MLDS links student and workforce data from MHEC and other agencies. Changes in student residency and eligibility status impact the data sets used for state-level analysis of educational outcomes and economic mobility.

OAG provides legal counsel to state institutions and agencies regarding the interpretation and implementation of education laws, including residency requirements and constitutional considerations for undocumented students.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and signs the annual state budget. The fiscal note indicates potential increases in general fund expenditures and aligns with the administration's broader policy goals regarding higher education access.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Helping Everyone Afford Life-Saving Treatments and Health Care (HEALTH) Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund designed to assist individuals with costs for legally protected health care services that are subject to federal restrictions. The fund provides grants to health care providers and is financed through an annual distribution of $20 million from abandoned property proceeds, unspent funds from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund, and specific sales, use, and property tax revenues derived from insurers.
stakeholders: Maryland Medical Assistance Program enrollees, insured and uninsured individuals seeking health care services impacted by federal funding restrictions, and Maryland health care providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Beginning in FY 2027, the bill redirects $20,000,000 annually from unclaimed property proceeds to the HEALTH Fund instead of the General Fund. It also requires that unspent money from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund be credited to the HEALTH Fund. Additionally, certain sales and use tax and State property tax revenues attributable to insurance companies are distributed to the Fund. The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is responsible for administering the fund through grants and contracts, while the Comptroller and State Treasurer handle accounting and investments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly designates the Executive Director of the Exchange to administer the HEALTH Fund, adopt regulations for its operation, provide grants to health care providers, and submit annual reports to the General Assembly.

The Comptroller, as the Administrator of abandoned property, is required to distribute $20 million annually from unclaimed funds to the HEALTH Fund. Additionally, the Comptroller is responsible for distributing specific sales and use tax revenue to the Fund.
The State Treasurer is required to hold the HEALTH Fund separately, invest its money in the same manner as other State funds, and serve as its custodian.

The bill requires that residual funds from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund, which is managed by the Department of Health, be credited to the HEALTH Fund at the end of each fiscal year. The Fund also provides assistance to Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) enrollees.

The bill amends the Insurance Article and relates to premium taxes. As the regulator of Maryland's insurance market, the MIA oversees the entities subject to the taxes that will now contribute additional revenue to the HEALTH Fund.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is involved in the creation of new special funds and the oversight of revenue shifts from the General Fund. The bill also references definitions in the State Personnel and Pensions Article which DBM manages.

The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, the Comptroller, and the Treasurer regarding the administration of the new fund and the implementation of grants and regulations.
The Governor oversees the executive agencies involved (MHBE, MDH) and is responsible for the state budget, which will be impacted by the redirection of millions in tax and abandoned property revenue.
The OLA will be responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of the HEALTH Fund and its administration by the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange.

The bill involves the distribution and imposition of specific tax revenues (sales, property, and premium taxes); the Tax Court serves as the administrative review body for disputes regarding these taxes.
The bill includes provisions regarding the distribution of State property tax revenue; these local boards handle disputes related to property tax assessments that contribute to that revenue.

bill_summary: The Utility RELIEF Act implements comprehensive reforms to Maryland's energy utility regulations and programs to mitigate cost inflation for families. It transfers the Electric Universal Service Program to the Office of Home Energy Programs, establishes the Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Program, and streamlines residential solar permitting. The bill modifies the EmPOWER Maryland program by excluding gas companies and reducing efficiency targets, restricts utility companies from recovering executive compensation and certain discretionary expenses through rates, and requires participation in regional transmission organizations. It also creates a registry for large load customers, such as data centers, and mandates a successor program to the current net energy metering system.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission, Maryland Energy Administration, Department of Human Services, and Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Residential and commercial utility customers, low-income households, nonprofit organizations, data center operators, and public service companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are significantly affected, most notably by $200,000,000 in contingent special fund appropriations from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) in FY 2027 ($100,000,000 for residential rate credits and $100,000,000 for renewable energy auctions). The bill also creates a mandated appropriation of unencumbered SEIF balances starting in FY 2028 and authorizes a $5,000,000 appropriation for the Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Fund. State administrative expenditures increase by approximately $2,200,000 in FY 2027 for expanded staffing and consulting at the Public Service Commission, Office of People's Counsel, and other agencies. Local governments face mandates related to solar permitting and potential administrative costs for municipal utilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directs the Governor to include specific appropriations in the annual budget (e.g., $100M for EmPOWER relief and SEIF balances). It also requires several reports to be submitted to the Governor regarding energy storage, net metering, and permitting streamlining.
The Comptroller is responsible for collecting the revenue from electric companies for the electric universal service program fund and placing it into the fund, which the bill reorganizes under OHEP.

The Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which is granted specific authority by the bill to waive the 'termination for convenience' clause in multi-year renewable energy procurement contracts.

The bill specifically authorizes the Attorney General to seek judicial enforcement against any county or municipality that fails to comply with the new residential solar permitting and software requirements.

The bill reallocates the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) proceeds, which the fiscal note identifies as eliminating the current SEIF funding source for the Urban Trees Program administered by the Trust, necessitating $10M in general fund replacement.

The bill defines agricultural buildings for exemptions in building performance standards and excludes agricultural facilities from certain large load customer regulations. The Maryland Department of Agriculture is also notified of CPCN applications.
The bill includes mandated appropriations and significant special fund shifts that directly impact the state budget process and long-term fiscal planning managed by DBM.
The Department is consulted on the energy site-readiness initiative and is a recipient of notice for Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) applications for large energy projects.
The bill allocates a portion of SEIF clean energy proceeds to be used for school electrification and electric school bus deployment programs.

MDE is responsible for developing building energy performance standards, consulting on emissions targets, and analyzing the adequacy of energy plans in meeting state climate goals established by the bill.

DGS is authorized to issue RFPs for long-term leases for renewable energy projects and is involved in recommending the waiver of contract clauses for renewable energy procurements to the Board of Public Works.

DHCD is responsible for administering the low-income weatherization component of the electric universal service program and receives half of the fees collected from the large load customer registry for its energy efficiency programs.

The bill transfers the administration of the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) to the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP) within DHS, making it a primary implementing agency for energy assistance changes.

The Commissioner of Labor and Industry is required to determine prevailing wage rates for solar projects and large load facilities, and the Department is tasked with enforcing these wage requirements.

The Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) within DNR is tasked with a significant study on streamlined permitting, identifying priority energy sites, and reviewing CPCN applications for energy projects.
MDP is a recipient of notice for CPCN applications and coordinates with other agencies on the sustainable development initiatives impacted by the bill's energy policy changes.
The Maryland Aviation Administration (under MDOT) must determine if proposed transmission lines or generating stations pose hazards to aviation safety as part of the CPCN review process.

The bill establishes the 'Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Program' (GREEN) within the Maryland Clean Energy Center to provide no-interest loans to nonprofits for energy efficiency and renewable systems.
MEA is a primary implementer, responsible for conducting alternative compliance fee auctions, managing the SEIF, providing renewable energy incentives, and coordinating multiple energy studies.
The bill explicitly states that the electric universal service program remains subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.

As the consumer advocate, OPC is required to consult on annual rate reports, participate in the development of the net metering successor program, and sit in on major regulatory proceedings established by the bill.

The PSC is the primary regulator for most provisions of the bill, including utility rate setting, the large load customer registry, CPCN modifications, net metering transitions, and oversight of the EmPOWER Maryland program.
The Board is granted the authority to waive 'termination for convenience' clauses in state procurement contracts for renewable energy to help suppliers secure project financing.

bill_summary: This bill adds lead to the list of prohibited ingredients in cosmetic products and classifies violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. It allows individuals to sue for civil damages and establishes the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund, administered by the Maryland Department of Health, to support research and treatment for conditions like uterine cancer and hair loss caused by harmful hair chemicals.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Consumers, cosmetic product manufacturers and retailers, and individuals suffering from health conditions caused by harmful hair chemicals.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by an estimated $540,793 in FY 2027, which includes $492,908 for enforcement by the Office of the Attorney General and $47,885 for administration by the Maryland Department of Health. General and special fund revenues increase minimally from penalties and interest, which are primarily directed to the newly established Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund. Local governments are not significantly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OAG's Division of Consumer Protection is a primary enforcer of the bill, as violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices. The OAG is also co-responsible for developing a plan for the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund and is expected to see increased expenditures for enforcement staff.

MDH is the primary agency responsible for the public health regulations involved. It is authorized to investigate complaints, inspect premises, and collect samples. Additionally, MDH is tasked with administering the new Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund and developing a plan for research and treatment in conjunction with the OAG.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency. The fiscal note indicates a need for additional staffing at both OAG and MDH to implement the bill, and the department will oversee the budget execution of the newly created special fund.

The bill establishes new civil liability for damages, including treble and punitive damages, and attorney's fees. The Judiciary will be responsible for adjudicating these civil actions brought by individuals for actual harm sustained.
As the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office will be responsible for the management and custody of the Harmful Hair Chemical Restitution Fund created by the bill.

The Comptroller acts as the state's chief financial officer and will likely be involved in the accounting and revenue collection processes related to the new restitution fund and its interest earnings.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDH and OAG) responsible for implementing the bill and will receive the required plan and reports regarding the new fund.

bill_summary: This bill establishes comprehensive operating and siting standards for data centers in Maryland. It requires the Department of the Environment to set regulations for sound levels, vibration controls, and backup power generation. Data centers located within 2,500 feet of a school are subject to additional requirements, including setbacks for electrical infrastructure, air quality monitoring, and mandatory funding for school HVAC filtration systems. Furthermore, the bill restricts the construction of data centers on high-quality agricultural land, eased land, and rural legacy areas, and it authorizes $10,000 civil penalties for violations.
stakeholders: Data center owners and operators, primary and secondary schools, local health departments, local approving authorities, and Maryland residents living near proposed or existing data center sites.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text; however, specific financial implications are identified. Data center operators who violate the new standards are subject to a civil penalty of $10,000 per violation. Additionally, operators near schools must fund the installation and annual maintenance costs of HEPA and MERV 13+ filters for the school's HVAC system. State and local government entities, particularly the Department of the Environment and local health departments, will likely incur indeterminate administrative costs related to regulation, monitoring, and the enforcement of emergency stop-work orders.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes Title 19 in the Environment Article, requiring the Department of the Environment to set regulations for sound, vibration, and air quality standards for data centers, and grants it enforcement powers including civil penalties and permit revocation.

The bill adds a new subtitle to the Land Use Article regarding data center siting and impacts sustainable growth policies and local zoning regulations which the Department of Planning oversees and provides technical assistance for.

The bill prohibits the construction of data centers on specific agricultural lands (Class I or II soil) and land encumbered by agricultural easements, which directly impacts the department's mission to protect farming and soil resources.
The bill prohibits the construction of data centers in Rural Legacy Areas, which are conservation areas defined and managed under the Natural Resources Article.

The bill mandates specific setbacks from school playgrounds and athletic fields, requires air filtration improvements in schools paid for by data center owners, and requires air quality monitoring at school intakes.
The bill empowers local health departments, which are overseen by the Maryland Department of Health, to issue emergency stop-work orders for violations of sound or air quality standards.
As the state's economic development agency, Commerce is impacted by the new operational and siting restrictions which affect the attractiveness and expansion of the data center industry in Maryland.

The bill mandates backup power requirements, Tier 4 emission standards, and on-site battery storage for large data centers, areas that fall within the agency's mission to manage energy efficiency and planning.

The bill sets setback requirements for electrical substations and high-voltage transmission lines (over 69 kilovolts), infrastructure that is generally under the regulatory and approval purview of the PSC.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates the Department of Planning and Department of the Environment on sustainable growth and land use, which are the primary areas of law modified by this bill.
The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the various implementing agencies and representing the state in any enforcement actions or appeals related to the new regulations.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDE, MDP, etc.) tasked with developing the new regulations and manages the intergovernmental relations affected by the land use changes.
DBM will oversee the fiscal impact and potential personnel needs of the Department of the Environment to implement and enforce the new regulatory framework.

MEDCO provides real estate development and advisory services for industry; the bill's requirement to evaluate decommissioned industrial or power plant sites directly relates to MEDCO's development mission.

The Department is authorized to contract with a third party to develop the application.
stakeholders: Recreational fishers who hold a Maryland angler's license or a Chesapeake Bay and coastal sport fishing license or registration, and the Department of Natural Resources.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a mandate for the Department of Natural Resources to develop a mobile application, which will involve expenditures for software development and ongoing maintenance. The department is permitted to contract with third parties for this purpose. Because a formal Fiscal Note with specific expenditure figures was not provided with the bill text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of Natural Resources to develop and manage a mobile application for recreational fishing reports and to oversee the reporting process for licensed anglers.

DoIT is responsible for the state's IT strategy and security. They would likely oversee the technical standards, cybersecurity, and implementation of any new mobile application developed by a state agency.

The bill permits the Department of Natural Resources to contract with a third party for the application's development. DGS is the central procurement authority responsible for overseeing such contracts.
DBM oversees the state budget and expenditures. The development and maintenance of a new mobile application will require budget allocation and fiscal oversight.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like DNR. They would be involved in reviewing the legal aspects of the app's terms of use, privacy policies, and any third-party development contracts.
As the office overseeing the executive branch and coordinating policy initiatives, the Governor's Office would provide high-level direction for this agency mandate.

bill_summary: The Maryland Enforcement Limits and Transparency (MELT) Act prohibits state and local government entities, employees, and contractors from voluntarily assisting in federal immigration enforcement unless required by a judicial warrant or law. The bill mandates documentation and record-keeping for interactions with immigration authorities, authorizes the Attorney General to investigate violations, and allows for civil lawsuits, contract termination, and professional license revocation as penalties for non-compliance.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General, Board of Public Works, and State licensing authorities
stakeholders: Immigrant residents, state and local government agencies, government contractors, and licensed professionals.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, state general fund expenditures increase by $214,800 in FY 2027 for additional staff in the Office of the Attorney General and computer programming for the Judiciary, with annual costs reaching $273,900 by FY 2031. There is a potential indeterminate decrease in federal fund revenues and a potential increase in local government expenditures for compliance and litigation. Violators are subject to a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Attorney General primary authority to investigate violations, issue subpoenas, and bring civil enforcement actions, including the recovery of costs and penalties.
The bill explicitly authorizes the Board of Public Works to void, decline, or condition State procurement contracts for persons who violate the immigration enforcement aid prohibitions.

As a primary licensing authority for business and professional occupations specifically mentioned in the bill, the Department is responsible for instituting disciplinary proceedings and collecting required certifications.
The bill impacts the Department as a licensing authority for health occupations and through operational requirements for documentation and notification in public health facilities.

MDOT faces high operational impacts due to the Motor Vehicle Administration's licensing role and the potential for reduced federal funding if state enforcement limits conflict with federal grant requirements.
The MVA is a key licensing authority impacted by the bill's disciplinary and certification requirements, and the fiscal note specifically identifies computer programming costs for its systems.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP is highly likely to have the 'interactions' defined in the bill, requiring extensive documentation, record retention, and adherence to aid prohibitions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department must implement new contract monitoring protocols and manage high-risk interactions within the correctional and parole systems to comply with the bill.
The Judiciary is responsible for system programming changes to licensing systems and will adjudicate civil suits authorized by the bill.
The Department and local school systems must update policies, train staff, and implement documentation systems to comply with the bill's restrictions and recordkeeping mandates.
The Comptroller serves as a licensing authority for several industries and is a member of the Board of Public Works, which enforces the procurement provisions of the bill.
The Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is tasked with overseeing procurement contract enforcement and ensuring fiscal responsibility regarding state contracts under this Act.
As the central procurement authority, DGS must ensure that all state contracts include the mandatory certifications and prohibitions against aiding immigration enforcement.
DHS manages social services involving personal information sharing, making the bill's notification and documentation requirements highly relevant to its operations.
The agency's supervision and detention of youth create frequent opportunities for interactions with law enforcement and immigration authorities that are regulated by this bill.
DoIT is responsible for overseeing the state's data procedures and will be involved in the implementation of records retention and privacy procedures required by current and new law.
OAH may be required to adjudicate contested cases arising from disciplinary actions taken by licensing authorities against individuals or entities that violate the bill.
As an independent licensing authority, the MCA must comply with the bill's requirements regarding disciplinary proceedings and applicant certifications.
The MIA serves as a licensing authority for the insurance industry and is subject to the bill's provisions regarding license suspension, revocation, and applicant certification.
The PSC regulates and licenses various common carriers and utility services, making it a licensing authority under the scope of this legislation.
The Department's Natural Resources Police must comply with the bill's restrictions on law enforcement cooperation with immigration authorities.
DBM is responsible for the overall fiscal management of state agencies and personnel policies that will be impacted by the bill's requirements and expenditures.
The Commission oversees policies for public and private institutions that are defined as 'persons' under the bill and must comply with its data and enforcement restrictions.
USM institutions are state entities whose personnel and procurement contracts are subject to the bill's prohibitions and documentation mandates.
As a state agency, the university must ensure its employees and contractors comply with the bill's requirements and include mandatory language in its procurement contracts.
The college is a state agency subject to the bill's provisions regarding personnel conduct and mandatory procurement contract requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS regulates EMS systems and providers; it is listed in the fiscal note as a relevant agency due to its regulatory role and the sensitive locations where EMS operates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency serves as a licensing authority for the gaming industry and must implement the certification and disciplinary provisions of the bill.
The Department conducts regulatory activities and issues licenses/permits, making it subject to the licensing authority requirements of the bill.
The Department is a state agency whose personnel and contractors must comply with the Act's prohibitions on aiding immigration enforcement.
The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies and licensing boards that must implement and enforce the bill's provisions.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to include screening for metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) as part of the state's coordinated newborn screening system for hereditary and congenital disorders.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no fiscal or operational impact because the Maryland Department of Health is already in the process of implementing screening for metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) following its addition to the federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel in December 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary implementing agency responsible for establishing the statewide newborn screening system, conducting the tests in its public health laboratory, managing follow-up activities, and adopting regulations for the screening of Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (MLD) as required by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
