bill_summary: The Maryland Generational Housing Act of 2026 requires local jurisdictions to authorize the development of at least one internal and one external accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on residential lots with a single-family detached home, regardless of density limits. The bill prohibits local governments from imposing development excise taxes or impact fees on ADUs smaller than 1,000 square feet and exempts ADUs occupied by family members from property taxes. It also restricts additional parking requirements and caps utility connection fees for units occupied by family members.
responsible_party: Local governments (counties and municipalities), utility providers, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT).
stakeholders: Single-family homeowners, qualified family members (parents, children, siblings, etc.), local governments, and utility providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in an indeterminate decrease in local revenues due to the prohibition of development excise taxes and impact fees for ADUs under 1,000 square feet. State and local property tax revenues will decrease because of the exemption for ADUs occupied by family members. Additionally, local and private utility providers will experience a reduction in revenue due to capped connection fees and permitted shared meters. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article, requiring local jurisdictions to authorize accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and excluding them from density calculations. This falls under the Department's mission to promote sustainable growth and provide policy guidance on land use.

As the primary agency for housing policy, DHCD is responsible for ensuring access to affordable housing. This bill, the 'Maryland Generational Housing Act of 2026,' aims to increase housing supply through ADUs, directly aligning with the Department's core mission.

The bill regulates water and sewer connection fees and mentions capacity charges related to septic systems. MDE regulates sanitary commissions and municipal authorities involved in these services, and provides oversight for environmental infrastructure.

The bill defines utilities to include private companies regulated under the Public Utilities Article. The PSC oversees these private companies, which would now be prohibited from charging certain fees for ADUs and must allow shared meters.

The bill specifically references septic system capacity as a factor in fee exemptions. MDH oversees local health departments and sets policies regarding environmental health, including the regulation and approval of septic systems.

The bill creates a new property tax exemption for ADUs occupied by qualified family members. PTAAB would be responsible for hearing appeals from property owners regarding the denial or valuation related to this specific exemption.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court would adjudicate appeals involving the new property tax exemption and local development excise tax prohibitions.

The bill's provision exempting certain ADUs from property tax has a fiscal impact on the State's revenue (specifically the portion of property tax used for debt service). DBM is responsible for estimating revenues and managing fiscal planning.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives like the 'Generational Housing Act.' The office would be responsible for the broader implementation of these housing and tax policies.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the various state agencies (MDP, DHCD, MDE) as they implement the new statutory requirements and regulations for ADUs and utility fees.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland Labor Relations Board as an independent unit of State government to oversee collective bargaining activities for certain private sector employees; establishing certain rights for employees and employers related to collective bargaining; establishing certain procedures related to elections and certification of exclusive representatives; and prohibiting an employer and employee organizations from engaging in certain unfair labor practices.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Labor Relations Act and creates the Maryland Labor Relations Board (MLRB) as an independent state agency to oversee collective bargaining for specific private sector employees. It grants employees the right to organize, join employee organizations, and engage in collective bargaining while prohibiting unfair labor practices by both employers and unions. The MLRB is empowered to supervise elections, certify exclusive representatives, and resolve labor disputes. The act is contingent on the repeal of the federal National Labor Relations Act or the federal government ceding jurisdiction to the state.
stakeholders: Private sector employees (excluding agricultural and domestic workers), private sector employers, and employee organizations (unions) in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The creation of the Maryland Labor Relations Board as an independent unit of State government will increase state expenditures to cover salaries for a full-time chair, four board members, and associated administrative and travel costs. These expenditures will be determined through the annual state budget process. As a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text, specific dollar estimates for these costs are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is responsible for appointing the Chair and all four members of the newly established Maryland Labor Relations Board, with the advice and consent of the Senate. Additionally, the Board is required to submit an annual report to the Governor summarizing its cases and actions.

The bill explicitly tasks the Maryland Department of Labor with monitoring federal government actions regarding the National Labor Relations Act and notifying the Department of Legislative Services when specific contingencies are met to trigger the effectiveness of the Act.

The bill creates a new independent state agency, the Maryland Labor Relations Board, with members and a full-time chair entitled to compensation and reimbursement as provided in the state budget, which is managed and executed by DBM.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in the recruitment, vetting, and recommendation of the five individuals to serve on the newly created Maryland Labor Relations Board.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the newly established Maryland Labor Relations Board and representing the state in legal matters arising from the Act's enforcement.

The bill prohibits employee organizations from discriminating against members based on protected classes such as race, sex, sexual orientation, and disability, which aligns with the anti-discrimination enforcement mandate of the MCCR.

Synopsis: Repealing the sunset termination of a requirement for the Governor to include $10,000,000 in the annual budget bill for certain purposes related to the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center; and altering certain findings by the General Assembly including that the University of Maryland Capital Region Health requires State support and investment to continue its mission to provide high-quality care and transform health care delivery in Prince George's County and the southern Maryland region.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the termination date for mandated state funding for the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center, effectively making a $10,000,000 annual appropriation permanent. It also updates the General Assembly's findings regarding the public-private partnership between the State, Prince George's County, and the University of Maryland Medical System aimed at improving healthcare access and outcomes in Prince George's County and the Southern Maryland region.
stakeholders: Residents of Prince George's County and the Southern Maryland region, the University of Maryland Medical System, and the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures will increase by $10,000,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2029, as the bill maintains a mandated appropriation that was previously scheduled to sunset after fiscal 2028. There is no impact on state revenues or local governmental finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the Governor include a specific $10,000,000 appropriation for the University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center in the annual budget bill for each fiscal year beyond 2028.

As the agency responsible for developing the state's budget and supervising budget execution, DBM is directly responsible for implementing the permanent mandated appropriation and managing the $10,000,000 annual fiscal impact on the general fund.

The bill amends the Health - General Article and concerns the state's role in transforming health care delivery and addressing chronic health conditions, which falls under the department's core public health and policy setting mission.

The bill discusses cost containment measures and preventing operating losses for the hospital, which directly relates to the commission's role in regulating hospital rates, revenues, and financial stability.

The bill's goals regarding access to high-quality clinical programs and healthcare delivery transformation align with the commission's responsibility for planning the state's health system needs and improving access to care.

The medical center is part of the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS), which is the academic medical system affiliated with USM institutions, and USM was consulted as an information source for the fiscal note.
The Comptroller, as the state's chief financial officer, is responsible for paying state bills and managing state expenditures, including the distribution of mandated operating grants.
The Treasurer is responsible for distributing state funds and sits on the Board of Public Works, which oversees significant state expenditures and fiscal integrity.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor and state agencies regarding the implementation of the statutory changes to the Health - General Article and the budget mandates.

Synopsis: Establishing the Workgroup to Study Extreme Risk Protective Orders; and requiring the Workgroup to report to the Governor and the General Assembly by May 1, 2027, on its policy recommendations for improving the use of extreme risk protective orders in the State.
Title: Workgroup to Study Extreme Risk Protective Orders (Sagar Ghimire Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:30 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill establishes the Workgroup to Study Extreme Risk Protective Orders, known as the Sagar Ghimire Act. The workgroup is tasked with studying the use of extreme risk protective orders in Maryland and developing policy recommendations for improvement. The workgroup, chaired by the Secretary of Health and staffed by the Maryland Department of Health, must report its findings to the Governor and General Assembly by May 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, Office of the Attorney General, Office of the Public Defender, Maryland Chiefs of Police Association, Maryland Sheriffs’ Association, mental health service providers, and individuals subject to or petitioning for extreme risk protective orders.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) estimated a cost of $94,335 in fiscal 2027 for a contractual program administrator to staff the workgroup. However, the Department of Legislative Services anticipates that MDH can staff the workgroup using existing budgeted resources. Expense reimbursements for workgroup members are expected to be minimal and absorbable within existing resources. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Health is designated as the chair of the Workgroup, and the Department of Health is responsible for providing the necessary staff and resources to support its operations.
The Attorney General, or their designee, is a mandatory member of the Workgroup, contributing legal expertise to the study of protective orders.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Defender, or their designee, is a mandatory member of the Workgroup, representing the perspective of indigent defense in the study of extreme risk protective orders.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new temporary workgroup, which falls under this collective category for bodies created by the General Assembly to study specific issues.
The Governor is responsible for appointing a member to the Workgroup representing mental health services and is the primary recipient of the Workgroup's final report.
Extreme Risk Protective Orders are judicial orders processed through the District Court; the AOC manages the court operations and records that will be a central focus of the Workgroup's study.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, the GOCPP has a significant interest in policies regarding the use of protective orders to prevent violence.
The fiscal note discusses potential staffing costs for the Maryland Department of Health, and DBM oversees state personnel resources and fiscal impacts.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are directly impacted by policies regarding the service and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders and firearm seizures.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in recruiting and vetting the representative of a mental health organization appointed to the Workgroup.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits any person doing business in Maryland from knowingly providing drugs, medical devices, or other goods and services intended for use in carrying out a death sentence. It requires health occupations boards to deny or revoke the licenses of individuals who violate this prohibition and establishes a civil penalty of $10,000 for each violation.
stakeholders: Healthcare professionals, pharmaceutical companies, medical device manufacturers, and health occupation licensing boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a civil penalty of $10,000 for violations. While these penalties could generate revenue for the State, specific aggregate revenue or expenditure estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new section to the Health - General Article and the Health Occupations Article, which the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) and its associated health occupations boards are responsible for administering and enforcing. The bill specifically mandates that health occupations boards deny or revoke licenses for violations.

As a division of the Maryland Department of Health responsible for enforcing the state's Controlled Dangerous Substance (CDS) Act and regulating the distribution of medications, this office would likely be involved in monitoring and investigating the prohibited supply of drugs or compounding of substances intended for use in death sentences.

The bill mandates that health occupations boards revoke or deny licenses for violations. Such actions are typically contested, leading to administrative hearings conducted by the OAH to ensure due process.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the health occupations boards and state agencies like MDH. It would likely be responsible for representing the boards in litigation related to license revocations and providing advice on the enforcement of civil penalties.

The bill prohibits any 'person doing business in the State' from supplying goods or services for death sentences. While the medical enforcement is handled by MDH, the Department of Labor regulates various businesses and professions and would have an interest in laws governing business conduct in the state.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Temporary Worker Oversight Unit within the Maryland Department of Labor to monitor and regulate the employment of temporary workers under H-2A and H-2B visas. It requires recruiters to register annually and post a $10,000 surety bond, prohibits the collection of recruitment fees, and protects workers from retaliation. Additionally, it grants temporary workers the right to host representatives from advocacy, legal, and health organizations in employer-provided housing and empowers the Department to conduct inspections and impose civil penalties.
stakeholders: Temporary workers (H-2A and H-2B visa holders), recruiters, employers who sponsor temporary workers, and worker advocacy or service organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in increased State expenditures for the Maryland Department of Labor to create and staff the Temporary Worker Oversight Unit, conduct inspections, and provide translation services. State revenue may increase from recruiter registration fees and civil penalties (up to $10,000 per violation), and recruiters are required to post a $10,000 surety bond. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable as the note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Temporary Worker Oversight Unit within this department and grants it primary authority for enforcement, regulation, and reporting on temporary worker recruiters and employers.
The bill specifically targets H-2A visa holders, who are agricultural workers, directly impacting the farming operations and agricultural employers overseen by this department.
Establishing a new unit within the Department of Labor requires budget allocation, personnel management, and fiscal oversight from DBM.
The OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the new Temporary Worker Oversight Unit and represent the state in enforcement actions or related litigation.
The bill creates a private right of action for temporary workers, which may lead to increased litigation and judicial administrative workloads.
Since H-2A workers are vital to rural agricultural sectors, the bill's regulatory impact on farmers and rural labor markets is highly relevant to the Council's mission.
The bill's protections against retaliation and interference with advocacy organizations relate to the Commission's mandate to protect worker rights and civil liberties.
Civil penalties imposed by the Department of Labor may be appealed to the OAH for adjudication by Administrative Law Judges.
The bill regulates employer-provided housing conditions and access for health service organizations, which falls under the department's interest in public health and worker safety.

The new requirements and liability for recruiters and employers of H-2B workers impact business climate, recruitment practices, and economic development in industries like hospitality and construction.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Maryland Justice Corps Program within the University System of Maryland, providing an alternative pathway to a license to practice law for graduates of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law. Participants commit to a three-year term with a public or private supervising organization, with priority given to those serving in underserved areas or legal fields. The program provides participants with an annual salary, a housing stipend, and student loan debt repayment assistance.
responsible_party: University System of Maryland, specifically the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law
stakeholders: Graduates of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law; public and private legal organizations; and Maryland residents in underserved communities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a significant State expenditure mandate by requiring the State to pay 50% of the benefits for each program participant. These benefits include a $75,000 annual salary, a $15,000 annual housing stipend, and up to $30,000 in student loan debt repayment per year, resulting in a State cost of up to $60,000 per participant annually. The remaining 50% is paid by the supervising organization. The total fiscal impact is indeterminate as the number of participants is not capped in the bill and a formal Fiscal Note with total aggregate estimates was not included in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maryland Justice Corps Program within the University System of Maryland (USM). The program is to be administered jointly by two USM institutions—the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law—and USM is tasked with adopting regulations to carry out the program.

The program provides an alternative pathway to a license to practice law. The Supreme Court of Maryland, which the Administrative Office of the Courts supports, is responsible for establishing the minimum qualifications for this alternative licensure and admitting successful participants to the Bar.

The bill has a significant fiscal impact as the State is required to pay 50% of the total cost of benefits for participants, which includes a $75,000 salary, a $15,000 housing stipend, and up to $30,000 for student loan debt annually. DBM oversees the state budget and fiscal planning necessary for such expenditures.

As the state's regulatory and coordinating board for higher education, the Commission oversees policies for universities and administers state financial aid. The program involves graduate law education and a significant student loan repayment component.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the University System of Maryland and the Judiciary. They would likely be involved in reviewing the new regulations and the legal framework for an alternative pathway to Bar licensure to ensure compliance with existing state laws.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Frederick County Special Education Video and Audio Recording Program. It requires the Frederick County Board of Education to install video recording devices in specialized instructional settings and audio recording devices in certain private areas, such as restrooms and changing areas, to document incidents of bullying, abuse, neglect, or harm. The program includes strict privacy protections, specific access protocols for parents and law enforcement, and requirements for unbiased third-party review and data retention.
stakeholders: Students with disabilities in Frederick County Public Schools, their parents or legal guardians, and school system employees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a significant indeterminate increase in local expenditures for the Frederick County Board of Education. Financial impacts include costs for purchasing, installing, and maintaining video and audio recording hardware; establishing and managing a secure, closed network for data storage; and potentially hiring or contracting personnel to fulfill the roles of unbiased third-party reviewers and custodians of recordings. Specific dollar estimates were not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new section to the Education Article and requires Frederick County to report to the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), which provides leadership and oversight for the state's public education system and special education services.

The bill establishes a program specifically targeting 'specialized instructional settings' for students with disabilities, impacting the delivery and documentation of services for the primary population the department supports.

The bill explicitly allows representatives from Child Protective Services, which is administered by the department through local offices, to review video and audio recordings of incidents involving suspected abuse or neglect.
The agency provides the impartial hearing process for special education disputes and contested cases; the bill requires that recordings be preserved until administrative proceedings are complete.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to state educational authorities regarding the bill's requirement to comply with federal privacy laws and the legal implications of recording in sensitive areas.
The office coordinates statewide efforts to improve the well-being and safety of Maryland's children, including initiatives to prevent child abuse and neglect in educational settings.

Located in Frederick County and dedicated to providing special education, the school is directly involved with the population addressed by the bill and may be impacted by local education policy precedents.
The commission oversees the funding and execution of school capital improvements and safety grants, which may be relevant to the installation and maintenance of the required recording systems.
The use of audio and video recording devices in restrooms and changing areas for students with disabilities may involve civil rights considerations and anti-discrimination law compliance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advocates for the welfare of deaf and hard of hearing residents, many of whom are served in the specialized instructional settings described in the bill.

bill_summary: This bill alters the homestead property tax credit for homeowners in Baltimore County who are at least 65 years old by setting the homestead credit percentage at 100%. This effectively caps annual property assessment increases at 0% for State, county, and municipal property tax purposes for eligible seniors.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Homeowners in Baltimore County who are at least 65 years old
fiscal_impact_summary: State Annuity Bond Fund revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $800,000 in FY 2027 and $600,000 in FY 2028. Baltimore County property tax revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $4,800,000 in both FY 2027 and FY 2028. The reduction in State property tax revenue may require an increase in the State property tax rate or a general fund appropriation to meet debt service obligations on general obligation bonds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill reduces State property tax revenues that flow into the Annuity Bond Fund (ABF). The Treasurer's Office manages this fund and oversees the debt service on the state's General Obligation bonds, which the fiscal note indicates may be impacted by the revenue decrease.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for estimating revenues and supervising budget execution. The fiscal note suggests the revenue loss from this bill may require a general fund appropriation to cover debt service, directly affecting the state budget managed by DBM.

As the independent agency responsible for hearing appeals regarding property tax assessment disputes and credits, PTAAB is relevant for adjudicating any disputes arising from the implementation or eligibility requirements of this new 100% homestead credit for seniors in Baltimore County.

The Maryland Tax Court performs the final administrative review of tax-related disputes, including those involving property tax assessments and credits. It would be the final venue for disputes regarding the age-based Homestead Property Tax Credit criteria established by this bill.

The bill specifically targets homeowners who are at least 65 years old to provide property tax relief. This aligns with the department's mission to protect the rights and improve the quality of life for older adults in Maryland.

The Board of Public Works oversees the state's fiscal integrity and approves general obligation bond issuances. Since the bill impacts property tax revenues dedicated to bond debt service, the Board has a significant oversight interest.

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller monitors state revenues and fiscal policy, including the impacts of property tax credit changes on state funds.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget. The fiscal impact on state property tax revenues and potential need for general fund appropriations would require coordination with the Governor's policy and budget staff.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation of new laws and would represent the state in the event of legal challenges to the new age-based tax credit structure.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the conditions under which owners of rental properties built before 1978 (affected properties) must meet lead risk reduction standards. It removes the requirement that an environmental investigation must first identify a defect in the property before an owner is mandated to perform lead hazard reduction treatments after receiving notice that a resident child or pregnant woman has an elevated blood lead level.
stakeholders: Owners of rental properties built before 1978, tenants, and children or pregnant women residing in such properties.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the provided text does not include a formal Fiscal Note. The bill expands the circumstances under which property owners must perform lead risk reduction measures, which will likely increase private-sector compliance expenditures. There may be minor administrative impacts on the Maryland Department of the Environment to oversee these modified standards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing the Lead Risk Reduction in Housing Act. This bill directly amends the Environment Article, which MDE oversees, by altering the triggers for property owners to meet lead risk reduction standards.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) monitors elevated blood lead levels (EBL) and coordinates with local health departments for case management. Since the bill links housing risk reduction requirements to EBL test results, MDH is a critical stakeholder in the identification and notification process.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to MDE and MDH and represents the state in enforcement actions. Removing the requirement for an environmental investigation to find a defect before triggering remediation alters the legal burden and enforcement protocols for lead-based paint violations.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) adjudicates contested cases from state agencies, including MDE. Disputes between property owners and MDE regarding compliance with the modified risk reduction standard and notices of lead risk are heard by Administrative Law Judges at OAH.

The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) manages programs for safe and affordable housing. While MDE handles lead-specific regulations, DHCD has a significant interest in housing quality standards and the impact of lead remediation requirements on the rental housing market.

The Judicial Branch manages civil litigation between landlords and tenants. Removing a prerequisite for requiring lead risk reduction measures may affect the volume and nature of civil suits brought by tenants seeking remediation or damages related to lead exposure.

Synopsis: Replacing the term "landlord" with "residential housing provider" and "tenant" with "resident" in the context of residential leases.

Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Economic Matters; Withdrawn
bill_summary: This bill updates the terminology used in the Annotated Code of Maryland by replacing the terms "landlord" and "tenant" with "rental property owner" and "resident," respectively, in provisions relating to residential leases.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Rental property owners (formerly landlords) and residents (formerly tenants) in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect state or local government operations or finances. The Maryland Judiciary may incur minor operational costs to update legal forms, brochures, and websites, but these expenses are expected to be absorbed during routine replenishment cycles.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly renames the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs to the Office of Resident and Rental Property Owner Affairs within this department and mandates the publication of a Maryland Residents' Bill of Rights.

The fiscal note indicates a moderate operational impact as the Judiciary must revise and reprint extensive court forms, notices, brochures, and websites to reflect the new terminology in summary ejectment and rent escrow proceedings.
The bill amends numerous sections of the Environment Article regarding lead-contaminated dust testing, risk reduction standards, and notifications provided to residents by property owners.
The bill updates terminology for social service programs that deduct rent from temporary cash assistance for residents in public housing.
The Division of Consumer Protection within the OAG is specifically tasked with enforcing rights related to the terminology changes in residential leases and assisted housing projects.
The bill amends the Public Utilities Article regarding utility billing, termination notices, and energy allocation systems involving residents and rental property owners.
The Secretary of State receives mandated notices and affidavits regarding the conversion of rental facilities into cooperative housing corporations or condominiums.
The bill updates terminology in the State Government Article pertaining to housing discrimination and reasonable modifications for residents with disabilities.
The bill requires property owners to provide residents with a link to a pet fact sheet published on the Department of Agriculture's website.
The bill amends protections for military personnel regarding the termination of residential leases due to changes in assignment.
The bill's changes to lease extension rights for senior citizens in converting properties directly impact the older adults served by this department.
The bill updates terminology regarding lease extensions and accessibility code relief for residents with disabilities.
The bill amends the Health - General Article to update terminology used in nursing home licensure applications regarding property ownership and management.
The bill updates terms in the Tax - Property Article regarding property tax credits for owners who provide reduced rents for certain residents.
The bill makes structural and nomenclature changes to an office within a cabinet-level department (DHCD) which is overseen by the Governor's Office.
The bill updates terminology in the Public Safety Article regarding lease protections for individuals in emergency management service.
The bill updates legal representation standards for residents and property owners within the Business Occupations and Professions Article.
As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the court may handle appeals involving the property tax credits updated by this bill.
The board hears appeals regarding property tax credits and exemptions, including those for rental dwellings cited in the bill.

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of "rental dwelling unit" within the context of lead risk reduction in housing. It removes the requirement that a unit be "independent" and specifies that a unit qualifies if it has either direct provisions or "access to" permanent facilities for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation.
stakeholders: Owners of rental properties, tenants in units with shared facilities, and the Maryland Department of the Environment.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The expansion of the definition of rental dwelling units likely increases the number of properties subject to lead risk reduction standards, which could increase State revenue from registration fees and raise administrative and enforcement expenditures for the Maryland Department of the Environment.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing lead risk reduction laws in housing. This bill directly amends the Environment Article to expand the definition of 'rental dwelling unit,' thereby increasing the number of properties subject to MDE's lead risk reduction regulations and enforcement actions.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) works closely with MDE on public health initiatives related to lead poisoning prevention. Expanding the scope of regulated rental units directly affects public health monitoring and services provided to residents at risk of lead exposure.

The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) oversees housing safety and affordability. Changes to the lead risk regulations for rental units impact the standards and compliance requirements for the housing stock that DHCD supports, finances, and revitalizes.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to MDE regarding environmental regulations and represents the state in civil and criminal enforcement of lead risk reduction laws. A broader definition of rental units will likely result in increased legal workload and advisory needs.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) adjudicates contested cases from various state agencies, including MDE. An expansion of regulated rental units could lead to an increase in administrative appeals regarding lead risk enforcement actions.

The judiciary handles litigation involving landlord-tenant disputes, including habitability and lead risk compliance. Changing the definition of what constitutes a rental dwelling unit may impact the volume and nature of these cases in state courts.

The Department of Human Services (DHS) provides assistance to vulnerable populations who often reside in rental housing. The inclusion of units with shared facilities under lead risk regulations may impact the availability or standards of units used by participants in DHS programs.

The Governor's Office for Children is focused on child well-being and reducing child poverty. Lead poisoning is a significant health and economic barrier for children in underinvested communities, making this regulatory expansion relevant to their policy goals.

Synopsis: Repealing the authority of the State to engage in eminent domain; and repealing certain provisions of law relating to the State's eminent domain and condemnation authority.
Title: Eminent Domain and Condemnation Authority - Repeal (Property Rights Protection Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/13 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

Article.Title: XI-B - City of Baltimore - Land Development and Redevelopment

bill_summary: The Property Rights Protection Act repeals the authority of the State of Maryland and its local governments to exercise eminent domain and condemnation. It proposes a constitutional amendment to prohibit the taking of private property for public use and strikes various statutory provisions that currently allow for such actions across the Maryland Code.
responsible_party: Maryland State and local government agencies with current condemnation authority, including the Maryland Department of Transportation and the State Highway Administration.
stakeholders: Private property owners, small businesses, and Maryland State and local government agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates a potential significant increase in State and local expenditures. Without the power of eminent domain, government agencies may face higher costs for acquiring land through voluntary negotiations or incur expenses related to modifying, delaying, or cancelling capital projects. Revenues are not affected. Specific dollar estimates for these impacts are currently unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Public Safety Article to repeal the Department's authority to acquire real property for the Maryland Air National Guard by condemnation.

The bill repeals various provisions of the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article related to condemnation proceedings and would fundamentally alter the judicial branch's role in adjudicating eminent domain cases.
The bill repeals multiple provisions requiring Board of Public Works approval for state-level condemnation and limits the Board's ability to oversee land acquisition through eminent domain.
The bill specifically amends the Financial Institutions Article to repeal the Authority's power to exercise condemnation for property in the park corridor.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller oversees significant state contracts and property acquisitions, which would be impacted by the repeal of eminent domain authority.
The bill repeals provisions related to the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF) and the Secretary's authority to acquire property by condemnation.
The bill has a significant fiscal impact on state capital projects, which are overseen by DBM during the budgeting and execution phases.

The bill amends provisions regarding site selection for power plants where the Secretary of Commerce provides advice, and general economic development projects often rely on property acquisition authority.
The bill repeals the authority of local boards of education and community colleges to bring condemnation proceedings for school purposes.
The bill repeals extensive authority within the Environment Article regarding the acquisition of property for water systems, sewerage systems, and the reclamation of mining lands.
DGS is the primary agency for state real estate acquisition and facility management; the bill repeals the general authority of DGS and the Board of Public Works to condemn property for State use.
The bill repeals the Department's authority to acquire sites for facilities by condemnation, particularly in cases of county default.
The bill repeals the condemnation authority used by the DHCD Administration for community development and housing projects.
The bill repeals and amends numerous sections of the Natural Resources Article regarding the acquisition of land for state parks, forests, and wildlife management areas.
The bill impacts state planning visions and utility corridor designations where the Department of Planning provides data and coordination.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the authority of counties to acquire sites for correctional facilities by condemnation.

As the overarching agency for transportation modal administrations, MDOT would be significantly impacted by the total repeal of eminent domain and quick-take authority for highway, transit, port, and aviation projects.
The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies whose statutory powers are being curtailed, and the bill proposes a constitutional amendment that must be coordinated by the executive department.
The bill amends the Education Article to remove the Commission's authority to acquire property within its boundaries by condemnation.
The bill's repeal of school-related condemnation authority affects the planning and execution of public school capital improvement projects overseen by the IAC.
The bill repeals the Administration's authority to acquire property or easements for airports and air navigation facilities by condemnation.
The bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article to update terminology regarding license transfers when premises are taken by condemnation.
The bill repeals MEDCO's authority to acquire property for development projects by condemnation.
The bill impacts energy planning and power plant site acquisition where the MEA Director provides advisory input.
The bill repeals the Service's authority to exercise eminent domain for environmental projects such as water and wastewater treatment facilities.
The bill repeals the Administration's authority to acquire land, riparian rights, or public land for port projects by condemnation.
The bill specifically repeals MSA's authority to use ordinary and quick-take condemnation for sports and entertainment facilities, including Camden Yards and racing facilities.
As the bill proposes a constitutional amendment, the Board is responsible for submitting the question to voters and managing the ballot process for the 2026 general election.
The bill repeals the authority to acquire property for library purposes via condemnation.
As a member of the Board of Public Works and the chief financial manager of state property, the Treasurer is relevant to the oversight of state land assets affected by this bill.
The bill repeals the MTA's authority to acquire property or interests in private carriers by condemnation for transit services.
The bill repeals the MDTA's authority to condemn property for transportation facilities projects.
The OAG would be the primary legal body advising state agencies on the implications of the repeal and representing the state in legal matters arising from the transition away from eminent domain.
The bill repeals the Commission's role in authorizing utility-related condemnation and amends multiple sections of the Public Utilities Article regarding franchise and acquisition rights.
The SHA is one of the primary users of 'quick-take' condemnation; the bill repeals these specific powers and the Board of Property Review Procedure used by the agency.

Synopsis: Establishing the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund; requiring, on or before July 1, beginning in 2028, a dog breeder to register annually with the Department of Agriculture and, at the time of registration, pay an annual registration fee of $150; requiring, beginning on July 1, 2029, and within 30 days after the birth of a litter, a dog breeder to apply to the Department for a puppy birth certificate for each puppy born in the litter; etc.
Title: Department of Agriculture - Regulation of Dog Breeders
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Technology -see also- AeroT; BioT; EnergyT; InfoT; MedT; etc
Transfer of Goods -see also- Goods&Svc; Leas&Rnt; RetailSale

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund to promote breeder registration and support animal shelters. It requires dog breeders to register annually with the Department of Agriculture starting in 2028, apply for puppy birth certificates for each puppy born starting in 2029, and ensure puppies born on or after July 1, 2030, are microchipped. It prohibits breeders from selling or transferring puppies to the public unless they are registered and have the required birth certificates and microchips.
stakeholders: Dog breeders, animal shelters, spay/neuter programs, puppy buyers, and the Maryland Department of Agriculture.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund, which will collect revenue from a $150 annual breeder registration fee and a $50 fee per puppy birth certificate application. The Department may also impose administrative penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Fund expenditures are designated for animal shelters and spay/neuter programs (50%), administrative costs (30%), and education and enforcement (20%). Interest earnings are credited to the General Fund. Total fiscal estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes Title 17 under the Agriculture Article, making the Department of Agriculture the primary agency responsible for registering dog breeders, issuing puppy birth certificates, administering the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund, and maintaining a public registry.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the newly established Dog Breeder Accountability Fund separately and to invest the money of the fund.
The bill requires the Comptroller to account for the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the Department of Agriculture regarding the adoption of new regulations and the enforcement of administrative penalties established in this bill.

The Department of Agriculture is required to submit an annual report to the Governor regarding the implementation of the breeder registration program and the impact of the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund.

DBM is responsible for supervising the state budget and personnel. The creation of a new special fund and the administrative requirements placed on the Department of Agriculture would involve DBM in fiscal and potentially personnel planning.

The bill authorizes the Department of Agriculture to impose administrative penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Contested cases involving these penalties would likely be adjudicated by the Office of Administrative Hearings.

Synopsis: Establishing a Class L beer, wine, and liquor license; authorizing a local licensing board to issue the license to a holder of a manufacturer's license; specifying that the license authorizes the license holder to sell or provide samples of certain beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption under certain circumstances; and establishing an annual license fee of $250.00.
Title: Alcoholic Beverages - Class L Beer, Wine, and Liquor License - Established
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Class L beer, wine, and liquor license, which local licensing boards may issue to holders of manufacturer's licenses. The license permits holders to sell or provide free samples of beer, wine, and liquor (produced by the holder or another manufacturer) for on-premises consumption.
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage manufacturers, local licensing boards, and consumers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes an annual license fee of $250 for the Class L license. While this will result in a revenue increase for local licensing boards, the total fiscal impact is indeterminate as the number of licenses to be issued is unknown and a formal Fiscal Note with aggregate estimates was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector and regulates the alcohol industry. This bill establishes a new Class L alcoholic beverages license for manufacturers, directly falling under the Comptroller's regulatory and revenue collection oversight.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including those involved in the regulation of alcoholic beverages, and would be responsible for interpreting the new license's legal framework and representing the state in related litigation.

Many alcoholic beverage manufacturers in Maryland, such as farm-breweries and wineries, are part of the state's agricultural community. This bill affects their ability to sell products and provide samples on-site, impacting the economic viability of these agricultural businesses.

The Department of Commerce is responsible for stimulating the economy and supporting Maryland businesses. This new license provides a business expansion opportunity for manufacturers (breweries, wineries, and distilleries) to increase on-premises sales.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies. Disputes regarding the issuance, suspension, or revocation of these new licenses by state-level regulators or local boards (where applicable for appeals) may be heard by Administrative Law Judges.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and coordinates intergovernmental relations. This bill involves changes to state law and local board authority that the Governor's staff would review and coordinate.

Synopsis: Requiring an order for guardianship of the person of a disabled person to allow for certain visitation; authorizing an interested person to file a certain petition for guardianship of the person of a disabled person on the grounds that the disabled adult's current guardian is medically or physically neglecting the adult; requiring a court to hear certain petitions within a certain amount of time; and authorizing an interested person to file a certain petition to appoint a temporary guardian of a disabled person.
Title: Estates and Trusts - Guardianship of the Person of a Disabled Person - Emergency and Temporary Guardianship Petitions
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Vulnerable Adults -see also- DevDisab; EldPers; PhysDisab

bill_summary: This bill establishes a rebuttable presumption that it is in the best interests of a disabled person under guardianship to have an access schedule for visits from relatives by blood or marriage. It also creates two distinct processes for urgent intervention—emergency guardianship and temporary guardianship—allowing petitions to be filed if a current guardian is medically or physically neglecting the disabled person. The bill requires expedited court rulings on these petitions (within one business day for emergency and seven calendar days for temporary) and lowers the evidentiary standard for such orders from 'clear and convincing evidence' to a 'preponderance of the evidence.'
responsible_party: The Maryland Judiciary (Circuit Courts) and the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Disabled adults under guardianship or in need of protective services, family members of disabled adults, and court-appointed guardians.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to have a direct or material impact on State or local finances. While the bill mandates expedited hearings and potentially increases the volume of petitions due to the lowered evidentiary standard, these administrative requirements are expected to be handled within existing resources. Small business impacts are noted as minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly impacts court operations by establishing new hearing timelines (ruling within 1 business day for emergency and 7 days for temporary petitions) and changing the evidentiary standard for guardianship cases from clear and convincing evidence to a preponderance of the evidence.

DHS is highly relevant because local departments of social services under its jurisdiction often serve as guardians of the person. The bill specifically references attorneys contracted by DHS to represent indigent persons in these proceedings.

The Secretary of Aging is specifically mentioned in the bill as an official who may be appointed as an emergency or temporary guardian. The department also oversees long-term care advocacy for the population impacted by the bill.

The bill addresses petitions for guardianship related to medical treatment and involves local departments of health in situations where forcible entry of a premises is required to provide protective services.

Law enforcement officers, including state police, are responsible for transporting individuals to medical facilities in emergencies and must accompany officials during authorized forcible entries as described in the bill.

The OAG serves as legal counsel to the state agencies directly impacted by these changes (DHS, Department of Health, and Department of Aging) and ensures that the implementation of new guardianship procedures complies with state law.

As the principal agency coordinating services for residents with disabilities, this department is relevant due to the bill's direct focus on the rights and legal protections of disabled individuals under guardianship.

Synopsis: Requiring the Comptroller, in consultation with certain entities, to study and report to the General Assembly by December 15, 2026, on exempting from the sales and use tax electricity used for agricultural purposes such as raising livestock or poultry, preparing, irrigating, or tending the soil, or planting, maintaining, or transporting seeds or crops; and requiring the report to include an estimate of the fiscal impact of the exemption.
Title: Sales and Use Tax - Electricity for Agriculture Purposes - Study and Report
Status: In the House - Returned Passed

Meat, Poultry, Seafood -see also- Clams; Crabs; Food; Oyster
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Office of the Comptroller, in consultation with the Public Service Commission and PJM Interconnection, LLC, to conduct a study on the potential effects of exempting electricity used for specific agricultural purposes from the state sales and use tax. The study must include a fiscal impact estimate and be reported to the General Assembly by December 15, 2026. Agricultural purposes covered in the study include raising livestock or poultry, soil preparation and irrigation, and various activities related to seeds and crops.
stakeholders: Maryland farmers, livestock and poultry producers, electric utility companies, the Public Service Commission, and PJM Interconnection, LLC
fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office may increase in fiscal 2027 to conduct the required study. The bill has no direct impact on state or local revenues as it mandates a report rather than an immediate change to tax law. Specific dollar estimates for the cost of the study are not provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of the Comptroller to lead the study and report on the proposed sales and use tax exemption for electricity used for agricultural purposes.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to consult with the Public Service Commission, which regulates the electric companies required to provide usage and billing data for the study.

The subject matter of the study—electricity used for livestock, soil irrigation, and crop management—directly impacts the economic viability of the agricultural community that the department supports and regulates.

The bill is expected to increase general fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office to conduct the study and involves long-term fiscal planning and revenue estimation related to the sales and use tax.
The proposed tax exemption would specifically benefit the agricultural and rural interests in Maryland's 18 rural counties that the council is tasked with advocating for and supporting.

As the administrative support for the Governor, the office oversees the executive branch agencies conducting the study and coordinates policy initiatives related to state taxation and agricultural support.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Comptroller and state agencies, which may be required to interpret existing tax laws and statutory definitions during the course of the study.

Synopsis: Altering the length of the term of the members of the Accountability and Implementation Board; authorizing a public school or local school system to appeal to the Office of Administrative Hearings after receiving a decision by the Accountability and Implementation Board to withhold certain funds after a certain appeals process; establishing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Stakeholder Advisory Council; establishing the Joint Oversight Committee on the Blueprint for Maryland's Future; etc.
Title: Education - Blueprint for Maryland's Future - Oversight Requirements

Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill establishes additional oversight mechanisms for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. It shortens the terms of Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB) members from six to four years and places the board under the jurisdiction of the Inspector General for Education. The bill establishes a Stakeholder Advisory Council to evaluate the classroom-level effectiveness of policies and a Joint Oversight Committee of the General Assembly to monitor implementation. Furthermore, it creates an appeals process through the Office of Administrative Hearings for local school systems contesting the withholding of funds by the AIB and mandates triennial performance audits of the AIB by the Office of Legislative Audits.
stakeholders: Local school systems, public school administrators, teachers, students, parents, and Maryland State education agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase to support triennial performance audits by the Office of Legislative Audits and administrative hearings conducted by the Office of Administrative Hearings. Additional operational costs will be incurred by the Department of Legislative Services to staff the new Joint Oversight Committee and the Stakeholder Advisory Council. While no specific appropriation is provided in the bill, it establishes a $1,000,000 threshold for the Joint Oversight Committee to review AIB decisions regarding the withholding of education aid. Local school systems may experience a fiscal impact if they successfully appeal and recover withheld State education funds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department is the primary agency responsible for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future implementation, and the bill establishes new legislative oversight over its implementation and enforcement decisions.

The bill designates the Office of Administrative Hearings as the body to adjudicate appeals from local school systems regarding decisions by the Accountability and Implementation Board to withhold Blueprint funding.
The bill mandates that the Office of Legislative Audits conduct a performance audit of the Accountability and Implementation Board at least once every three years beginning in 2026.
The Governor is responsible for appointing members of the Accountability and Implementation Board, and the bill alters their terms and the appointment cycle for these members.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Stakeholder Advisory Council as a new advisory body under this category to offer expertise to the General Assembly.
The Comptroller must be notified of the Accountability and Implementation Board's final decisions regarding the release or withholding of education aid funds for accounting and payment purposes.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in the recruitment and vetting of members for the Accountability and Implementation Board, whose membership terms are restructured by this bill.

As the chief legal representative for state boards, the OAG would provide legal counsel and representation to the Accountability and Implementation Board during the new administrative appeal processes.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from placing an advertisement for a sugary beverage on certain property unless the advertisement includes a certain warning.
Title: Business Regulation - Sugary Beverage Advertisements - Warning Labels
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the placement of advertisements for sugary beverages on property owned by the State, a county, or a municipal corporation unless the advertisement includes a specific health warning label. The label must be in bold, boxed, and highly visible, warning that added sugar can contribute to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and tooth decay. The bill applies to beverages containing added sugars or nonnutritive sweeteners like aspartame or stevia.
responsible_party: Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Manufacturers and advertisers of sugary beverages, State and local government agencies that manage advertising space on public property, and Maryland residents.
fiscal_impact_summary: State General Fund revenues may increase by an indeterminate amount due to civil penalties of up to $1,000 per day for each violation. State and local government entities could experience an indeterminate impact on advertising revenue if beverage companies choose not to place advertisements on government-owned property to avoid the warning label requirement. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General with enforcing the new advertising requirements and imposing civil penalties for violations.

As the primary manager of state-owned facilities and the central procurement authority, DGS must ensure that all advertisements and vending contracts on state property comply with the required health warnings.
The MTA manages extensive advertising space on state-owned transit vehicles and facilities, all of which would be subject to the bill's mandatory labeling requirements.

The MSA manages large state-owned sports and entertainment complexes where sugary beverage advertisements are a significant presence; the agency will be responsible for ensuring compliance with label mandates.

As the parent agency for several modal administrations that manage state property with advertising space (such as MTA and MAA), MDOT oversees the implementation of these regulations across its network.
The bill focuses on public health outcomes like obesity and diabetes, and it designates the required text as a 'Maryland State Health Warning,' making MDH a key stakeholder and policy expert.
The MAA operates BWI and Martin State Airport, which are state-owned properties featuring significant commercial advertising that would require the specified warning labels.
DNR manages half a million acres of state-owned public lands and parks where advertisements on vending machines or signage must now include the health warning.
The Board of Public Works approves significant state procurement and concession contracts, including those for food and beverage services on state property that involve advertising.
The bill applies to advertisements on county property, which includes local public schools; MSDE would likely provide guidance and oversight to ensure compliance within school systems.
USM governs various state-owned university campuses where sugary beverage advertisements on vending machines or at athletic venues would need to comply with the bill.
As a state agency managing its own urban campus, Morgan State must ensure all advertisements for sugary beverages on its state-owned property include the required warning labels.
As an independent state honors college, SMC must ensure that advertisements on its state-owned campus property meet the new health labeling standards.
The MPA manages state-owned maritime terminals where beverage advertisements or vending machines must comply with the bill's labeling mandate.
The MFCA manages state-owned wholesale food distribution facilities; any advertisements for sugary beverages within these centers would require the specified health warning.
The OTD manages state welcome centers; any beverage advertisements or signage in these state-owned facilities must include the required labeling.
Since the bill applies to municipal and county-owned property, the Maryland State Library Agency will likely coordinate with local library systems to ensure their signage and vending machines comply.

Synopsis: Establishing a Real Estate Advisory Committee in the Department of General Services to advise the Department, the Board of Public Works, and the General Assembly on certain real estate matters; establishing additional requirements for the Board of Public Works before approving the acquisition or lease of certain real property; providing that the Board may not approve the sale, transfer, exchange, or grant of certain property under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Procurement - Real Estate Advisory Committee and Property Acquisition and Lease Requirements
Status: In the House - Passed Enrolled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Real Estate -see also- Agents and Brokers
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Real Estate Advisory Committee within the Department of General Services (DGS) to provide guidance to the Department, the Board of Public Works, and the General Assembly on commercial real estate trends, asset management, and long-term planning. Additionally, it extends existing reporting and justification requirements for state property acquisitions valued at $500,000 or more to include real property leases with annual payments of at least $500,000.
stakeholders: Maryland state agencies (particularly DGS, MDOT, and higher education institutions), the Board of Public Works, the General Assembly, and commercial real estate landlords and developers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $90,000 in FY 2027, which accounts for a 90-day startup delay following the bill's effective date of July 1, 2026. These costs cover the hiring of one administrative staff member at DGS to support the new advisory committee and manage the increased reporting requirements to the Legislative Policy Committee. Out-year expenditures are projected to increase annually for salary and inflation, reaching $121,000 by FY 2031. The bill has no effect on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is a primary body impacted by the bill's new reporting and advisory requirements. Additionally, the new Real Estate Advisory Committee must submit its annual findings and recommendations directly to the Governor.

The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works. The bill mandates that the Board receive advisory reports and detailed justifications/cost-benefit analyses for real estate acquisitions and leases exceeding $500,000.

The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works. The bill requires the Board to review expanded justifications and cost-benefit analyses for major real estate transactions and receive annual reports from the new advisory committee.
As the state's principal personnel and budget agency, DBM is impacted by the bill's requirement for a new staff position at DGS and the associated general fund expenditures ($90,000+ annually).

DGS is the primary implementing agency. The bill establishes the Real Estate Advisory Committee within DGS, requires the Secretary of General Services to chair and appoint members, mandates DGS to provide staffing, and increases DGS's reporting obligations for property acquisitions and leases.

The fiscal note identifies MDOT as one of the agencies responsible for producing and disseminating the detailed justifications and cost-benefit analyses required by the bill for its specific real estate acquisitions and leases.

The Board of Public Works is a central entity in the bill. It is the recipient of the advisory committee's findings and is prohibited from approving certain acquisitions or leases without providing specific justifications and analyses to the Legislative Policy Committee.

As a state institution of higher education that manages its own property, Morgan State is included in the fiscal note's group of agencies responsible for producing the bill's required reporting information for real estate transactions.

As a public honors college and state agency, it falls under the institutions of higher education identified in the fiscal note as responsible for the bill's expanded real estate reporting requirements.

The fiscal note explicitly names USM as an agency responsible for producing and disseminating the relevant required information for real estate acquisitions and leases under the bill's expanded oversight provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new permanent advisory body, the Real Estate Advisory Committee, which falls under this category of executive entities tasked with providing expertise and recommendations to the state government.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a licensing and regulatory framework for anesthesiologist assistants (AAs) in Maryland under the State Board of Physicians. It defines the scope of practice for AAs, mandates that they practice under the supervision of a licensed anesthesiologist, and requires the Board to adopt regulations concerning qualifications, fees, and disciplinary procedures for the profession.
stakeholders: Anesthesiologist assistants, licensed anesthesiologists, medical facilities, and patients requiring anesthesia services.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State Board of Physicians special fund expenditures increase by $70,800 in FY 2027 and $207,100 in FY 2028 for staffing and software updates, with ongoing annual costs between approximately $85,000 and $94,000. Maryland Department of Health general fund expenditures increase by $1,800 in FY 2028 for database updates. Board special fund revenues and state general fund revenues (from fines and registration fees) will increase by an indeterminate amount starting in FY 2028.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new licensure category for Anesthesiologist Assistants under the State Board of Physicians, which is an entity within the Maryland Department of Health. The department will oversee the implementation of the new regulatory framework and is responsible for the fiscal impact on special funds.

As a division of the Department of Health, the OCSA is responsible for issuing Controlled Dangerous Substance (CDS) registrations. The bill allows Anesthesiologist Assistants to order controlled substances, necessitating a database update and new registration process for these practitioners as noted in the fiscal note.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal representative for the state and its boards. This bill specifically assigns the OAG a role in the disciplinary process, requiring it to file certified docket entries with the Board of Physicians regarding certain criminal convictions.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency for the state, DBM is relevant because the bill requires the creation of a new Licensure Analyst position and has a fiscal impact on the state's special and general funds.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Board of Physicians pay all collected licensure fees to the Comptroller, who is then responsible for distributing those funds back to the Board to cover administrative costs.

The Office of Administrative Hearings is responsible for providing impartial hearings for contested cases across state agencies, including disciplinary matters and regulatory enforcement related to health professionals.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and appointments to state boards, including the State Board of Physicians which will implement this new licensing program.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the placement of children in unlicensed settings under the out-of-home placement program required to be established by the Social Services Administration; altering the duties of the pediatric hospital overstay coordinators; establishing the Child and Youth Placement Review Panel in the Governor's Office for Children with the Senior Advisor for Children and Families as its head;  establishing the Advisory Council on Maryland's System of Care for Children, Youth, and Families; etc.
Title: Children in Unlicensed Settings and Pediatric Hospital Overstay Patients - Placement
