bill_summary: This bill authorizes volunteer fire, rescue, and ambulance companies, as well as their auxiliary organizations, in Frederick County to accept credit from individuals as payment to play gaming devices during gaming events held for the organization's own benefit.
stakeholders: Frederick County volunteer fire, rescue, and ambulance companies and their auxiliaries, and participants in local gaming events.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no state or local fiscal impact. The bill does not affect Frederick County's finances, and local impact grants from gaming revenues are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for all commercial and state gaming operations in Maryland, this agency is directly relevant to any legislation that modifies gaming laws, payment methods, or compliance requirements for gaming events, even those conducted by local volunteer organizations.

The OAG is responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies and interpreting state law. This bill amends the Criminal Law Article regarding gaming violations, which requires legal oversight and potential enforcement guidance.

The Comptroller's Office was consulted for the fiscal note and serves as the state's chief financial officer. While the bill primarily affects local non-profit gaming, the Comptroller oversees general revenue collection and regulatory compliance for various industries.

The Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing the state's criminal laws. Since the bill modifies what constitutes a misdemeanor under the Criminal Law Article regarding gaming events, it impacts their law enforcement scope.
The bill impacts the judicial branch because it creates or modifies exceptions to criminal misdemeanors related to gaming, which are adjudicated within the state court system.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement that a school bus be constructed with materials that enable it to meet all criteria of the school bus seat upholstery fire block test established by the National School Transportation specifications and procedures adopted by the most recent National Congress on School Transportation.
Title: Education - School Bus - Fire Safety Standards
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations
bill_summary: This bill repeals the statutory requirement that school buses be constructed using materials that meet specific upholstery fire block test criteria established by the National School Transportation specifications. Instead, it mandates that the Motor Vehicle Administration, with advice from the Maryland State Department of Education, adopt regulations to promote school bus fire safety standards.
responsible_party: Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration and the Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: Local school systems, school bus manufacturers, and Maryland students
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill shifts the authority for school bus fire safety standards from statutory requirements to administrative regulations, which may have future implications for school bus procurement costs depending on the standards adopted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Motor Vehicle Administration to adopt regulations to promote fire safety standards for school buses, replacing a specific statutory material requirement with agency-led regulation.

The bill amends the Education Article and specifies that the Department of Education must provide advice to the Motor Vehicle Administration during the development and adoption of school bus fire safety regulations.

As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the implementation of vehicle safety standards for state-regulated transport like school buses.

The Maryland Center for School Safety coordinates school safety policies and standards; changes to fire safety equipment standards for school buses fall within their mission to foster safe learning environments.

The Office of the Attorney General would likely provide legal counsel to the Motor Vehicle Administration and the Department of Education regarding the repeal of statutory requirements and the subsequent drafting of new administrative regulations.

The Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle laws and ensure traffic safety; they may be impacted by changes to equipment standards and fire safety compliance for school buses operating on state highways.

As a state agency that operates its own educational facilities and student transportation, the Maryland School for the Deaf is directly impacted by changes to the fire safety standards required for school bus construction and procurement.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the eligibility requirements for a local option property tax credit available to certain disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. It increases the income threshold for eligibility from $100,000 to $150,000 for individual filers and $300,000 for joint filers, and grants local governments the authority to establish additional eligibility criteria regarding income and disability ratings.
responsible_party: Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a county or municipal corporation
stakeholders: Honorably discharged veterans with service-connected disabilities of at least 50%, surviving spouses of such veterans, and local taxing authorities in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Local property tax revenues may decrease starting in fiscal 2027 to the extent that local jurisdictions grant the property tax credit and the increased income limits allow additional individuals to qualify. Specific dollar estimates for the revenue loss are unavailable as they depend on local adoption and the number of newly eligible veterans, though the Fiscal Note identifies approximately 45,500 veterans in Maryland who could potentially qualify for the credit depending on local implementation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal state agency for assisting veterans in securing benefits, this department is directly involved in advocating for and providing information regarding benefits like property tax credits for disabled veterans. They are also listed as an information source in the fiscal note.
This agency provides administrative review for disputes concerning property tax assessments and property tax credits, which would include the specific local option credits modified by this bill.

The Tax Court adjudicates appeals from taxing authorities regarding property tax assessments and credits, serving as the highest level of administrative review for the tax matters affected by this bill.
As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller oversees tax law enforcement and is consulted on changes to tax eligibility criteria involving federal adjusted gross income.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the interpretation and implementation of new tax laws and eligibility criteria.

This department coordinates policies for residents with disabilities; while not the primary administrator, it has a secondary interest in legislation defining disability ratings for state or local benefits.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing the legislation into law and overseeing the general administration of state policy regarding veterans.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors legislation for fiscal impacts, although the bill primarily affects local rather than state revenues.

Synopsis: Repealing the prohibition on applicants for and holders of video lottery operation licenses and persons who own an interest in video lottery facility operations in the State from directly or indirectly making contributions to certain campaign finance entities; and requiring the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency to study and report to the Governor and the General Assembly by January 1, 2027, on certain matters concerning certain independent evaluators for sports wagering content.

bill_summary: The bill repeals the prohibition on campaign contributions from applicants for and holders of video lottery operation licenses (casinos) and their owners to nonfederal candidates in Maryland. Additionally, it requires the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency to conduct a study and report on the use of independent evaluators for sports wagering content by January 1, 2027.
responsible_party: State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency
stakeholders: Applicants for and holders of video lottery operation licenses, casino owners, nonfederal political candidates, and sports wagering operators.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances. The State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency can conduct the required study on independent evaluators for sports wagering content using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the agency to conduct a study and report to the Governor and General Assembly regarding independent evaluators for sports wagering content. The agency also regulates the video lottery facilities and sports wagering licensees mentioned in the bill.

The bill repeals a significant prohibition within the Election Law Article regarding campaign contributions from gaming entities. The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering election laws and enforcing campaign finance regulations.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is responsible for investigating and prosecuting criminal offenses related to the electoral process and public ethics laws. Repealing a contribution prohibition directly impacts the legal framework they enforce.

The Governor's Office receives the required study and report from the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency. As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies involved and sets policy priorities regarding gaming and election law.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency. They would likely advise on the implementation of the new law and the legal parameters of the required study.

The commission is responsible for maintaining public confidence in the integrity of state government. Changes to campaign finance laws regarding specific industries (like gaming) intersect with the broader mandate of ethics and influence in state government.
OAH may be involved in adjudicating administrative disputes or contested cases arising from changes to gaming or election law regulations.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance and performance audits of the involved agencies; changes in regulatory requirements for the Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency or the State Board of Elections would be subject to their oversight.

Synopsis: Specifying that the inspector for the Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County is the county codes administrator or an individual the Board appoints as inspector.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the appointment process for the inspector for the Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County. It specifies that the inspector may be either the county codes administrator or an individual specifically appointed by the Board, and clarifies that the Board determines the inspector's duties regarding the enforcement of local alcoholic beverages laws.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage licensees in Caroline County, the Board of License Commissioners, the Caroline County government, and potential inspector appointees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill provides that the salary of the inspector shall be as provided in the county budget. While the bill expands the pool of eligible candidates for the inspector position, specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes are not provided in the bill text and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the source text.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County is a permanent regulatory body established by state law to oversee alcoholic beverages. This bill directly modifies the Board's authority and specifies the appointment process for its inspector, making the Board the primary entity affected by and responsible for implementing the legislation.

The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing state alcohol laws. As this bill changes the structure of local enforcement and administration of those laws in Caroline County, it is relevant to the Comptroller's regulatory oversight.

The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing the members of the Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County. This bill impacts the powers and administrative structure of that Governor-appointed body.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting individuals for state boards and commissions, including local Boards of License Commissioners. Changes to the Board's authority over its staff (inspectors) are relevant to the management of these positions.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions. The OAG would be responsible for providing legal interpretations of the amendments to the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article for the Caroline County Board.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) to use automated lane use control signal monitoring systems on highways, bridges, and tunnels under its jurisdiction to enforce red lane signals. It establishes tiered civil penalties of $90, $180, and $270 for violations occurring on the same trip and outlines the administrative and judicial procedures for issuing, contesting, and processing citations.
stakeholders: Motorists and vehicle owners using Maryland Transportation Authority highways (including bridges and tunnels), the Maryland Transportation Authority, and the District Court of Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill results in a one-time State general fund expenditure of $22,900 in FY 2027 for Judiciary programming costs. If the Maryland Transportation Authority implements the monitoring system, its nonbudgeted expenditures could exceed 10,000,000 annually, which may be offset by revenues from civil penalties remitted by the District Court to the Authority. No local fiscal impact is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) to implement and operate lane use control signal monitoring systems on highways under its jurisdiction, adopt relevant regulations, and receive remitted civil penalties.

The Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) and the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) are both administrations within the Department of Transportation, and the bill modifies the Transportation Article of the Maryland Code.

The bill authorizes the MVA to refuse or suspend vehicle registrations if civil penalties for lane use violations are not paid, and it specifies that such violations may not be recorded on a driver's record.

The District Court, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, is responsible for processing citations, adjudicating contested cases, and remitting penalty revenues to the MDTA. The fiscal note indicates a $22,900 one-time programming cost for the Judiciary.

The bill amends the Insurance Article to prohibit insurers from considering civil penalties from lane use monitoring systems for the purpose of reclassifying an insured in a manner that increases premiums.
The bill requires the Chief Judge of the District Court and the Comptroller to agree upon a system for remitting costs, fines, and penalties to the State.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the MDTA and is responsible for signing the bill into law and appointing members to relevant boards that may oversee transportation policy.

Synopsis: Providing that reserve funds of a cooperative housing corporation or condominium may be used for purposes other than those specified in the funding plan in an emergency and if the use of funds is approved by an affirmative vote of the members or unit owners having at least two-thirds of the votes in the cooperative housing corporation or the council of unit owners, respectively.

Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing bodies of cooperative housing corporations and condominiums to use reserve funds for purposes other than those specified in their funding plans during an emergency. This use is permitted only if the funds are repaid to the reserve within five years and the use is approved by an affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the members or unit owners in good standing.
responsible_party: Governing bodies of cooperative housing corporations and condominiums
stakeholders: Cooperative housing corporations, condominiums, cooperative members, and condominium unit owners
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill relates to the internal financial management of private entities and has no direct impact on State or local government revenues or expenditures. Specific dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note are unavailable as no formal note was included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is explicitly charged with the registration and oversight of condominiums, which are one of the two types of entities governed by the proposed legislation.

The bill governs the financial management and emergency readiness of cooperatives and condominiums, impacting the agency's mission to ensure residents have access to safe, secure, and well-maintained housing.
The OAG enforces state laws regarding consumer protection and provides legal counsel on the interpretation of the Real Property and Corporations and Associations Articles, which this bill amends.

A significant portion of the older adult population in Maryland resides in condominiums and cooperatives; the agency has an interest in the financial stability and structural safety of these housing models for seniors.

The bill introduces new legal requirements for emergency reserve usage, including specific voting thresholds and repayment timelines, which may lead to litigation requiring adjudication by the state's courts.

Synopsis: Authorizing a mutual insurance holding company that, directly or indirectly, owns 100% of the capital stock of a reorganized stock insurer to convert its mutual insurance holding company system to a mutual insurer on adoption and approval of a plan of conversion; and establishing certain requirements related to the plan of conversion and its submission to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner for approval.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a mutual insurance holding company that owns 100% of a reorganized stock insurer's capital stock to convert its system into a mutual insurer. The conversion requires the adoption and approval of a plan of conversion by the company's board of directors, at least 75% of its voting members, and the Maryland Insurance Commissioner. The bill outlines specific requirements for the conversion plan, including the transition of membership interests, the dissolution of the holding company system, and the filing of necessary documents and financial plans with the Maryland Insurance Administration.
stakeholders: Mutual insurance holding companies, reorganized stock insurers, and their policyholders and members.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) special fund expenditures and revenues may increase correspondingly if the Commissioner hires experts to review conversion plans, as the converting companies are required to reimburse MIA for these costs. This results in no net fiscal impact on the State. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as they depend on the frequency and complexity of future conversion applications. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Maryland Insurance Commissioner with reviewing and approving plans for mutual insurance holding companies to convert into mutual insurers. The agency is responsible for overseeing the submission process, potentially holding hearings, adopting regulations, and may retain experts to assist in the evaluation of such plans.

As the legal representative for all state agencies, the OAG would provide counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration regarding the legality of conversion plans and the development of new regulations. They would also represent the state in any civil appeals if the Commissioner's decisions are challenged in court.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies. If the Maryland Insurance Commissioner disapproves a conversion plan or imposes additional conditions that a company disputes, the OAH may be involved in the resulting administrative hearing process.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal agency. The fiscal note indicates that this bill will increase special fund expenditures and revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) to the extent that experts are retained for reviews, which requires DBM oversight of MIA's budget execution.

The Governor oversees the executive branch, including the Maryland Insurance Administration. The Governor also appoints the Insurance Commissioner, who is the primary official charged with implementing the requirements of this bill.

bill_summary: This bill allows Maryland counties to establish 'health innovation zones' in areas with documented health disparities and limited access to healthcare and grocery stores. While the program is optional for most counties, Prince George's County is required to designate two specific zones. The bill requires the Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO) to provide funding to incentivize grocery stores, pharmacies, and healthcare providers to locate within these zones in Prince George's County and exempts such businesses from local zoning and land use laws.
responsible_party: Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO), Prince George’s County Council, and local zoning authorities
stakeholders: Residents of communities with high health disparities, low-income households, minority populations, immigrant populations, grocery store owners, pharmacy operators, and primary and specialty healthcare providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least 250,000 in fiscal 2028 for MEDCO administrative costs, with indeterminate but significant expenditure increases beginning in fiscal 2029 to provide business incentives in Prince George’s County. Prince George’s County expenditures will increase as early as fiscal 2027 to provide local incentives for its mandated zones. Other counties that choose to designate zones will also see increased expenditures, and local revenues may decrease depending on the specific tax incentives implemented.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MEDCO is the primary state entity tasked with implementing the bill's fiscal incentives, managing the distribution of funding to businesses in health innovation zones, and seeking additional funding sources.

The bill adds a new subtitle to the Health – General Article and establishes health innovation zones based on clinical health outcomes and disparities, which are core areas of public health policy overseen by this department.

The bill explicitly exempts grocery stores, pharmacies, and healthcare providers within these zones from local zoning and land use laws, directly impacting the department's role in promoting sustainable growth and land use guidance.
The bill authorizes the Governor to include a significant annual appropriation in the state budget for MEDCO starting in fiscal year 2028, which DBM would manage and supervise.
The Governor has the authority to include appropriations for the zones in the annual budget bill and coordinates the inter-agency policy goals related to health and economic mobility.

The commission's mission includes planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to health care, which aligns with the bill's goal of establishing healthcare providers in underserved areas.
The bill targets 'food deserts' by incentivizing the establishment of grocery stores, which aligns with the department's work in food quality assurance and marketing local agricultural products.
The bill specifically mandates that health innovation zones address disability-related health disparities, particularly in rural communities.
OAG would likely provide legal counsel regarding the bill's preemption of local zoning authority and oversee legal agreements between the state and MEDCO.
The bill's focus on maternal and newborn health complications in disadvantaged communities aligns with the office's mission to improve well-being for Maryland's children and families.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill targets 'communities of color' and 'economically disadvantaged communities' for business development, which relates to the office's oversight of socioeconomic procurement and development.
The team is charged with piloting novel initiatives to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility, which are the intended outcomes of designating these zones in underinvested communities.
The bill addresses health disparities in rural communities, and the council is tasked with advocating for rural interests and addressing geographic challenges in Maryland's 18 rural counties.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of the Environment, in coordination with the Department of Commerce, to streamline the environmental permitting process for manufacturing businesses in NAICS sectors 31, 32, and 33. The Department must establish a single digital application portal, provide a dedicated navigator to assist applicants personally, and issue permit determinations within 60 days of application receipt.
stakeholders: Manufacturing businesses (NAICS sectors 31, 32, and 33) and the Maryland Department of the Environment.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided; however, the bill creates significant new administrative requirements for the Department of the Environment, including the development and maintenance of a single digital portal and the provision of dedicated navigators for permit applicants, which will likely increase state expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency for environmental protection and permitting, MDE is tasked with implementing the bill's requirements, including adopting streamlined procedures, meeting a 60-day determination deadline, providing dedicated navigators, and establishing a single digital portal for specific manufacturing sectors.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of the Environment to coordinate with the Department of Commerce to adopt the streamlined permitting procedures, aligning with Commerce's mission to support businesses and economic development in the manufacturing sector.

The mandate to establish a single digital portal for permit applications directly involves DoIT, which is responsible for the state's IT strategy, infrastructure, and ensuring efficient digital services for government operations.

Implementing the 'dedicated navigator' role and building a new digital portal will likely have fiscal and personnel impacts, requiring DBM's involvement in budgeting for new positions and IT expenditures.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MDE and Commerce. They would be responsible for reviewing the newly adopted permitting procedures and digital portal requirements for compliance with state and federal environmental laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives between departments. This bill affects two cabinet-level departments (MDE and Commerce) and relates to economic and environmental policy priorities.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the requirements for the development of the 28-acre State Center property in Baltimore City. It establishes the State Center Advisory Group to provide community input, facilitate transparency, and leverage benefits for surrounding neighborhoods. The bill replaces previous requirements for agreements with the State Center Neighborhood Alliance with requirements for a community benefit agreement with the new Advisory Group. It also updates the preferred tenant profile from State agencies to anchor institutions providing public or community services, removes the requirement for parking facilities, and extends the timeline for a developer to begin construction from 18 to 24 months after contract execution.
responsible_party: The State or its reporting agency (specifically the Department of General Services and Department of Budget and Management per the Fiscal Note)
stakeholders: Residents and neighborhood associations within a one-mile radius of State Center, anchor institutions in Baltimore City, minority- and women-owned businesses, and real estate developers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates there is no material financial impact on State or local government operations or finances. The creation of the State Center Advisory Group is expected to be handled within existing governmental resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for the planning, design, and management of state-owned facilities and real estate leasing, DGS is the primary 'reporting agency' for the State Center redevelopment project. The bill directly impacts DGS operations by altering contract requirements and requiring the department to convene and engage with a new advisory group.

The Board of Public Works must approve significant state procurement contracts and the lease or transfer of state property. Any new or modified development contract for State Center, as described in the bill, would require BPW approval.

DBM is responsible for long-term fiscal planning and the state's budget execution. The department is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note and is involved in the oversight of state-owned property usage and personnel policies related to the development.

The University of Baltimore, which is a member institution of the University System of Maryland, is explicitly named as a member of the State Center Advisory Group and is identified as an anchor institution for the project area.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the Board of Public Works. It would be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new contract requirements and the enforceable community benefits agreements mandated by the bill.

The bill references the Baltimore City Department of Planning's directory for advisory group membership and relates to large-scale urban development and land use planning, which falls under the broad policy and technical assistance scope of MDP.

The Governor oversees the executive branch departments involved in the project (DGS and DBM) and serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which has final approval over the development contracts.
The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is the body that must approve the modified development contracts and property transfers for State Center.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is the body that must approve the modified development contracts and property transfers for State Center.

The bill also provides that any redisclosure of records by an inspector general is subject to the provisions of the Public Information Act.

stakeholders: State and local government inspectors general, custodians of public records, and state and local government agencies subject to oversight.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text. The legislation likely has an administrative impact on state and local governments as it codifies access protocols for inspectors general, but it does not specify any direct financial allocations, revenue changes, or spending mandates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies regarding the Public Information Act and houses the Ombudsman, who handles disputes and appeals regarding record access and denials.
MSDE houses the Office of the Inspector General for Education, a major state-level oversight body that will directly utilize the expanded record access authority provided by this bill.
MDOT houses its own statutory Office of Inspector General, which requires robust access to multi-modal transportation and administrative records to fulfill its oversight mandates.

MDH houses an Office of Inspector General and serves as the custodian for sensitive public health and Medicaid data that may be subject to inspection by oversight officials notwithstanding other PIA restrictions.
DJS houses an Office of Inspector General whose investigative duties regarding youth and facility management require access to confidential records that this bill clarifies can be inspected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS houses an Office of Inspector General that investigates matters within the state's correctional and parole systems, necessitating access to sensitive security and personnel records.
DHS houses an Office of Inspector General that monitors large-scale social service programs and serves as a custodian for sensitive beneficiary and administrative data.
The Department of Labor houses an Office of Inspector General responsible for overseeing unemployment insurance and workforce programs, requiring access to regulatory and employer records.

As the primary law enforcement agency and a custodian of sensitive investigative records, MSP is impacted by changes to the Public Information Act that prioritize Inspector General access over traditional denials.

The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and a major custodian of tax and revenue records which are frequently the subject of financial and compliance investigations by Inspectors General.

The Secretary of State is a principal custodian of official state records and is directly affected by amendments to the Public Information Act governing the inspection and redisclosure of such records.

As the central depository for government records of permanent value, the Archives is impacted by any legislative changes affecting access rights for oversight bodies and subsequent redisclosure rules.
DBM is the central personnel agency and custodian of state employee records, which are frequently scrutinized by Inspectors General during investigations into misconduct or fiscal waste.
DoIT manages statewide data governance and information security, impacting the technical and policy frameworks through which Inspectors General access digital public records.
The Governor oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy for the various departments whose internal Inspectors General and record custodians are the primary parties affected by this bill.
DGS is the central procurement authority for the state; its contract and facility records are essential to the oversight work of Inspectors General investigating procurement integrity.

Synopsis: Requiring certain wastewater treatment plants to maintain a publicly accessible website on which certain information relating to certain discharges is required to be published in a certain manner; and requiring certain wastewater treatment plants to begin certain testing within 24 hours after a bypass, overflow, or treatment failure that requires testing for certain chemicals or bacteria.
Title: Wastewater Treatment Plants - Discharges - Requirements
Status: In the Senate - Favorable with Amendments Report by Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut
Hazardous and Toxic Substances -see also- Asbestos; Radiatn

bill_summary: This bill requires wastewater treatment plants with an annual average effluent flow of at least 50 million gallons per day to maintain a publicly accessible website. These facilities must publish monthly bacteria results, provide plain-language explanations and volume estimates for any bypass, overflow, or treatment failure within five days, and begin required water quality testing within 24 hours of such incidents, publishing the results within 24 hours of receipt.
stakeholders: Owners and operators of large wastewater treatment plants (specifically Baltimore City's Back River and Patapsco plants) and the general public residing near or using affected waterways.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. The local fiscal impact is anticipated to be minimal; while the bill imposes new operational requirements on Baltimore City for its two affected wastewater treatment plants, both the city and the Maryland Association of Municipal Wastewater Agencies expect the costs to be negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary regulatory agency responsible for issuing discharge permits and enforcing the environmental laws modified by this bill. The bill requires MDE to receive reports, manage a searchable database for industrial pretreatment permits, and oversee the monitoring and testing requirements for wastewater treatment plants.

The bill involves public health determinations related to sewer overflows and treatment plant bypasses. The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) coordinates with MDE and local health departments to develop procedures for public notification and to address health risks associated with wastewater discharges.

The Maryland Environmental Service (MES) provides technical and operational services for wastewater treatment and management to state and local governments. As an agency that operates many wastewater facilities on a fee-for-service basis, it would be directly impacted by the new testing, monitoring, and reporting requirements.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of the Environment and the Department of Health. It would be involved in interpreting the new regulations, providing guidance on compliance, and representing the state in enforcement actions related to wastewater discharge violations.

The bill requires immediate notification to the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) in the event of sewer overflows or treatment plant bypasses that impact State surface waters or state parks, as DNR is responsible for managing these resources and ensuring their conservation.

The bill requires the Department of the Environment to establish a publicly available and searchable database of industrial users with pretreatment permits and their compliance status. DoIT would likely support the strategy, infrastructure, and security required for this state database.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including the Department of the Environment. Disputes regarding discharge permits, industrial pretreatment permits, or penalties issued under the new requirements would be heard by this agency.

The Maryland Department of Emergency Management (MDEM) coordinates responses to emergencies and disasters. Significant wastewater treatment failures or massive overflows that threaten public safety or property would fall under their interagency coordination efforts.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including MDE and MDH. The bill adds new reporting requirements for wastewater treatment plants to the General Assembly and involves high-level policy initiatives related to environmental protection and public safety.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This council coordinates interagency efforts to restore the Chesapeake Bay. Since the bill regulates nutrient discharges (nitrogen and phosphorus) and bacterial levels in major treatment plants affecting the Bay watershed, it aligns with the Council's management and restoration goals.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the budget execution of the Department of the Environment. Any administrative or fiscal changes required for MDE to manage the new database and oversight programs would be reviewed by DBM.

The Office of Legislative Audits (OLA) conducts performance and fiscal compliance audits of the Department of the Environment. OLA would be responsible for auditing MDE's implementation and enforcement of the new wastewater discharge and database requirements.

Synopsis: Repealing certain provisions authorizing a county or municipal corporation to impose certain assessments on transportation network services; prohibiting a county or municipal corporation from imposing an assessment, a tax, a fee, or a charge on transportation network services; repealing the Transportation Network Assessment Fund; prohibiting the Maryland Aviation Administration from fixing any charges, rentals, or fees on the privilege of providing transportation network services at an airport or a facility; etc.
Title: Maryland Aviation Administration and Local Governments - Transportation Network Services - Prohibition on Taxes, Fees, and Charges
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations

bill_summary: This bill prohibits local governments and the Maryland Aviation Administration from imposing taxes, fees, or charges on transportation network services (ridesharing). It repeals the existing authority of counties and municipalities to collect assessments on these services, eliminates the Transportation Network Assessment Fund, and prevents airports from charging fees for the privilege of providing rideshare services.
stakeholders: Transportation network companies, rideshare drivers, rideshare passengers, local governments, and the Maryland Aviation Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a revenue decrease for local governments and the Maryland Aviation Administration. By repealing the authority of local jurisdictions to impose assessments on transportation network service trips (previously capped at 25 cents per trip) and prohibiting airports from fixing charges for rideshare access, the bill removes established revenue streams. The Transportation Network Assessment Fund is also repealed. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Comptroller as the primary authority responsible for enforcing the provisions regarding transportation network company impact fees and managing the collection and remittance of these revenues following the repeal of the Transportation Network Assessment Fund.

The bill explicitly prohibits the Maryland Aviation Administration from fixing any charges, rentals, or fees on the privilege of providing transportation network services at its airports and facilities, which directly impacts its revenue and operational policy.
The bill amends the Public Utilities Article concerning the regulation and data-sharing requirements of transportation network companies, which fall under the Commission's regulatory jurisdiction.

As the parent department of the Maryland Aviation Administration, MDOT is affected by the changes to airport revenue policies and the broader regulation of transportation network services in the state.
The Treasurer is the current custodian of the Transportation Network Assessment Fund, which this bill repeals.
The bill identifies the Maryland Tax Court as a body for appeals and the disclosure of records related to transportation network services assessments and impact fees.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary agencies involved (Comptroller, MAA, and PSC) regarding the interpretation and enforcement of the new prohibitions on taxes and fees.
The bill repeals a state fund and prohibits certain local and state-level revenue collections, which impacts the state's fiscal planning and budget oversight.
The bill references the requirement for court orders to disclose certain transportation network company information, involving the administrative processes of the judiciary.
The bill reenacts language requiring the Maryland Aviation Administration to refer alleged employment practice violations by airport contractors to the Commission on Civil Rights.

Synopsis: Constituting the Village Council of Drummond as the governing body of the special taxing district constituted as the Village of Drummond in Montgomery County; providing for the structure, membership, duties, and obligations of the Village Council; altering the eligible uses of funds derived from the Village's annual special tax levy; and providing for the Village's annual appropriations process.
Title: Special Taxing Districts - Village of Drummond - Authority and Organization MC 20-26
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 149

bill_summary: This bill reconstitutes the governing body of the Village of Drummond, a special taxing district in Montgomery County, from a citizens' committee to a Village Council. It defines the council's organization, membership, and duties, and establishes procedures for annual budgeting, auditing, and public procurement.
stakeholders: Residents and property owners within the Village of Drummond special taxing district in Montgomery County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. Locally, the Village of Drummond anticipates minor costs for surety bonds for two individuals, with each bond estimated to cost between $1,000 and $5,000. The bill maintains existing tax levy rates of $0.14 per $100 of assessable value for real property and $0.35 per $100 for personal and public utility operating real property.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifies that the annual election of members of the Village Council of Drummond must be conducted in accordance with the election laws of the State of Maryland.
The bill establishes a specific right of appeal to the Circuit Court for Montgomery County for parties affected by the final decisions of the Village Council regarding special tax assessments.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office is responsible for the final review and signing of this local law, and the Governor is specifically mentioned in the signature block.
The Secretary of State is the custodian of Maryland's official records and laws, including the Public Local Laws of Montgomery County modified by this bill.
The Maryland Department of Planning provides technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments regarding land use and jurisdiction organization, including special taxing districts.
The bill grants the Village Council authority over public ways, including the power to construct, maintain, and light streets and roads, which relates to MDOT's broader transportation oversight.
As the state's principal financial officer, the Comptroller's office monitors local revenue collection and tax laws; this bill authorizes a specific property tax levy and collection process.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the legality and interpretation of changes to local governance and special taxing district authority.
The bill authorizes a specific property tax levy within the village; the PTAAB provides administrative review for disputes related to property tax assessments and credits.
The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals from final decisions regarding tax disputes, including those that might arise from the special taxing district levies authorized in this legislation.

bill_summary: This bill requires a custodian of public records to allow an inspector general from a state or local office to inspect records if the inspector general is authorized by law to access those records and requires them for official duties. The bill also stipulates that any redisclosure of these records by an inspector general is governed by the Public Information Act.
responsible_party: State and local public record custodians
stakeholders: State and local inspectors general and government agency record custodians
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, and the bill text itself contains no explicit financial mandates, allocations, or revenue changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the chief legal officer for the State of Maryland, the Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to all state agencies on the interpretation and implementation of the Public Information Act, which this bill directly amends.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives for the departments and offices that serve as primary custodians of public records and house many Inspectors General.

The Secretary of State is a principal custodian of official state records, including executive orders and commissions, and is directly affected by mandates regarding mandatory disclosure to Inspectors General.
The Archives serves as the central depository for government records of permanent value, making it a key custodian impacted by laws governing the access of oversight bodies to public information.

This office investigates and prosecutes offenses related to the integrity of state officials and institutions, a function that requires access to public records similar to the access expanded for Inspectors General.
The OLA performs audits to ensure financial accountability and legal compliance, an oversight role that intersects with the investigative record access duties of Inspectors General.
The MLDS serves as the central state repository for linked student and workforce data, making it a critical custodian of the types of public records subject to inspection by Inspectors General.
The Commission manages public financial disclosure records and investigates ethics violations, necessitating regular management of and access to records governed by this bill.
The AOC provides support for judicial records management and must ensure that the judicial branch complies with state laws regarding public information access by oversight entities.
As the chief financial officer and an auditor of taxpayers, the Comptroller is a major custodian of sensitive fiscal and revenue records subject to oversight access provisions.
The Department of Education oversees the public education system and acts as a primary custodian of significant public and student-related records that are subject to Inspector General review.
A massive regulatory agency and custodian of public health records, the Department of Health is subject to frequent oversight by state and internal Inspectors General.
The department and its modal administrations act as custodians for extensive transportation and operational records and house a specific Inspector General office impacted by this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency overseeing state correctional facilities and community supervision, it maintains significant public and administrative records subject to integrity oversight.
The MSP is the primary custodian of state criminal and motor vehicle records, making its data sets prime targets for inspection by state and local Inspectors General.
As the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM manages executive branch personnel records and oversees policies related to the management of state information.

Synopsis: Altering the amount of fees the Maryland Department of Health may establish for newborn testing under the newborn screening program; requiring the State Advisory Council on Hereditary and Congenital Disorders to advise the Department on certain information related to the implementation of testing for a core condition added to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel and provide recommendations regarding whether testing should be implemented; etc.
Title: Public Health - Newborn Screening Program - Fees and Core Conditions
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/01 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the Maryland Department of Health's newborn screening program by altering fee structures to ensure they cover administrative and laboratory costs and updating the process for adding new screening conditions. It requires the State Advisory Council on Hereditary and Congenital Disorders to advise on the implementation of new conditions added to the federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP), while granting the Department of Health the authority to implement, delay, or decline the implementation of testing for those conditions based on that advice.
stakeholders: Newborn infants in Maryland, parents and guardians, healthcare providers, hospitals, and the Maryland Department of Health public health laboratory.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) can implement the bill's administrative changes using existing resources. However, if MDH increases newborn screening fees to cover performance costs as authorized by the bill, MDH special fund revenues will increase. Additionally, because Medicaid covers approximately half of all births in Maryland, Medicaid expenditures (funded 50% by State general funds and 50% by federal funds) would increase to pay its share of higher fees. Specific dollar estimates for the fee increases are currently unavailable as the timing and magnitude of such changes cannot be reliably estimated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for the Newborn Screening Program and its public health laboratory. The bill grants MDH the authority to establish fees, determine which core conditions are screened, and manage the implementation timeline for new conditions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly expands the duties of the State Advisory Council on Hereditary and Congenital Disorders, requiring them to advise MDH on the risks, harms, accessibility, and costs of implementing testing for any condition added to the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel.
The bill mandates that all fees collected under the Newborn Screening Program be paid to the Comptroller, who is then responsible for distributing them to the Newborn Screening Program Fund.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is impacted because any increase in newborn screening fees will lead to higher Medicaid expenditures, which include state general funds overseen by the department.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to MDH and would be responsible for reviewing and approving the new regulations required for the implementation and fee structures of the newborn screening program.

Synopsis: Establishing the Food Security Coordination Office within the Department of Agriculture; requiring the Department to establish a rural-to-urban produce distribution program to connect local farmers with urban and suburban communities experiencing food insecurity; requiring the Department to establish the Maryland Rural-to-Urban Produce Financing Program to provide financial assistance for projects that stabilize and expand the movement of Maryland-grown produce to certain communities; etc.

bill_summary: The Maryland Food Security, Access, and Equity Act establishes the Food Security Coordination Office within the Department of Agriculture to oversee statewide food access initiatives. The bill requires the Department to create a rural-to-urban produce distribution program and a financing program to provide grants, loans, and other financial assistance to farmers and organizations for food infrastructure projects. Additionally, it expands the Jane Lawton Farm-to-School Program to include early childhood education facilities and encourages partnerships between healthcare providers and food access organizations for produce prescriptions and nutrition education.
stakeholders: Maryland farmers and farming cooperatives, food-insecure residents in urban and suburban communities, nonprofit and community-based organizations, local government entities, health care providers, and schools including pre-kindergarten and child care facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates significant new expenditures for the Maryland Department of Agriculture to staff and operate the Food Security Coordination Office and manage several new grant and financing programs. While specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not provided in the text, the bill explicitly mandates financial assistance through grants, low-interest loans, and potential bond issuances. Local school systems and private child care facilities will also face new reporting requirements and eligibility for the expanded Farm-to-School Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Department of Agriculture as the primary agency responsible for implementing the Maryland Food Security, Access, and Equity Act, establishing the Food Security Coordination Office, and managing various distribution and financing programs.

The bill authorizes the Department of Agriculture to establish financial mechanisms including bond issuance and to enter into significant third-party contracts for program administration, both of which typically require Board of Public Works approval.

The Treasurer's Office manages state bond issuances and sits on the Board of Public Works; the bill specifically mentions bond issuance as a financial mechanism for the new Rural-to-Urban Produce Financing Program.

The bill requires the Department of Agriculture to support partnerships with health care providers for produce prescription programs and medically tailored groceries, requiring coordination with health policy and provider reporting.
The bill expands the Jane Lawton Farm-to-School Program, which is operated in consultation with the State Department of Education, to include more school types and support school gardens.
The OAG will be required to provide legal counsel for the drafting of new regulations, the creation of the Food Security Coordination Office, and the review of third-party contracts.

DBM oversees the state budget and personnel; the creation of a new office within the Department of Agriculture and the administration of new grant and loan programs will have significant fiscal and staffing implications.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO provides financial services and loans to Maryland's agricultural industry; its mission overlaps with the bill's proposed Maryland Rural-to-Urban Produce Financing Program.

RMC is housed within the Department of Agriculture and works to address challenges in rural counties, including agricultural support and healthcare access, which aligns with the bill's focus on connecting rural farmers to urban markets.
The GOC coordinates efforts to reduce child poverty and food insecurity, directly aligning with the mission of the newly established Food Security Coordination Office.
The Innovation Team is charged with piloting novel initiatives to address child poverty and economic mobility; the data-driven strategies for food security in this bill align with their mandate.
DHS administers food assistance programs (SNAP) and assists vulnerable populations; the bill's focus on eliminating food insecurity complements DHS's social service mission.
The bill requires the development of a statewide data dashboard on food access and technology platforms for logistics, which would fall under DoIT's oversight of state IT strategy.
DGS serves as the central procurement authority; the bill involves third-party contracts for program administration and logistics that must comply with state procurement laws.
As a member of the Board of Public Works and the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller would oversee the fiscal integrity of the new financing and grant programs.
The bill creates a new executive office and requires statewide reporting on food security, a key policy priority for the executive branch.
The bill includes provisions for supporting urban agriculture and community gardens, which are often components of the neighborhood revitalization projects managed by DHCD.
As a state-operated school with early childhood programs, MSD would be eligible to participate in the expanded Jane Lawton Farm-to-School Program and nutrition education initiatives.

Synopsis: Providing that the Office of the Inspector General for Howard County shall have access to and inspect certain public records under certain circumstances; prohibiting a custodian from denying the Office of the Inspector General for Howard County access to a public record under certain circumstances; and providing that redisclosure of certain information is subject to certain restrictions.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that the Howard County Office of the Inspector General be granted access to inspect public records for the purpose of auditing the county government, county agencies, or the county public school system. It prohibits record custodians from denying access to the Office of the Inspector General when such access is authorized by law and deemed necessary for an audit, while also ensuring that any redisclosure of obtained information complies with existing state public record laws.
responsible_party: Office of the Inspector General for Howard County
stakeholders: Howard County Government, Howard County Public School System, Howard County Office of the Inspector General, and record custodians within Howard County agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The bill establishes administrative procedures for record access to facilitate audits, which is expected to have a minimal fiscal impact without specific spending mandates or revenue changes identified in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Attorney General is the primary legal advisor for the State on matters regarding the Public Information Act (PIA), which is codified in the General Provisions Article being amended by this bill. The bill creates new mandates for custodians regarding the disclosure of records to a local Inspector General.

The bill specifically facilitates audits of the Howard County public school system by granting the local Inspector General access to its records. The Maryland State Department of Education provides oversight and leadership for all 24 local school systems in the state.

The Office of Legislative Audits is responsible for conducting audits of local school systems in Maryland. This bill establishes specific statutory record-access rights for a local auditing entity (Howard County Inspector General) to perform similar functions, which is relevant to the state's broader audit and accountability framework.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the implementation of state laws, including changes to the General Provisions Article and intergovernmental relations between state authorities and local county governments.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement that a proposed new academic program be a graduate program in order for the Maryland Higher Education Commission or institutions of higher education in the State to file an objection to implementation of the proposed program.
Title: Higher Education - Academic Program Approval - Objections
Status: In the House - Rereferred to Appropriations

NarrowSubjects.Name: Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.

bill_summary: This bill expands the existing academic program objection process in Maryland to include all new academic programs at public and private nonprofit institutions of higher education that are implemented using existing resources. Currently, the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) and other institutions can only file objections against proposed graduate programs. The bill allows for objections to any proposed program (including undergraduate and associate degrees) based on mission inconsistency, lack of regional or statewide need, or unreasonable or unnecessary program duplication.
stakeholders: Maryland public and private nonprofit higher education institutions, community colleges, and students.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal impact on the State and local governments is indeterminate. While MHEC and institutions can handle the expanded objection process using existing resources, the volume of administrative work and program evaluations may increase. The bill could lead to delays, modifications, or rejections of proposed academic programs, which may in turn affect institutional enrollment patterns and tuition revenues. The Fiscal Note provides an illustrative example stating that a change of 30 full-time students at a public senior institution could impact tuition and fee revenue by approximately $336,000.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for higher education in Maryland, MHEC is responsible for overseeing the academic program approval process. This bill directly impacts MHEC by expanding its workload and oversight responsibilities, allowing it or other institutions to file objections for all academic programs rather than just graduate programs.

USM is the state's largest public higher education system. Its constituent institutions are directly affected by the expanded objection process for undergraduate and other non-graduate programs. Additionally, the USM Board of Regents must approve programs for its institutions, making it a key stakeholder in the new regulatory environment.

As an independent public senior higher education institution, Morgan State is directly subject to MHEC's program approval and objection process. The bill significantly expands the scope of programs for which Morgan State may receive objections from other institutions or file objections itself.

As an independent public honors college and a state agency, Saint Mary's College is subject to the program approval process outlined in the Education Article. The bill expands the potential for external objections to its proposed programs and grants it expanded authority to object to programs at other institutions.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MHEC and public institutions of higher education. It may be called upon to interpret the legal criteria for objections, such as consistency with missions and equal educational opportunity obligations, and represent the state in administrative disputes.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state. While the bill focuses on programs implemented with existing resources, shifts in academic programming can influence enrollment patterns and long-term fiscal planning for the state's higher education sector.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to establish regulatory standards for the discharge of patients from drug and alcohol treatment programs and for referral services. It prohibits discharging a patient to homelessness if they require residential care and mandates referrals to halfway houses or recovery residences. Additionally, it requires that treatment plans facilitate access to medical, mental health, and social services.
stakeholders: Patients with substance use disorders, drug and alcohol treatment program providers, and recovery residences.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health must establish new regulations and submit a status report by December 1, 2026. These administrative and enforcement requirements will likely result in State expenditures, but a formal Fiscal Note was not provided and specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Maryland Department of Health to establish standards by regulation for the discharge of patients from drug and alcohol treatment programs and for referral services. MDH is also required to submit an enforcement plan and status report to the Governor and General Assembly.
The bill specifically requires treatment programs to implement referrals to the Maryland Division of Rehabilitation Services (DORS), which is a division of the Maryland State Department of Education.

The bill prohibits discharging patients into homelessness if residential care is needed and requires referrals to recovery residences and halfway houses. The Department of Housing and Community Development manages homeless solutions and community-based housing initiatives.

The bill requires treatment programs to refer patients for financial support and social services. DHS is the primary agency providing cash assistance, SNAP, and other social services for vulnerable individuals.
The bill mandates that discharge standards include referrals for employment support, which falls under the workforce development and training responsibilities of the Maryland Department of Labor.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health. They would be involved in drafting and reviewing the new regulations and ensuring that the required referral agreements between treatment programs and other entities are legally sound.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM will be responsible for overseeing the fiscal impact on the state budget related to MDH's regulatory enforcement and any potential increase in state-funded residential or social services resulting from the new referral requirements.
The bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to submit a report on the status of regulations and an enforcement plan to the Governor by December 1, 2026.

bill_summary: The Maryland Energy Savings Guarantee Act repeals numerous energy-related programs, surcharges, and taxes to reduce consumer utility costs. It also repeals the public service company franchise tax and mandates that Maryland withdraw from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI). State expenditures will decrease due to the abolition of associated programs like the Electric Universal Service Program and EmPOWER Maryland. The bill requires Maryland to withdraw from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) and repeals carbon dioxide reduction requirements for power plants. It also impacts the Maryland Clean Air Fund which MDE manages.

The bill repeals the low-income weatherization component of the electric universal service program and impacts other community-based energy conservation grants and loans managed by the department.
The bill repeals the Public Service Company Franchise Tax and modifies the collection of environmental surcharges, both of which fall under the Comptroller's revenue collection and auditing duties.
The bill specifically mandates the Governor to withdraw the State from RGGI and submit reports to the General Assembly regarding the withdrawal process and future carbon reduction plans.
The bill repeals the environmental surcharge that funds the Environmental Trust Fund, which the DNR uses to support various environmental research and restoration activities.

The bill mandates that State energy programs be funded through direct legislative appropriations from the General Fund rather than utility surcharges, requiring significant changes to the State's fiscal planning and budget development.
The Treasurer is the custodian of the funds being restructured, including the Strategic Energy Investment Fund and the Environmental Trust Fund.

The repeal of the Public Service Company Franchise Tax would eliminate a category of tax disputes currently adjudicated by the Tax Court.
The bill changes the definition of clean energy and modifies the funding levels and mechanisms (SEIF) that support the Center's green bank activities.
The bill alters statutory definitions related to advanced clean energy and impacts economic development funding related to the Maryland Energy Innovation Fund.
DGS is responsible for state energy procurement; the bill's changes to renewable energy contract terms and the repeal of green power goals for state facilities affect their operational role.
The OAG would be involved in the legal process of withdrawing Maryland from RGGI and advising agencies on the repeal of complex utility and environmental regulations.
The bill's repeal of the franchise tax and impact on the renewable energy sector affects the department's mission of business retention and economic stimulation in the clean tech sector.

The bill mentions job training for energy efficiency technology, which falls under the department's workforce development oversight.
The bill involves changes to the PSC's consideration of historic sites and aesthetics in utility construction, which often coordinates with MDP's Maryland Historical Trust.
The team's mission to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility is directly linked to energy costs and assistance programs for low-income families that this bill modifies.

stakeholders: Maryland judges (Supreme Court, Appellate Court, Circuit Courts, and District Court), administrative judges, magistrates, the State Prosecutor, the Public Defender, Workers' Compensation Commission members, and local government officials with salaries tied to judicial pay.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $3.3 million in fiscal 2027, rising to $11.7 million by fiscal 2030. Special fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $63,325 in fiscal 2027, rising to approximately $300,000 by fiscal 2030. These costs account for salary increases for 322 judges, higher fringe benefits, stipends for administrative judges, and increased compensation for senior/recalled judges and magistrates. Additionally, salaries for the Public Defender, State Prosecutor, and members of the Workers' Compensation Commission will increase due to their statutory link to judicial pay. Local government expenditures will increase minimally in counties that tie local official salaries to judicial salaries.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the central support agency for the Maryland Judicial Branch, the AOC is responsible for implementing the salary increases, stipends, and benefit adjustments for the 322 judges and 70 magistrates affected by this resolution.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The salary of the Public Defender is tied by statute to the salary of a circuit court judge; therefore, the judicial salary increases proposed in this resolution directly impact the compensation for the head of this agency.
The salary of the State Prosecutor is tied by statute to the salary of a circuit court judge, meaning the resolution directly dictates the compensation for the head of this agency.

The salaries of the ten members of the Workers' Compensation Commission are tied by statute to those of District Court judges. The resolution's proposed increases will result in a notable fiscal impact on this agency's special fund expenditures.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM must account for the multi-million dollar general fund expenditure increases necessitated by these judicial salary and pension adjustments in the state budget.
The SRA manages the State Retirement and Pension System, including the Judicial Retirement System. Changes in judicial salaries impact actuarial valuations and future pension contribution rates.

The Governor appoints the members of the Judicial Compensation Commission, receives their recommendations, and proposes the state budget which must include the funding for these mandated salary levels.

The Comptroller is responsible for paying state employees and will be the entity processing the increased salary payments for judges and related officials.

The Office of Appointments facilitates the Governor's recruitment and vetting of the members for the Judicial Compensation Commission, which is the body responsible for the recommendations in this resolution.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a 120-day deadline for the State Highway Administration (SHA) to approve, deny, or return as incomplete any application for the use of speed monitoring systems on State highways within municipal corporations. bill_summary: This bill modernizes the methodology for setting reimbursement rates for behavioral health services in Maryland. It requires the Maryland Department of Health to conduct a cost-driven rate-setting study by June 30, 2028, and establishes the Workgroup on Behavioral Health Rate Methodology Modernization within the Maryland Health Care Commission to develop transparent, cost-based reimbursement models for clinics and outpatient providers.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Health Care Commission
stakeholders: Community behavioral health providers, certified community behavioral health clinics, outpatient mental health centers, independent outpatient providers, and individuals receiving behavioral health services.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State expenditures increase by $392,000 in FY 2027 and $356,100 in FY 2028. Specifically, Maryland Department of Health general fund expenditures increase by $181,700 in FY 2027 and $158,500 in FY 2028 for staff to conduct the rate study. Maryland Health Care Commission special fund expenditures increase by $210,300 in FY 2027 and $197,600 in FY 2028 for contractual staff and services to support the workgroup. The bill does not mandate immediate rate increases or specific appropriations for provider services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Workgroup on Behavioral Health Rate Methodology Modernization within the Commission. MDH is mandated to conduct an independent cost-driven, rate-setting study by 2028. Its sub-units, the Behavioral Health Administration and the Medical Care Programs Administration, are tasked with developing and implementing a new payment system based on the study's findings. The Secretary must also designate a technical liaison to coordinate with the Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages the rehabilitation of justice-involved individuals, for whom behavioral health services are a key component of reducing recidivism. Improvements in rate methodologies for these services directly impact the providers DPSCS relies on.
