bill_summary: This bill alters the regulations for Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses in Wicomico County. It prohibits the local Board of License Commissioners from issuing new Class A licenses to restaurants with Class B licenses after July 1, 2026, while grandfathering existing licenses. Additionally, the bill increases the maximum number of Class A licenses allowed in the county from three to seven by permitting one license per county councilmanic district and requires license holders to purchase liquor from county dispensaries rather than wholesalers.
responsible_party: Wicomico County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Restaurant owners and alcoholic beverage license holders in Wicomico County, alcoholic beverage wholesalers, and Wicomico County dispensaries.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or Wicomico County operations or finances. While the potential number of Class A licenses increases from three to seven (each with an annual fee of $4,400), the overall fiscal impact is estimated as minimal by the Department of Legislative Services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the principal regulator of the state's alcohol industry and oversees tax collection and industry compliance. This bill modifies licensing rules and purchasing requirements for liquor retailers in Wicomico County, which directly pertains to the agency's regulatory and oversight functions.

As the primary legal representative for the state and its agencies, the OAG provides counsel on the interpretation and enforcement of state laws. This bill alters local alcoholic beverages regulations in the Maryland Code, which may require legal guidance or defense regarding the implementation of license limits and grandfathering provisions.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "eligible project"; requiring an appropriation of a certain amount to the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program if the Governor appropriates less than $80,000,000 to the Community College Construction Grant Program in each fiscal year; increasing the number of grants, from 8 to 16, the Maryland Higher Education Commission may make in each fiscal year; etc.
Title: Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program - Alterations
Status: In the Senate - Unfavorable Report by Budget and Taxation; Withdrawn
bill_summary: The bill expands the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program by removing project cost limits and increasing the number of grants that can be awarded each year from 8 to 16. It also sets a new funding requirement: if the state's main community college construction fund receives less than $80 million in a fiscal year, the state must provide enough funding to the renewal program to make up the difference. Additionally, it removes the rule that prevents colleges from receiving grants in consecutive years and requires funds to be distributed equally among eligible colleges.
stakeholders: Maryland community colleges and Baltimore City Community College
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a state funding mandate for the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program. If the annual appropriation for the Community College Construction Grant Program is less than $80,000,000, the Governor must appropriate the difference to the Facilities Renewal Grant Program. This ensures a baseline funding level when construction appropriations are below the $80,000,000 threshold. The bill also doubles the number of possible grants from 8 to 16 and removes the $1,000,000 project cost cap and the $500,000 individual grant limit. Specific state expenditure increases are indeterminate as they depend on future annual budget cycles, but the $80,000,000 figure serves as the primary fiscal benchmark.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Higher Education Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program, determining grant awards in consultation with colleges, and adopting necessary regulations.

The bill mandates the Governor to make specific annual appropriations for the Program within the state's operating or capital budget, contingent on funding levels for the Community College Construction Grant Program.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for developing the budget and ensuring the implementation of the bill's mandatory appropriation requirements for facility renewal grants.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and capital projects, which include the facilities renewal grants and construction funding for community colleges addressed in this bill.

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is involved in overseeing state expenditures and distributing the grant funds appropriated for the program.

The State Treasurer's Office manages state funds and serves on the Board of Public Works, participating in the oversight of significant procurements and bond-funded projects related to community college facilities.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Higher Education Commission and would be responsible for reviewing the regulations required to implement the program's changes.

Synopsis: Establishing a consumption-only nonprofit swim club license in Anne Arundel County which authorizes the license holder to allow members of the swim club and their guests to bring beer, wine, and liquor onto the licensed premises for on-premises consumption during designated events; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Anne Arundel County to issue the license to a nonprofit swim club in Anne Arundel County; and providing for an annual license fee of $100.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a consumption-only nonprofit swim club license in Anne Arundel County. The license allows nonprofit swim clubs to permit members and guests to bring and consume beer, wine, and liquor on the premises during designated events for up to five days per year, with the possibility of three additional days if authorized by the Board of License Commissioners. Consumption is limited to designated areas between 2:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., and the license holder must provide 10 days' notice to the board before an event.
responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Nonprofit swim clubs in Anne Arundel County, their members, and their guests.
fiscal_impact_summary: Anne Arundel County revenues are expected to increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027 through the collection of license fees. The annual license fee is $100, and a club may pay an additional $50 per day for up to three additional days. There is no impact on State finances or county expenditures, as the board can administer the license using existing staff.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Governor is responsible for signing into law or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state boards and agencies and represents the state in legal matters concerning the enforcement of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.
The Maryland State Police enforce state motor vehicle and criminal laws, including those related to alcohol consumption and public safety.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This category includes bodies such as the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners, which is the primary agency authorized to issue and manage the new consumption-only license established by this bill.

Synopsis: Establishing a presumption that the sentencing of a minor convicted as an adult should be transferred to the juvenile court, under certain circumstances, and authorizing the court to do so; and requiring the juvenile court to make a juvenile determination under certain circumstances.

bill_summary: This bill establishes that a court sentencing a minor convicted as an adult may transfer the case to juvenile court for sentencing if the minor was a victim of a sex crime or human trafficking by their victim within three months of the offense. It also prohibits life sentences without parole for minors and permits courts to impose sentences below statutory minimums.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Department of Juvenile Services
stakeholders: Minors convicted as adults who were victims of sex crimes or human trafficking, the Maryland Judiciary, and the Department of Juvenile Services
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided; however, the bill may result in a shift of costs from adult correctional facilities to juvenile services and potential reductions in long-term incarceration expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts court procedures by authorizing the transfer of sentencing for certain minors from adult criminal court to juvenile court and requiring the juvenile court to make a disposition.

DJS is responsible for managing youth in the juvenile justice system. This bill allows for more minors to be transferred to its jurisdiction for sentencing and disposition rather than remaining in the adult correctional system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent minors in criminal and juvenile proceedings. This bill provides a significant legal mechanism for their clients to seek transfer to the juvenile system for sentencing.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages adult correctional facilities. Provisions that allow for the transfer of minors to juvenile court for sentencing would affect the population of justice-involved youth held in adult facilities under their jurisdiction.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates criminal justice strategies and policy development related to juvenile delinquency and public safety, making the changes to minor sentencing highly relevant to their mission.
The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides legal counsel on matters of criminal procedure and state law, including the implementation of sentencing reforms.

The bill specifically references minors who were victims of sex crimes or human trafficking. DHS provides protective services and support to such vulnerable populations and may be involved in the history of the minor being considered for transfer.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including DJS and DPSCS, and sets policy initiatives regarding criminal justice and juvenile rehabilitation.

bill_summary: This bill establishes an exemption to the population ratio quota for Class A and Class D (off-sale) alcoholic beverages licenses in Anne Arundel County for applications filed on or after January 1, 2023, and approved by the Board of License Commissioners before July 1, 2025.
responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage license applicants and business owners in Anne Arundel County.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, Anne Arundel County revenues will increase by $5,160 annually starting in fiscal 2027 due to the issuance of three licenses that were previously restricted by the population ratio quota. There is no impact on State finances and no effect on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry. As this bill amends the 'Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis' Article concerning license quotas, it falls within the Comptroller's broad regulatory subject matter.
The Governor's Office is responsible for the executive branch and for the final review and signing of legislation passed by the Maryland General Assembly.
The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of Maryland's official records, including the laws and acts passed by the General Assembly that are recorded as part of the state's legal history.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement to include taxes in the total price for a ticket on a ticket listing and at each step of a ticket purchase transaction; authorizing a consumer, an artist, or a venue to file a  private right of action against a ticket issuer, secondary ticket exchange, or reseller for a certain violation; authorizing a court to award economic and punitive damages; and establishing the circumstances under which damages may not exceed certain amounts.

bill_summary: This bill modifies ticket sale and resale disclosure requirements by removing the mandate that taxes be included in the total price of a ticket during listing and throughout the purchase transaction. It also establishes a private right of action, allowing consumers, artists, or venues aggrieved by violations of these regulations to sue ticket issuers, secondary ticket exchanges, or resellers for economic and punitive damages.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division)
stakeholders: Ticket purchasers, musical artists, entertainment venues, ticket issuers, secondary ticket marketplaces, and ticket resellers.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is unavailable. The bill establishes civil liability for ticket sellers, authorizing courts to award punitive damages of up to $10,000 for a first violation and $25,000 for subsequent violations. While these private actions may increase the workload of the state court system, specific dollar estimates for state or local revenue and expenditures are not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Consumer Protection Act (Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article), which is primarily enforced by the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General. The agency would be responsible for oversight and enforcement of the new ticket price disclosure rules and the newly authorized private causes of action.

The Maryland Stadium Authority operates major sports and entertainment venues, such as the Camden Yards Sports Complex. As a venue operator and potential ticket issuer, the agency must comply with the modified price disclosure requirements and the mandatory refund provisions for counterfeit or canceled events.

The bill creates a specific private cause of action for consumers, artists, and venues to sue ticket issuers and resellers, and it establishes specific statutory limits for economic and punitive damages ($10,000 to $25,000). This may increase civil litigation and requires the judiciary to handle new categories of claims.

Member institutions within the University System of Maryland operate numerous stadiums, arenas, and theaters that host athletic and entertainment events. These institutions act as 'ticket issuers' and are directly subject to the bill's requirements for price transparency and refunds.

As a public university with its own athletic programs and entertainment venues, Morgan State University acts as a ticket issuer and venue operator, making the bill's disclosure and refund requirements relevant to its operations.
Saint Mary's College operates venues for performing arts and other events that require ticketing, making it subject to the bill's regulations on price disclosure and consumer protection.

The bill specifically repeals the requirement to include 'taxes' in the total disclosed price of a ticket at each step of a transaction (though they must still be itemized). As the state's chief tax officer, the Comptroller is relevant to any legislative changes affecting how tax information is communicated to consumers during sales.

The Department of Commerce oversees the state's economic development, including the film, arts, and tourism industries. Regulations affecting ticket sales and venues directly impact the businesses and cultural organizations within the department's portfolio.

The agency promotes Maryland as a destination for events and entertainment. Changes to consumer protection laws regarding event ticketing and pricing transparency can affect the state's reputation and the consumer experience for tourists attending Maryland events.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates casinos, many of which house entertainment venues and theaters. These venues act as ticket issuers and are subject to the bill's consumer protection and price disclosure requirements.

Maryland Public Television (MPT) occasionally hosts ticketed cultural and educational events. As an entity that may sell tickets to the public, it would be required to follow the revised disclosure and refund rules.

The Commission operates a museum and archaeological park that hosts ticketed events and entertainment. It would be classified as a venue operator under the bill and required to comply with its provisions.

The corporation manages the Reginald F. Lewis Museum, which hosts ticketed entertainment and cultural events. As a ticket issuer and venue operator, the agency is impacted by the bill's consumer protection standards.

The Governor's Office coordinates state policy initiatives and oversees the executive branch. This bill represents a shift in state consumer protection policy regarding the entertainment and secondary ticket industries.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is involved in assessing the fiscal impact of legislation on other state agencies, including the operational costs for state-run venues to comply with new ticketing laws.

Synopsis: Establishing that damages to be awarded for the taking of land in a condemnation proceeding include, in addition to the fair market value of the land taken, any legal, expert, or other fees or costs of the action incurred by a defendant.

Status: In the Senate - Hearing 2/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's eminent domain laws to require that damages awarded to a property owner in a condemnation proceeding include the property's fair market value as well as any legal, expert, or other fees and costs incurred by the defendant during the action.
responsible_party: Maryland State and local government entities with condemnation authority and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Property owners facing condemnation proceedings, state and local government agencies, and legal and expert service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in an indeterminate increase in expenditures for state and local government entities that exercise eminent domain, as they will be required to reimburse the defendant's legal and expert fees in addition to paying for the land taken. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary operational support agency, DGS is responsible for the acquisition of real estate for most executive branch agencies. This bill would significantly increase the costs associated with land acquisition by requiring the state to pay for a defendant's legal, expert, and other fees in condemnation proceedings.

MDOT is one of the primary users of eminent domain in Maryland for highway, transit, port, and aviation projects. Requiring the payment of defendants' legal and expert fees would significantly increase the capital costs of infrastructure projects throughout the state.

DNR frequently acquires land for state parks, forests, and conservation efforts. The bill would increase the fiscal burden on the department during land acquisition and specifically mentions damages for land designated as park land or open space.

MDTA is an independent agency that utilizes eminent domain to acquire property for toll facilities, bridges, and tunnels. The bill would directly increase their project expenditures which are funded by toll revenues.

The OAG represents state agencies in all civil litigation, including condemnation proceedings. This bill would change the scope of damages and likely increase the complexity and duration of litigation as legal and expert fees would now be a contested part of the award.
The bill explicitly references the Maryland Historical Trust, which is overseen by the Department of Planning, regarding the valuation of donated easements in condemnation proceedings.

The Board of Public Works must approve significant state expenditures and the acquisition of state property. This bill would increase the total cost of land acquisitions presented to the Board for approval.

The bill contains specific provisions relating to the taking of land or interests in land granted pursuant to the Agriculture Article (§ 2–504), impacting the department's agricultural land preservation programs.

DBM oversees state budget development and execution. The requirement to pay additional fees in condemnation proceedings would represent a notable increase in state capital expenditures across multiple departments.
Condemnation is a judicial proceeding handled in Maryland courts. This bill changes the statutory calculation of damages that must be applied in these court actions.

The Stadium Authority plans and builds various sports and public facilities, often requiring significant land acquisition and the use of eminent domain, which would become more expensive under this bill.
USM and its member institutions occasionally utilize eminent domain for campus expansion and research facility development, and would be subject to the increased costs for legal and expert fees.
The bill specifically mentions the Maryland Environmental Trust regarding the awarding of damages for land with donated easements.
DHCD is involved in community revitalization and infrastructure projects that may involve land acquisition or the coordination of condemnation actions in urban areas.
As a member of the Board of Public Works and the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees the fiscal impacts of increased state expenditures for property acquisition.

As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Treasurer is involved in the approval of state land acquisitions and the financing of capital projects that would be impacted by higher condemnation costs.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies primarily responsible for land acquisition and proposes the state budget which must account for these increased project costs.
MES provides technical services and manages infrastructure projects like landfills or treatment plants that sometimes require the acquisition of land.

Synopsis: Repealing a certain provision of law relating to a certain school police officer's authorization to carry a firearm under certain circumstances; and requiring a school resource officer to carry a firearm while present on the premises of the school to which the officer is assigned.

bill_summary: This bill requires all school resource officers (SROs), including Baltimore City school police officers, to carry a firearm while on the premises of the public school to which they are assigned. responsible_party: Maryland local school systems and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: School resource officers, Baltimore City school police officers, public school students, and school staff
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state fiscal impact as it applies only to local school systems and law enforcement agencies. It is also estimated to have no material effect on local governmental operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Center for School Safety is the primary agency responsible for the statewide coordination of school safety. The bill directly amends section 7-1508, which governs the Center's duties regarding SRO training curricula, data collection on the use of force, and reporting on SRO coverage to the Governor and General Assembly.

As the oversight body for Maryland's public education system, MSDE is directly impacted by changes to the requirements for School Resource Officers (SROs) stationed in schools. Additionally, the Maryland Center for School Safety is an independent unit within MSDE.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires SRO training programs to be approved by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission (MPTSC), which is an entity housed within this department. MPTSC is responsible for certifying SROs and approving the specialized safety curriculum mentioned in the bill.

The Governor receives annual reports on SRO and law enforcement coverage in schools from the Center. Furthermore, the bill references the Governor's statutory mandate to include $10 million in the annual budget for SRO-related grants.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the primary coordinating body for public safety and advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies, including those involving law enforcement officers and youth programs, making the policy shift regarding armed SROs relevant to their mission.

As the primary law enforcement agency for the state, the Maryland State Police is involved in general safety standards and coordinates with local agencies that provide the law enforcement officers defined as school resource officers in the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE, the Center for School Safety, and other state entities regarding the implementation of statutory mandates and potential liability issues related to requiring firearms for school-based personnel.
DBM is responsible for the development and execution of the state budget, which includes the $10 million mandated annual appropriation for SRO grants cited in the bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes local jurisdictions and the State Highway Administration to deploy crosswalk monitoring systems in school zones to record images of vehicles failing to stop for pedestrians. It establishes a civil penalty of up to $40 for recorded violations, outlines procedures for the issuance and adjudication of citations, and requires that fine revenue be used to cover program costs or support public safety and pedestrian programs.
responsible_party: Local law enforcement agencies, the State Highway Administration, the Maryland District Court, and the Motor Vehicle Administration.
stakeholders: Maryland motorists, pedestrians in school zones, local governments, and state transportation and judicial agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a civil penalty not to exceed $40 for violations. Local jurisdictions may use collected fines to recover the costs of implementing and administering the systems, with any remaining funds restricted to public safety purposes such as pedestrian or highway safety programs. While the bill text identifies these revenue and expenditure mechanisms, specific aggregate dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly involves the State Highway Administration (SHA) and the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA). SHA is authorized to approve crosswalk monitoring systems on State highways in school zones and is responsible for placing signage. MVA is authorized to refuse or suspend vehicle registrations for unpaid citations.

The District Court is granted exclusive original civil jurisdiction over crosswalk monitoring system violations. The Chief Judge of the District Court is tasked with adopting procedures for citations, trials, and collection, and the Administrative Office must manage the adjudication of these new civil infractions.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police may be responsible for issuing and reviewing citations generated by crosswalk monitoring systems on State highways and in school zones within their jurisdiction.

The bill includes the Maryland Transportation Authority in the framework for remitting and distributing civil penalties collected by the District Court, and the agency manages its own police force and monitoring systems that may be integrated with these new crosswalk requirements.
The Comptroller is responsible for the distribution of fines and civil penalties remitted by the District Court to agencies like the State Highway Administration for implementation and safety costs.

The bill explicitly prohibits crosswalk monitoring system violations from being considered for motor vehicle insurance coverage, which falls under the regulatory and enforcement oversight of the Maryland Insurance Administration.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the implementing agencies, including MDOT and the State Police, regarding the enforcement and implementation of the new automated monitoring system.
DBM oversees the fiscal impact on the state budget, including the potential increase in Special Fund revenue from civil penalties and expenditures for system implementation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and manages funds for law enforcement; this bill introduces a new automated enforcement tool that aligns with their mission to improve public and pedestrian safety through policy development.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Human Services (DHS) to conduct a study and make recommendations regarding the impact of the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 on the Heat and Eat Program within the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). The study must determine the number of households excluded from automatic standard utility allowance eligibility, broken down by county and demographic characteristics (specifically elderly and disabled members), and evaluate the administrative costs and logistics for providing additional assistance. A final report of findings is due to the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: SNAP recipients, households participating in the Heat and Eat Program, elderly individuals (60+), individuals with disabilities, and the Maryland Department of Human Services.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Human Services (DHS) can implement the bill's study requirements with existing budgeted resources. The fiscal note indicates that while the bill mandates a study, conforming state law to federal eligibility changes potentially avoids an annual general fund expenditure of approximately 107700000 that might otherwise be required to maintain benefit levels for 108,136 households no longer automatically eligible for the federal standard utility allowance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHS is the primary agency responsible for administering the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the Heat and Eat Program. The bill specifically mandates DHS to conduct the study, evaluate administrative logistics, and submit the final report.

The bill requires the study to specifically identify and count the number of households with a member who is at least 60 years old, which directly relates to the department's mission to protect the rights and well-being of older adults.

The bill requires the study to specifically identify and count households with a member who is disabled, directly impacting the department's role in coordinating and improving services for Marylanders with disabilities.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is affected by the bill's findings. The fiscal note indicates that in the absence of this bill, the State might have faced significant general fund expenditures (estimated at $107.7 million annually) to maintain benefit levels.

The office's mission is focused on reducing child poverty and improving access to health and economic opportunities. Reductions in SNAP and energy assistance benefits directly impact the financial stability of families with children.

The Heat and Eat Program is linked to utility assistance (MEAP). As the advocate for residential utility consumers, the OPC is concerned with programs that help low-income households afford essential utility services.

The team is tasked with addressing child poverty and economic mobility. The study evaluates a reduction in federal food and energy benefits, which are key factors in economic mobility and poverty reduction.
As the executive department overseeing DHS and the state budget, the Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives related to the fiscal findings of the required study.

OLA conducts performance audits of state programs. The results of the DHS study regarding administrative costs and benefit distribution will serve as relevant data for future audits of SNAP efficiency.
The PSC regulates the utilities that provide services tied to the Heat and Eat program's energy assistance components. Changes in program eligibility affect the consumer base they oversee.

The study requires a breakdown of households by county. The Rural Maryland Council advocates for the interests of residents in Maryland's 18 rural counties where utility assistance and SNAP are vital services.

Synopsis: Providing that during the trial of a criminal case in which a defendant is charged with an assault in the second degree, a certain statement is not excluded by the hearsay rule if the statement is offered against a party that has engaged in, directed, or conspired to commit wrongdoing that was intended to and did procure the unavailibility of the declarant of the statement, under certain circumstances.
Title: Criminal Procedure - Admission of Out-of-Court Statements - Assault in the Second Degree
Status: In the Senate - Returned Passed
bill_summary: This bill expands a hearsay rule exception to include criminal trials for assault in the second degree. It allows a witness's out-of-court statement to be admitted as evidence if the court finds that the defendant's wrongdoing caused the witness to be unavailable to testify, provided specific procedural requirements and reliability standards are met.
stakeholders: Defendants charged with second-degree assault, victims and witnesses of second-degree assault, the Maryland State's Attorneys' Association, and the state court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is procedural in nature and does not materially affect State or local government finances or operations. There are no specific revenue or expenditure estimates provided as the impact is expected to be negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies evidentiary procedures within the Maryland court system. The Administrative Office of the Courts is responsible for providing operational and legal support to the state's courts, which will be tasked with conducting the mandated hearings and applying the expanded hearsay exception.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender is responsible for defending indigent individuals in criminal cases. This bill expands the conditions under which out-of-court statements can be used against a defendant in second-degree assault cases, directly impacting their legal defense strategies and constitutional advocacy.

The Office of the Attorney General represents the State in criminal appeals. Changes to the rules of evidence, particularly regarding hearsay exceptions, are frequently the subject of appellate litigation, requiring the OAG to handle cases arising from these procedural shifts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the Governor's primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategy, this office is relevant because the bill alters the prosecution's tools for addressing witness intimidation and second-degree assault, which are key components of state crime prevention policy.

Synopsis: Altering the membership, duties, and reporting requirements for the Maryland Reparations Commission.
Title: State Government – Maryland Reparations Commission – Revisions
Status: In the Senate - Unfavorable Report by Education, Energy, and the Environment; Withdrawn

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

bill_summary: This bill modifies the composition, duties, and reporting requirements of the Maryland Reparations Commission. It expands the commission's membership to include faith leaders and a representative from the Maryland Commission for African American History and Culture, changes the appointment process for certain members, mandates at least three public hearings for public input, and extends the commission's termination date and reporting deadlines to 2029.
stakeholders: Individuals impacted by historical inequality, members of the Maryland Reparations Commission, faith leaders, historians, mental health experts, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. The bill is likely to result in indeterminate increases in administrative expenditures and member reimbursements due to the addition of commission members, the requirement to conduct at least three public hearings, and the extension of the commission's operational lifespan from 2028 to 2029. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing several specialized members to the Commission and receives both the preliminary and final reports detailing findings and recommendations on reparations for historical inequality.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies and commissions, the OAG would provide legal counsel and representative services to the Maryland Reparations Commission regarding its duties and the legality of its recommendations.

This department oversees state personnel and budget execution, which is relevant given the bill's extension of the Commission's lifespan and the introduction of mandatory public hearings that require fiscal oversight.

This office assists the Governor in fulfilling the responsibility to recruit and vet experts—such as historians, mental health experts, and legal counsel—appointed to the Maryland Reparations Commission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the membership structure, reporting deadlines, and statutory lifespan of the Maryland Reparations Commission, which is an executive commission established to study historical inequality.

The bill's focus on studying and recommending benefits for individuals impacted by historical inequality and housing segregation aligns with this agency's mission to address and prevent discrimination in Maryland.

This office oversees ethnic, cultural, and faith-based commissions, including the Maryland Commission for African American History and Culture, which is explicitly assigned a representative on the Reparations Commission by this bill.

As the central depository for permanent government records, the Archives will be essential for the Commission’s mandated study of the historical impacts of enslavement and systemic inequality in Maryland.

Synopsis: Altering the period from 5 to 12 years that a licensed real estate appraiser must retain certain records; establishing a statute of limitations for certain civil actions against a person for certain real estate appraisal-related actions; extending the statute of limitation for certain civil actions for an alleged discriminatory housing practice related to the appraisal of residential real property; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Civil Actions - Real Estate Appraisals - Record Retention and Statute of Limitations
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/26 at 2:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Real Estate -see also- Agents and Brokers
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill increases the required record retention period for licensed real estate appraisers from 5 years to 12 years. It also establishes a statute of limitations for civil actions against appraisers for acts or omissions related to an appraisal, requiring that such actions be filed within 2 years of discovery or 4 years after the service was provided. Furthermore, it extends the statute of limitations for civil actions involving alleged discriminatory housing practices related to residential real property appraisals to 12 years.
responsible_party: State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors (Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Licensed real estate appraisers, appraisal management companies, home buyers, home sellers, and individuals filing civil suits related to property appraisals or discriminatory housing practices.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect Maryland State or local government finances or operations. However, it may have a meaningful fiscal impact on small businesses involved in real estate appraisal-related litigation due to the adjusted record retention requirements and statutes of limitations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Business Occupations and Professions Article, which governs the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors, a regulatory body within the Department of Labor. It changes the mandatory record retention period for its licensees from 5 years to 12 years.

The bill amends the State Government Article regarding discriminatory housing practices, which the Commission on Civil Rights is responsible for enforcing. It specifically extends the statute of limitations for filing a civil action related to appraisal discrimination from 2 years to 12 years, significantly impacting the agency's enforcement window.

The bill creates new statutes of limitations for civil actions and modifies existing ones in the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article. This impacts the adjudication of civil damages and housing discrimination cases within the Maryland judicial system.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal counsel for state agencies, including the Department of Labor and the Commission on Civil Rights. They would be responsible for advising these agencies on the implementation and legal implications of the altered record retention and statute of limitations provisions.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "dually enrolled student" to include both a nonpublic secondary school student and a homeschool student in Washington County so that these students are eligible to apply for the Part-Time Grant Program and the Early College Access Grant.
Title: Washington County - Institutions of Higher Education - Dually Enrolled Students
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

Private Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: The bill expands the definition of a 'dually enrolled student' in Washington County to include students attending nonpublic secondary schools and students who are homeschooled. This change makes these students eligible for the Part-Time Grant Program and the Early College Access Grant administered by the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC). Additionally, the bill prohibits public institutions of higher education from charging tuition to these dually enrolled students.
stakeholders: Nonpublic secondary school students in Washington County, homeschooled students in Washington County, and Maryland public institutions of higher education.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases eligibility for state-funded grants, specifically the Part-Time Grant Program and the Early College Access Grant, for certain students in Washington County. It also mandates that public institutions of higher education cannot charge tuition to these newly eligible dually enrolled students. These provisions imply an increase in state expenditures for grants and a potential decrease in tuition revenue for public higher education institutions; however, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Commission to establish and administer the Part-Time Grant Program and the Early College Access Grant for dually enrolled students, including setting guidelines and adopting regulations.

As the primary regulatory body for postsecondary education, this agency is tasked with the administration of the financial aid programs and the oversight of the institutions of higher education affected by the tuition changes.

MSDE oversees the secondary school systems, nonpublic schools, and homeschooling standards. The bill's changes to the definition of dually enrolled students directly impact the students under MSDE's jurisdiction and requires coordination with local school systems like Washington County.

USM constituent institutions are 'public institutions of higher education' which, under this bill, are prohibited from charging tuition to dually enrolled students, including the newly eligible nonpublic and homeschool students from Washington County.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University is subject to the provision that prohibits charging tuition to dually enrolled students and would serve as an eligible institution for the expanded grant programs.
As the state's public honors college, it must comply with the tuition prohibitions for dually enrolled students and participate in the grant programs expanded by this legislation.

The bill specifies that the Governor must provide funds for the Early College Access Grant in the annual budget, a process managed by DBM, which also oversees the fiscal impact of these grant expansions on state resources.
The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual state budget which must include funding for the Early College Access Grant as expanded by this bill.
The agency tracks student performance and workforce outcomes; expanding grant eligibility and dual enrollment definitions changes the data sets and student populations they monitor and report on.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Higher Education Commission and the Department of Education regarding the implementation of the new grant eligibility criteria and tuition regulations.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Off-Highway Recreational Vehicle (OHRV) Recreation Oversight Board to advise the Secretary of Natural Resources on the operation, acquisition, regulation, and general oversight of OHRV trails and recreation in Maryland.
stakeholders: Off-highway recreational vehicle drivers (ATV, UTV, motorcycle), vehicle dealers, the Maryland Off-Highway Vehicle Alliance, and the American Motorcyclist Association.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Natural Resources (DNR) can handle the board's staffing and support requirements using existing resources. The bill has no impact on state revenues and no direct effect on local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary agency impacted by the bill. The board is established to advise the Secretary of Natural Resources, and the department is responsible for providing staffing and support from the Maryland Park Service, Forest Service, and Wildlife and Heritage Service.
The Governor is responsible for appointing all five members of the newly established Off-Highway Recreational Vehicle Recreation Oversight Board and filling any vacancies that occur.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in the recruitment, vetting, and recommendation of the five members required to be appointed to the new board.
The OAG serves as legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and its constituent boards, and would likely provide legal guidance regarding the board's regulatory and oversight advice.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new permanent advisory board within the executive branch, which falls under this collective category for state bodies created to address specific government issues.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the State Highway Administration (SHA) and local jurisdictions to implement speed monitoring systems in 'safety corridors,' which are segments of highways identified as high-risk areas for vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists. It establishes a tiered civil penalty structure for speeding violations, requiring a 30-day warning period for newly installed systems. Revenue generated from these citations will be used to fund the program's administration, with remaining balances directed to the Transportation Trust Fund for highway safety and infrastructure preservation.
stakeholders: Motorists, pedestrians, bicyclists, and local government jurisdictions.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase State special fund revenues and expenditures, potentially by millions of dollars annually; the Fiscal Note provides an illustrative estimate of $26,800,000 in citation revenue based on specific deployment scenarios. Revenue will first cover SHA's administrative costs, with the remainder supporting highway safety and system preservation. Local governments that choose to implement their own safety corridor programs will also see increases in both revenues and expenditures. General fund revenues may increase slightly from contested cases in the District Court.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Highway Administration is the primary implementing agency authorized by the bill to identify safety corridors, implement speed monitoring systems, and manage the resulting permit program for local jurisdictions.

The District Court has exclusive original jurisdiction over contested speed monitoring citations. The Chief Judge is also responsible for adopting procedures for citation issuance and penalty collection in consultation with SHA.
The MVA is responsible for refusing to register or suspending the registration of motor vehicles when owners fail to pay civil penalties or contest violations.

MDOT is the parent agency of the State Highway Administration and the Motor Vehicle Administration. The bill also directs citation revenue (after administrative costs) into the Transportation Trust Fund managed by MDOT.
The Comptroller is explicitly required to distribute revenue from civil fines collected through State-controlled safety corridor speed monitoring systems into a special fund.
The MDTA is identified as an agency that can operate speed monitoring systems and may receive civil penalty payments for violations recorded by its systems.
The bill prohibits insurers from considering these civil penalties when reclassifying an insured or increasing premiums, a regulation falling under the oversight of the MIA.
The bill's primary purpose is the protection of vulnerable road users, which the legislation explicitly defines to include individuals using wheelchairs and mobility devices.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP is involved in the enforcement of motor vehicle laws and preservation of traffic safety on state highways impacted by this legislation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on public safety strategies and coordinates criminal justice policy, which includes automated traffic enforcement and highway safety initiatives.
The bill requires the use of recorded images and data processing that must comply with state standards for automated enforcement systems, which are governed by DoIT’s IT and data security policies.

As an insurer of last resort for Maryland residents, MAIF is subject to the bill's provisions prohibiting the use of these specific speed citations for premium reclassification or insurance coverage decisions.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the implementing agencies, including SHA and the Judiciary, and represents the State in legal matters involving traffic enforcement laws.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Board of Physicians to issue a limited medical license to physicians who were trained and licensed in foreign countries, provided they meet specific educational, training, and character requirements. These licensees must be employed full-time by a designated health care facility and may transition to a full medical license after meeting additional criteria, such as completing a period of supervised practice and passing standardized examinations.
stakeholders: Internationally trained physicians, the Maryland Board of Physicians, Maryland health care facilities, and MedChi (the Maryland State Medical Society).
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, Maryland Board of Physicians special fund expenditures increase by $68,600 in FY 2028, growing to $93,800 by FY 2031, primarily to fund a new licensure analyst position to manage regulations and applications. Special fund revenues will increase starting in FY 2029 by an indeterminate, but likely minimal, amount through application fees for the limited licenses. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Board of Physicians (MBP) is a regulatory body within the Maryland Department of Health and is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill's provisions, including issuing the new limited licenses, evaluating foreign credentials, and promulgating regulations. Additionally, local health departments are included in the bill's definition of health care facilities that may employ these licensees.

The fiscal note identifies a need for a new licensure analyst position and increased special fund expenditures starting in FY 2028. As the state's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is responsible for overseeing the creation of new positions and managing employee benefits and resources.

The University System of Maryland includes schools of medicine, which are specifically defined in the bill as 'health care facilities' authorized to employ and supervise physicians holding a limited license. USM institutions will also be involved in the evaluation and attestation of these physicians' competence for future full licensure.

The OAG serves as legal counsel to the Maryland Board of Physicians and the Department of Health. The agency will be responsible for reviewing the new regulations and policies required by the bill and advising on the legal aspects of the new limited licensure category.

As the state's regulatory board for postsecondary education, the commission oversees policies for schools of medicine. The bill establishes new educational equivalency standards and pathways for international medical graduates, which intersect with the commission's role in coordinating higher education policy.

The bill addresses physician workforce shortages by creating a new pathway for internationally trained professionals. This aligns with the board's mission to develop innovative workforce solutions and coordinate partnerships to strengthen Maryland's talent pipeline.

OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal and performance audits of state agencies. The agency will eventually be responsible for auditing the Maryland Board of Physicians' compliance with the new licensing laws and the financial management of the associated fees and expenditures.

bill_summary: This bill implements the federal Workforce Pell Grant Program in Maryland, establishing a framework for students in short-term vocational programs to receive federal Pell Grants. The Governor, with the Governor's Workforce Development Board, must approve programs based on criteria like completion rates, job placement, and alignment with high-demand industries.
responsible_party: Governor's Workforce Development Board (GWDB) and the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC)
stakeholders: Maryland postsecondary students, community colleges, private career schools, and employers in high-demand industry sectors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by 300000 in FY 2027 to implement the program, covering staffing costs at GWDB and MHEC as per a contingent appropriation. Subsequent years require approximately 236000 to 270000 annually. General fund revenues from application fees are indeterminate but expected to increase. Local community colleges and public universities may see fiscal changes if they choose to seek program approval.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the Governor, after consultation with the Governor's Workforce Development Board, determines whether short-term programs are eligible for federal Pell Grant funds. The Governor also has the authority to revoke approvals based on findings of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

The board is a primary implementing entity, tasked with consulting the Governor on program approvals, requesting and collecting performance data from institutions, and jointly reporting to the General Assembly. The board is also authorized to adopt regulations and collect application fees.

MHEC is a central agency for the program's administration, responsible for joint reporting to the General Assembly, adopting regulations, collecting evaluation fees, and verifying compliance of short-term programs at postsecondary institutions.

The department staffs the Governor's Workforce Development Board and oversees the Maryland Apprenticeship and Training Council, both of which are integral to the bill's implementation. The fiscal note also identifies a $300,000 contingent appropriation directed to this department for implementation.

The bill specifies that if the Attorney General finds an institution has engaged in unfair, deceptive, or abusive trade practices related to the program, the Governor must revoke the program's approval.

The system's constituent institutions are eligible to offer short-term programs under the bill and would be subject to the approval process, tuition limits, and reporting requirements established by the legislation.

As a public institution of postsecondary education, Morgan State University may seek approval for short-term programs under the Workforce Pell Grant Program, requiring compliance with the bill's regulatory and reporting mandates.

As a public institution of postsecondary education, the college is eligible to offer short-term programs and may participate in the federal Pell Grant program expansion, necessitating adherence to the bill's criteria.
DBM is relevant due to the fiscal impact of the bill, including the creation of new personnel positions and the management of a $300,000 contingent appropriation to support implementation.

The bill references findings by a court of appropriate jurisdiction as a trigger for the revocation of program approval. Additionally, the agency was identified as a source of information for the fiscal analysis.

Synopsis: Altering the education requirements an individual must meet to practice funeral direction or as a licensed apprentice; and prohibiting the practical examination qualification required for a license to practice funeral direction from including a practical examination demonstrating competency in the preparation of dead human bodies for final disposition and sanitary science.
Title: State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors - Funeral Direction Licensure and Apprentices - Requirements

bill_summary: This bill modifies the education and examination requirements for individuals seeking licensure as funeral directors or apprentices in Maryland. It distinguishes requirements between morticians and funeral directors, notably prohibiting the practical examination for funeral director applicants from requiring competency in the preparation of dead human bodies or embalming. The bill also establishes specific credit hour requirements for funeral director licensure and updates apprenticeship enrollment standards.
responsible_party: State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors
stakeholders: Individuals seeking licensure as morticians or funeral directors, licensed apprentices, mortuary science students, and the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires applicants to pay licensure fees to the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors. However, as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the context, specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Health Occupations Article and directly impacts the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors, which is a regulatory agency under the Maryland Department of Health.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors is a permanent regulatory body responsible for the licensing and examination of funeral service professionals impacted by this bill.
The bill alters educational requirements for licensure, including Associate of Arts degree specifications and mortuary science program credit hour approvals.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and boards, including those regulating health occupations.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch departments and is responsible for appointing members to the state regulatory board for morticians.
The Department of Budget and Management oversees the personnel and fiscal planning of state agencies, including the board that administers these licenses.

Synopsis: Increasing the penalties for stalking to a period of imprisonment of up to 10 years or a fine of up to $10,000 or both if the victim had a protective order in effect against the defendant at the time of the offense or the defendant had previously been convicted of stalking.
Title: Criminal Law - Stalking - Penalties
Status: In the Senate - Returned Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill elevates the crime of stalking from a misdemeanor to a felony if the offender has a prior stalking conviction or was subject to a protective or court order involving the victim at the time of the offense. It increases the maximum penalties for these specific cases to 10 years of imprisonment and a $10,000 fine, up from the standard 5 years and $5,000.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Victims of stalking, individuals charged with or convicted of stalking, and the Maryland state and local court systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in a minimal increase in State general fund expenditures due to longer incarceration sentences for felony stalking. There is also a potential minimal decrease in State general fund revenues and a corresponding minimal increase in local revenues as fine-collecting jurisdiction shifts from the District Court to the circuit courts. The Fiscal Note does not provide a specific dollar estimate, characterizing the impact as minimal.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill increases the maximum term of imprisonment for stalking from 5 years to 10 years and reclassifies certain offenses as felonies. DPSCS is the primary agency responsible for managing correctional facilities, pretrial detention, and parole and probation supervision for individuals convicted under these provisions.

The bill alters the classification of certain stalking offenses from misdemeanors to felonies, which shifts jurisdiction from the District Court to the Circuit Courts. The AOC provides the administrative support necessary to manage these changes in court processing and sentencing.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD is responsible for providing legal representation to indigent defendants. The reclassification of certain stalking charges to felonies with increased prison time increases the complexity and potential caseload for public defenders representing these individuals.

As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating criminal law violations, including stalking, and enforcing the penalties associated with these crimes.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. They manage funding for law enforcement and victim services, which are directly related to the enforcement and impact of stalking laws.
The OAG represents the state in criminal appeals. Stalking convictions, particularly those involving the new felony provisions and enhanced penalties, may be subject to appeal in state courts.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the enforcement of state laws. The Governor is also responsible for signing the bill into law and setting overall policy priorities regarding public safety and criminal justice.

Synopsis: Authorizing the county councils of certain charter counties, notwithstanding certain provisions of law, to set by simple majority vote of its members then serving a property tax rate that is higher than the property tax rate authorized under a county's charter or collect more property tax revenues than the revenues authorized under the county's charter for the purpose of funding the approved public safety budget of the county; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after June 30, 2026.
Title: Property Tax - Charter Counties - Application of County Tax Limitation on Public Safety Budget
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/31 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Chartered Counties -see also- AACo; BCo; CecilCo; etc.

Emergency Services -see also- Ambul; Emergencies; etc.
