bill_summary: This bill requires hospitals in Maryland to adopt and implement policies regarding how they will respond to immigration enforcement actions on their premises. These policies must align with guidance from the Attorney General, be made available to all hospital staff, and be supported by annual staff training. The bill also tasks the Health Services Cost Review Commission with developing and publishing a model policy in consultation with the Attorney General and the Maryland Hospital Association.
responsible_party: Maryland Health Services Cost Review Commission
stakeholders: Hospital staff and administrators, patients, guests, and the Maryland Hospital Association.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect state or local governmental operations or finances. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the bill relates to administrative policy requirements and training for hospital staff, which do not carry a direct state expenditure or revenue change according to the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) to develop a model policy for hospitals regarding immigration enforcement actions and to publish this policy on its website by October 1, 2026.

The HSCRC must consult with the Attorney General to develop the model policy. Additionally, the bill requires hospital policies to be consistent with guidance already issued by the Attorney General under existing state law.

The HSCRC is an independent agency within the Maryland Department of Health. Furthermore, MDH regulates the hospitals that are required to adopt these policies and was a primary information source for the fiscal note.
The bill includes a technical amendment to the section of law that governs the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, which the MHCC oversees in conjunction with the HSCRC.
As the executive department overseeing state agencies and policy coordination, the Governor's Office is relevant to the implementation of new hospital protocols and the signing of the bill into law.

Synopsis: Authorizing an individual who enrolls for coverage or enrolls a dependent for coverage during a certain special enrollment period for pregnancy to choose a certain date option on which the coverage will become effective; and requiring the carrier, if the individual fails to select the effective date, to select a certain date option.
Title: Health Insurance - Special Enrollment Period for Pregnancy - Coverage Effective Date

bill_summary: This bill allows individuals who enroll for health insurance or enroll a dependent during a special enrollment period for pregnancy to choose the effective date of their coverage. The individual may choose to have coverage begin on either the first day of the month in which pregnancy was confirmed or the first day of the month following the selection of the plan. If the individual does not select an option, the insurance carrier is required to select one of these two dates.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange
stakeholders: Pregnant individuals and their dependents, health insurance carriers, the Maryland Insurance Administration, and the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration will increase minimally in FY 2027 due to $125 rate and form filing fees. Operational impacts on the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange are expected to be handled within existing budgeted resources. There is no fiscal impact on local governments or the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary regulatory body for health insurance in the state. This bill requires carriers to modify their enrollment processes and effective dates for pregnancy-related special enrollment periods, which will require the MIA to review and approve updated rate and form filings.

The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange (MHBE) administers the Maryland Health Connection, the state's individual insurance marketplace. Since the bill mandates changes to special enrollment periods both inside and outside the Individual Exchange, MHBE must implement system and operational changes to allow enrollees to select their preferred coverage start dates.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange. They would be responsible for ensuring that the implementation of the new enrollment rules complies with state and federal insurance laws.

The Maryland Department of Health oversees public health policy and the Maryland Health Care Commission. While MIA and MHBE are the primary implementers, MDH has a general interest in policies that expand or clarify access to maternal health coverage and healthcare practitioner confirmation processes.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that employers with workers exposed to temperatures of at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit, whether indoors or outdoors, develop and implement a heat-related illness prevention plan. The bill requires employers to provide drinking water and shade, monitor work area temperatures, and establish specific high-heat procedures when temperatures reach 90 degrees. Additionally, it requires acclimatization protocols for new or returning employees, emergency response planning, and annual heat stress training for all staff and supervisors.
responsible_party: Maryland Commissioner of Labor and Industry
stakeholders: Maryland employers and employees working in conditions of 80 degrees Fahrenheit or higher, excluding certain emergency services and incidental exposures.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the bill text, so specific dollar estimates for State or local revenue and expenditures are unavailable. The bill creates financial obligations for employers to provide drinking water, shaded areas, and heat stress training. The Maryland Commissioner of Labor and Industry will also incur administrative costs to oversee the implementation of these standards and review submitted acclimatization plans.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor is the primary implementing agency, as the Commissioner of Labor and Industry oversees the Maryland Occupational Safety and Health (MOSH) program, which is responsible for developing, adopting, and enforcing heat stress standards and safety regulations.

MDOT oversees a massive outdoor workforce across highways, transit, ports, and aviation. The bill's requirements for heat-related illness prevention plans, shade, water, and rest breaks will significantly impact operations and fiscal expenditures for all MDOT administrations.

DNR employs numerous park rangers, foresters, and field staff who work in outdoor environments. This bill mandates specific safety protocols and equipment (shade, water monitoring) for these employees during high-heat conditions.

Agriculture is one of the sectors most impacted by heat stress standards. The department provides leadership to the agricultural community, which will face significant compliance requirements regarding hydration, acclimatization, and rest breaks for farm labor.

DGS manages state-owned facilities and construction projects. Maintenance crews and contractors working on state projects will be subject to these safety standards, requiring DGS to update its operational procedures and procurement for safety equipment.

As a service provider for water, wastewater, and solid waste, MES has a large workforce of field technicians and operators frequently exposed to outdoor and industrial heat conditions, requiring rigorous adherence to the bill's safety plans.
The OAH would be responsible for adjudicating contested cases and appeals involving citations issued by the Department of Labor for violations of these new heat stress standards.

DBM is the central personnel agency for Maryland. It will need to coordinate with other agencies to ensure state employee policies align with the training, acclimatization, and rest break mandates of the bill.

The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor during the regulatory development process and represent state agencies in litigation or enforcement actions related to these heat stress standards.

MDH provides expertise in public health and medical safety. The bill's focus on heat-related illness symptoms (heat stroke, exhaustion) and medical care protocols overlaps with MDH's mission to protect resident health.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages correctional facilities where staff and justice-involved individuals may be exposed to extreme heat in older buildings or during outdoor work assignments, requiring the development of prevention and high-heat procedures.

The commission adjudicates claims for workplace injuries. These new standards will likely impact the volume and evaluation of workers' compensation claims related to heat-related illnesses and employer negligence.
As a major employer with extensive campus grounds and facilities, USM will need to implement these safety standards for its maintenance, groundskeeping, and construction personnel.

The PSC regulates utilities whose employees often perform outdoor maintenance on electric, gas, and water infrastructure. While emergency restoration is exempt, routine maintenance work will be subject to these heat standards.

MSA manages sports complexes and large-scale construction projects (including schools). These sites frequently involve heat-exposed work, requiring MSA to ensure compliance among its staff and contractors.

While emergency response is exempt, MSP personnel performing routine duties such as highway patrol, commercial vehicle inspections, and facility maintenance are subject to the bill's heat protection requirements.
The council advocates for rural interests, including the agricultural sector, which will be significantly affected by the operational costs and labor requirements associated with the bill.
The BPW oversees significant state contracts and expenditures. Large procurement orders for water, shade structures, or specialized cooling equipment for state agencies may require BPW approval.
PERB oversees collective bargaining for public sector employees. Heat-related working conditions, rest break schedules, and safety protocols are often subjects of labor negotiations and disputes.

bill_summary: This bill alters the calculation of the Maryland Homeowners' Property Tax Credit and increases the maximum combined gross income eligibility threshold from $60,000 to $100,000. It also expands the income brackets and modifies the percentages used to determine the credit amount, effectively increasing the benefit for eligible homeowners.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland homeowners with combined gross incomes up to $100,000 and a combined net worth of $200,000 or less.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase state general fund expenditures because the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit is a state-funded program that reimburses local governments for lost property tax revenue. By increasing the income eligibility limit and adjusting calculation brackets to be more generous, the bill will increase the number of qualifying homeowners and the size of the credits awarded. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the eligibility and calculation of the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit. The Board is explicitly responsible for hearing appeals regarding disputes over various property tax credits and tax exemptions.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court hears appeals from decisions regarding real property assessments and tax credits, making it a critical venue for legal challenges arising from these credit changes.

Expanding the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit has a significant fiscal impact on the state budget. DBM is responsible for revenue estimation, budget execution, and long-term fiscal planning affected by the reduction in property tax revenue.

The Homeowners' Property Tax Credit is a vital program for older Marylanders on fixed incomes. Changes to income limits and credit calculations directly impact the financial stability and housing security of the department's primary constituents.

This agency's mission includes ensuring safe, affordable housing and supporting homeownership. Alterations to this tax credit directly affect the affordability of homeownership for low-to-moderate income residents.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and enforcement of tax laws, including the Tax - Property Article modified by this bill.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees revenue collection and fiscal integrity, and sits on the Board of Public Works which handles significant state expenditures related to tax reimbursements.
The Treasurer manages and protects state funds and anticipates monetary needs, which are impacted by changes in tax credit expenditures and state revenue flows.
The Governor's Office is responsible for proposing the annual state budget, which must incorporate the fiscal changes resulting from the expanded property tax credit eligibility.

Synopsis: Prohibiting certain service agreements for residential property entered into before June 1, 2023, if the service provider is not considered in good standing with the State Department of Assessment and Taxation on or after June 1, 2026.
Title: Residential Property - Service Agreement - Defunct Service Providers
Status: In the Senate - Returned Passed
bill_summary: This bill voids residential property service agreements made before June 1, 2023, if the service provider is defunct or not in good standing with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation on or after June 1, 2026. It limits the duration of such agreements to two years and prohibits them from creating property liens or binding subsequent owners. Additionally, it allows property owners to sue in circuit court to have such agreements declared void and to seek compensatory damages and legal fees.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Residential property owners and service providers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. While it creates a cause of action for individuals to seek damages and attorney's fees in circuit court, these private legal actions do not represent a significant fiscal impact on the State or local budgets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a specific cause of action in Maryland's Circuit Courts, allowing individuals to seek a judicial determination that a service agreement is void and unenforceable. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides the operational and legal support necessary for the judicial branch to handle these new proceedings.

The bill regulates service providers who contract for the maintenance, purchase, or sale of residential property. Many of these providers, such as real estate brokers and home service professionals, are licensed and regulated by the Maryland Department of Labor.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the Office of the Attorney General provides counsel on the interpretation of the Real Property Article. Furthermore, these types of residential service agreements are often linked to the Consumer Protection Act, which the OAG enforces.

This agency is responsible for ensuring residents have access to secure housing and for managing community revitalization. The bill's provisions regarding the voiding of liens and encumbrances on residential properties directly impact homeownership security and property title integrity.

stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals, Maryland Correctional Enterprises, and Maryland institutions of higher education
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in a significant increase in State general fund expenditures in fiscal 2027 and 2028, with the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services estimating contract costs between $150,000 and $200,000 to complete the study and report. Higher education revenues and expenditures may also be affected depending on whether a public or private institution is selected for the collaboration. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to lead the study, collaborate with a higher education institution, and submit both interim and final reports regarding Maryland Correctional Enterprises and reentry outcomes.

The bill requires collaboration with an institution of higher education, and the University System of Maryland is explicitly identified in the fiscal note as a source of information and potential partner for the study.

As a state university, Morgan State is a potential candidate for the higher education collaboration required by the bill and is specifically named in the fiscal note as a source of information for the report.
As an independent state-governed honors college, Saint Mary's is a potential institution for the higher education collaboration mandated to support the study of correctional industry programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office is responsible for coordinating criminal justice strategies and reducing recidivism, which aligns with the bill's focus on improving correctional industries to achieve successful reentry outcomes.

The Department of Labor oversees workforce development and adult learning programs; the improvement of job training through correctional industries directly relates to their mission of fostering economic growth and worker protection.

The bill is expected to have a significant fiscal impact on the general fund (estimated between $150,000 and $200,000), which falls under the oversight and budget execution responsibilities of this department.
The bill requires that both interim and final reports be submitted to the Governor, who oversees the policy initiatives and executive branch agencies involved in the study.

The commission coordinates statewide policies for higher education institutions, which are the designated partners for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services in fulfilling the bill's requirements.

The board sets the vision for the state's workforce system and aligns education and government partnerships, making it relevant to recommendations for improving job training and post-release employment outcomes for incarcerated individuals.

This bill impacts the business climate and economic development for electric vehicle manufacturers. Changes to dealer licensing laws are a significant factor for companies looking to establish a direct-to-consumer presence in the state.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a moratorium on the implementation and enforcement of State energy efficiency and conservation programs, services, and plans starting July 1, 2026. It requires the Public Service Commission to continue current rate-making policies until electric and gas companies recover all unpaid and unamortized costs incurred for these programs prior to the moratorium. After full cost recovery is achieved, the Commission must submit a report to the General Assembly recommending whether the moratorium should be rescinded.
stakeholders: Electric and gas companies, Maryland utility customers, and State government agencies involved in energy efficiency oversight.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a moratorium on energy efficiency programs, which will impact future State expenditures and utility customer surcharges. It specifically mandates the recovery of utility costs incurred before July 1, 2026. Specific dollar estimates for the fiscal impact are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency named in the bill, responsible for managing utility cost recovery, overseeing the moratorium on energy efficiency programs, and submitting a final report and recommendation to the General Assembly.

As the state's principal agency for maximizing energy efficiency and coordinating energy planning, the MEA's core mission is directly impacted by a moratorium on implementing or enforcing energy efficiency and conservation programs.

The OPC represents residential utility consumers in proceedings regarding rates and service quality; the bill's changes to the EmPOWER Maryland surcharges and energy efficiency programs are a central focus of their advocacy work.
The MCEC's mission to advance the adoption of energy efficiency technologies is directly challenged by a legislative moratorium on the implementation of state energy efficiency programs and services.

bill_summary: The Utility RELIEF Act overhauls Maryland's energy policy by transferring the electric universal service program to the Department of Human Services, establishing a no-interest loan program for nonprofits to adopt renewable energy, and reforming utility rate-making processes. It introduces new transparency requirements for customer bills, limits the recovery of executive compensation through rates, and mandates utility membership in regional transmission organizations. The bill also addresses the impact of large load customers like data centers by creating a registry and specific rate schedules, modifies EmPOWER Maryland energy reduction targets, and streamlines the permitting and interconnection process for residential solar and energy storage systems.
responsible_party: Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC), Maryland Energy Administration (MEA), and Department of Human Services (DHS)
stakeholders: Residential utility customers, low-income households, nonprofit organizations, large industrial and commercial energy users (including data centers), solar energy installers, and electric and gas utility companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill effectuates $334,500,000 in contingent special fund appropriations from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) for fiscal 2027, with an additional $150,000 in SEIF funds allocated for a public school study. Major financial impacts include $100 million for renewable energy and storage auctions, $100 million for EmPOWER Maryland residential program costs, $38 million for limited-income rate relief, and approximately $91.5 million for public school HVAC upgrades and heat pump installations. Local governments are impacted by mandates to implement automated solar permitting software and specific inspection timelines, though Baltimore City receives targeted school funding. Various State agencies, including the PSC and MEA, will incur unquantified administrative costs for staffing and implementation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, coordinates policy initiatives, and the Governor serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which is authorized by the bill to waive certain contract clauses for renewable energy procurement.

The Comptroller serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which is involved in contract waivers under the bill. Additionally, the agency is tasked with providing funding for a study of public school HVAC systems and collecting revenue for the Electric Universal Service Program fund.
The Treasurer serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which is granted authority by the bill to waive certain termination for convenience clauses in state energy contracts.
The OAG is specifically authorized by the bill to seek judicial enforcement against counties or municipalities that fail to comply with the new residential solar permitting requirements.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency and the bill involves significant transfers of hundreds of millions of dollars within the Strategic Energy Investment Fund and new appropriations for various state programs.

The bill prohibits the construction of data centers in certain development districts in Baltimore City and requires assessments of the economic and fiscal impacts of data center development in the state.
The bill impacts the public education system through funding for HVAC systems and coordination with the Interagency Commission on School Construction for capital improvements in schools.

MDE is responsible for implementing and enforcing Building Energy Performance Standards (BEPS), which are directly altered by the bill's reduction of alternative compliance fees for certain buildings. The agency also conducts greenhouse gas emission studies mentioned in the bill.
DGS is authorized to issue requests for proposals for long-term leases on state-owned sites for new or expanded energy generating stations identified in state studies.
The agency is responsible for administering the low-income residential weatherization component of the Electric Universal Service Program, which the bill restructures.
The bill transfers the administration of the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) to the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP), which is a unit within the Department of Human Services.
The bill imposes new prevailing wage requirements on the construction of solar energy generating stations, which falls under the agency's responsibility for enforcing labor laws.
The Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) within DNR is required to conduct studies on permitting processes for energy development and identify priority energy sites.
MDP is involved in the 'Site-Readiness Initiative' and coordinates with other agencies to identify parcels suitable for rapid energy deployment.
MDOT is tasked with studying methods for reducing transmission-constrained areas through the use of existing rights-of-way.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires input from panels or roundtables of interested parties and involves various committees in reviewing energy policy scenarios and implementation strategies.
The BPW is specifically authorized by the bill to waive the inclusion of termination for convenience clauses in multi-year state contracts for the procurement of renewable energy.
The bill allocates millions of dollars from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) to the IAC for upgrades to public school HVAC systems in Baltimore City.
The bill establishes the Green and Renewable Energy Efficiency for Nonprofits Loan Program and an associated fund within the MCEC.

MEA is the primary administrator of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) and is responsible for conducting alternative compliance fee auctions and managing numerous energy grant programs modified or created by the bill.
The bill explicitly states that the Electric Universal Service Program, in its new administrative home, remains subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.
As the advocate for residential utility consumers, the OPC is heavily impacted by the bill's changes to utility rate-making, cost recovery limitations, and clean capacity rating programs.

The PSC is the primary regulator for the utilities and programs affected by this bill, including rate plan approvals, the large load customer registry, CPCN process changes, and the successor net energy metering program.

bill_summary: The bill corrects technical errors, omissions, and obsolete references in the Annotated Code of Maryland and the Public Local Laws of Maryland. It reorganizes certain sections and clarifies language without making substantive changes to the law.
stakeholders: Maryland residents, legal professionals, and state and local government agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state or local fiscal impact, as it is purely technical in nature and does not affect governmental operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill makes numerous technical corrections and updates to the Education Article, affecting education funding, teacher induction programs, school safety funds, and special education services.

The bill corrects multiple sections within the Health - General and Health Occupations articles, including language regarding the AHEAD Model State Agreement, firearm violence reduction programs, and physician assistant regulations.
The bill contains extensive technical updates to the Transportation Article, affecting modal administrations, zero-emission bus procurement, and emergency vehicle regulations.
The bill includes drafter's notes clarifying the role and definition of the Secretary of Budget and Management regarding capital project planning and performance incentive programs.
The bill clarifies the approval authority of the Secretary of General Services concerning the design and implementation of state capital projects.
The bill explicitly adds definitions for the Secretary and Department of Disabilities to the Human Services Article to clarify the administration of assistive technology and self-advocacy programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill corrects the agency's name in multiple sections of the Annotated Code following its renaming from the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention, Youth, and Victim Services.
The bill updates sections regarding nonvisual access standards for information technology and the reporting of cybersecurity incidents.
The bill corrects technical errors in the Labor and Employment and Business Occupations articles, including provisions related to unemployment insurance and professional licensing.
The bill updates the Land Use Article to change the term 'visions' to 'planning principles' in alignment with recent legislative changes.
The bill makes technical corrections to the Environment Article regarding groundwater permits, the Water Quality Revolving Loan Fund, and packaging inspections.
The bill updates cross-references within the Tax - General Article that the Comptroller is responsible for enforcing.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill corrects language in the Correctional Services Article and updates retirement provisions for correctional officers.
The bill reorganizes definitions related to sustainable communities and the Sustainable Growth Subcabinet within the Housing and Community Development Article.
The bill makes technical corrections to the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding juvenile detention and traffic citation penalties.
The bill updates technical provisions in the State Personnel and Pensions Article regarding investment managers and retiree reemployment.
The bill corrects technical errors in the Public Utilities Article regarding community choice aggregators and hazardous liquid pipelines.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill corrects the terminology regarding Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) participation goals in state procurement contracts.
The bill clarifies the use of the Safe Schools Fund for grants and training, which is administered by this center.
The bill identifies the State Police as a coordinating partner in multidepartmental firearm violence reduction efforts.
The bill specifies the Treasurer's role in investing money within the Safe Schools Fund.
The bill repeals an obsolete cross-reference to the Insurance Article within the Health - General Article affecting health maintenance organizations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill updates language regarding the distribution of proceeds from online sports wagering.
The bill makes multiple corrections to the State Government Article and defines the Sustainable Growth Subcabinet located within the Executive Department.
The bill clarifies that certain guidance and policies are not subject to standard administrative procedures, affecting the OAG's advisory role.
The bill updates the Interstate Compact on Educational Opportunity for Military Children, which impacts the families served by this department.
The bill corrects federal law references regarding National Guard members on active duty orders within the Education Article.
As a modal administration of MDOT, it is impacted by technical corrections to road safety and work zone speed control provisions.
As a modal administration of MDOT, it is impacted by corrections to vehicle registration and driver education accounts.
As a modal administration of MDOT, it is impacted by corrections regarding zero-emission bus procurement and reporting.
The bill updates definitions related to transportation facilities projects managed by the MDTA.
The bill makes technical corrections to nonresident tuition exemptions at public institutions of higher education.

Synopsis: Requiring an election director of a local board of elections to immediately remove a registered voter from the statewide voter registration list when the local board receives a certain report that the registered voter is deceased; requiring the election director to take certain action if the election director receives information that a voter removed from the statewide voter registration list is not in fact deceased; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires local election directors to immediately remove deceased individuals from the statewide voter registration list upon receiving reports from the Maryland Department of Health, the Social Security Administration, or vital statistics agencies in other states. It replaces the previous requirement to mail a notice and wait for a response before removal. The bill also establishes oversight procedures for the State Board of Elections to ensure local compliance, including the authority to mandate corrective action plans, require staff retraining, and withhold discretionary election funds from noncompliant local boards.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections and local boards of elections
stakeholders: Maryland registered voters, local boards of elections, the State Board of Elections, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Financial implications identified in the bill text include the potential withholding of discretionary election administration funds from local boards that fail to comply with registration list maintenance requirements and costs associated with mandatory staff retraining or audits by the Office of Legislative Audits for noncompliant jurisdictions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for supervising elections and managing the statewide voter registration list. This bill directly mandates procedures for the State Administrator and local boards regarding the immediate removal of deceased voters and grants the State Board enforcement authority over non-compliant local boards.

The Maryland Department of Health is explicitly required by the bill to report names and addresses of individuals reported deceased in the State to the State Administrator, serving as a primary data source for updating the voter registration list.
The bill authorizes the State Board of Elections to refer local boards that are persistently non-compliant with voter registration list maintenance requirements to the Office of Legislative Audits.

The bill amends Section 3-504 of the Election Law Article, which defines reporting requirements for the clerks of the circuit courts and administrative clerks of the District Courts regarding felony convictions and name changes, both of which are managed under the AOC's operational oversight.

Title: Electric and Gas Companies - Energy Efficiency, Conservation, and Demand Response Programs - Alterations (Utility Affordability and Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026)

bill_summary: The Utility Affordability and Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026 requires that utility energy efficiency, conservation, and demand response programs provide demonstrable bill savings to residential customers. It extends the deadline for electric and gas companies to eliminate certain unamortized program costs from 2032 to 2040 and mandates that the Public Service Commission establish caps or limits on residential assessments for these programs by July 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Residential electric and gas customers, electric and gas utility companies, and midsize electric cooperatives.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill shifts the timeline for utilities to recover unamortized energy program costs by extending the recovery deadline from 2032 to 2040. It also requires the Public Service Commission to set caps on residential assessments to reduce customer costs. These changes will likely decrease immediate ratepayer charges but extend the duration of those charges over a longer period. Specific state or local fiscal estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulator for the electric and gas utilities affected by this bill. The bill specifically mandates the Commission to establish cost caps, limit residential assessments, review energy efficiency plans for demonstrable bill savings, and submit a progress report to the General Assembly.

The Office of the People's Counsel is the statutory advocate for residential utility consumers. Since the bill's primary purpose is 'Utility Affordability and Ratepayer Protection' for residential customers, the OPC will play a critical role in representing consumer interests during the Commission's implementation of these new requirements.

In the Public Utilities Article, 'the Department' referenced in Section 7-222 is the Department of Housing and Community Development. The agency is directly responsible for developing and implementing energy efficiency and conservation programs for low-income residential sectors that are part of the state's broader energy strategy modified by this bill.

The Maryland Energy Administration coordinates state energy policy and manages programs related to energy efficiency and demand response. Changes to utility-led conservation programs and their cost-recovery mechanisms directly impact the state energy strategies overseen by the MEA.

The bill explicitly links utility energy efficiency and demand response programs to the state's greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals. The Department of the Environment is the lead agency responsible for monitoring and implementing these environmental targets.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits state and local government officials, employees, and contractors from entering into nondisclosure agreements with entities involved in economic development activities, specifically including those establishing or operating data centers. It also expands the Maryland Public Information Act by defining public service companies as instrumentalities of the State, thereby making their records subject to public disclosure requirements.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Economic Development, Maryland General Assembly, local governing bodies, and public service companies.
stakeholders: State and local government employees, contractors, and consultants; businesses involved in economic development projects; data center operators; public service companies; and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill may result in indeterminate administrative costs for state and local agencies and public service companies due to expanded Public Information Act compliance requirements. Additionally, the prohibition on nondisclosure agreements may impact the negotiation and execution of economic development projects, which could have broader implications for state and local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new title to the Economic Development Article specifically prohibiting the Department of Commerce, including its employees, contractors, and consultants, from entering into nondisclosure agreements related to economic development activities.

The bill amends the Public Information Act to define 'public service companies'—which are regulated by the PSC—as instrumentalities of the State, thereby making their records subject to public disclosure.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG will be responsible for advising all state agencies and instrumentalities on the implementation of the expanded Public Information Act and the new prohibitions on nondisclosure agreements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This entity includes the State Public Information Act Compliance Board, which will have its jurisdiction expanded to include disputes over the public records of public service companies.
As an entity governed by the Economic Development Article, MEDCO is directly impacted by the new prohibition against using nondisclosure agreements in economic development activities.

The OPC represents residential utility consumers; making public service companies subject to the Public Information Act provides the OPC with a new mechanism for accessing records to support its advocacy efforts.
The bill impacts executive branch policy regarding economic development negotiations and transparency, requiring oversight from the Governor's Office and coordination among executive agencies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As a quasi-public corporation focused on economic development within the agricultural sector, MARBIDCO is likely subject to the new restrictions on nondisclosure agreements.
The bill specifically amends the Health - General Article to update notice requirements for death certificates issued by the Chief Medical Examiner and the rights of a 'person in interest' to appeal.
The bill amends the Transportation Article to update the definition of 'personal information' as it relates to MVA records and the Public Information Act.
As the central personnel and fiscal agency, DBM may need to update state employment and contracting policies to ensure compliance with the ban on nondisclosure agreements.
The bill references the Tax - General Article for the definition of 'data center,' an area within the Comptroller's tax regulatory scope, though the bill's impact on the agency is minimal.

bill_summary: This bill extends the term of the Workgroup on the Affordability of Private Passenger Automobile Insurance to June 30, 2027, and expands its membership and specific duties. The workgroup is required to develop concrete, data-driven legislative recommendations to reduce automobile insurance premiums and address rating factors that may cause geographic or racial disparities, with an updated report due to the Governor and General Assembly by January 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Maryland motorists, private passenger automobile insurance companies, insurance producers, and consumer advocacy organizations
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) is expected to handle the bill's requirements with existing budgeted resources. There may be a minimal increase in special fund expenditures if the MIA needs to expand its contract with an actuary for additional data-driven analyses. The bill has no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) is the primary agency responsible for establishing, chairing, and supporting the Workgroup on the Affordability of Private Passenger Automobile Insurance. The bill expands the workgroup's duties to include specific legislative recommendations regarding rating factors and extends its operational life until 2027.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund (MAIF) is a statutory member of the workgroup. As the state's insurer of last resort, MAIF is directly impacted by findings and legislative recommendations concerning the affordability of automobile insurance, particularly in majority-minority and lower-income communities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly alters the membership, legislative duties, and termination date of the Workgroup on the Affordability of Private Passenger Automobile Insurance, which is a state-authorized body tasked with conducting special studies and providing policy recommendations.

The workgroup is required to submit its findings and recommendations to the Governor. Additionally, the Governor oversees the executive branch, including the primary implementing agency (MIA), and the workgroup serves to inform the Governor's policy initiatives regarding insurance affordability.

bill_summary: This bill expands the scope and responsibilities of the Maryland Aerospace and Technology Commission to include promoting innovation in space science, space technology, and aeronautics. It alters the commission's membership, requires the appointment of an executive director, and establishes a grant program to support eligible businesses, nonprofits, government entities, and higher education institutions in aerospace research, technology development, workforce training, and infrastructure improvements.
stakeholders: Aerospace businesses and nonprofit entities, Maryland institutions of higher education, state and local government agencies, and the aerospace and technology workforce.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $144,930 in FY 2027 to hire an executive director. Beginning in FY 2028, general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $5,000,000 annually to cover ongoing administrative costs and the new grant program. Local government revenues and expenditures may also increase starting in FY 2028 to the extent that local entities apply for and receive grants from the commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Aerospace and Technology Commission is established within the Department of Commerce. The Department is responsible for providing staff support to the Commission, and the Secretary of Commerce (or their designee) serves as a member of the Commission.

The Chief Executive Officer of TEDCO is a designated member of the Commission. Additionally, the bill requires the Commission's staff to coordinate and connect the Commission with TEDCO for relevant projects and initiatives.

The Executive Director of MEDCO is a designated member of the Commission. The bill also explicitly requires Commission staff to coordinate with MEDCO to align efforts regarding the aerospace industry.

The Presidents of the University of Maryland, College Park and the University of Maryland Baltimore County (both USM institutions) are designated members of the Commission. Furthermore, institutions of higher education are eligible for the grants established by the bill.

The bill expands the Commission's scope to include aeronautics and aviation industries. The Chair of the Maryland Aviation Commission, which is part of MDOT's modal administrations, is a designated member of the Commission.

The bill adds the Chair of the Maryland Aviation Commission to the Commission's membership and expands the Commission's purpose to include aeronautics and aviation, which directly aligns with the MAA's mission to foster aviation vitality in the state.

The Governor is responsible for appointing several members of the Commission with the advice and consent of the Senate. Additionally, the appointment of the Commission's Executive Director is subject to the Governor's approval.

The bill creates a mandated annual appropriation of $30,000,000 starting in fiscal year 2028 for the Commission’s administrative costs and grant program, which significantly impacts state budget planning managed by DBM.

The bill defines 'institution of higher education' based on the standards and regulations prescribed by the Maryland Higher Education Commission. Furthermore, these institutions are eligible to receive grants for aerospace research and development.

As a public institution of higher education that may conduct aerospace research, Morgan State University is an 'eligible entity' that can apply for and receive grants from the Commission established under this bill.

As a public institution of higher education, Saint Mary's College of Maryland is eligible to apply for grants provided by the Commission for aerospace-related research, development, or workforce training.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland Workforce Launch Pilot Program in the Department of Commerce to provide customized, no-cost workforce training as a business attraction tool, to recruit strategic industries and qualified business entities to the State; requiring the Department to partner with not more than two community colleges in the State to deliver training services; etc.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Maryland Workforce Launch Pilot Program within the Department of Commerce. The program is designed to attract new businesses and strategic industries to the state by providing them with customized, no-cost workforce training. The Department of Commerce will partner with up to two community colleges to deliver these training services and must report on the program's effectiveness by the end of 2028.
stakeholders: Business entities located outside of Maryland that are in active negotiations to relocate to the state, Maryland community colleges, and individuals receiving workforce training through the program.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by 1,000,000 in FY 2027 and FY 2028, reflecting a contingent appropriation in the FY 2027 budget and assumed discretionary funding thereafter. These funds will support one contractual position at the Department of Commerce and provide training grants to partner community colleges. Minimal expenditures of 42,600 are expected in FY 2029 for final administrative duties. Local community colleges selected as partners will see an increase in revenues and expenditures to develop and deliver the training curriculum.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Department of Commerce as the primary agency responsible for establishing, administering, and reporting on the Maryland Workforce Launch Pilot Program. Commerce must manage the budget, negotiate with business entities, and partner with community colleges.

The bill creates a workforce training program as an economic development tool. As the chief policy-making body for the state's workforce system, the GWDB is relevant to the strategic alignment of this pilot with state workforce goals.

The fiscal note identifies a need for $1.0 million in general fund expenditures and the creation of a new contractual finance specialist position, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget and personnel management.

The program requires the Department of Commerce to partner with community colleges to deliver training. As the regulatory and coordinating board for higher education, MHEC is relevant to the integration of these programs into the community college system.

The Department of Labor oversees workforce development and adult learning programs. This pilot program provides similar workforce training services, creating a direct overlap or coordination point with Labor's mission.

The bill requires the Department of Commerce to submit a report on the program's effectiveness to the Governor by 2028. The Governor's Office also oversees executive policy initiatives like the state's economic strategic plan mentioned in the bill.

The Department of Commerce must enter into formal agreements with qualified business entities, including performance metrics and reimbursement provisions. OAG provides the necessary legal counsel to draft and enforce these state contracts.

As an agency responsible for conducting fiscal compliance and performance audits of executive branch programs, OLA will eventually be responsible for auditing the financial management and performance outcomes of this pilot program.

The Comptroller, as the state's chief financial officer, is responsible for the collection of revenues and payment of state bills, including the $1.0 million in general fund expenditures allocated for this program.

The Treasurer's Office manages and protects state funds. This includes the disbursement of the $1.0 million in general funds and the handling of any reimbursements from businesses that fail to meet performance metrics.
The team is tasked with piloting novel initiatives to enhance economic mobility. This workforce pilot is directly related to providing pathways for economic opportunity through job training.

The pilot program requires tracking performance metrics such as jobs created and salaries. MLDS links and analyzes student and workforce data, which may be relevant for evaluating the long-term outcomes of the trainees.

Synopsis: Providing that punitive damages may be awarded in a civil action only if the plaintiff proves by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with gross negligence; requiring the State Court Administrator to assess a certain surcharge on a defendant against whom a judgment for punitive damages is entered; requiring the Administrator to deposit money collected from the surcharge into the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund; applying the Act prospectively; etc.
Title: Civil Actions - Punitive Damage Awards - Surcharge

bill_summary: This bill provides that punitive damages in civil negligence actions may only be awarded if gross negligence is proven by clear and convincing evidence. It requires the State Court Administrator to assess a 50% surcharge on such awards, to be paid by the defendant and deposited into the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund.
stakeholders: Plaintiffs and defendants in civil litigation, the Maryland Judiciary, and the Maryland public education system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a 50% surcharge on punitive damage awards in civil actions, with the revenue designated for the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund. Because the bill text does not provide specific revenue projections or a formal Fiscal Note, the total financial impact is indeterminate, although it would result in a revenue increase for the State based on the amount of future punitive judgments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the State Court Administrator, who heads the Administrative Office of the Courts, to assess a 50% surcharge on punitive damage awards and deposit the funds into the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund.

The surcharge collected from punitive damage awards is dedicated to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, which is the primary funding mechanism for state education reform initiatives overseen by the Department of Education.

The bill significantly alters Maryland civil law by changing the evidentiary standard for punitive damages from 'actual malice' to 'gross negligence' and abrogating long-standing judicial precedent, which impacts civil litigation and state legal policy.

The creation of a new revenue surcharge for a major state fund (Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund) requires DBM to incorporate these revenue estimates into state fiscal planning and budget execution.
The bill affects the funding of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a key policy priority of the state, and involves oversight of executive branch revenue collection and budgeting.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is responsible for the oversight of state revenue distributions and the accounting of funds such as the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund.
The State Treasurer's Office acts as the custodian of state funds, including the investment and management of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund into which the surcharge will be deposited.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that all recovery residences in Maryland be certified by a state-approved credentialing entity before they are permitted to operate. It explicitly exempts recovery residences from standard behavioral health program licensure while requiring a certificate of compliance. The bill also tasks the Maryland Department of Health with maintaining a public list of certified residences and credentialing entities and establishes civil penalties for residences that falsely claim to be certified.
stakeholders: Owners and operators of recovery residences, individuals with substance-related or addictive disorders, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Maryland Department of Health general fund expenditures increase by $323,000 in FY 2027, which accounts for the bill's October 1, 2026, effective date. These costs are projected to grow to $431,500 by FY 2031. The expenditure covers the hiring of four staff members (three investigators and one program manager) to manage the certification, inspection, and complaint investigation process for an estimated 215 additional residences. There is no reported impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, MDH is responsible for approving the credentialing entity, overseeing the certification process, maintaining public records of certified residences, and enforcing civil penalties. The bill also necessitates significant new general fund expenditures for MDH staffing.

DBM is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution. This bill requires the creation of four new positions and the allocation of over $323,000 in general funds, which falls under DBM's oversight.
OAH adjudicates administrative disputes. Civil penalties imposed by MDH on recovery residences that violate advertising or certification requirements may be contested through the OAH hearing process.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees individuals in the justice system. Certified recovery residences are a key resource for the Division of Parole and Probation and for successful reentry programs for individuals with substance-related disorders.

DHCD handles affordable housing and community revitalization. Recovery residences represent a specialized form of supportive housing that impacts the availability and regulation of secure housing options for vulnerable residents.

DVMF provides advocacy for veterans, a population often served by recovery residences. Ensuring these facilities are certified provides additional protections and quality assurance for veterans seeking these services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety and criminal justice strategies. High-quality recovery housing is essential to GOCPP's mission to reduce recidivism and address substance abuse as a driver of crime.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and other state agencies. They would likely be involved in drafting regulations and providing guidance on the enforcement of the new certification requirements and civil penalties.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and behavioral health policy initiatives. The Governor would be responsible for the broad administrative implementation of the SERVE Act-related goals and general public safety/health improvements.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a three-year pilot program authorizing the use of stop sign monitoring systems in school zones within the 41st Legislative District of Baltimore City. Fines collected from these systems, which are capped at $40, are distributed such that 50% of the revenue is allocated to the local management board for Baltimore City to provide youth programming and services for residents or students in the 41st district, with the remaining funds used for program administration and public safety.
stakeholders: Drivers in school zones within Baltimore City's 41st Legislative District, students and youth residing in or attending school in the 41st Legislative District, and the Baltimore City local government.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by approximately $5,938 in FY 2027 for one-time programming costs for the Judiciary. General fund revenues may increase minimally from contested citations paid to the District Court. For Baltimore City, revenues and expenditures will increase as the city implements the system, collects civil penalties of up to $40, and distributes 50% of those fines to youth programming in the 41st district. If net revenues exceed 10% of the county's total revenue, the excess must be remitted to the State Comptroller.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Judiciary, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, is responsible for the District Court where contested stop sign monitoring citations are adjudicated. The agency faces direct fiscal impacts for programming costs to update its systems for the new legislative district and oversees the collection of fines.

The bill explicitly requires the State Highway Administration (a modal administration of MDOT) to authorize the placement of monitoring systems on State highways and to install required signage notifying drivers of the systems. The Baltimore City Department of Transportation is also mandated to report on the program.

The bill requires that if fine revenues (after costs) exceed 10% of a county's total revenue, the excess must be remitted to the Comptroller, who serves as the state's chief financial officer and revenue collector.

The bill directs 50% of collected fines to the Baltimore City Local Management Board for youth programming. The Governor's Office for Children coordinates the state's network of Local Management Boards and supports youth-focused initiatives and support networks.

As the independent unit within MSDE responsible for coordinating school safety, the Center has a direct interest in the pilot program's focus on school zone traffic enforcement and its impact on student and pedestrian safety.

DBM is responsible for supervising state budget execution and estimating revenues. The fiscal note indicates that the bill will affect general fund revenues and require state expenditures for programming costs.

The bill requires the Baltimore City Department of Transportation and the City of Takoma Park to submit comprehensive reports on the pilot program's effectiveness, costs, and revenue to the Governor by December 1, 2027.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including MDOT and the Judiciary, regarding the implementation and enforcement of automated traffic monitoring systems and the distribution of related fine revenues.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP advises on public safety strategies and coordinates criminal justice policy. Automated traffic enforcement systems in school zones are a component of broader public safety and pedestrian injury prevention strategies managed by the office.

As the primary law enforcement agency responsible for enforcing the Maryland Vehicle Law, the State Police have a secondary interest in the expanded use of automated systems to monitor traffic violations on state and local highways.
The monitoring systems are specifically deployed in school zones within public school systems overseen by MSDE. MSDE also serves as the parent agency for the Maryland Center for School Safety.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a State income tax credit for individuals employed full-time in Maryland public primary or secondary schools who have outstanding student loan debt and participate in the teacher career ladder. The Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) is authorized to award up to $5,000,000 in tax credit certificates annually on a first-come, first-served basis, with 70% of the funds prioritized for individuals who graduated from both a Maryland high school and a Maryland institution of higher education in the previous year. Recipients must use the credit for student loan repayment or face recapture of the credit.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Full-time educators in Maryland public primary and secondary schools who have outstanding student loan debt and are participating in the state career ladder.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues will decrease by up to $5,000,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027 (tax year 2026) due to the cap on tax credit certificates authorized by the bill. While a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, the bill explicitly limits the annual award of certificates to $5,000,000. Administrative expenditures for MHEC and the Comptroller to implement the application and certification process are expected but not specified.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Commission is the primary implementing agency for the educator student loan tax credit. It is responsible for accepting and certifying applications, awarding certificates within a $5 million annual limit, verifying continued educator employment and career ladder status, rescinding credits for non-compliance, and conducting an annual impact report for the General Assembly.

As the state's regulatory and coordinating board for postsecondary education, this agency (alternatively listed as the Maryland Higher Education Commission) is tasked with the direct administration of the tax credit program, including applicant certification, award management, and annual reporting on teacher retention impacts.

The Comptroller's office is responsible for the administration of the Maryland income tax system. This bill creates a new income tax credit, requiring the Comptroller to update tax forms, manage the application of the credit against tax liabilities, and oversee the recapture of funds if the credit is used improperly or the recipient fails to meet statutory requirements.

The bill targets full-time educators in Maryland public schools who participate in the 'Career Ladder' established under Title 6, Subtitle 10 of the Education Article. The Department of Education oversees the public education system and the implementation of the Career Ladder, making its data and policy standards essential for verifying the eligibility of individuals claiming the credit.

As the state’s principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for monitoring the $5 million annual fiscal impact on state revenues and ensuring the program aligns with the state's overall budget and personnel management strategies for the public workforce.

The bill requires an annual report evaluating the tax credit's impact on teacher recruitment and retention. The MLDS Center links student and workforce data across state agencies to provide the type of research and data analysis required by this specific reporting mandate.

The Office of the Attorney General will provide legal counsel to the implementing agencies regarding the drafting of necessary regulations and the legal enforcement of the tax credit's recapture provisions.

bill_summary: Authorizes the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to license and regulate internet skill-based gaming, such as poker, backgammon, and chess, in Maryland. It establishes licensing requirements, fees, and a distribution framework for gaming proceeds to support education through the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund, as well as horse racing and small businesses.
responsible_party: State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission (SLGCC)
stakeholders: Video lottery operators, sports wagering licensees, minority-owned businesses, internet skill-based gaming players, the horse racing industry, and Maryland public schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: In FY 2027, total revenues from internet skill-based gaming are projected to be $11,000,000, with $7,500,000 distributed to the State and local jurisdictions. Special fund expenditures for regulatory oversight by the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency are estimated at $2,100,000. By FY 2031, total revenues are expected to reach $31,100,000. Local impact grants to jurisdictions with casino facilities are projected to increase by $280,000 in the first year.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is the primary regulator and implementer for the bill, responsible for licensing internet skill-based gaming operators, regulating the industry, and overseeing the collection and distribution of proceeds.

The Governor is authorized to enter into multijurisdictional internet skill-based gaming agreements and receives annual reports from the Commission regarding the operation and impact of the new gaming program.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the revenue generated under the bill and executing the distribution of proceeds to various state funds and local jurisdictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is required to consult on the establishment of minority business enterprise (MBE) goals for the new gaming industry and monitor diversity plans submitted by licensees.
The department oversees the Maryland Center of Excellence on Problem Gambling, which receives funding and is tasked with reporting on the impact of internet gaming on gambling addiction.
The Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund, which supports public education, is the primary recipient of the state's share of gaming proceeds and license fees.
The OAG must be consulted in establishing MBE participation goals and procedures for the new industry and provides legal counsel for the new regulatory framework.
The bill explicitly requires internet skill-based gaming licensees to provide transactional data and metrics to the university for research and analysis purposes.
The bill mandates that transactional data and metrics be provided to Bowie State University, which is a member institution of the University System of Maryland.
The bill directs a portion of gaming proceeds to the Small, Minority, and Women-Owned Businesses Account, which is under the authority of the department.
DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning; the bill establishes new revenue streams and necessitates the creation of additional state personnel positions to manage the program.
The department regulates the state's racing industry, which benefits from distributions to the Purse Dedication Account and the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account established or modified by the bill.
The board would likely need to approve significant state procurements, such as a central monitoring system, required for the implementation and regulation of the new gaming platform.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to license and regulate internet gaming and online bingo in Maryland, subject to approval by a statewide voter referendum in November 2026. It establishes a licensing framework for casino operators, sports wagering licensees, and social equity applicants, while creating a tax structure for gaming proceeds. The revenue generated is primarily directed to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund for public education, but also supports problem gambling programs, the horse racing industry, and a new fund for casino employees displaced by online gaming.
responsible_party: State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission
stakeholders: Potential online gamblers, video lottery facility operators, commercial bingo operators, social equity applicants for gaming licenses, displaced casino employees, and Maryland public school students and administrators.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill generates state revenue through initial license fees (ranging from $250,000 to $1,000,000) and a share of internet gaming and online bingo proceeds (between 20% and 40% of gross receipts). The State distributes these funds to several accounts, including the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, the Purse Dedication Account, and the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account. A specific allocation of up to $10,000,000 is mandated for the Video Lottery Facility Employee Displacement Fund during the first year. Local jurisdictions receive 5% of all gaming proceeds for education, in addition to fixed annual distributions for local impact starting at $6,500,000 in fiscal year 2028 and increasing annually.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is authorized to enter into multijurisdictional Internet gaming agreements upon recommendation from the Commission. The bill also affects the Governor's policy priorities regarding revenue for education and small business support.
The Comptroller is responsible for the control and distribution of gaming and bingo proceeds as directed by the bill, including transfers to the State Lottery Fund and various dedicated accounts.
The State Treasurer is tasked with holding the new Video Lottery Facility Employee Displacement Fund and investing its money.
The OAG must be consulted by the Governor's Office of Small, Minority, and Women Business Affairs to establish a plan for minority business participation goals and procedures.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency and will oversee the budget execution of the new Video Lottery Facility Employee Displacement Fund and the distribution of revenues to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund.
The bill requires certain licensees to commit to building live gaming or film production studios under the auspices of the Maryland Film Office, which is housed within the Department of Commerce.

The bill provides a significant new revenue stream for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund and modifies how local jurisdictions meet education funding requirements using internet gaming proceeds.
The bill mandates coordination with the Maryland Center of Excellence on Problem Gambling (typically overseen via MDH Behavioral Health) regarding voluntary exclusion lists and annual impact reports.
The Department of Labor is designated to administer the Video Lottery Facility Employee Displacement Fund, including job training and supplemental unemployment payments for displaced workers.
MHEC coordinates policy for higher education institutions; the bill specifically names Morgan State and Bowie State (part of the USM) as recipients of gaming data and metrics.

The bill authorizes multijurisdictional gaming agreements with other governments, which involves the diplomatic and intergovernmental coordination functions of this division within the Secretary of State.
The authorization for multijurisdictional Internet gaming agreements effectively creates or utilizes interstate compact-like structures for regulatory cooperation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office is specifically required to establish a plan for setting minority business enterprise participation goals for the procurement of goods and services related to internet gaming.
The requirement for licensees to build studios under the Maryland Film Office (within the same division as Tourism) impacts the state's promotional and cultural infrastructure.
The bill is subject to a referendum of the qualified voters of the State in November 2026, and the Board of Elections is tasked with conducting this referendum.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Commission and Agency are the primary regulators for the new internet gaming and online bingo programs, responsible for licensing, oversight, and accounting of all proceeds.
The bill explicitly requires internet gaming licensees to provide annual transactional data and metrics to Morgan State University.
OLA will be responsible for fiscal compliance and performance audits of the new funds and distributions established by this bill.
The bill requires licensees to enter into labor peace agreements and maintain neutrality on unionization, areas falling under PERB's jurisdiction for labor relations and collective bargaining.
Bowie State University, a member of the USM, is specifically designated to receive transactional data and metrics related to internet gaming.
